The daily protocol

  1. Answer out loud, from memory, before reading the hint or opening the link. Reading feels like learning; recall is learning.
  2. Then read the hint and note the gap between what you said and what it lists.
  3. Only then open Answer and compare. What you missed is the day's real lesson; the study link is for repairing it.
  4. Write code for anything code-shaped. Never accept a conceptual answer to a mechanical question.
  5. For system design, draw it on paper — you will be drawing under pressure, so practise drawing.
  6. Do the named DSA problems yourself before looking at any solution. A read solution teaches nothing.
  7. Log every fumble to a weak-spots list. Days 78 and 84 exist to clear that list.

If you cannot explain it out loud, at speed, without notes, you do not know it yet.

Object identity and the hash contract

Explain == vs equals() vs hashCode(). What exactly breaks in a HashMap when you override equals but not hashCode?

Must coverReflexive/symmetric/transitive/consistent contract; unequal hashCodes send equal objects to different buckets so get() returns null; mutable key fields after insert strand the entry permanently.

StudyHashMap API + implementation notes →

Do a back-of-envelope capacity estimate for a service with 1M DAU, 20 requests/user/day, 500-byte records, 3-year retention. Derive QPS, peak QPS, storage, bandwidth.

StudySystem Design Primer →

What actually happens between calling setState and the DOM updating? Walk through render phase vs commit phase and automatic batching.

Must coversetState enqueues an update and schedules work; render phase is pure and interruptible, produces a new element tree, diffs it; commit phase applies mutations synchronously then runs layout effects, then paints, then passive effects. React 18 batches across promises/timeouts too.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start by separating the three. == compares references — are these the same object in memory. equals() compares logical equality — do these two objects represent the same value, and it is yours to define. hashCode() returns an int used to place the object into a bucket in hash-based collections; it is a placement function, not an equality function.

The contract binds them: if two objects are equal, they must return the same hashCode. The converse is not required — unequal objects may collide, and hash collections handle that by chaining. The full equals contract is reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and x.equals(null) is false.

Now the actual failure. Override equals without hashCode and you inherit Object.hashCode, which is identity-based. So map.put(new Key(1), "v") hashes to bucket A. Later map.get(new Key(1)) creates a different object, hashes to bucket B, HashMap searches bucket B, finds nothing, and returns null. The entry is not lost — it is sitting in bucket A, permanently unreachable and un-removable, because every lookup will compute the wrong bucket. It is simultaneously a correctness bug and a memory leak.

The second, subtler failure is mutating a key after insertion. The entry stays physically in the old bucket while the key now hashes elsewhere. Same result. This is why HashMap keys should be immutable, and why String — immutable with a cached hash — is the ideal key.

Java
class Key {
    final int id;
    Key(int id) { this.id = id; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Key k && k.id == id; }
    // hashCode deliberately NOT overridden
}

Map<Key,String> m = new HashMap<>();
m.put(new Key(1), "value");
m.get(new Key(1));       // null - equal, but a different bucket
m.containsKey(new Key(1)); // false

// correct pairing
@Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(id); }
Follow-ups they will ask

Does a hashCode need to be unique?

No — it needs to be well distributed. A constant hashCode is legal and turns the map into a linked list with O(n) lookups. HashMap defends against poor hashes by spreading bits with h ^ (h >>> 16) and by converting a bucket's chain into a red-black tree at 8 entries when capacity is at least 64.

getClass() or instanceof in equals?

getClass() guarantees symmetry but breaks with proxies and Hibernate subclasses. instanceof works with proxies but needs the class to be final, otherwise a subclass adding a field breaks symmetry. For JPA entities the usual compromise is instanceof plus comparing only a stable business key.

Why is String a good key?

Immutable, so the hash cannot change after insertion; the hash is cached after first computation, so repeated lookups are cheap; and it is safely shareable across threads with no synchronization.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Do this out loud and write the numbers down — the interviewer is scoring whether you quantify before designing. Traffic: 1M DAU × 20 requests = 20M requests/day. 20M ÷ 86,400 ≈ 230 QPS average. Traffic is never flat, so apply a peak multiplier of 2–3x → ~600 QPS peak. State the multiplier as an assumption rather than hiding it.

Storage: if every request writes a 500-byte record, that is 20M × 500B = 10 GB/day. Over 3 years: 10 GB × 365 × 3 ≈ 11 TB. Add replication (×3) and indexes/overhead (roughly ×1.3) and you are budgeting for 40–45 TB. That number immediately tells you this is not a single-node database.

Bandwidth: 230 QPS × 500 B ≈ 115 KB/s average, ~350 KB/s at peak. Trivially small — which is itself the useful conclusion: bandwidth is not your constraint, storage and QPS are.

Then state the number that actually drives the design: the read:write ratio. At 100:1 reads you design around caching and read replicas. At 1:1 you design around write throughput, partitioning, and possibly an LSM-based store. Ask for it if it was not given — asking is a positive signal, not a gap.

Finally, anchor with the latency ladder so your estimates are grounded: L1 ~1 ns, main memory ~100 ns, SSD random read ~100 µs, same-datacentre round trip ~0.5 ms, cross-continent ~150 ms. A cache hit versus a cross-region call is a factor of a hundred thousand, and that is what justifies most caching decisions.

Estimation
DAU            1,000,000
req/user/day          20
-> req/day    20,000,000
-> avg QPS  20e6 / 86400  = 231
-> peak QPS       231 x 3 = ~700

record               500 B
-> per day    20e6 x 500 = 10 GB/day
-> 3 years    10 x 365 x 3 = 11 TB  (x3 replication, x1.3 index) = ~43 TB

bandwidth     231 x 500 = 115 KB/s   (not the bottleneck)
Follow-ups they will ask

Why round so aggressively?

Because the decision you are making is "one box or a hundred", and that survives a 2x error. Precision beyond one significant figure is false confidence and wastes interview time.

Where does the peak multiplier come from?

Daily and weekly cycles. Most consumer traffic peaks 2–3x the daily average; a system with a scheduled event (payroll, market open, a flash sale) can peak 10–50x, and you must ask which kind you are designing for.

What do you do with the 43 TB number?

It rules out a single Postgres instance and forces a conversation about partitioning, retention tiering (hot 90 days, cold to object storage), and whether all of it needs to be online at all.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Answer in the two phases React actually uses. Calling setState does not update anything — it enqueues an update on the component's fiber and schedules work. Your local variable is unchanged for the rest of that function, because state is a snapshot of that render.

Render phase: React calls your component function to produce a new element tree, and diffs it against the previous one. This phase must be pure — no side effects, no mutation — because React may pause, abandon, or restart it under concurrent rendering. Nothing is on screen yet.

Commit phase: React applies the computed mutations to the DOM in one synchronous pass, then runs layout effects (useLayoutEffect, refs) before the browser paints. The browser paints. Then passive effects (useEffect) run asynchronously afterwards. That ordering is exactly why measuring layout belongs in useLayoutEffect — doing it in useEffect means you measure after paint and cause a visible flicker when you correct it.

Batching: multiple setState calls in the same tick produce one re-render. Before React 18 this only happened inside React event handlers; automatic batching now covers promises, setTimeout and native handlers too. So three setState calls in an async function now cause one render, not three.

The practical consequence worth stating: because state is a snapshot, setCount(count + 1) three times in a row increments once. Use the functional form setCount(c => c + 1) when the next value depends on the previous one.

JSX
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  function handle() {
    setCount(count + 1);
    setCount(count + 1);   // count is still 0 in this render -> ends at 1
    console.log(count);    // 0 - state is a snapshot of this render
  }

  function handleCorrect() {
    setCount(c => c + 1);
    setCount(c => c + 1);  // queued updaters -> ends at 2
  }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

What breaks if the render phase is not pure?

Under concurrent rendering React can render, discard, and re-render. A side effect in render therefore runs an unpredictable number of times. StrictMode double-invokes components in development specifically to surface this.

Why does useEffect run after paint but useLayoutEffect before?

useEffect is deliberately deferred so it never blocks the browser from painting. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutation but before paint, so you can measure and adjust without the user seeing an intermediate frame — at the cost of blocking paint.

Does setState always re-render?

No. If the new value is Object.is-equal to the current one, React bails out — though it may still render once before bailing. That is also why mutating an object and setting the same reference appears to do nothing.

CostKnow the ladder: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ)Reach for itBefore writing any solution, and to read the constraints. n ≤ 20 means exponential is intended; n ≤ 10⁵ means you need n log n.
n <= 20      -> O(2^n) backtracking or bitmask
n <= 500     -> O(n^3) triple loop is fine
n <= 5000    -> O(n^2)

Strings, pools, and stateless scale

Must coverFinal char/byte array, cached hash, no defensive copy needed; pool lives in heap since Java 7; compact strings since Java 9. Contrast StringBuilder (unsynchronized) vs StringBuffer, and why + in a loop is O(n^2).

StudyJDK API docs →

StudySystem Design Primer →

Why do list keys matter? Explain React reconciliation and what concretely goes wrong when you use array index as key.

Must coverSame-position/same-type elements are reused, state is keyed by position+key; index keys on a reordering or filtering list bind stale state (input values, animation) to the wrong row. Keys are scoped to siblings, not global.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

String is immutable because its backing array is private final and never escapes — no method hands it out or mutates it. Every apparent modification (substring, toUpperCase, +) returns a new String.

Four things follow. Thread safety for free: no synchronization is ever needed to share a String. Cached hash: the hash is computed once and stored, so repeated map lookups are cheap. Safe as a HashMap key: the hash cannot change after insertion, so entries stay findable. Security: a validated filename or URL cannot be altered between the check and the use — the classic time-of-check/time-of-use attack is impossible.

The string pool is a JVM-managed table of canonical instances. Literals are interned automatically at class load, so two identical literals are the same object — which is why == deceptively works for literals and fails for runtime-built strings. Since Java 7 the pool lives in the heap rather than PermGen, so heavy interning is a GC concern rather than a PermGen overflow.

For building strings, StringBuilder is the answer; StringBuffer is its synchronized legacy twin and almost never needed. Concatenating in a loop is O(n²) because each += allocates and copies everything so far — though a single expression like a + b + c is compiled efficiently via invokedynamic since Java 9.

Java
String a = "hello";
String b = "hello";
String c = new String("hello");
a == b;            // true  - same pooled literal
a == c;            // false - distinct heap object
a == c.intern();   // true  - canonical instance
a.equals(c);       // true  - the only comparison you should write

// O(n^2) - do not do this
String s = ""; for (String p : parts) s += p;
// O(n)
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (String p : parts) sb.append(p);
Follow-ups they will ask

Is String really immutable, given reflection can reach the array?

Reflection with setAccessible can mutate it, which corrupts the pool and breaks every sharer. The immutability guarantee holds for well-behaved code; module encapsulation on modern JDKs makes the reflective route harder.

When would you call intern() deliberately?

Rarely — parsing huge inputs with massive duplication, such as repeated column names or log tags. Measure first: the pool is itself a hash table with a cost, and a plain HashMap-based canonicalizer is often better and more controllable.

What are compact strings?

Since Java 9, Strings store Latin-1 text in a byte[] with a coder flag instead of always using char[], roughly halving memory for ASCII-heavy applications. One of the biggest free wins in modern JDKs.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Vertical scaling is a bigger machine: no code changes, no distributed-systems problems, and it is genuinely the right first answer for a lot of systems. Its limits are a hard ceiling on machine size, cost that grows superlinearly, and — decisively — it remains a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds machines: effectively unbounded, cheaper per unit, and gives redundancy, at the cost of needing a load balancer, coordination, and a tolerance for partial failure.

The precondition for adding a second instance is that the service is stateless — no request may depend on in-memory state left behind by a previous request. Anything a subsequent request needs must live somewhere shared: session in Redis or encoded in a signed token, uploaded files in object storage, caches in a shared cache or accepted as per-node and short-lived, and scheduled jobs guarded by a lock or leader election so they do not run N times.

Sticky sessions route a user to the same instance so in-memory session works. It is a workaround, not a design: it breaks load balancing (an instance can be hot while others idle), makes deploys disruptive (draining an instance logs those users out), defeats autoscaling, and turns one node's failure into a user-visible session loss. Externalize the session instead.

Close by naming what horizontal scaling does not fix — because that is the senior half of the answer. You have now moved the bottleneck to the shared dependencies: the database, the cache, and the load balancer itself. Ten stateless app servers hammering one Postgres primary is not a scaled system.

Checklist
Before you can add instance #2:
  [ ] no in-memory session          -> Redis / signed token
  [ ] no local file writes          -> object storage
  [ ] no in-process scheduler       -> leader election or a lock with TTL
  [ ] no in-memory cache as truth   -> shared cache, or accept staleness + TTL
  [ ] no local rate-limit counters  -> shared counter
  [ ] graceful shutdown + drain     -> so deploys do not drop in-flight requests
Follow-ups they will ask

When is vertical scaling the right answer?

When you are nowhere near the machine ceiling and the engineering cost of distribution exceeds the hardware cost — which is most systems, most of the time. Buying a bigger box for six months while you fix the real bottleneck is a legitimate, senior decision.

How do you scale the database once the app tier is stateless?

In order of increasing pain: read replicas for read-heavy load, caching to remove reads entirely, vertical scaling of the primary, then functional partitioning by domain, then sharding. Sharding is last because it costs you cross-shard joins and transactions.

Does the load balancer become a single point of failure?

It can, which is why it is deployed redundantly behind DNS or anycast with health-checked failover. Managed load balancers handle this, but you should still be able to say it out loud.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Keys exist because of how reconciliation works. When React diffs two element trees, it compares children by position by default. Same position and same type means "this is the same component" — so React keeps its state and DOM node and just updates props. Different type means unmount, discard state, and mount fresh.

For lists, position is the wrong identity, because inserting or reordering shifts everything. A key overrides positional matching: React matches children by key across renders, so it can move a DOM node instead of rebuilding it, and each item's state follows its key. Keys only need to be unique among siblings, not globally.

Now the concrete bug with index keys. Render a list with key={index}, each row containing an uncontrolled input. Delete the first row. React sees key 0 still exists (it is now the old second item), so it keeps the DOM node and its component state, and only updates the props. The user's typed text stays on the row above where it belongs. The same mechanism strands checkbox state, focus, animation state, and any state held inside the row component.

So the rule: index keys are safe only if the list is never reordered, filtered, inserted into, or deleted from — effectively, a static list. Otherwise use a stable id from the data. And never use Math.random() as a key: it changes every render, so React unmounts and remounts every row, destroying state and performance simultaneously.

JSX
// broken: state follows the index, not the item
{items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} item={item} />)}

// correct: state follows the item
{items.map(item => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />)}

// deliberate remount: changing the key resets a component's state
<ProfileForm key={userId} userId={userId} />   // switching user clears the form
Follow-ups they will ask

When is key={index} acceptable?

When the list is static — never reordered, filtered, appended to in the middle, or deleted from — and items hold no state. A rendered set of constants is fine. Anything driven by user actions is not.

Can you use a key to force a reset?

Yes, and it is an idiomatic technique. Changing the key of a component unmounts and remounts it, clearing all internal state. It is the cleanest way to reset a form when the entity being edited changes.

Why must keys be unique only among siblings?

Because matching happens within one parent's child list. Two different lists on the page may both use key 1 without conflict — React never compares across parents.

Arrays & Hashing II
  • Group AnagramsMedium
  • Top K Frequent ElementsMedium
  • Product of Array Except SelfMedium

Two indices walking a sorted array, usually from both ends inward. Each step discards one candidate, so a quadratic pair search becomes linear.

CostO(n) time, O(1) space, after sortingReach for itFinding a pair with a target sum, container-with-most-water, or any 'find two things' question on sorted data.
def two_sum_sorted(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        s = a[lo] + a[hi]
        if s == target: return (lo, hi)
        if s < target:  lo += 1     # need bigger -> move left pointer up
        else:           hi -= 1     # need smaller -> move right pointer down
    return None

Immutability by design

Must coverfinal class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copy in constructor AND getters for mutable types, BigDecimal not double for money, currency-mismatch guard, equals/hashCode/compareTo consistency. Then show it as a record and say what a record does not give you.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

State the five rules, then apply them. To make a class immutable: mark the class final (or the constructor private) so behaviour cannot be overridden; make every field private final; provide no setters or mutators; defensively copy mutable inputs in the constructor; and defensively copy mutable state on the way out of any getter.

For Money specifically there are two domain rules that carry as much weight: never use double — use BigDecimal or an integer count of minor units — and reject arithmetic across mismatched currencies rather than silently coercing. Validate in the constructor so an invalid Money can never exist.

The defensive-copy pair is where candidates usually lose the point. Missing the copy in means the caller keeps a reference to your internal state and can mutate your object from outside. Missing the copy out means the caller mutates the object you handed back. Either one destroys immutability entirely — the class only looks immutable.

Close with what immutability buys: safe publication. A correctly constructed object with only final fields cannot be observed half-initialized by another thread — the JMM's final-field freeze guarantees it — so it is thread-safe with zero synchronization, and it is safe to cache, share, and use as a map key.

Java
public final class Money implements Comparable<Money> {
    private final long minorUnits;      // paise/cents - exact, no float
    private final Currency currency;

    private Money(long minorUnits, Currency currency) {
        this.currency = Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency");
        this.minorUnits = minorUnits;
    }
    public static Money ofMinor(long minor, Currency c) { return new Money(minor, c); }

    public Money plus(Money other) {
        requireSameCurrency(other);
        return new Money(Math.addExact(minorUnits, other.minorUnits), currency);
    }
    private void requireSameCurrency(Money o) {
        if (!currency.equals(o.currency))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
    }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Money m && m.minorUnits == minorUnits && m.currency.equals(currency);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(minorUnits, currency); }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Where exactly would a defensive copy be needed here?

Not for long or Currency (both immutable). It becomes essential the moment a field is a List, Date, array, or any mutable object: this.tags = List.copyOf(tags) in the constructor, and return an unmodifiable view or copy from the getter.

Would a record be enough?

It gives you final fields, accessors, equals/hashCode/toString — but only shallow immutability, and no validation unless you add a compact constructor. record Money(long minorUnits, Currency currency) with a compact constructor doing the null check is a good answer; a record holding a List without List.copyOf is not immutable.

Why minor units rather than BigDecimal?

Both are correct. Longs are faster, exactly representable, and make rounding decisions explicit; BigDecimal handles currencies with unusual exponents and very large values more naturally. The wrong answer is double.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

L4 operates at the transport layer: it forwards TCP connections using IP and port, never looks at the payload, and is therefore extremely fast and protocol-agnostic. L7 terminates the connection and understands HTTP, so it can route by path, host or header, terminate TLS, retry idempotent requests, rewrite, compress, and enforce rate limits. You pay latency and CPU for that visibility. Modern systems usually run both: L4 at the edge for raw throughput, L7 inside for routing.

Algorithms: round-robin is the simple default and assumes uniform requests and uniform servers. Least-connections is better when request durations vary, because it naturally avoids piling onto a slow instance. Weighted handles heterogeneous instance sizes. Consistent hashing or hash-by-key routes the same key to the same instance, which is what you want in front of a cache tier so you do not duplicate cache entries across every node.

Health checks come in two kinds, and conflating them causes outages. A liveness check asks "is this process broken and in need of a restart"; a readiness check asks "should this instance receive traffic right now". An instance that is warming up, has lost its database connection, or is shutting down should fail readiness without being killed. Check something meaningful — a shallow endpoint that returns 200 while the database is down is worse than no check.

Connection draining is the deploy-safety mechanism: when an instance is removed, the LB stops sending it new requests but lets in-flight ones finish, up to a timeout. Without it, every deploy drops live requests. The instance must cooperate — fail readiness first, keep serving, then shut down after the drain window. Finally, note that the LB is itself a single point of failure, so it is deployed redundantly behind DNS failover or anycast.

Deploy sequence
1. new version starts, fails readiness while warming (JIT, caches, pool)
2. passes readiness  -> LB adds it to the pool
3. old instance told to stop:
     a. starts failing readiness   -> LB stops sending new requests
     b. keeps serving in-flight    -> drain window (e.g. 30s)
     c. process exits
   result: zero dropped requests
Follow-ups they will ask

What happens if liveness and readiness are the same check?

A transient dependency failure fails liveness, the orchestrator restarts the pod, the dependency is still down, and you get a restart loop — turning a partial degradation into a total outage.

When would you use hash-based routing?

In front of a cache tier or any node holding per-key state, so a given key consistently lands on the node that already has it. Use consistent hashing so adding or removing a node remaps only a fraction of keys rather than all of them.

How does the LB know a server is slow rather than dead?

It usually does not, which is the argument for least-connections (a slow server accumulates connections and stops receiving new ones) plus outlier detection that ejects instances whose error rate or latency deviates from the pool.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Give a one-line decision rule first: useState when a change must re-render; useRef when it must not; useReducer when several fields change together as one action.

useState is for values the UI is derived from. It is a snapshot per render, updates are batched, and setting it schedules a re-render. Use the functional form when the next value depends on the previous.

useRef is a mutable box that survives renders and never triggers one. Two distinct jobs: holding a DOM node (ref={el}), and holding mutable non-render state — a timer id, a WebSocket, a previous value, an "is this the first render" flag, or the latest-callback pattern that avoids re-subscribing an effect. The rule is never read or write a ref during render; it belongs in effects and event handlers.

useReducer is right when the next state depends on the previous in non-trivial ways, when several fields must move together atomically, or when you want the transition logic testable outside the component. A form with data, errors, touched and submitting as four useStates lets you render illegal combinations — submitting and errored at once. One reducer with explicit actions makes those states unrepresentable, and it also stabilizes the dispatch identity, so passing it deep through context causes no re-render churn.

The case where each is the only correct choice: a value shown to the user → useState. A setInterval id you must clear on unmount → useRef, because storing it in state would re-render on every tick. A wizard where advancing a step must simultaneously clear errors, mark the previous step complete and reset scroll → useReducer.

JSX
// ref: mutable, no re-render
const timer = useRef(null);
useEffect(() => {
  timer.current = setInterval(tick, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(timer.current);
}, []);

// reducer: one atomic transition instead of four setStates
function reducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'submit':  return { ...state, submitting: true, errors: {} };
    case 'failure': return { ...state, submitting: false, errors: action.errors };
    default: return state;
  }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does mutating a ref not re-render?

React does not track ref mutations at all — ref.current is a plain property on a plain object. That is precisely the point: it is the documented escape hatch for values the render output does not depend on.

Is useReducer faster than useState?

Not meaningfully. You choose it for correctness and testability, not performance — though the stable dispatch identity does remove a class of unnecessary re-renders when passed through context.

What is the latest-callback ref pattern?

Store a frequently-changing callback in a ref, update it in an effect on every render, and have a long-lived subscription call ref.current(...). The subscription never needs to tear down and re-create just because the callback identity changed.

Halve the search space each step by comparing against the middle. Requires sorted (or monotone) data.

CostO(log n) time, O(1) spaceReach for itAny lookup in sorted data. Use the bisect form — it avoids the off-by-one bugs the classic form is famous for.
def lower_bound(a, x):
    """First index where a[i] >= x. This form handles duplicates and
       'insert position' without special cases."""
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1
        else:          hi = mid
    return lo

# Use mid = lo + (hi-lo)//2 in languages where lo+hi can overflow.

Type hierarchies and consistency models

Abstract class vs interface after Java 8 default methods. How does Java resolve a diamond when two interfaces provide the same default method? When do you actually prefer composition over inheritance?

Must coverClass wins over interface, most-specific interface wins, otherwise compile error forcing explicit Iface.super.m(). Inheritance couples you to a superclass invariant you do not control; favour composition + delegation. Cite the Liskov violation classic (Square extends Rectangle).

StudyJava Language Specification →

CAP theorem, and why PACELC is the more useful framing in practice. Explain strong, eventual, read-your-writes, and monotonic-read consistency with a real example each.

Must coverCAP only applies during a partition; PACELC adds the latency-vs-consistency tradeoff in normal operation. Payments need strong/linearizable; a feed can be eventual; a user reading their own just-posted comment needs read-your-writes (sticky routing to primary or version tokens).

StudyJepsen — consistency models →

Explain useEffect precisely: when it runs, when cleanup runs, and the two classic bugs (stale closure, missing/lying dependency array). When should you NOT use an effect at all?

Must coverCleanup runs before the next effect and on unmount. Stale closure = the effect captured an old render value. Do not use effects to derive state (compute during render), to transform props, or to handle user events - only for external synchronization.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Since Java 8 the line is no longer "interfaces have no code". The distinction that survives is state: an interface still cannot have instance fields, and a class implements many interfaces but extends exactly one class. So the modern rule is — use an interface for a capability that unrelated types can have, and an abstract class only when subtypes genuinely share mutable state or construction logic.

Default methods were added for API evolution, not to make interfaces into classes. Adding stream() to Collection would otherwise have broken every implementation in existence. Interfaces also have static methods (factories that belong to the type) and, since Java 9, private methods to share code between defaults without exposing it.

The diamond — two interfaces supplying the same default — is resolved by three rules in order: class wins over interface (a concrete inherited method beats any default, for backward compatibility); the most specific interface wins (a sub-interface beats its parent); otherwise it is a compile error and you must override explicitly, optionally delegating with A.super.method(). Java refuses to guess, which is why default methods did not reintroduce the C++ multiple-inheritance mess.

On composition over inheritance: inheritance couples you to a superclass's internal call patterns. Extend HashSet to count additions and you double-count, because addAll internally calls add — and a future JDK could change that silently. Composition with delegation depends only on the published interface. The test for when inheritance is right is Liskov: a subtype must be usable anywhere the supertype is. Square extends Rectangle fails it, because code that sets width and height independently and asserts the area breaks.

Java
interface A { default String hello(){ return "A"; } }
interface B { default String hello(){ return "B"; } }
class C implements A, B {
    @Override public String hello() { return A.super.hello(); }  // must be explicit
}

// composition instead of extending HashSet
class CountingSet<E> implements Set<E> {
    private final Set<E> delegate; private int addCount;
    public boolean add(E e){ addCount++; return delegate.add(e); }
    public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c){
        addCount += c.size(); return delegate.addAll(c);   // no double count
    }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Does a default method break a functional interface?

No — a functional interface needs exactly one abstract method; any number of default and static methods is fine. That is how Comparator carries thenComparing, reversed and a dozen others while still being a lambda target.

When is an abstract class clearly right?

Template Method: the parent owns the algorithm's skeleton and shared state, subtypes fill in steps. AbstractList and Spring's JdbcTemplate family are the canonical cases.

How do you decide in a code review?

Ask what happens when the parent changes its internal call sequence. If the answer is "we break silently", it should have been composition. Effective Java's rule: design and document for inheritance, or forbid it with final.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

State CAP precisely, because most candidates state it wrongly. During a network partition you must choose between consistency and availability. That is all it says. It is not "pick two of three" — partitions are a fact of distributed systems, not an option, so the real choice is CP or AP, and only while partitioned.

PACELC is the more useful framing: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. It captures the tradeoff you actually make every day — even with a perfectly healthy network, waiting for a quorum or a cross-region acknowledgement costs latency. Postgres with synchronous replication is PC/EC; DynamoDB with eventual consistency is PA/EL.

Then the models, each anchored to a symptom the user notices. Strong / linearizable: every read sees the latest committed write, as if there were one copy — required for payments and inventory. Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop; fine for a follower count. Read-your-writes: you always see your own writes — violated when a user posts a comment, the read hits a lagging replica, and their comment vanishes on refresh. Monotonic reads: you never see time move backwards — violated when consecutive reads hit replicas with different lag and a counter appears to decrease.

Finish with how you get read-your-writes without going fully strong, because that is the practical part: route a user's reads to the primary for N seconds after they write, pin them to one replica, or pass a version/LSN token the replica must have caught up to. That answer shows you have shipped this, not just read about it.

Choosing
payment / ledger balance      -> strong (linearizable). Correctness > uptime.
inventory, seat booking       -> strong, or a DB constraint that forbids oversell
user's own profile edit       -> read-your-writes (sticky or version token)
social feed, follower count   -> eventual. Nobody notices 2s of staleness.
notification counter          -> monotonic reads at minimum, or it flickers
Follow-ups they will ask

Is a system with no partitions CA?

Only trivially — a single node. Any real distributed system will be partitioned eventually, so CA is not a design you can choose; it is a description of a system that has not failed yet.

Where does the choice actually appear in code?

In quorum settings and replication mode: synchronous_commit in Postgres, W+R>N in Dynamo-style stores, acks=all plus min.insync.replicas in Kafka. Each is a concrete dial on the consistency/latency tradeoff.

Give one system that deliberately chose AP.

DNS. It is eventually consistent by design with TTL-based caching, and that is why it stays available globally — and also why a DNS change takes minutes to propagate.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Define it as synchronization, not lifecycle. useEffect exists to synchronize your component with an external system — a subscription, a network request, a timer, a DOM API. It runs after the browser paints, so it never blocks rendering.

Timing: after the commit and paint. Cleanup runs before the next effect re-runs and on unmount. The dependency array does not choose when to run — it declares what the effect reads, and React re-runs it whenever any of those change. Empty array means "nothing reactive, run once"; no array means "every render".

Stale closure is the most common React bug. An effect captures the values from the render it was created in. If you write [] to "run once" but the effect reads count, it captures count from the first render forever, and no amount of re-rendering changes what it sees. Lying to the dependency array does not make the code correct — it hides the fact that it is wrong. The real fixes are: use the functional updater so you do not need the value, move the value into a ref if it should not re-trigger, or accept the re-subscription.

When not to use an effect at all — this is where senior candidates separate. Do not use one to compute derived state (calculate it during render), to transform props for display, to handle a user event (put it in the handler), or to reset state when a prop changes (change the component's key instead). An effect that sets state which triggers another render is usually a value you should have computed inline; every one you remove eliminates a render pass and a class of bugs.

JSX
// stale closure: reads count from the first render, forever
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);                       // lying about the dependency

// fix: functional updater removes the dependency honestly
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => setCount(c => c + 1), 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);

// not an effect at all - derive during render
const fullName = first + ' ' + last;          // NOT useEffect(() => setFullName(...))
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does the cleanup run before every re-run, not only on unmount?

Because the effect is a synchronization: before syncing to new values it must un-sync from the old ones. Subscribing to room A then room B without unsubscribing from A leaves two live subscriptions — the leak the cleanup exists to prevent.

Why does StrictMode mount effects twice in development?

To surface missing cleanup. If your effect is correctly symmetric, mount-unmount-mount is harmless. If it leaks a subscription or double-fires a request, you see it immediately in development rather than in production.

How do you fetch data in an effect without a race?

Use an ignore flag set in the cleanup, or an AbortController. Otherwise a slow response for an old prop can land after a fast response for the new one and overwrite it. In practice, use a query library that handles this structurally.

  • Two Sum II - Input Array Is SortedMedium

Keep a window of exactly k elements. Instead of recomputing the sum each step, add the entering element and subtract the leaving one.

CostO(n) time, O(1) spaceReach for itMax/min/average of every k-length subarray. The moment you see 'every window of size k', this is it.
def max_sum_k(a, k):
    s = sum(a[:k]); best = s
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        s += a[i] - a[i - k]     # add entering, remove leaving
        best = max(best, s)
    return best

Wrap-and-rethrow preserving cause. AutoCloseable closes in reverse order and suppression preserves the primary failure.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Checked exceptions are part of the method signature and the compiler forces the caller to handle or declare them; use them for conditions a caller can reasonably recover from — a file missing, a remote call failing. Unchecked (RuntimeException) are for programming errors and unrecoverable conditions — a null argument, an illegal state, a bug. The honest position is that checked exceptions have fallen out of favour: they do not compose with lambdas and streams, and in practice they get wrapped or swallowed, which is worse than not having them.

For a public service API, design the exception contract like the API it is. Define a small hierarchy meaningful to callers — NotFoundException, ConflictException, ValidationException, DownstreamUnavailableException — rather than leaking SQLException or FeignException upward. Each maps to one HTTP status and one stable error code the client can branch on. Wrap and rethrow, always preserving the cause, so the stack trace survives.

The rules that matter: never swallow (catch (Exception e) {} is how outages become invisible), never catch Exception broadly at a low level, never use exceptions for control flow, and never let an internal message or stack trace reach the client — log the detail server-side with a correlation id and return something safe.

try-with-resources closes every declared AutoCloseable in reverse declaration order, even on exception. The subtlety worth naming: if the body throws and close() throws, the close exception is attached as a suppressed exception rather than replacing the original — retrievable via getSuppressed(). Before this existed, a failure in a finally-block close routinely masked the real cause, and people lost hours to it.

Java
try (var conn = pool.getConnection();
     var stmt = conn.prepareStatement(SQL)) {          // closed first
    return map(stmt.executeQuery());
} catch (SQLException e) {
    throw new RepositoryException("loading order " + id, e);  // cause preserved
}

@ExceptionHandler(NotFoundException.class)
ProblemDetail handle(NotFoundException e) {
    log.info("not found: {}", e.getMessage());         // detail stays server-side
    return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Order not found");
}
Follow-ups they will ask

When is catching and ignoring acceptable?

Almost never, and when it is, it needs a comment saying why. The one common legitimate case is catching InterruptedException where you cannot propagate — and even then you must restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt().

Why do checked exceptions break streams?

A lambda passed to map cannot throw a checked exception, because Function.apply does not declare one. You end up wrapping in a RuntimeException inside every lambda, which is exactly the ceremony checked exceptions were meant to avoid.

What should a 500 response body contain?

A correlation id, a stable error code, and a generic message. Never a stack trace, SQL, class name or internal hostname — those are reconnaissance for an attacker and useless to a legitimate client.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Walk it hop by hop, and attach a failure mode and mitigation to each — that pairing is what is being scored, not the recitation.

DNS: the browser resolves the hostname, possibly via GeoDNS to the nearest region. Fails as stale records after a failover, bounded by TTL. Mitigate with short TTLs on failover-critical records and anycast so the IP itself moves. TLS handshake: one to two extra round trips. Mitigate with session resumption, TLS 1.3, and terminating at a nearby edge. CDN edge: static assets served locally. Fails as serving stale HTML you cannot recall — mitigate with hashed asset filenames plus no-cache on HTML.

Load balancer: health-checked routing. Fails as sending traffic to a warming or dying instance — mitigate with readiness checks distinct from liveness, plus connection draining. API gateway: authentication, rate limiting, routing. Fails as becoming a bottleneck or a business-logic monolith. Service: your code. Fails as thread-pool or connection-pool exhaustion — mitigate with bounded pools, timeouts, and bulkheads per dependency.

Cache: Redis in front of the database. Fails as a stampede when a hot key expires, or a cache outage becoming a database outage — mitigate with single-flight, TTL jitter, and a circuit breaker. Database: the usual last stop. Fails as slow queries, lock contention, replica lag — mitigate with indexes, read replicas, and query timeouts.

Then say the thing that ties it together: every hop needs a timeout, and the budget must shrink down the chain. If the client waits 3 s, the gateway should wait 2.5 s and the service 2 s, so a failure surfaces as a clean error rather than a cascade of resources held until everything times out at once.

Timeout budget
client        3000 ms
 gateway      2500 ms   (retry: 0 - it is not idempotent at this layer)
  service     2000 ms
   cache        50 ms   (fail open -> fall through to DB)
   db          800 ms   (statement_timeout enforced server-side too)
   downstream  600 ms   + circuit breaker + retry with jitter (idempotent only)
Follow-ups they will ask

Where would you put a circuit breaker and why not everywhere?

On calls to dependencies that can fail independently — a payment provider, a recommendation service. Not on your own database, where the correct response to failure is usually to fail the request, not to serve a degraded fallback that hides data loss.

What breaks if timeouts do not shrink down the chain?

The client gives up at 3 s while every layer below is still holding threads and connections for its own longer timeout. Under load those resources are never released fast enough and the whole chain saturates — a retry storm on top of an already-slow dependency.

Which hop surprises people most in a real incident?

DNS TTL and connection pools. Both are invisible in normal operation and both turn a small failure into a long one — a 24-hour TTL means a failover nobody can complete, and an exhausted pool looks exactly like a slow application.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Controlled: React state is the single source of truth — value={x} plus onChange. Every keystroke sets state and re-renders. You get instant validation, derived UI, and a form you can drive programmatically. Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value and you read it with a ref or on submit. No re-render per keystroke, but no live derivation either.

For a 40-field form, naive controlled state is the wrong answer, and saying why is the point: one useState object at the form level means every keystroke re-renders all 40 fields plus any validation and derived UI. That is where the input lag people complain about comes from.

The scaling answer is subscription-based form state — which is what react-hook-form does. Fields register themselves and are largely uncontrolled; the library holds values in a ref and notifies only the components that subscribe to a given field. Typing in field 12 re-renders field 12, not the form. Validation runs on a schema (Zod) shared with the backend so the rules exist once.

If you must stay controlled — say the design needs cross-field reactivity — the mitigations are: keep state in a useReducer at the form level but memoize each field component so only the changed one re-renders; split the form into sections with their own state; and debounce expensive derived work rather than the input itself, so typing stays instant. Close by naming what the choice really trades: re-render cost against live derivability.

JSX
// scales: field-level subscription, form values live in a ref
const { register, handleSubmit, formState:{ errors } } =
      useForm({ resolver: zodResolver(schema) });

<input {...register('email')} />        // typing re-renders this field only
{errors.email && <span>{errors.email.message}</span>}

// does not scale: one state object, 40 fields re-render per keystroke
const [form, setForm] = useState({});
<input value={form.email} onChange={e => setForm({...form, email: e.target.value})} />
Follow-ups they will ask

When is fully controlled clearly correct?

Small forms, and any field whose value drives other UI live — a search box filtering a list, a slider updating a preview, a field that enables or disables another. There the re-render is the feature.

How do you validate without re-rendering on every keystroke?

Validate on blur and on submit by default, and only switch a field to onChange validation after it has already failed once. That is the standard UX pattern and it removes most of the work.

Why share the schema with the backend?

Because client validation is a UX affordance, not a security control — the server must validate regardless. Deriving both from one schema means the rules cannot drift, and the client gets the same error messages the server would produce.

Two Pointers II
  • Container With Most WaterMedium
  • Trapping Rain WaterHard

Precompute cumulative totals once, then any range sum is a single subtraction.

CostO(n) build, O(1) per queryReach for itMany range-sum queries on static data, or counting subarrays with a target sum when combined with a hash map.
pre = [0]*(len(a)+1)
for i, v in enumerate(a): pre[i+1] = pre[i] + v
range_sum = pre[r+1] - pre[l]        # sum of a[l..r], O(1)

# Count subarrays summing to k - prefix sums + hash map
from collections import defaultdict
def count_subarrays(a, k):
    seen = defaultdict(int); seen[0] = 1
    run = res = 0
    for v in a:
        run += v
        res += seen[run - k]     # how many prefixes make a[j..i] == k
        seen[run] += 1
    return res

Generics and the storage decision

Explain type erasure and its consequences. What do List<?>, List<? extends T>, List<? super T> each allow, and what is PECS?

Must coverNo generic type at runtime: no new T[], no instanceof List<String>, bridge methods, heap pollution/@SafeVarargs. Producer Extends (read-only), Consumer Super (write-only). Show why Collections.copy has both.

StudyOracle tutorial — Generics →

Give a decision framework for SQL vs NoSQL. For each of: user profiles, an audit log, a session store, a social graph, transaction ledger - pick a store and defend it.

Must coverDrive it from access patterns, consistency needs, and cardinality of relationships, not hype. Postgres is the correct default; justify moving off it. Mention that NoSQL means you model the query, not the entity.

StudyDesigning Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann) →

How does Context actually propagate? Why does a context update re-render every consumer, and what are the three standard fixes?

Must coverProviders bypass memoization - any consumer re-renders on value identity change. Fixes: split into multiple contexts (state vs dispatch), memoize the value object, or use a subscription store (useSyncExternalStore/Zustand) so consumers select slices.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Erasure: generics are a compile-time feature. The compiler checks types, then erases them — T becomes its bound (Object if unbounded) and casts are inserted. At runtime List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class. This was a compatibility decision so generic and pre-generic code could share a JVM.

The consequences are the interview material: no new T() or new T[n]; no x instanceof List<String>; you cannot overload on List<String> versus List<Integer> because they have the same erasure; static fields are shared across all parameterizations; and bridge methods are synthesized to make covariant overriding still work after erasure.

Generics are invariant — List<String> is not a List<Object> — precisely to avoid the ArrayStoreException hole that array covariance leaves open. Wildcards restore the flexibility safely. ? extends T is a producer: you can read T out, but cannot write in (except null), because the actual subtype is unknown. ? super T is a consumer: you can write T in, but reads come back as Object.

That is PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Apply it to any parameter you only read from or only write to, and your API becomes usable with subtypes and supertypes. The corollary worth stating: wildcards belong in parameters, never in return types — a wildcard in a return type propagates into every caller's code.

Java
// src produces T, dst consumes T
static <T> void copy(List<? extends T> src, List<? super T> dst) {
    for (T t : src) dst.add(t);
}
copy(List.of(1,2,3), new ArrayList<Number>());   // only compiles because of PECS

List<? extends Number> producer = List.of(1,2);
// producer.add(3);        // illegal - could be a List<Double>
Number n = producer.get(0);  // fine

// the standard erasure workaround: pass a Class token
static <T> T create(Class<T> type) throws Exception {
    return type.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
}
Follow-ups they will ask

How do Jackson and Spring read generic types at runtime if they are erased?

With a super type token: an anonymous subclass captures the type argument in its class file (new TypeReference<List<Order>>(){}) and reflection reads it from the generic superclass signature. Generic information survives in class metadata — it is only absent from instances.

What is heap pollution?

A variable of a parameterized type referring to an object that is not of that parameterization — possible because erasure removed the runtime check. Generic varargs are the usual gateway, which is why they warn and why @SafeVarargs exists.

Why not reify generics like C#?

Backward compatibility: in 2004 the entire Java ecosystem was non-generic, and reification would have required a new incompatible runtime. Project Valhalla is revisiting parts of this now.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Refuse the tribal framing and drive it from access patterns, consistency needs, and relationship cardinality. Say your default out loud: Postgres unless there is a specific reason not to be — it handles JSON, full-text search, geospatial, and scales further than most teams ever need. Then justify moving off it.

Relational when: you need transactions across entities, the data is genuinely relational, you need ad-hoc queries you cannot predict, and consistency matters more than raw write throughput. NoSQL when: you know every access pattern up front, you need write throughput or multi-region writes beyond one primary, or the shape genuinely does not fit rows. The key mental shift for NoSQL is that you model the query, not the entity — denormalize deliberately and accept duplicated writes.

Now the five: User profiles — Postgres. Low volume, relational, needs consistency, and you will inevitably want ad-hoc queries. Audit log — append-only, huge, immutable, queried by time range and entity: partitioned Postgres tables or Cassandra, with cold data tiered to object storage. Never mix it into the OLTP tables. Session store — Redis. Ephemeral, key-value, needs TTL and sub-millisecond reads, and losing it is an inconvenience, not a data loss. Social graph — traversal-heavy ("friends of friends"), which is where recursive SQL joins get expensive: a graph database, or in practice an adjacency table with heavy caching, because most teams never actually need Neo4j.

Transaction ledger — Postgres, and say why emphatically: it needs ACID, double-entry rows that must balance, unique constraints for idempotency, and full auditability. This is the case where eventual consistency is simply wrong. If it outgrows one node, shard by account id so a single account's entries stay together, rather than reaching for a store that cannot give you a transaction.

Decision order
1. What are the access patterns?  (point lookup / range / ad-hoc / traversal)
2. What consistency does it need?  (linearizable / read-your-writes / eventual)
3. What is the read:write ratio and absolute volume?
4. Does it need transactions across entities?
5. Only now: pick the store, and say what you give up.
Follow-ups they will ask

When does Postgres genuinely stop being enough?

Write throughput past what one primary can absorb, a need for multi-region active-active writes, or a working set far larger than can be indexed economically. Note that read scaling is solved earlier and more cheaply with replicas and caching.

What do you lose by moving to NoSQL?

Ad-hoc querying, joins, and multi-entity transactions. You are trading query flexibility for scale, so you must know the access patterns before you choose — and any new access pattern later may mean a migration or a second copy of the data.

Can you use both?

Yes, and most real systems do — Postgres as the system of record, Redis for sessions and caching, Elasticsearch for search, object storage for blobs. The discipline is a single source of truth per fact, with everything else derived and rebuildable.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Mechanism first. A Provider stores a value on the fiber tree. Any component calling useContext registers as a consumer of that context. When the provider's value changes by reference identity (Object.is), React re-renders every consumer — and crucially, this bypasses React.memo. A memoized component still re-renders if it consumes a changed context.

So the cost is not the propagation itself; it is that context has no granularity. One field changing in a large context object re-renders every component reading any part of it. Combine that with an inline object as the value and you get a re-render of every consumer on every parent render, because {{user, setUser}} is a new object each time.

The three standard fixes. 1. Memoize the value — useMemo the object so its identity only changes when the data does. This is the minimum and fixes the accidental case. 2. Split the context — separate the rarely-changing state from the never-changing dispatch. Components that only dispatch subscribe to a context whose value never changes, so they never re-render. 3. Use a subscription store — Zustand, Redux, or useSyncExternalStore — where components select a slice and re-render only when that slice changes. That is the real answer for high-frequency state.

Close with the rule: context is a dependency-injection mechanism for low-frequency, widely-needed values — theme, locale, the current user, a service client. It is the wrong tool for anything that changes often, and reaching for it as a state manager is how apps end up re-rendering the whole tree on every keystroke.

JSX
// bug: new object identity every render -> every consumer re-renders
<Ctx.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>

// fix 1: stable identity
const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, setUser }), [user]);

// fix 2: split - dispatch consumers never re-render
<StateCtx.Provider value={state}>
  <DispatchCtx.Provider value={dispatch}>   {/* dispatch is stable */}

// fix 3: selector-based subscription
const name = useStore(s => s.user.name);   // re-renders only when name changes
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does React.memo not protect a consumer?

memo compares props. Context is not a prop — the consumer subscribes directly to the provider — so a context change bypasses the comparison entirely. This surprises people who have memoized aggressively and still see re-renders.

Does splitting context always help?

It helps when the split matches how components actually consume the data. If most components need both halves you have doubled the plumbing for nothing. Profile first: React DevTools shows which context caused a render.

When is a context re-render actually fine?

When it is genuinely rare — theme, auth, locale. A re-render of the tree once when the user logs in costs nothing. The problem is exclusively with high-frequency updates.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design the interface before the implementation — that is what is being assessed. A minimal, honest API: V get(K key) that loads on miss, void put(K,V), void invalidate(K), and a builder taking max size, TTL, and a loader function. Make the loader a Function<K,V> so it is testable and the cache knows nothing about your data source.

Types: Cache<K,V> with the loader as Function<? super K, ? extends V> — PECS applied, so a loader for a supertype key or subtype value is accepted. Do not make the cache itself generic over the loader; keep the type parameters minimal.

Now the race, which is the real question. The naive if (map.containsKey(k)) return map.get(k); else { v = load(k); map.put(k,v); } is a check-then-act race: N concurrent misses all call the loader. On a cold cache with a hot key, that is a stampede against your database — the failure mode that turns a cache outage into a database outage.

The fix is single-flight: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent, which guarantees the mapping function runs at most once per absent key while other threads block on that bin. Two caveats to name: the function runs while holding the bin lock, so it must not recursively update the same map (the JDK throws IllegalStateException for some cases and can otherwise corrupt the table), and a long-running loader blocks other keys hashing to the same bin. For a production cache the honest answer is use Caffeine — it gives you TTL, size-based eviction with a better-than-LRU policy, async loading, and refresh-ahead — but you should be able to write the core by hand.

For TTL and max size without Caffeine: wrap values in a record carrying the expiry instant and treat expired entries as absent on read; for size, a LinkedHashMap in access order with removeEldestEntry, or accept an approximate policy. Say explicitly that eviction and expiry are where hand-rolled caches usually go wrong.

Java
public final class Cache<K, V> {
    private record Entry<V>(V value, long expiresAtNanos) {
        boolean expired() { return System.nanoTime() > expiresAtNanos; }
    }
    private final ConcurrentMap<K, Entry<V>> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Function<? super K, ? extends V> loader;   // PECS
    private final long ttlNanos;

    public V get(K key) {
        Entry<V> e = map.get(key);
        if (e != null && !e.expired()) return e.value();
        map.remove(key, e);                                  // drop the stale entry
        // single-flight: the loader runs at most once per absent key
        return map.computeIfAbsent(key, k ->
                new Entry<>(loader.apply(k), System.nanoTime() + ttlNanos)).value();
    }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the danger inside computeIfAbsent?

The mapping function runs while the bin is locked. Recursively updating the same map can deadlock or corrupt it, and a slow loader blocks every other key in that bin. Keep it short, and never call back into the cache.

How would you add refresh-ahead?

Return the stale value immediately and trigger an asynchronous reload when an entry passes a soft threshold before its hard TTL. It removes the latency spike on expiry entirely — Caffeine's refreshAfterWrite does exactly this.

What if the loader throws?

computeIfAbsent propagates the exception and stores nothing, so the next call retries — which under a persistent downstream failure means every request retries. Add a circuit breaker or negative caching with a short TTL so a broken dependency does not get hammered.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Requirements first. Functional: shorten a URL, redirect, optional custom alias, optional expiry, click analytics. Non-functional: extremely read-heavy (say 100:1), redirects must be fast (tens of milliseconds), high availability — a dead shortener breaks every link ever shared. Then estimate: 100M new URLs/year ≈ 3 writes/s, but 10B redirects/year ≈ 300 reads/s average and maybe 1,000 at peak. Storage at ~500 bytes/row is ~50 GB/year — small. The numbers say this is a caching problem, not a storage problem.

Key generation is the core decision, so compare the options. Hash and truncate (MD5 of the URL, take 7 chars) needs collision detection and a retry loop. Random has the same problem. Base62 of a monotonic counter is collision-free by construction and gives the shortest keys — 62^7 is 3.5 trillion — but a single counter is a bottleneck and sequential ids are enumerable, so use a distributed id generator (Snowflake-style, or ranges handed out in blocks to each node) and optionally scramble the output. Pre-generated key pool is my usual answer: a background job fills a table of unused keys, and creation is one atomic claim — no collisions, no coordination on the hot path.

Storage and read path: a simple table keyed by short code, and because it is 100:1 read-heavy and immutable after creation, cache aggressively — this is close to an ideal caching workload since entries never change. Put the mapping in Redis with a long TTL, and the CDN can even cache the redirect itself.

Redirect: 301 is permanent and browsers cache it — fastest, but you stop seeing the clicks. 302 is temporary, so every click reaches you and analytics work. Choose 302 if analytics matter, and say that tradeoff explicitly — it is the detail interviewers look for. Analytics: never write synchronously on the redirect path; publish an event to Kafka and aggregate asynchronously. Custom aliases need a uniqueness check under concurrency — rely on a unique constraint and handle the violation, not a read-then-write.

Read path
GET /aX9k2Bq
  -> CDN / edge cache            (optional; kills most traffic)
  -> app: Redis GET short:aX9k2Bq
       hit  -> 302 + async click event to Kafka
       miss -> Postgres lookup -> populate Redis -> 302
  -> not found -> 404 (cache negatives briefly to stop scan abuse)
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you stop someone enumerating every link?

Do not use a raw sequential counter — scramble it, or use the pre-generated pool so keys are non-sequential. Add rate limiting per IP on 404s, since a scanner produces a distinctive burst of misses.

What happens when Redis goes down?

Every redirect falls through to Postgres. At 1,000 QPS that is survivable with connection pooling and an index, which is worth stating — the cache is an optimization, not a dependency. Add a small local in-process cache as an L1 so a Redis outage does not fully expose the database.

How would you support link expiry and deletion?

Store an expires_at and check it on read, evicting from cache on expiry. For deletion, remove from Postgres and explicitly invalidate the cache key — and remember that a 301 already cached in users' browsers cannot be recalled, which is another argument for 302.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Build it as four concerns and address each: input handling, request lifecycle, keyboard navigation, and accessibility. Say that structure up front; it is what separates a designed answer from a coded-in-a-panic one.

Debounce the query at 250–300 ms so you fire one request per pause, not per keystroke. Debounce the request, not the input value — the field must stay controlled and instant, or typing feels laggy. Do not fire below a minimum length (usually 2 characters), and cache results by query string so backspacing to a previous query is free.

Request lifecycle is where correctness lives. Every new request must abort the previous one with an AbortController, otherwise a slow response for "ap" can land after a fast one for "apple" and overwrite the results with stale data. Aborting also stops wasted network work. Handle the three states explicitly — loading, empty results, and error — because an autocomplete that silently shows nothing on failure is indistinguishable from no matches.

Keyboard: ArrowDown/ArrowUp move a highlighted index (wrapping or clamping — pick one and be consistent), Enter selects the highlighted item, Escape closes the list and restores the typed value, Tab closes and moves on. Track the highlight as an index in state, and scroll the highlighted option into view.

Accessibility is the part most candidates skip and it is cheap to score on. The input gets role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-controls pointing at the listbox, and aria-activedescendant set to the id of the highlighted option — so the screen reader announces the highlighted item while focus stays in the input. The list is role="listbox" with role="option" children and aria-selected. Add an aria-live region announcing the result count. Finally, for very large lists, virtualize the dropdown.

JSX
const [q, setQ] = useState('');
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
const [active, setActive] = useState(-1);
const deferred = useDeferredValue(q);           // or a debounce hook

useEffect(() => {
  if (deferred.length < 2) { setItems([]); return; }
  const ctrl = new AbortController();
  fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(deferred)}`, { signal: ctrl.signal })
    .then(r => r.json()).then(setItems)
    .catch(e => { if (e.name !== 'AbortError') setError(e); });
  return () => ctrl.abort();                    // cancels the stale request
}, [deferred]);

<input role="combobox" aria-expanded={items.length > 0}
       aria-controls="ac-list"
       aria-activedescendant={active >= 0 ? `ac-${active}` : undefined}
       value={q} onChange={e => setQ(e.target.value)} onKeyDown={onKey} />
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is AbortController better than an ignore flag?

An ignore flag prevents the stale state update but the request still completes, consuming bandwidth and a server connection. Abort cancels the work end to end — which matters when the user types ten characters and would otherwise fire ten live requests.

Where should the debounce live?

On the request trigger, not the input state. Keeping the input controlled and instant while deferring only the fetch is what makes it feel responsive. useDeferredValue gives you a similar effect with React scheduling instead of a timer.

What does aria-activedescendant buy over moving focus?

Focus stays in the text input, so the user can keep typing while arrowing through options. Moving DOM focus into the list would break typing entirely — this is the standard combobox pattern for exactly that reason.

MOCK - 45 min, timed, narrate throughout
  • Merge IntervalsMedium
  • Longest Substring Without Repeating CharactersMedium

Two mediums in 45 minutes. State brute force before optimizing, state complexity before coding.

Split in half, sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves in one linear pass. The merge step is where the useful variants live.

CostO(n log n) time, O(n) space, stableReach for itLearning divide and conquer, and as the basis for counting inversions and other 'count pairs across a split' problems.
def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1: return a
    m = len(a) // 2
    L, R = merge_sort(a[:m]), merge_sort(a[m:])
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(L) and j < len(R):
        if L[i] <= R[j]: out.append(L[i]); i += 1   # <= keeps it stable
        else:            out.append(R[j]); j += 1
    return out + L[i:] + R[j:]
