Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Four kinds. A static nested class is a top-level class scoped inside another — no link to any outer instance. An inner (non-static nested) class holds an implicit reference to its enclosing instance, so it can read the outer object's fields. An anonymous class is a one-off subclass or implementation declared inline. A local class is a named class declared inside a method.

The leak follows directly from that implicit reference. The compiler adds a synthetic this$0 field pointing at the outer object. If an inner-class instance outlives its outer object — stored in a static registry, handed to a long-lived listener, submitted to an executor that queues it for minutes — the entire outer object and everything it references stays reachable and cannot be collected. In a heap dump you see it immediately: follow the dominator tree and the path terminates at this$0.

The fix is almost always the keyword static: make the nested class static and pass what it needs explicitly. Lambdas are better behaved — a lambda only captures this if it actually references an instance member; one that touches only parameters and effectively-final locals compiles to a static method and captures nothing.

On enums: an enum is a fixed set of instances created at class-initialization time, which the JVM performs lazily under the class-init lock. That makes the enum singleton the safest one in Java — thread-safe, lazy, and uniquely immune to the two attacks that break other singletons, since the JVM forbids reflective enum construction and handles enum serialization specially so a second instance cannot be created. Enums also carry state and per-constant behaviour, which is Strategy with no boilerplate, and EnumMap/EnumSet are array- and bitmask-backed rather than hash-based, so they are dramatically faster and smaller.

Java
class Service {
    private byte[] cache = new byte[10_000_000];
    class Task implements Runnable { public void run(){} }        // holds Service.this
    static class SafeTask implements Runnable { public void run(){} } // holds nothing
}
// registry.add(service.new Task());  // pins the 10MB cache forever

enum Operation {
    PLUS("+") { public long apply(long a, long b){ return a + b; } },
    TIMES("*") { public long apply(long a, long b){ return a * b; } };
    private final String symbol;
    Operation(String s){ this.symbol = s; }
    public abstract long apply(long a, long b);
}
enum Singleton { INSTANCE; }   // safest singleton in Java
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you confirm this leak in a heap dump?

Look for the synthetic this$0 field on the inner-class instance, then run "path to GC roots" — it leads straight to the outer object and its retained size tells you the cost.

Why not persist enum.ordinal()?

Ordinal is positional, so inserting a constant in the middle silently remaps every stored value. Persist name() or an explicit stable code field.

When is an inner (non-static) class actually right?

When it genuinely needs the outer instance and has the same lifetime — an iterator implementation inside a collection is the classic legitimate case.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Serial dependencies multiply. Three components at 99.9% each give 0.999³ = 0.997, so 99.7% — about 2 hours of downtime a month, not 43 minutes. That is the number people find surprising and it is the whole point: every dependency you add lowers your ceiling, so a service calling five others cannot be more available than their product.

Redundancy adds nines because parallel components fail independently: two instances at 99.9% give 1 − (0.001)² = 99.9999%, assuming genuinely independent failure. That assumption is where real systems break — two instances in the same rack, availability zone, or behind the same load balancer are not independent, and a bad deploy hits both simultaneously. Say that out loud; it is the difference between reciting the formula and understanding it.

SLA is the contractual promise to customers with financial consequences. SLO is your internal target, deliberately stricter than the SLA so you have margin. SLI is the actual measurement — the indicator, such as the proportion of requests served under 300 ms without a 5xx. The order matters: SLI is measured, SLO is chosen, SLA is promised.

The error budget is what makes this operational rather than decorative: 99.9% over 30 days allows 43 minutes of failure. That budget is a resource you spend. If it is intact, ship faster and take risks. If you have burned it, the policy is to freeze feature work and spend on reliability. It converts an argument about "how much reliability is enough" into an arithmetic decision, which is why it is worth naming in an interview.

Know the ladder cold: 99% = 7.2 h/month, 99.9% = 43 min, 99.99% = 4.3 min, 99.999% = 26 s. And note each nine costs roughly an order of magnitude more, so pick the lowest one the business genuinely needs.

Availability maths
serial:    0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 = 0.997      -> 99.7%  (~2h/month)
parallel:  1 - (1-0.999)^2      = 0.999999   -> 99.9999% (if independent)

budget @ 99.9% over 30 days = 43m 12s
  burned 40m in week 2  ->  freeze features, spend on reliability
  burned 2m by week 4   ->  ship, take risks, the budget is there to spend
Follow-ups they will ask

Why should the SLO be stricter than the SLA?

Because you need to detect and react before you breach the contract. If they are equal, the first signal that you are failing is a customer invoking penalties.

What makes redundancy fail to deliver its theoretical nines?

Correlated failure: shared rack, shared AZ, shared config, shared deploy, shared dependency. Independence is an assumption you have to engineer for, not one you get for free.

How do you pick an SLO?

From what users actually notice and what the business will pay for. Measure current performance first — an SLO you are already breaching is a project plan, and one you never come close to breaching is too loose to be useful.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

StrictMode is a development-only wrapper that renders nothing and changes no production behaviour. Its job is to make latent bugs loud now rather than mysterious later, particularly the ones concurrent rendering will expose.

It does this by double-invoking: component function bodies, state updater functions, and — since React 18 — mounting each effect, immediately unmounting it, and mounting it again. So you see setup → cleanup → setup on first mount in development.

That double effect mount surfaces exactly one class of bug: missing or asymmetric cleanup. If your effect subscribes, opens a socket, starts a timer or fires a request without a matching teardown, you now get two live subscriptions on mount and you notice at once. If your cleanup is correct, the sequence is harmless — which is the test. The classic complaint "my API is called twice in development" is StrictMode correctly telling you the request has no cancellation.

The double render of the component body surfaces impurity: mutating a prop, pushing to an array defined outside, incrementing a module-level counter, or generating an id during render. Under concurrent rendering React may render, discard, and re-render at will, so anything non-idempotent in the render path is already broken — StrictMode just makes it visible.

On the lifecycle mapping: componentDidMount ≈ useEffect(fn, []), componentDidUpdate ≈ useEffect(fn, [deps]), componentWillUnmount ≈ the cleanup return. The important difference is conceptual: hooks describe synchronization to a value, not points in a lifetime, which is why the dependency array is a declaration of what the effect reads rather than a list of when to fire.

JSX
// StrictMode reveals this: two live subscriptions after mount
useEffect(() => {
  socket.subscribe(onMessage);
});                                   // no cleanup - bug

// symmetric: setup -> cleanup -> setup is harmless
useEffect(() => {
  socket.subscribe(onMessage);
  return () => socket.unsubscribe(onMessage);
}, [onMessage]);

// impure render - StrictMode's double render exposes it
let id = 0;
function Row() { const myId = ++id; }   // different value each render
Follow-ups they will ask

Should you disable StrictMode because effects run twice?

No — that is removing the smoke detector. If double-mounting breaks something, the effect lacks cleanup or the request lacks cancellation, and that same bug appears in production as a leak or a race.

Does StrictMode run in production?

No. The double-invocation is development-only, so it costs nothing in the shipped bundle's behaviour.

What else does it warn about?

Legacy APIs — string refs, legacy context, findDOMNode — and deprecated lifecycle methods, so you find them before they are removed.

Sliding Window I
  • Best Time to Buy and Sell StockEasy
  • Longest Substring Without Repeating CharactersMedium
  • Longest Repeating Character ReplacementMedium

Grow the window on the right; shrink from the left while it violates the constraint. Each element enters and leaves once.

CostO(n) time, O(k) spaceReach for itLongest/shortest subarray with a property: no repeats, at most k distinct, sum ≥ target. State the shrink condition in one sentence and the code writes itself.
def longest_no_repeat(s):
    last, left, best = {}, 0, 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last and last[ch] >= left:
            left = last[ch] + 1        # shrink past the duplicate
        last[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

# The template: expand right always, shrink left WHILE invalid.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Arrays are covariant: String[] is a subtype of Object[]. That compiles, but arrays are also reified — they carry their real component type at runtime — so storing the wrong type throws ArrayStoreException at the point of the store, not at compile time.

Generics deliberately went the other way: they are invariant and erased. List<String> is not a List<Object>, so the entire class of error is caught by the compiler instead. The reason arrays are covariant at all is historical: Java 1.0 had no generics, so covariance was the only way to write a general sort(Object[]). It cannot be removed without breaking compatibility.

That reified-versus-erased mismatch is why generics and arrays mix badly: you cannot write new T[n], and a generic varargs parameter T... args secretly creates a T[] the compiler cannot make safe. That is heap pollution, and it is why such methods warn. @SafeVarargs suppresses the warning and is a promise you are making: the method only reads from the array and never stores or leaks it. It is restricted to static, final and private methods precisely because an overridable method could be replaced by an unsafe implementation.

Two utility gotchas worth having ready. Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list backed by the array — set writes through, add and remove throw. And List.of(...) is genuinely immutable but rejects nulls throughout, which surprises people migrating from Arrays.asList.

Java
Object[] objs = new String[2];
objs[0] = 42;                 // compiles; ArrayStoreException at runtime
// List<Object> l = new ArrayList<String>();   // will not compile - invariant

@SafeVarargs                  // promise: read only, never stored or leaked
static <T> List<T> listOf(T... items) { return new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(items)); }

static <T> T[] leak(T... items) { return items; }   // UNSAFE
// String[] s = leak("a","b");   // ClassCastException - it is really an Object[]

List<Integer> fixed = Arrays.asList(1,2,3);
fixed.set(0, 9);   // ok, writes through to the array
// fixed.add(4);   // UnsupportedOperationException
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you create a generic array safely?

You do not, directly. Use (T[]) new Object[n] confined to a private field that never leaks as T[], or Array.newInstance(clazz, n) when you have a Class<T>. ArrayList does exactly the former internally.

Why is multidimensional not a rectangular block?

Java has arrays of arrays, so rows are separate heap objects and may have different lengths. That also means worse cache locality than a flattened single array with index arithmetic — relevant in numeric hot paths.

What is the safest signature for a generic varargs API?

Take a Collection<T> instead of T.... It sidesteps the array entirely and therefore the whole heap-pollution question.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Little's law is L = λ × W: the average number of items in a system equals arrival rate times average time in the system. For the example — 200 req/s at 50 ms — that is 200 × 0.05 = 10 concurrent requests in flight. That single number is what you size thread pools, connection pools and concurrency limits against, and it is the fastest sanity check in a design interview.

It also runs backwards, which is the more useful direction: if you know your pool has 20 connections and each query takes 10 ms, your ceiling is 20 / 0.01 = 2,000 QPS. Beyond that, requests queue no matter how many application threads you add. That is how you prove a proposed design cannot meet its target without simulating anything.

Why latency explodes past ~70–80% utilization: queueing delay grows roughly as 1/(1−ρ). At 50% utilization the wait is about 1× the service time; at 90% it is 9×; at 95% it is 19×. The curve is a hockey stick, so a system "comfortably" at 85% CPU is one traffic bump away from a latency cliff — and the bump does not need to be large.

This is why you size for headroom rather than efficiency, and it explains several things that otherwise look unrelated: why a GC pause at high utilization causes a latency spike far larger than the pause itself; why losing one instance out of four can take the remaining three over the cliff; and why averages are useless here — at 85% utilization the mean may look fine while p99 has already collapsed. Always quote and alert on percentiles.

Little's law
L = lambda x W
  200 req/s x 0.050 s = 10 concurrent requests

backwards - capacity from a known limit:
  20 db connections / 0.010 s per query = 2,000 QPS ceiling

queueing multiplier ~ 1/(1-rho):
  rho = 0.50 ->  2x service time
  rho = 0.80 ->  5x
  rho = 0.90 -> 10x
  rho = 0.95 -> 20x     <- the cliff
Follow-ups they will ask

How does this change how you size a thread pool?

It tells you the pool only needs to cover concurrency, not throughput: 10 in-flight requests need ~10 threads, not 200. Oversizing just moves the queue from the pool into the downstream dependency, where it is harder to see.

Why are averages dangerous for latency?

Averages hide the tail, and the tail is what users experience — one slow request in a page that makes 20 calls means most page loads hit it. Track p50, p95 and p99, and set SLOs on p99.

What utilization should you target?

Typically 50–70% for latency-sensitive services, leaving room for spikes, deploys, and the loss of one instance or availability zone. Batch systems can safely run much hotter because queueing delay does not hurt them.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

React does not attach a listener to each element. It uses event delegation: since React 17 it attaches listeners at the root container where your app is mounted (in React 16 it was document, and the change matters when embedding multiple React apps or mixing with non-React code on the same page).

When a native event fires, it bubbles up the real DOM to that root, React works out which fiber it corresponds to, and then synthesizes its own propagation through the React tree, calling your onClick handlers as it goes. The SyntheticEvent you receive is a cross-browser normalized wrapper — consistent properties and behaviour across browsers. Note that event pooling, which used to require e.persist(), was removed in React 17; the object is no longer reused, so you can hold on to it.

The consequence that gets asked about is portals. A modal rendered with createPortal into document.body is elsewhere in the DOM, but React propagates events through the React tree, not the DOM tree — so a click inside the portal still bubbles to the React parent that rendered it. That is usually what you want (a form's onChange still fires) and occasionally surprising (a click-outside handler on the parent fires for clicks inside the modal).

Two practical notes. e.stopPropagation() stops React-tree propagation, but a native listener you attached with addEventListener on document may already have run or may still run, because it sits at a different level — mixing the two is the usual cause of "my click-outside handler fires immediately when I open the menu". And for capture-phase behaviour React provides onClickCapture and friends.

JSX
// portal: rendered into document.body, but events bubble through the React tree
function Modal({ children }) {
  return createPortal(<div className="modal">{children}</div>, document.body);
}

<div onClick={() => console.log('parent')}>   {/* fires for clicks inside Modal */}
  <Modal><button>Click</button></Modal>
</div>

// click-outside: use capture or check containment, and mind the ordering
useEffect(() => {
  const onDoc = e => { if (!ref.current?.contains(e.target)) close(); };
  document.addEventListener('mousedown', onDoc);   // mousedown, not click
  return () => document.removeEventListener('mousedown', onDoc);
}, []);
Follow-ups they will ask

Why did React move delegation from document to the root container?

So multiple React versions or apps can coexist on one page without intercepting each other's events, and so React plays better with non-React code that also listens on document.

Why use mousedown rather than click for click-outside?

Because the click that opened the menu may still be propagating; listening on mousedown and attaching after the opening event has settled avoids the menu closing instantly. It also feels more responsive.

Do all DOM events get delegated?

Most, but some cannot be — media events, scroll, and a few others are attached directly to the element because they do not bubble. You rarely need to know which, but knowing the rule exists is the point.

When you cannot compute the answer directly but you can check whether a candidate works, binary search the candidate.

CostO(n log(range)) timeReach for it'Minimise the maximum' or 'maximise the minimum' — that phrasing is this technique nearly every time. Ship capacity, splitting arrays, Koko eating bananas.
def min_capacity(weights, days):
    def can(cap):                       # monotone: bigger cap is never worse
        d, cur = 1, 0
        for w in weights:
            if cur + w > cap: d += 1; cur = 0
            cur += w
        return d <= days

    lo, hi = max(weights), sum(weights)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if can(mid): hi = mid
        else:        lo = mid + 1
    return lo

Must coverThey help when (a) the computation is genuinely expensive, or (b) the value is a dependency of a memoized child/effect. They cost an allocation + comparison otherwise. Note the React Compiler changes the calculus.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A HashMap is an array of buckets. For a key it takes hashCode(), then spreads it with h ^ (h >>> 16) so the high bits influence the outcome, then indexes with h & (capacity - 1) — which is why capacity is always a power of two: that mask is equivalent to modulo but far cheaper.

Collisions chain in a linked list. Since Java 8, once one bucket reaches 8 nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets, that chain converts to a red-black tree, changing worst-case lookup from O(n) to O(log n). This was added as a defence against hash-collision denial-of-service, where an attacker sends keys engineered to land in one bucket. It converts back at 6 nodes — the gap between 8 and 6 is deliberate hysteresis so a map hovering at the boundary does not thrash between representations.

Resize triggers when size exceeds capacity × loadFactor. The default 0.75 is a measured balance: lower wastes memory, higher increases collision probability sharply. Capacity doubles, and because it doubles, each old bucket's entries split into exactly two destinations — the same index, or that index plus the old capacity — decided by a single additional bit. That is an elegant detail worth stating.

The Java 8 change people ask about: Java 7 reversed the order of entries during a resize, and under concurrent access two threads resizing simultaneously could create a cycle in a bucket's linked list, so a later get would spin forever at 100% CPU. Java 8 preserves relative order during the split, which removes that particular failure — but HashMap is still not thread-safe, and concurrent use can still lose entries. Use ConcurrentHashMap.

Java
// power-of-two capacity makes this a cheap mask instead of a modulo
int index = (n - 1) & (h ^ (h >>> 16));

// pre-size to avoid repeated grow-and-rehash
int expected = 10_000;
Map<String,Order> m = new HashMap<>((int)(expected / 0.75f) + 1);

// treeify:   bucket >= 8 nodes AND table capacity >= 64
// untreeify: bucket <= 6 nodes   (hysteresis)
Follow-ups they will ask

Why treeify at 8 rather than sooner?

With a decent hash function the probability of 8 collisions in one bucket is vanishingly small (Poisson, roughly 1 in 10 million), so the tree path should never trigger in normal operation. It is an attack defence, not an optimization — and trees cost more memory per node.

Why does capacity >= 64 also matter for treeify?

Below that the right fix is to resize, not to treeify — a small table with a full bucket is under-sized rather than adversarially collided.

What makes a good HashMap key?

Immutable, with equals and hashCode over the same fields, and a well-distributed hash. String, Integer, enum and records qualify. A mutable entity whose id is assigned on persist is a bad key — its hash changes after insertion.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Name the patterns and, for each, the failure mode — that pairing is the answer.

Cache-aside (lazy loading): the application checks the cache, and on a miss loads from the database and populates it. Simplest and most common. Failure modes: a cold cache means every request hits the database, and there is a race where a read repopulates a stale value concurrently with a write. Read-through is the same shape but the cache library does the loading, which centralizes the single-flight logic.

Write-through: write to cache and database together, so the cache is never stale. Cost is write latency on every write, and you cache data that may never be read. Write-behind (write-back): write to cache and flush asynchronously — very fast writes, but you can lose acknowledged data if the cache node dies before the flush. That makes it unacceptable for a ledger and fine for a view counter. Refresh-ahead: proactively reload entries before they expire, removing the latency spike on expiry, at the cost of refreshing things nobody asked for.

Eviction: LRU is the sensible default; LFU is better when popularity is stable but adapts poorly to shifting workloads; TTL bounds staleness rather than size and you almost always want both; and modern caches such as Caffeine use W-TinyLFU, which beats plain LRU by admitting a new entry only if it is likely more valuable than what it would evict.

Then the one to volunteer: what happens when the cache node fails. Every request becomes a miss simultaneously, and a cache outage becomes a database outage. Defend with a small in-process L1 in front of Redis, single-flight so concurrent misses for one key produce one load, TTL jitter so entries do not expire in lockstep, and a circuit breaker that sheds load rather than letting the database collapse.

Cache-aside
value = cache.get(key)
if value is null:
    value = db.load(key)          <- N concurrent misses = N db queries
    cache.set(key, value, ttl + jitter)
return value

// single-flight fixes the stampede
value = cache.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> db.load(k))   // loader runs once per key
Follow-ups they will ask

Which pattern did the 96% latency win use, and what did it risk?

Almost certainly cache-aside with a TTL. The risk you accepted is bounded staleness: for up to one TTL a client can read a value that has since changed. Be ready to say what the worst-case wrong value was and why that was acceptable.

How do you invalidate rather than wait for TTL?

Explicitly delete the key on write (simple, but there is a small race with a concurrent read repopulating it), or publish an invalidation event that every node's L1 cache consumes. Versioned keys — including a version in the key — sidestep invalidation entirely at the cost of garbage.

When should you not cache at all?

When the data changes as often as it is read, when staleness is unacceptable and you cannot invalidate reliably, or when the query is already fast. A cache adds a consistency problem — it needs to buy something real.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start with what they actually are: useMemo caches a value between renders, useCallback caches a function identity. useCallback(fn, deps) is exactly useMemo(() => fn, deps). Neither prevents a re-render on its own — they only stabilize what gets passed along.

They genuinely help in two cases. One: the computation is expensive — sorting or filtering thousands of rows, a heavy derivation — and repeating it every render is measurable. Two, and far more common: the value is a dependency of something that compares by identity — a React.memo child, a useEffect dependency array, or a context value. Here the real motivation is referential equality: {} !== {} and () => {} !== () => {}, so an inline object or function is a new value every render and defeats every memoized consumer downstream.

They are pure cost otherwise. Each one allocates the dependency array, runs a comparison on every render, and adds code you must keep correct — a wrong dependency array turns a performance hint into a stale-value bug. Memoizing a cheap computation whose result nothing compares by identity is strictly worse than not memoizing.

The honest closing point: the React Compiler changes this calculus by inserting memoization automatically, so hand-written useMemo/useCallback becomes largely unnecessary in codebases that adopt it. Until then, the discipline is to profile first — add memoization to fix a measured problem, not preemptively.

JSX
// pointless: cheap, and nothing compares it by identity
const total = useMemo(() => a + b, [a, b]);

// worth it: expensive derivation
const sorted = useMemo(() => rows.slice().sort(cmp), [rows, cmp]);

// worth it: stabilizes a prop for a memoized child
const onSelect = useCallback(id => setSelected(id), []);
<MemoizedList items={items} onSelect={onSelect} />

// defeated anyway - inline object is a new identity every render
<MemoizedList items={items} style={{ margin: 8 }} />
Follow-ups they will ask

Does useMemo guarantee the value is cached?

No — React may discard memoized values, for example to free memory. It is a performance hint, not a semantic guarantee, so never rely on it for correctness or to avoid re-running something with side effects.

What is the cost of over-memoizing?

Allocation and comparison on every render, more code to keep correct, and dependency arrays that drift out of sync with the body and cause stale-closure bugs. It also makes the code harder to read for no measured benefit.

How do you decide in practice?

Open the React Profiler, record the interaction, and look at which components re-render and how long each takes. Memoize the ones that show up. If nothing shows up, the memoization would have bought nothing.

CostO(n) time, O(1) spaceReach for itMaximum subarray sum, and its variants — max product, best time to buy/sell stock, circular arrays.
def max_subarray(a):
    cur = best = a[0]
    for v in a[1:]:
        cur = max(v, cur + v)     # start fresh, or extend
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

# The whole insight: a prefix with a negative sum is never worth keeping.

Concurrent maps and cache pathologies

Must coverJava 8 dropped segments for per-bin CAS + synchronized on the first node; size() is an estimate via CounterCells; iterators are weakly consistent, never throw ConcurrentModificationException. Compound operations still need putIfAbsent/compute.

StudyConcurrentHashMap API docs →

Explain cache stampede, thundering herd, and hot keys. Give three concrete mitigations for each.

Must coverStampede: request coalescing/single-flight, probabilistic early expiry, stale-while-revalidate. Hot keys: key splitting with random suffix, local L1 cache in front of Redis, dedicated replicas. Never let all keys share one TTL - add jitter.

StudyAWS — Caching challenges and strategies →

React.memo: exactly what does it compare, and name three situations where it silently does nothing.

Must coverShallow prop compare only. Defeated by: inline object/array/function props, children as JSX (new element each render), and context updates. Show the fix for each.

Studyreact.dev — memo reference →
Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Hashtable is the legacy answer: every method synchronized on the whole object, so all access serializes. Collections.synchronizedMap is the same idea applied as a wrapper — one global lock, and iteration still requires you to synchronize manually on the map or you get a ConcurrentModificationException. Both are effectively single-threaded under contention.

ConcurrentHashMap in Java 8 was rewritten. The old lock-striping segments are gone; it is now a single table where a write CASes the first node into an empty bin and takes a synchronized lock on that bin's head node only when a chain already exists. So lock granularity is per-bucket, and reads are entirely lock-free — get never blocks, because the table and nodes use volatile reads.

size() is an estimate. It sums a base counter plus striped CounterCells — the same technique as LongAdder — without locking, so a concurrent update may or may not be counted. If you need an exact size you need coordination outside the map, which is usually a sign the design is wrong.

Iterators are weakly consistent: they never throw ConcurrentModificationException, they traverse elements as of some point at or after creation, and they never return an element twice — but they may or may not reflect concurrent updates. Finally, the API point that catches people: individual methods are atomic, but if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) is not — two threads can both pass the check. Use putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, compute or merge.

Java
ConcurrentMap<String, List<Order>> m = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

// atomic; the mapping function runs at most once per absent key
m.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()).add(order);
m.merge(key, 1L, Long::sum);        // atomic counter

// NOT atomic - classic check-then-act race
// if (!m.containsKey(k)) m.put(k, v);

// CHM also forbids null keys and values, deliberately:
// get() returning null would be ambiguous under concurrency
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does CHM forbid null values when HashMap allows them?

Because get(k) == null would be ambiguous — absent, or present with a null value? In a single-threaded map you can disambiguate with containsKey; under concurrency the answer could change between the two calls, so nulls are banned outright.

What is the risk inside computeIfAbsent?

The mapping function runs while the bin is locked. Recursively updating the same map can deadlock or corrupt the table — the JDK detects some cases and throws IllegalStateException. Keep the function short and free of callbacks into the map.

When is synchronizedMap still acceptable?

When contention is genuinely negligible and you want the simplest possible wrapper around an existing map, or when you need null keys. Otherwise ConcurrentHashMap is better in essentially every dimension.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Cache stampede (thundering herd): a popular key expires and every concurrent request misses simultaneously, so N requests all hit the database with the same query. The database, sized for the cached load, collapses — and because the cache is now empty and the database is slow, it cannot recover on its own.

Three mitigations. Single-flight / request coalescing: only the first miss loads; the others wait for that result — computeIfAbsent in-process, or a short-lived lock key in Redis across nodes. Probabilistic early expiry: each reader independently decides, with rising probability as the TTL approaches, to refresh early — so the refresh is spread out rather than synchronized. Stale-while-revalidate: serve the expired value immediately and refresh in the background, which removes the latency spike entirely and is usually the best answer when slight staleness is tolerable.

Hot keys: one key receives a disproportionate share of traffic — a celebrity profile, a flash-sale product — and saturates the single shard that owns it, because consistent hashing sends every request for that key to one node. Mitigations: key splitting, writing the value to key#1..key#N and having readers pick a random suffix; a local L1 cache in each application process so most reads never leave the box; and dedicated replicas for known-hot keys.

Two more to volunteer. Cache penetration is repeated misses for keys that do not exist — an attacker requesting random ids — which passes straight through to the database; fix with negative caching (short TTL on "not found") or a Bloom filter in front. And the simplest, most-forgotten rule: add jitter to every TTL. Populating a cache in a batch with identical TTLs guarantees they all expire at the same instant, which manufactures a stampede on a schedule.

Mitigations
stampede   -> single-flight lock, or stale-while-revalidate
              ttl = base + random(0, base * 0.1)      <- always add jitter
hot key    -> key#0..key#9 with a random read suffix
              + in-process L1 cache with a 1-5s TTL
penetration-> cache the negative result briefly, or a Bloom filter
cache down -> circuit breaker + load shedding, so the DB is not killed
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you find a hot key in production?

Redis has --hotkeys and keyspace sampling; more generally, sample a percentage of requests and aggregate by key. A single shard whose CPU is far above its peers is the operational tell.

Is stale-while-revalidate always safe?

No — it means someone reads a value you know is expired. Fine for a product listing or a feed; not fine for a balance or a permission check. It is a business decision about the tolerable staleness window.

What happens if the single-flight lock holder dies?

Everyone else waits until the lock's TTL expires, so the lock must have a short TTL and waiters must have a timeout that falls back to loading directly. Never take a distributed lock without an expiry.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

React.memo wraps a component and does a shallow comparison of props. If every prop is Object.is-equal to last render's, React skips re-rendering that subtree. It compares props only — it does not deep-compare and it does not track anything else.

Where it silently does nothing. 1. Inline object, array or function props. style={{margin: 8}}, items={[...]} or onClick={() => …} create a new identity on every parent render, so the shallow comparison always fails and memo costs you a comparison for zero benefit. 2. children as JSX. <Memoized><Child /></Memoized> passes a new element object every render — children is a prop like any other, so the memo never hits. 3. Context. A consumer re-renders when its context value changes regardless of memo, because it subscribes to the provider directly rather than receiving a prop.

The fixes map one-to-one: hoist constant objects out of the component or wrap them in useMemo; wrap handlers in useCallback; for children, pass a memoized element or restructure so the expensive part is memoized inside; for context, split the context or use a selector-based store.

Finish with the judgement: memo is not free. It costs an extra comparison per render and adds coupling to prop identity throughout the tree. Apply it to components that are expensive to render or that render frequently with unchanged props — and verify with the Profiler that it actually removed renders, because a memo that never hits is pure overhead plus a false sense of having optimized.

JSX
const Row = React.memo(function Row({ item, onSelect }) { /* ... */ });

// defeated: new identities every render
<Row item={item} onSelect={() => select(item.id)} style={{ padding: 4 }} />

// works: stable identities
const onSelect = useCallback(id => select(id), []);
const style = useMemo(() => ({ padding: 4 }), []);
<Row item={item} onSelect={onSelect} style={style} />

// custom comparator - use sparingly, it is easy to make it wrong
React.memo(Row, (prev, next) => prev.item.id === next.item.id);
Follow-ups they will ask

When is a custom comparator a bad idea?

When it compares fewer fields than the component reads — then a real change is skipped and the UI silently goes stale. It is also easy to make it more expensive than the render you avoided. Prefer fixing prop identity.

Does memo help if the parent re-renders constantly?

Yes — that is exactly its purpose, provided the props are stable. If props change every time anyway, the parent's render frequency is the problem and memo cannot fix it.

How do you verify memo is working?

React DevTools Profiler: record an interaction and check whether the component appears in the commit. If it still renders, inspect "why did this render" — it will point at the prop whose identity changed.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Give the textbook answer, then correct it — that contrast is the point. On paper LinkedList wins for insertion and deletion (O(1) at a known node) and loses for indexed access (O(n)); ArrayList is the reverse. In practice LinkedList loses almost everywhere, because Big-O ignores cache locality. ArrayList's elements sit in one contiguous array, so the CPU prefetcher streams through them. LinkedList's nodes are scattered across the heap, so nearly every step is a cache miss — and each node also costs an object header plus two pointers, roughly 24 extra bytes.

There is also a hidden cost people miss: to insert "in the middle" of a LinkedList you must first walk there, which is O(n) anyway. The O(1) advantage only materializes when you already hold an iterator positioned at the spot.

For queue and stack use cases the right answer is ArrayDeque — a circular array, no per-element nodes, faster than both LinkedList and the legacy Stack (which extends Vector, is synchronized, and iterates bottom-up, which is the wrong order). ArrayDeque forbids null elements deliberately, so poll() returning null unambiguously means empty.

Fail-fast iterators track a modCount on the collection; the iterator snapshots it and compares on every next(), throwing ConcurrentModificationException if anything other than the iterator structurally modified the collection. It is a best-effort bug detector, not a guarantee — modCount is not volatile, so under real concurrency a modification may go unseen. Never write code that depends on catching it. Fail-safe (weakly consistent) iterators never throw: CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates an immutable snapshot, ConcurrentHashMap reflects some state at or after creation.

CopyOnWriteArrayList copies the entire backing array on every mutation, so reads are lock-free and iteration is snapshot-safe, but writes are O(n) and allocation-heavy. It is correct only for read-dominant, small collections — listener registries, cached configuration, routing tables that change on deploy. N sequential adds allocate N arrays.

Java
Deque<Task> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();  stack.push(t); stack.pop();
Deque<Task> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();  queue.offer(t); queue.poll();

// ConcurrentModificationException
for (String s : list) if (s.isBlank()) list.remove(s);
// correct
list.removeIf(String::isBlank);

// COW: right for this, wrong for anything write-heavy
private final List<Listener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
for (Listener l : listeners) l.on(e);   // no lock, no CME, safe under mutation
Follow-ups they will ask

Is LinkedList ever the right choice?

When you hold an iterator and repeatedly insert or remove at that position in a very large list, or when you need a Deque that permits null elements. Both are rare enough that "I would use ArrayList or ArrayDeque" is the honest default answer.

Why does COW get O(n squared) under a burst of writes?

Each write allocates a full new array, so N sequential adds allocate N arrays and all but the last become immediate garbage. Use addAll to batch them into one copy, or pick a different structure.

Why is fail-fast only best-effort?

The modCount check is unsynchronized and modCount is not volatile, so a concurrent modification may not be observed. It reliably catches the single-threaded mistake, which is what it exists for.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Split the answer by content type, because the caching rules are opposite for each. Hashed static assets — app.9f2a1c.js — get Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. The content hash is in the filename, so a new build produces a new URL and the old one can be cached forever. immutable additionally tells the browser not to revalidate even on reload. HTML gets no-cache, which means "cache it but revalidate every time" — the HTML references the hashed assets, so it must always be fresh. API responses get private plus a short max-age, or an ETag for conditional requests.

ETag enables revalidation without re-sending the body: the client sends If-None-Match, and the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body if unchanged. It saves bandwidth but still costs a round trip, which is why max-age beats ETag for assets you can version. stale-while-revalidate lets the browser serve the cached copy immediately while refreshing in the background — the best of both for content that tolerates brief staleness.

CDN: a pull CDN fetches from your origin on first miss and caches at the edge — simple and self-maintaining, at the cost of a slow first request per region. A push CDN has you upload in advance — better for large, predictable assets like video. An origin shield is a mid-tier cache that absorbs edge misses so a global cold start does not send hundreds of simultaneous requests to your origin.

Then volunteer the failure mode, because it is the memorable part: a wrong Cache-Control on HTML is an outage you cannot roll back. If you accidentally serve max-age=86400 on your HTML, every client that received it will not check back for a day, and there is nothing you can deploy to reach them. Purging the CDN does not help — the copies are in users' browsers. That asymmetry is why HTML is always no-cache and assets are always hashed.

Cache-Control
/static/app.9f2a1c.js   public, max-age=31536000, immutable
/index.html             no-cache                     <- always revalidate
/api/profile            private, max-age=0, must-revalidate
/api/products           public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300

# no-cache  = cache, but revalidate before every use
# no-store  = never write it to disk at all (auth pages, PII)
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the difference between no-cache and no-store?

no-cache means store it but revalidate before use — you still benefit from a 304. no-store forbids storing it at all, which is what you want for pages containing PII or on shared machines.

How do you invalidate a CDN?

An explicit purge by path or tag, but propagation takes seconds to minutes and does not touch browser caches. The reliable strategy is versioned URLs, which make invalidation unnecessary.

Why does immutable exist if max-age is already a year?

Because browsers revalidate on an explicit reload even within max-age. immutable suppresses that, which measurably reduces requests for users who habitually hit refresh.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Virtualization renders only the rows currently in the viewport plus a small buffer, so a 100,000-row list has perhaps 30 DOM nodes instead of 100,000. Without it you pay for 100,000 elements at mount, and every re-render diffs all of them — the page freezes for seconds.

The fixed-height maths is short and you should be able to write it. A scroll container has an inner spacer of totalHeight = rowCount × rowHeight so the scrollbar is correct. Then startIndex = floor(scrollTop / rowHeight), visibleCount = ceil(viewportHeight / rowHeight), and you render startIndex − overscan to startIndex + visibleCount + overscan. Each rendered row is absolutely positioned at top = index × rowHeight, or you translate a container by startIndex × rowHeight.

Overscan — rendering a few extra rows above and below — is what stops blank flashes during fast scrolling, since scroll events fire after the paint. Three to five rows is typical.

Variable heights change the problem qualitatively, because you can no longer compute an index from an offset. You need a measurement cache: render with an estimated height, measure actual heights with ResizeObserver as rows mount, store them, and maintain a prefix-sum (or Fenwick tree) of offsets so you can binary-search from scrollTop to the start index. Total height becomes an estimate that converges as more rows are measured — which is why the scrollbar sometimes shifts slightly in naive implementations.

In practice use TanStack Virtual or similar rather than hand-rolling; the value in an interview is being able to explain the mechanism and name the hard parts — scroll restoration, sticky headers fighting absolute positioning, keyboard focus on unmounted rows, and Ctrl+F not finding text that is not in the DOM.

JSX
const rowHeight = 40, overscan = 4;
const start = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / rowHeight) - overscan);
const visible = Math.ceil(viewportHeight / rowHeight) + overscan * 2;
const rows = items.slice(start, start + visible);

<div onScroll={e => setScrollTop(e.currentTarget.scrollTop)}
     style={{ overflowY: 'auto', height: viewportHeight }}>
  <div style={{ height: items.length * rowHeight, position: 'relative' }}>
    {rows.map((item, i) => (
      <div key={item.id}
           style={{ position:'absolute', top:(start+i)*rowHeight, height:rowHeight }}>
        {item.name}
      </div>
    ))}
  </div>
</div>
Follow-ups they will ask

What accessibility problems does virtualization create?

Screen readers and browser find-in-page only see rendered rows, and aria-setsize/aria-posinset must be set manually so assistive tech knows the real list length. Keyboard navigation must also scroll the target row into view before focusing it.

How do you restore scroll position when returning to the list?

Persist scrollTop (not the index) and restore it after the container has its full height, otherwise you scroll before the spacer exists and land at the top. With variable heights you may need to restore by item id and re-measure.

When is virtualization not worth it?

Below a few hundred simple rows the overhead and the complexity are not repaid. Measure first — pagination or simply rendering less per row is often the cheaper fix.

  • Daily TemperaturesMedium
  • Car FleetMedium

A stack kept sorted (increasing or decreasing). Popping while the incoming element breaks the order is what finds the 'next greater' in one pass.

CostO(n) total — each element is pushed and popped at most onceReach for itNext/previous greater or smaller element, largest rectangle in a histogram, daily temperatures, trapping rain water.
def next_greater(a):
    res, st = [-1]*len(a), []          # st holds INDICES, decreasing values
    for i, v in enumerate(a):
        while st and a[st[-1]] < v:
            res[st.pop()] = v          # v is the next greater for that index
        st.append(i)
    return res

# Anything left on the stack has no next greater element.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

TreeMap is a red-black tree — a self-balancing BST where get, put and remove are O(log n) and iteration is in sorted key order. TreeSet is a TreeMap with dummy values. The reason to choose it over a HashMap is not the ordering alone but the NavigableMap API: floorKey, ceilingKey, higherEntry, headMap, tailMap, subMap, firstEntry, pollFirstEntry. Range and nearest-neighbour queries are precisely what a hash map cannot do at any price.

Comparable is the type's own natural ordering, implemented on the class as compareTo. Comparator is an external, swappable ordering — you can have many, and they work on types you do not own. Modern comparators compose: Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...).reversed(), with primitive-specialized comparingInt/comparingLong to avoid boxing on every comparison inside a sort.

Now the contract violations, which is what is really being asked. compareTo should be consistent with equals — and when it is not, sorted collections misbehave in a way that looks like a JDK bug. A TreeSet ordered by salary treats two employees earning the same amount as duplicates and silently drops the second, because TreeSet decides membership by compare, never by equals. The fix is always a tie-breaker that makes the comparator a total order.

The second violation is worse: a non-transitive comparator. TimSort detects the inconsistency and throws IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract! — but usually only on large inputs, because small arrays take a simpler sort path. So it passes every test and fails in production. Two more traps: reversed() applies to the entire chain built so far, not just the last key; and TreeMap rejects null keys, because it must compare them.

Java
NavigableMap<Instant, Rate> rates = new TreeMap<>();
Rate inEffect = rates.floorEntry(when).getValue();     // nearest at-or-before
Map<Instant,Rate> window = rates.subMap(from, true, to, false);

// silently drops the second employee - compare() says they are equal
Set<Emp> s = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Emp::salary));

// fix: total order via a tie-breaker
Comparator<Emp> c = Comparator.comparingInt(Emp::salary).thenComparing(Emp::name);
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does the JDK throw rather than just sorting wrongly?

TimSort's merge invariants depend on the contract; a violation can cause an ArrayIndexOutOfBounds deep inside the sort. The explicit check converts an incomprehensible crash into a diagnosable message.

TreeMap or sort a list?

TreeMap when the data changes and you keep querying — each change costs O(log n). A sorted array with binary search is faster and more compact for static data, but every insertion is O(n).

Which collections use equals and which use compare?

Hash-based collections use equals and hashCode; sorted collections use the comparator exclusively. The same two objects can therefore be duplicates in a TreeSet and distinct in a HashSet — a genuine source of confusion.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ): competing consumers, each message delivered to one consumer, and deleted after acknowledgement. Good for work distribution. Pub/sub (SNS, Google Pub/Sub): each message fans out to every subscriber, typically without retention. Distributed log (Kafka): messages are retained on disk for a configured period and consumers track their own offset, so multiple independent consumer groups read the same stream at their own pace, and any of them can rewind and replay. That replay capability is the defining difference, and it is why Kafka is used as an integration backbone rather than just a queue.

At-most-once: acknowledge before processing. If you crash in between, the message is gone. Acceptable only for lossy telemetry. At-least-once: acknowledge after processing. If you crash after processing but before acknowledging, the message is redelivered — so duplicates are guaranteed to happen eventually. This is the default in essentially every real system.

Exactly-once is where the honest answer scores. As a delivery guarantee over an unreliable network it is impossible — the acknowledgement itself can be lost, and the sender cannot distinguish a lost message from a lost acknowledgement. What is achievable is exactly-once effect, built from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing: give every message a stable id, record processed ids, and make the handler safe to run twice. Kafka's transactions give exactly-once within Kafka (consume-transform-produce with the offset commit in the same transaction), but the moment you write to an external database that guarantee ends unless you make the write idempotent too.

So the design rule to state: assume at-least-once, and make every consumer idempotent. Use a natural idempotency key — an order id, a payment reference — with a unique constraint in the database, or a processed-events table with a bounded retention window. "We are exactly-once because we use Kafka" is the answer that fails.

Idempotent consumer
onMessage(event):
  # unique constraint on event_id does the work atomically
  BEGIN
    INSERT INTO processed_events(event_id) VALUES (?)   -- fails if duplicate
    apply(event)                                        -- same transaction
  COMMIT
  ack()

# duplicate -> unique violation -> skip and ack, no double effect
# crash before ack -> redelivered -> insert fails -> safe
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does ordering only hold per partition?

Because partitions are consumed independently and in parallel — that is what gives you throughput. Global ordering would require a single partition and a single consumer, which caps you at one core. So the partition key is the design decision: it defines what is ordered relative to what.

How long should the processed-events table be retained?

Long enough to cover your maximum redelivery window — retention plus retry topics plus a safety margin, typically days. Then partition by time and drop old partitions, or the table becomes the bottleneck.

When is a queue better than a log?

When you need per-message acknowledgement, per-message retry with visibility timeouts, and priority — SQS-style semantics. Kafka replays by offset, which makes "retry this one message later" awkward and is why retry topics exist.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Name all three, then fix each — the structure is what makes this answer land.

Waterfalls. A parent fetches, renders, and only then does the child mount and start its own fetch. Three nested components means three sequential round trips, so a 300 ms API becomes a 900 ms page. Fix by hoisting and parallelizing: fetch both at the parent with Promise.all, or move data loading to the route boundary (route loaders, RSC, or a prefetch on hover) so requests start before components mount. The tell in DevTools is a network waterfall shaped like a staircase.

Race conditions. Props change from A to B; the request for A is slow, the request for B is fast, B's response lands first, then A's overwrites it — and the UI shows the wrong data with no error anywhere. Fix with an ignore flag in the cleanup or, better, an AbortController, which also cancels the wasted network work. This is the single most common bug in hand-rolled data fetching, and it is invisible on a fast connection.

Fetch-on-render. The component must mount before the request starts, so you always pay one render's delay and you get a guaranteed loading flash. The alternative is render-as-you-fetch: kick off the request when the navigation begins, not when the component renders, and let Suspense read from the in-flight promise. Route loaders and RSC do this by construction.

Close with the practical recommendation: a query library — TanStack Query or SWR — solves races, deduplication, caching and background refetch structurally, so you stop rewriting this in every component. Reserve hand-rolled effects for genuinely one-off cases.

JSX
// race: stale response can overwrite fresh data
useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;
  fetchUser(id).then(u => { if (!ignore) setUser(u); });
  return () => { ignore = true; };            // minimum viable fix
}, [id]);

// better: cancels the network work too
useEffect(() => {
  const c = new AbortController();
  fetchUser(id, { signal: c.signal }).then(setUser)
    .catch(e => { if (e.name !== 'AbortError') setError(e); });
  return () => c.abort();
}, [id]);

// waterfall -> parallel
const [user, prefs] = await Promise.all([fetchUser(id), fetchPrefs(id)]);
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is the ignore flag not enough on its own?

It prevents the stale state update but the request still completes, consuming bandwidth, a server connection and a browser connection slot. Under fast typing that is ten live requests where one would do.

How does a query library fix races structurally?

It keys every request by its inputs and only commits the response for the currently active key, so an out-of-order response for an old key is discarded automatically. You cannot forget to handle it.

What causes a waterfall you cannot see in the code?

A component that suspends or conditionally renders its child — the child's fetch cannot start until the parent resolves. Also authentication gates: waiting for the session before starting any data fetch serializes everything behind it.

Sort by start, then walk: if the next interval overlaps the current one, extend it; otherwise close it and start a new one.

CostO(n log n) time, dominated by the sortReach for itMerging, inserting, or counting overlapping intervals — meeting rooms, calendar booking, range consolidation.
def merge(iv):
    iv.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    out = [iv[0]]
    for s, e in iv[1:]:
        if s <= out[-1][1]:                     # overlap
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
        else:
            out.append([s, e])
    return out

# Sorting by START is what makes one pass sufficient.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A pipeline is a source, zero or more intermediate operations, and one terminal operation. Intermediate operations are lazy — they build a description and do nothing. Only the terminal operation triggers execution, which is why a stream with no terminal operation runs no code at all.

Execution is then fused: elements flow through the whole chain one at a time rather than each stage materializing a full intermediate collection. That is why filter().map().findFirst() can stop after examining a single element, and why putting filter before map matters — the expensive stage then sees fewer elements. Short-circuiting operations (findFirst, anyMatch, limit) stop consuming once the answer is known, which makes infinite sources like Stream.iterate usable.

Stateless operations — filter, map, peek — hold nothing between elements and fuse perfectly. Stateful ones — sorted, distinct, limit, skip — retain information, and sorted and distinct are full barriers: sorting must see every element before emitting the first, so laziness stops there and memory grows to the size of the stream. That is why sorted().limit(10) sorts everything to take ten, and a bounded priority queue is the right structure for top-K.

Parallel streams split work across the common ForkJoinPool, which is sized to cores−1 and shared by the entire JVM. They help when the source splits cheaply (array, ArrayList, IntStream range), N is large, and the per-element work is CPU-bound and substantial. They hurt when N is small (split and merge overhead dominates), when the source splits poorly (LinkedList, Files.lines, iterators), and catastrophically when the work is blocking — one slow IO call occupies a common-pool thread and starves every other parallel stream in the JVM, including framework internals. If you must, submit to your own ForkJoinPool, or just use an ExecutorService. Always measure; parallel streams are frequently slower.

One more: a stream is single-use. Consuming it twice throws IllegalStateException.

Java
// nothing executes - no terminal operation
Stream<Order> s = orders.stream().filter(Order::isPaid);

// fused and short-circuiting: enrich runs only until the first match
orders.stream().filter(Order::isPaid).map(this::enrich).findFirst();

// sorts everything to take 10
orders.stream().sorted(byTotalDesc).limit(10).toList();
// O(n log 10), bounded memory
PriorityQueue<Order> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(comparing(Order::total));
for (Order o : orders) { heap.offer(o); if (heap.size() > 10) heap.poll(); }

// dangerous: blocking work in the shared common pool
// urls.parallelStream().map(this::httpGet).toList();
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is peek discouraged outside debugging?

It is specified for debugging, and implementations may skip it entirely when a result can be computed without traversing every element — count() on a sized stream, for example. Using it for side effects makes behaviour version-dependent.

When are streams the wrong choice?

Tight numeric loops where lambda overhead matters, logic needing indices or complex early exit, and anything you will need to step through in a debugger. A plain loop is often clearer, and clarity is the main reason to use streams in the first place.

What is encounter order and when can you drop it?

The defined element order of the source. Calling unordered() tells the pipeline you do not need it, which lets parallel distinct and limit use substantially cheaper algorithms.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Topics and partitions. A topic is split into partitions; each partition is an ordered, append-only log on disk. Partitions are the unit of parallelism and of ordering — ordering is guaranteed within a partition only. So the partition key is the central design decision: keying by account id means one account's events are strictly ordered while different accounts process in parallel. A null key round-robins and gives no ordering at all.

Consumer groups. Within a group each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer, so your parallelism ceiling is the partition count — adding consumers beyond that leaves them idle. Different groups consume the same topic independently, which is what makes Kafka an integration backbone rather than a queue.

Offsets and commits. Turn off auto-commit and commit after processing. Auto-commit fires on a timer, so a crash between the commit and the processing silently loses messages. Manual commit after processing gives at-least-once, which means duplicates, which means the handler must be idempotent. Rebalancing happens when a consumer joins, leaves, or misses max.poll.interval.ms — the classic incident is slow processing exceeding that interval, so the broker assumes the consumer died, rebalances, the work is reassigned, and it happens again in a loop. Use cooperative-sticky assignment to avoid the stop-the-world variant.

For your own pipeline, the numbers to have ready are: topic and partition count, consumer instances, average and p99 processing time, the lag alert threshold, and DLQ volume. When a consumer falls behind, lag grows; the first response is to scale consumers up to the partition count, and if you are already at that ceiling you must add partitions (which changes key-to-partition mapping and therefore breaks ordering for in-flight keys) or make processing faster. Consumer lag is the key SLI — alert on lag and its rate of growth, because growth predicts a breach long before latency alarms fire. If lag exceeds retention, you lose data permanently, which is the failure to name.

Kafka
acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2      # durability
enable.idempotence=true              # dedupes producer retries
enable.auto.commit=false             # commit AFTER processing
max.poll.records=100                 # keep a poll cycle under max.poll.interval.ms

lag = latest_offset - committed_offset
  alert on: lag > threshold  AND  d(lag)/dt > 0 sustained
  scale: consumers <= partitions, then add partitions, then optimize handler
Follow-ups they will ask

What happens to ordering when you add partitions?

The key-to-partition mapping changes, so a key that used to land on partition 3 may now land on partition 7 — and messages for that key can be processed out of order across the transition. Plan repartitioning as a deliberate migration, not a scaling reflex.

How do you handle a poison message without blocking the partition?

Bounded retries with backoff, then publish to a DLQ and commit the offset so the partition advances. Classify first: a deserialization failure will never succeed, so send it straight to the DLQ; a downstream timeout deserves retries.

Why prefer retry topics over blocking retries?

A blocking retry holds the consumer thread and can exceed max.poll.interval.ms, triggering a rebalance and making things worse. Retry topics with increasing delays move the wait off the main consumption path.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A custom hook is just a function that calls other hooks and whose name begins with use. That prefix is not decoration — it is what lets the linter enforce the rules of hooks on it.

When to extract: when logic is stateful and reused, or when it isolates an external system (a subscription, a media query, a WebSocket, localStorage). Extraction gives you a named concept and a place to test the logic. When not to: pure functions with no hooks should be plain functions, not hooks — they are easier to test and can be called anywhere. And a hook that returns JSX should have been a component.

The design rules that matter: a hook should do one thing and return the minimum surface; prefer returning an object for three or more values so callers are not order-dependent; keep returned callbacks stable with useCallback so they can be effect dependencies; and never accept a component as an argument. Give it a name describing the concept — useDebounce, useOnlineStatus — not the mechanism.

Why the rules of hooks exist is the part that separates a memorized answer. Hooks are stored in a linked list on the component's fiber, and they are resolved by call order, not by name — React has no idea which useState is which; it simply advances a pointer on each call. So if you call a hook conditionally, on the next render the sequence shifts and every subsequent hook reads the previous one's slot: your count state suddenly holds your name state's value. That is why the rules are "top level only, never in conditions, loops or nested functions, and only from components or other hooks" — and why the eslint plugin is not optional.

JSX
function useDebounced(value, delay = 300) {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(id);      // cleanup cancels the pending timer
  }, [value, delay]);
  return debounced;
}

// why the rules exist: hooks resolve by call order on the fiber
if (isLoggedIn) { const [a] = useState(1); }   // ILLEGAL
const [b] = useState(2);                       // b reads a's slot when the
                                               // condition flips
Follow-ups they will ask

Do two components sharing a hook share state?

No. Each call site gets its own independent state — the hook shares the logic, not the data. Sharing state requires lifting it, context, or an external store.

How do you test a custom hook?

With React Testing Library's renderHook, or by rendering a tiny test component that uses it. Better still, keep the pure logic in a plain function and unit-test that directly, leaving only the React wiring in the hook.

What is the sign a hook is doing too much?

It returns six values, or its name has an "and" in it. Split it — small composable hooks read better and can be reused independently.

When the values are a permutation of 1..n, put each value at its own index by swapping. No extra space needed.

CostO(n) time, O(1) spaceReach for it'Array of n numbers in range 1..n' — find the missing, the duplicate, or all of them. The constraint is a strong hint.
def cyclic_sort(a):
    i = 0
    while i < len(a):
        j = a[i] - 1                     # where a[i] belongs
        if a[i] != a[j]: a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
        else: i += 1
    return a

# After sorting, the first index where a[i] != i+1 is the missing number.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Optional exists to make "there might be no result" explicit in a signature, so callers cannot forget. That is its whole purpose, and it defines its correct use: as a return type.

The anti-patterns, because interviewers probe them. Not as a field — it is not Serializable and adds an object per instance. Not as a parameter — provide an overload instead; forcing callers to wrap arguments in Optional.of is worse than a null check. Not as a collection element — an empty collection already means nothing. And never call get() without isPresent(); use orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, map, filter.

The specific bug worth naming: orElse evaluates its argument eagerly, even when a value is present. findUser(id).orElse(loadDefaultFromDb()) hits the database on every call including the hits. orElseGet(() -> loadDefaultFromDb()) only on absence. This is a real production performance bug that reads as correct.

On functional interfaces: one abstract method, so a lambda can implement it. The core set is Function, Supplier, Consumer, Predicate, plus Bi- and primitive-specialized variants (ToIntFunction, IntPredicate) that exist to avoid boxing in hot pipelines. They compose through default methods — andThen, compose, and, or, negate.

Effectively final is the capture rule: a lambda captures the value of a local, not the variable, so the compiler requires the local never be reassigned — otherwise you would have two diverging copies with no defined semantics. Fields are exempt because they are reached through the captured this. And unlike an anonymous class, this inside a lambda refers to the enclosing instance, which matters when registering callbacks.

Java
Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);        // correct use: return type

String name = findByEmail(e).map(User::name)
        .filter(n -> !n.isBlank()).orElse("anonymous");
User u = findByEmail(e).orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(e));

int factor = 2;
nums.stream().map(n -> n * factor);   // factor must stay effectively final
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is Optional not Serializable?

A deliberate design decision to discourage its use as a field. The API authors said explicitly that it was designed as a limited-purpose return type, not a general-purpose container.

andThen or compose?

f.andThen(g) runs f then g; f.compose(g) runs g then f. Same operations, opposite order — getting the name right is a small precision signal.

Is Optional appropriate in a Spring Data repository?

Yes — Optional<Entity> findById(id) is the intended idiom: the return type honestly says no row may match, and the caller cannot forget to handle it.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start from the guarantee you actually have: at-least-once delivery. Duplicates will happen — a retry after a lost acknowledgement, a redelivery after a consumer crash, a rebalance replaying uncommitted offsets. So the design goal is not to prevent duplicates but to make them harmless.

Idempotency keys. Every message or request carries a stable id supplied by the producer — an order id, a payment reference, a client-generated UUID in an Idempotency-Key header. The consumer records processed ids and skips repeats. The critical detail is that recording the id and applying the effect must be atomic: insert the id and perform the write in one database transaction, with a unique constraint on the id doing the work. If you record first and apply second, a crash in between loses the effect permanently; if you apply first and record second, a crash duplicates it. For an API, also store the original response against the key so a retry returns the same answer rather than a conflict.

The transactional outbox solves the sibling problem — the dual write. You cannot atomically update your database and publish to Kafka; if you write the row then the broker call fails, you have state with no event, and if you publish then the transaction rolls back, you have an event for something that never happened. The outbox writes the domain row and an event row in the same local transaction, and a separate relay (a poller, or CDC reading the write-ahead log with Debezium) publishes from the outbox and marks it sent. The relay may publish twice — which is fine, because consumers are idempotent.

Dedup windows. The processed-ids store must be bounded or it grows forever. Size the retention to cover your maximum redelivery window — broker retention plus retry topics plus a margin, typically days — and partition by time so you drop old partitions rather than running deletes. Redis SET key NX EX works for short windows; a database table with a unique constraint is the durable option. State the tradeoff: too short a window and a late redelivery duplicates; too long and the store becomes a cost and a bottleneck.

Outbox + idempotent consumer
-- producer side: one local transaction, no dual write
BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO orders(id, ...) VALUES (...);
  INSERT INTO outbox(id, topic, payload) VALUES (...);
COMMIT;
-- relay polls outbox (or CDC reads the WAL) -> publishes -> marks sent

-- consumer side: dedupe and effect in one transaction
BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO processed_events(event_id) VALUES (?);   -- unique constraint
  UPDATE balances SET amount = amount + ? WHERE id = ?;
COMMIT;                                                -- duplicate -> violation -> skip
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is CDC better than polling the outbox?

Polling adds query load and latency, and you must handle the ordering and cleanup yourself. CDC reads the write-ahead log, so it adds no query load, captures deletes, and preserves commit order — at the cost of operating Debezium and coupling to the database's replication.

What if the effect is not a database write?

Sending an email or charging a card cannot be rolled back. Then the idempotency key must be passed to the downstream provider — every serious payment API accepts one — so the provider deduplicates. If it does not, you need a pending-state record and reconciliation.

Does Kafka's exactly-once feature remove the need for this?

Only within Kafka — consume, transform and produce with the offset commit in the same transaction. The moment you write to an external database the guarantee ends, so the idempotent consumer is still required.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design the states first, then the boundaries. Every data-driven region has four states — loading, empty, error, success — and the common failure is treating empty as loading, or having no error state at all so a failure renders as a permanent spinner.

Error boundaries catch errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of the tree below them. State clearly what they do not catch: event handlers, asynchronous code (setTimeout, promise rejections), server-side rendering, and errors thrown in the boundary itself. Those need ordinary try/catch or a rejection handler. Error boundaries must still be class components — there is no hook equivalent — which is why most teams use react-error-boundary.

Suspense handles the loading state declaratively: a component suspends while its data or code is pending, and the nearest Suspense boundary shows a fallback. Pair each Suspense boundary with an error boundary — one handles "not ready yet", the other handles "it failed" — and they compose naturally because both work on the tree.

The architectural decision is boundary granularity. One boundary at the page root means any slow call blanks the whole page and any failure kills it. Instead place a boundary per independent region — sidebar, main content, recommendations — so a slow or failing recommendations service degrades to a small error card while the rest of the page renders. Design skeletons that match the final layout so there is no layout shift when content arrives.

Two practical additions: give the error fallback a reset action (retry the query, remount the subtree via the boundary's reset key), and always report the caught error to your monitoring in componentDidCatch — a boundary that silently swallows failures is worse than a crash, because now nobody knows.

JSX
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<ErrorCard onRetry={refetch} />}>
  <Suspense fallback={<FeedSkeleton />}>
    <Feed />
  </Suspense>
</ErrorBoundary>

// per-region isolation: a failing sidebar does not take down the page
<Layout>
  <ErrorBoundary fallback={<SidebarError />}><Sidebar /></ErrorBoundary>
  <ErrorBoundary fallback={<MainError />}><Main /></ErrorBoundary>
</Layout>

// NOT caught by a boundary - needs its own handling
onClick={async () => { try { await save(); } catch (e) { setError(e); } }}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why can an error boundary not catch event handler errors?

Because handlers run outside the render phase — React is not on the stack, so there is nothing to intercept. The upside is that a failed click does not need to unmount your UI; handle it locally and show a toast.

What is the reset key pattern?

Give the boundary a resetKeys array; when a value in it changes, the boundary clears its error state and re-renders the children. It is how you make "Try again" actually retry rather than showing the same cached failure.

Should every component have a boundary?

No — too many boundaries fragment the UI into isolated broken cards and hide systemic failures. Place them at meaningful product boundaries: a page, a panel, a widget that can genuinely fail on its own.

Walk the list rewiring each next pointer backwards, carrying three pointers: previous, current, and the saved next.

CostO(n) time, O(1) spaceReach for itReversing a whole list, a sub-list, or in k-groups. Also the second half of 'is this a palindrome list'.
def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next     # save it before you destroy it
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    return prev            # new head
