Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

With LinkedHashMap it is five lines. Construct it with accessOrder = true, so every get or put moves the entry to the end of its internal linked list, then override removeEldestEntry to return true when size exceeds capacity — the map evicts the head, which under access order is the least recently used.

From scratch the structure is a HashMap from key to node, plus a doubly linked list of nodes ordered from least to most recently used. get: look up the node, unlink it, append at the tail, return the value. put: if present, update and move to tail; otherwise create, append at tail, and if over capacity remove the head node and delete its key from the map. Both are O(1) because the map gives you the node directly, so unlinking needs no traversal. Use sentinel head and tail nodes — they remove every null check in the unlink and append code, which is where hand-written versions usually break.

Two details interviewers look for: the linked list must be doubly linked, because unlinking a node in O(1) requires its predecessor; and eviction must remove the entry from the map as well as the list, or you leak keys and the map grows unbounded while the list stays at capacity.

Thread safety. The honest first answer is a single lock around both structures, because get mutates the list — so even reads are writes, and a read-write lock buys nothing. Say that explicitly; it is the insight. Only if the lock is proven hot do you reach for striping, and at that point you should use Caffeine, which records accesses into per-thread ring buffers and applies them asynchronously so reads do not contend, and uses W-TinyLFU rather than plain LRU. Also note what this design lacks: no TTL, and no protection against a scan flushing the whole cache — the classic LRU weakness.

Java
// 1. LinkedHashMap
class LruCache<K,V> extends LinkedHashMap<K,V> {
    private final int max;
    LruCache(int max) { super(16, 0.75f, true); this.max = max; }   // access order
    @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K,V> e) { return size() > max; }
}

// 2. from scratch - sentinels remove all null checks
class Node { K key; V val; Node prev, next; }
private final Map<K,Node> map = new HashMap<>();
private final Node head = new Node(), tail = new Node();   // head <-> tail

V get(K k) {
    Node n = map.get(k);
    if (n == null) return null;
    unlink(n); appendTail(n);            // O(1): no traversal needed
    return n.val;
}
void put(K k, V v) {
    Node n = map.get(k);
    if (n != null) { n.val = v; unlink(n); appendTail(n); return; }
    n = new Node(k, v); map.put(k, n); appendTail(n);
    if (map.size() > max) { Node lru = head.next; unlink(lru); map.remove(lru.key); }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does a ReadWriteLock not help here?

Because get mutates the recency list, so every read is structurally a write. There are no pure readers to run concurrently, which is exactly the situation where a read-write lock costs more than a plain mutex.

What is LRU's weakness?

A single large scan touches every entry once and evicts the genuinely hot working set. LFU resists that but adapts badly to shifting popularity; W-TinyLFU (Caffeine) admits a new entry only if it is likely more valuable than the victim, which handles both.

How would you add TTL?

Store an expiry timestamp on each node and treat an expired entry as absent on read, evicting it lazily. A background sweeper is only needed if expired entries must be reclaimed promptly rather than on next access.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Requirements: 1,000 requests per minute per API key, 10,000 keys, several gateway nodes. So the counter must be shared — per-node counters would let a client with N nodes get N times the limit. And the check sits in the hot path of every request, so it must be a single fast operation.

Algorithms, with their failure modes. Fixed window: one counter per key per minute — trivial, but allows a 2x burst at the boundary (1,000 at 11:59:59 and 1,000 at 12:00:00). Sliding window log: store every request timestamp and count those inside the window — exact, but O(requests) memory per key, which at scale is unacceptable. Sliding window counter: keep the current and previous window counts and interpolate by how far into the current window you are — approximate, tiny memory, no boundary burst. This is the practical default. Token bucket: tokens refill at a fixed rate up to a cap, each request takes one — the right model when bursts are legitimate, and the one to choose if the API should tolerate a client catching up after being idle.

Implementation. Redis with a Lua script so the read-modify-write is atomic in one round trip — otherwise two gateway nodes can both read 999 and both allow. Compute tokens lazily from elapsed time rather than running a refill job. Key it rl:{apiKey} and set a TTL so idle keys expire on their own; 10,000 keys with a handful of fields each is trivial memory.

The latency-conscious variant worth volunteering: check a local in-process counter first and only synchronize with Redis periodically or when near the limit. You trade exactness — a client may briefly exceed — for removing a network hop from every request. And the operational decision that interviewers wait for: fail open or fail closed when Redis is down? For a public API protecting a fragile backend, fail closed. For a limiter that exists only to stop accidental abuse, fail open, because taking the whole API down to enforce a rate limit is a worse outcome. Say which and why. Finally, return 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining so clients can back off intelligently rather than hammering.

Redis Lua (token bucket)
-- KEYS[1]=bucket  ARGV: now, rate, capacity, cost
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[3])
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
local delta  = math.max(0, tonumber(ARGV[1]) - ts)
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[3]), tokens + delta * tonumber(ARGV[2]))
if tokens < tonumber(ARGV[4]) then return 0 end          -- reject
redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens - ARGV[4], 'ts', ARGV[1])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 3600)
return 1                                                  -- allow
Follow-ups they will ask

Why must this be a Lua script rather than GET then SET?

Because two gateway nodes can interleave: both read 999, both decide to allow, both write 1000. The script runs atomically on the Redis server, so the check and the decrement cannot be split.

How do you rate limit by user when requests arrive unauthenticated?

Limit by IP first at the edge (coarse, and beware shared NATs and proxies — use the correct forwarded header), then by user id after authentication. Two layers with different limits is normal.

What if one Redis node becomes a hot shard?

The limiter keys are spread by key hash, so hot shards mean one client dominates. Shard the limiter itself, or move to local-first counting with periodic sync so the hot key stops being a single point of contention.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The defining requirement is that anything must be able to trigger a toast — a component, an API interceptor, a route loader, a plain utility function that knows nothing about React. That rules out putting the state in a component and passing a callback down, and it is the constraint that drives the whole design.

So keep the state in a module-level store outside React and subscribe to it with useSyncExternalStore. The store exposes an imperative API — toast.success('Saved') — importable anywhere, and a single <Toaster /> mounted once near the app root subscribes and renders. That separation is what makes it callable from non-component code, and it is the correct use of useSyncExternalStore: it guarantees a consistent snapshot under concurrent rendering, avoiding tearing.

Rendering goes through a portal so the toasts escape any parent's overflow: hidden or stacking context — a very common bug when toasts are rendered inline. Cap the number visible (three or four) and queue the rest, otherwise a burst of failures produces a wall of toasts.

Behaviour details that separate a real implementation: auto-dismiss on a timer, but pause the timer on hover and on focus so a user reading it is not cut off; dedupe identical messages fired in quick succession, or increment a count on the existing toast; allow a toast to be updated by id, which is how you turn a "Saving…" toast into "Saved"; and clean up timers on unmount.

Accessibility is the part most candidates skip: the container needs aria-live="polite" (or assertive for errors) with role="status", so screen readers announce it without moving focus. Never move focus to a toast — it interrupts the user's task. Any action inside a toast must be keyboard reachable, and a toast carrying an important action should not auto-dismiss at all, because a keyboard or screen-reader user may not reach it in time.

JSX
// store outside React - callable from anywhere
let toasts = [], listeners = new Set();
const emit = () => { toasts = [...toasts]; listeners.forEach(l => l()); };

export const toast = {
  show(msg, opts = {}) {
    const id = crypto.randomUUID();
    toasts.push({ id, msg, ...opts }); emit();
    if (opts.duration !== 0) setTimeout(() => toast.dismiss(id), opts.duration ?? 4000);
    return id;
  },
  dismiss(id) { toasts = toasts.filter(t => t.id !== id); emit(); }
};

function useToasts() {
  return useSyncExternalStore(
    cb => { listeners.add(cb); return () => listeners.delete(cb); },
    () => toasts);
}

function Toaster() {
  const items = useToasts();
  return createPortal(
    <div aria-live="polite" role="status">{items.map(t => <Toast key={t.id} {...t} />)}</div>,
    document.body);
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why useSyncExternalStore rather than a plain useState plus subscription?

Under concurrent rendering, two components reading the same mutable external store mid-render can observe different values — that is tearing. This hook forces a consistent snapshot and is the supported way to integrate an external store.

Why not just use context?

Context requires a provider ancestor, so only components can publish. An axios interceptor or a utility module cannot reach it. The module store has no such constraint, which is exactly the requirement.

How do you handle a burst of identical errors?

Dedupe by a caller-supplied key: if a toast with that key is visible, update it and increment a counter instead of pushing a new one. Otherwise one failing poll loop fills the screen in seconds.

One pointer moves one step, the other two. If there is a cycle they must eventually meet; if not, the fast one reaches the end.

CostO(n) time, O(1) spaceReach for itCycle detection, finding the cycle's start, the middle node, and 'happy number' style problems on functional graphs.
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
        if slow is fast: break
    else:
        return None                 # no cycle
    slow = head                     # reset one pointer to the head
    while slow is not fast:         # they now meet AT the cycle start
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next
    return slow

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The plain fluent builder breaks under inheritance. If Builder.name() returns Builder, then after calling a parent method you can no longer chain a subclass method — new UserBuilder().name("x").email("y") fails to compile, because name() handed back the parent type. Forcing callers to order their calls a particular way is a fragile API.

The fix is a recursive generic bound, the self-type idiom: abstract class Builder<T extends Builder<T>> with an abstract T self(). Every parent method returns self(), which is typed as the concrete subclass, so chaining works in any order. It reads as "T is a Builder of itself" and it is the same shape as <T extends Comparable<T>> — comparable to its own type.

Be honest about when it is worth it: only when you genuinely have a builder hierarchy. For a single builder, methods returning the builder type are simpler and better, and for a small immutable value a record with with-style copy methods beats a builder entirely.

On wildcards in a public API, the rule is accept the widest type you can consume, return the narrowest useful type. So parameters take ? extends T when you only read and ? super T when you only write — PECS. And the corollary that matters most: never put a wildcard in a return type. It propagates into every caller's variable declarations and infects their code with wildcards they cannot get rid of. If a method returns List<? extends Number>, callers cannot add to it and must keep the wildcard everywhere they pass it on.

One more API-design point: prefer a Function<? super K, ? extends V> for a caller-supplied strategy, so a loader written for a supertype key or a subtype value is still accepted. Small, but it is exactly the kind of signature a reviewer notices.

Java
abstract class Builder<T extends Builder<T>> {
    protected String name;
    public T name(String n) { this.name = n; return self(); }
    protected abstract T self();                       // the self-type hook
}
class UserBuilder extends Builder<UserBuilder> {
    private String email;
    public UserBuilder email(String e) { this.email = e; return this; }
    @Override protected UserBuilder self() { return this; }
}
new UserBuilder().name("asha").email("a@b.c");   // chains in any order

// PECS in a public signature; no wildcard in the return type
static <T> void copy(List<? extends T> src, List<? super T> dst) { ... }
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is a wildcard return type harmful in practice?

List<? extends Number> xs = f(); means the caller cannot add anything to xs and must keep the wildcard on every variable and parameter it flows into. You have exported your internal uncertainty into their code.

Is the self-type worth the complexity?

Only for a real hierarchy. If there is one builder, plain methods returning the builder are clearer. Mention that judgement — reaching for the clever generic when it buys nothing is itself a design smell.

What does the compiler not check about self()?

Nothing forces self() to return this — a subclass could return another instance and break the chain. It is a convention the type system cannot enforce, which is a fair criticism of the idiom.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design it as layers, each with its own policy: browser cache, CDN edge, an optional shared cache (Redis), and the application. The mistake is a single blanket policy; the right answer assigns a different one per content type and says why.

Hashed static assets — app.9f2a1c.js: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. The content hash means a new build is a new URL, so the old one can be cached forever, and immutable stops the browser revalidating even on an explicit reload. HTML shell: no-cache — store it, but revalidate every time. It references the hashed assets, so it must always be fresh. JSON API: private (never let a shared cache hold one user's data) with a short max-age, or an ETag for conditional revalidation.

ETag mechanics, precisely: the server sends ETag: "abc123"; the client's next request carries If-None-Match: "abc123"; if unchanged the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body. It saves bandwidth but still costs a full round trip — which is exactly why max-age beats ETag whenever you can version the URL. A strong ETag means byte-identical; a weak one (W/"abc") means semantically equivalent, which is what you want if you gzip at the edge. ETags also give you optimistic concurrency on writes via If-Match, returning 412 Precondition Failed.

stale-while-revalidate decouples freshness from latency: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300 means serve from cache for 60 s, then for the next 300 s keep serving the stale copy immediately while refreshing in the background. The user never waits for a revalidation. Its sibling stale-if-error serves stale content when the origin is failing, which turns an outage into slightly old data.

Close with the failure mode, because it is the memorable part: a wrong Cache-Control on HTML is an outage you cannot roll back. Ship max-age=86400 on your HTML and every client that received it will not check back for a day. Purging the CDN does not help — the copies are in users' browsers. That asymmetry is the entire reason HTML is no-cache and assets are hashed.

Layered policy
browser  |  CDN edge  |  Redis  |  app  |  db

/static/app.9f2a1c.js   public, max-age=31536000, immutable   (browser + CDN)
/index.html             no-cache                              (CDN may hold briefly)
/api/me                 private, no-store                     (never shared)
/api/products           public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300

ETag flow:  200 + ETag  ->  If-None-Match  ->  304 (no body, still a round trip)
Follow-ups they will ask

When is ETag better than max-age?

When the resource changes unpredictably and you cannot version the URL, and when the payload is large — a 304 saves the body even though it costs the round trip. For versioned assets, max-age is strictly better.

Why must user-specific responses be private?

Otherwise a shared cache — a CDN or corporate proxy — can store one user's response and serve it to another. That is a real data-leak class of bug, and private plus Vary: Authorization is the defence.

What does Vary do?

It tells caches which request headers change the response, so a cache keys separate entries per value. Vary: Accept-Encoding is routine; Vary: Cookie is usually a sign the response should not be shared-cached at all.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Both run after React has mutated the DOM. The difference is when, relative to paint. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutation and before the browser paints. useEffect is deferred and runs after paint, asynchronously.

So the rule is: use useLayoutEffect only when you must measure the DOM and change it before the user sees anything — positioning a tooltip or popover against its trigger, measuring text to decide on truncation, reading and restoring scroll position. Do it in useEffect and the browser paints the wrong position first, then you correct it, and the user sees a visible flicker — one frame of the element in the wrong place. That flicker is the entire reason the hook exists.

What breaks if you pick wrong the other way: useLayoutEffect blocks paint. Any expensive work there delays the frame, which shows up directly in INP and makes the UI feel unresponsive. So data fetching, subscriptions, logging and analytics all belong in useEffect — everything that does not need to happen before paint.

Why it warns during SSR: there is no DOM and no layout on the server, so a layout effect can never run there. React warns because the code implies it depends on measurements that will not exist, meaning the server-rendered output may not match what the client produces. The standard workaround is an isomorphic hook that picks useLayoutEffect in the browser and useEffect on the server — or better, avoid needing measurement for the first paint, using CSS or the Popover/anchor positioning APIs instead.

JSX
// correct: measure and position before paint - no flicker
useLayoutEffect(() => {
  const rect = triggerRef.current.getBoundingClientRect();
  setPos({ top: rect.bottom + 8, left: rect.left });
}, [open]);

// wrong here: paints at (0,0) first, then jumps into place
useEffect(() => { /* same measurement */ }, [open]);

// SSR-safe isomorphic hook
const useIsomorphicLayoutEffect =
  typeof window !== 'undefined' ? useLayoutEffect : useEffect;
Follow-ups they will ask

Does useLayoutEffect hurt performance?

It can — it runs synchronously in the commit phase and delays paint, so heavy work there directly costs you interaction latency. Keep it to a measurement and a state set, nothing more.

Why does setting state inside useLayoutEffect not cause a visible double render?

React flushes the resulting re-render synchronously before yielding to the browser, so both renders happen within one frame and the user only ever sees the final result. That is precisely the guarantee you are paying for.

Is there a way to avoid it entirely?

Often yes — CSS anchor positioning, position: sticky, container queries, or the native Popover API solve many positioning problems declaratively, with no measurement and no JavaScript in the paint path.

heapq.heappushpop(h, x)          # cheaper than push then pop

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Collectors is where most real stream work happens, and the highest-value idiom is groupingBy with a downstream collector. The second argument transforms each group rather than just collecting it to a list: counting(), summingInt, averagingDouble, mapping, toSet, maxBy, or a nested groupingBy for multi-level grouping. Reaching for the downstream form instead of post-processing a Map<K, List<V>> is the fluency signal.

toMap has two sharp edges that bite in production. It throws IllegalStateException on a duplicate key unless you supply a merge function — and real data has duplicates. And unlike HashMap it throws NullPointerException on a null value, because its implementation uses Map.merge, which treats null as absent and so cannot represent it unambiguously. Both fail fast rather than silently dropping entries, which is the right design but surprises people.

partitioningBy is the boolean special case and is worth knowing for one property: it always returns both true and false keys, even when a group is empty, so you never need to null-check. teeing (Java 12+) runs two collectors over the same stream in one pass and merges the results — count and sum together without writing a custom collector.

A custom Collector has five parts: supplier (fresh mutable container), accumulator (fold one element in), combiner (merge two containers), finisher (transform to the result), and characteristics (IDENTITY_FINISH, UNORDERED, CONCURRENT). The trap is the combiner: it is never called in a sequential stream, so a wrong combiner passes every test and only corrupts results when someone later adds .parallel(). If you cannot write a correct one, say the collector is sequential-only.

Java
Map<String, Long> countByDept = employees.stream()
        .collect(groupingBy(Employee::dept, counting()));

Map<String, List<String>> namesByDept = employees.stream()
        .collect(groupingBy(Employee::dept, mapping(Employee::name, toList())));

// duplicates are real - always supply a merge function
Map<String, Employee> byEmail = employees.stream()
        .collect(toMap(Employee::email, e -> e, (a, b) -> a));

// one pass, two aggregates
var summary = employees.stream().collect(teeing(
        counting(), summingInt(Employee::salary), Summary::new));

Collector<Order, StringJoiner, String> ids = Collector.of(
        () -> new StringJoiner(", ", "[", "]"),   // supplier
        (j, o) -> j.add(o.id()),                   // accumulator
        StringJoiner::merge,                       // combiner - parallel only
        StringJoiner::toString);                   // finisher
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you control the Map implementation groupingBy returns?

Use the three-argument form with a map factory: groupingBy(Employee::dept, TreeMap::new, toList()). Same for the four-argument toMap. Useful when you need sorted or insertion-ordered output.

What does IDENTITY_FINISH mean?

The mutable container is already the result, so the framework can skip the finisher entirely. toList has it; a collector that returns a different type does not.

When is CONCURRENT safe on a collector?

Only when the container is thread-safe and the accumulator can be called concurrently on it — groupingByConcurrent backed by a ConcurrentHashMap. It also needs UNORDERED to actually help.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start with the split that defines the system: metadata in a database, bytes in a blob store. The metadata service holds object keys, sizes, checksums, content types, ownership and versions and is queryable; the blob store holds immutable content addressed by an internal id. Never put multi-megabyte blobs in your relational database — it destroys backup times, replication and buffer-cache efficiency.

Presigned URLs are the most important decision: bytes must never traverse your API servers. The client asks your API to authorize an upload; you return a short-lived signed URL; the client PUTs directly to storage; storage notifies you (or the client confirms) and you mark the object complete. This keeps your service stateless and cheap, and means a 1 GB upload does not occupy an application thread for minutes.

Multipart and resumable uploads for 1 GB: split client-side into parts (typically 5–100 MB), upload each independently with its own checksum, retry only failed parts, and issue a final complete call listing the part ids and their ETags. Resumability follows for free — ask the server which parts it already has and skip them. Parallel parts also saturate the connection far better than one stream. Add a lifecycle rule to abort and reclaim incomplete multipart uploads, or they silently accumulate cost.

Deduplication via content addressing: hash the content (SHA-256) and use the hash as the storage key. Identical content maps to one blob with a reference count, and metadata rows point at it. The subtlety is that the client must hash before uploading to get the saving, and you should verify server-side rather than trusting the client's hash.

Durability: replication (3 copies) is simple and fast to reconstruct but costs 3× storage. Erasure coding — splitting into k data and m parity fragments — gives comparable durability at roughly 1.5× storage, at the cost of CPU on reconstruction and higher read latency on a degraded read. Use replication for hot, small, latency-sensitive objects and erasure coding for cold bulk storage; tier between them with lifecycle policies.

Upload flow
1. POST /uploads            -> app: create metadata row (state=pending), return
                               uploadId + presigned URLs per part
2. PUT part 1..N            -> client uploads DIRECTLY to blob store, in parallel
                               (retry only failed parts; each part checksummed)
3. POST /uploads/{id}/done  -> app: verify parts, complete multipart,
                               state=available, dedupe by content hash

lifecycle rule: abort incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you stop someone abusing a presigned URL?

Scope it tightly: short expiry (minutes), one specific key, one method, a content-length range and content-type condition. It is a bearer capability, so the constraints in the signature are your only control.

What if the client dies after uploading but before confirming?

The metadata row stays pending and a reaper cleans it up after a timeout, along with the incomplete multipart upload. This is why the metadata row is created first — otherwise you have orphaned bytes nobody can find.

Where does the strong-consistency question appear?

In the metadata store, not the blob store. The row must not say available until the bytes are durable, or a reader gets a 404 for an object your API claims exists. Order the writes so metadata trails the data.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The problem it solves is tearing. Concurrent rendering lets React pause a render, do something else, and resume. If the component tree reads a mutable external store — a Redux store, a Zustand store, a module-level variable — and that store changes mid-render, components rendered before the change see the old value and those rendered after see the new one. The result is a single committed UI showing two inconsistent versions of the same state. That cannot happen with React state, because React controls when it changes.

useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot) fixes it by forcing React to read a consistent snapshot: it checks the snapshot before and after rendering and, if the store changed, re-renders synchronously rather than committing a torn tree. In effect it opts that subtree out of concurrent-safe reads in exchange for consistency.

Two mechanical requirements. getSnapshot must return a cached, referentially stable value — returning a newly created object each call (() => ({a, b})) causes an infinite render loop, because React compares snapshots by identity and always sees a change. subscribe must be stable too, or the store re-subscribes on every render. And getServerSnapshot is required for SSR, since there is no store to subscribe to on the server.

This is not a hook you use daily — it is the integration primitive for library authors. Redux, Zustand, Jotai and Valtio all use it internally, which is how they became concurrent-safe in React 18. You reach for it directly when you subscribe to something outside React: a module store (the toast example), navigator.onLine, a media query, localStorage changes across tabs, or a WebSocket connection state.

JSX
// online status - a browser API is an external store
function useOnlineStatus() {
  return useSyncExternalStore(
    cb => {
      window.addEventListener('online', cb);
      window.addEventListener('offline', cb);
      return () => {
        window.removeEventListener('online', cb);
        window.removeEventListener('offline', cb);
      };
    },
    () => navigator.onLine,      // snapshot: a primitive, so it is stable
    () => true                   // server snapshot
  );
}

// INFINITE LOOP - new object identity on every call
// () => ({ user: store.user, theme: store.theme })
// fix: cache the object in the store and return the same reference
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does returning a new object from getSnapshot loop forever?

React compares the snapshot by Object.is to decide whether to re-render. A fresh object never equals the previous one, so it re-renders, calls getSnapshot again, and repeats. Cache the derived object in the store, or select a primitive.

How do you select a slice without re-rendering on unrelated changes?

Return a primitive from getSnapshot, or use useSyncExternalStoreWithSelector from use-sync-external-store/shim, which adds a selector and an equality function. That is exactly what Zustand's selector API does under the hood.

Is it a replacement for context?

No — different jobs. Context distributes a value down a tree; this hook subscribes to a store that lives outside React entirely. They compose: a context can hold the store instance, and components use this hook to read from it.

Keep a heap of size k, not n. Push each element and pop the worst, so the heap always holds the best k seen so far.

CostO(n log k) time, O(k) spaceReach for itK largest/smallest/most frequent. Beats sorting when k is much smaller than n, and works on a stream where sorting cannot.
import heapq
def top_k(a, k):
    h = []                          # min-heap of the k largest
    for v in a:
        heapq.heappush(h, v)
        if len(h) > k: heapq.heappop(h)   # evict the smallest
    return h

# For k largest use a MIN-heap (so the weakest is on top and easy to evict).
# For k smallest use a MAX-heap. Getting this backwards is the classic bug.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A String in memory is Unicode; bytes on disk or the wire are an encoding of it. Every conversion needs a charset, and if you do not name one Java uses a platform default that differs between your laptop, CI and the production container — which is exactly how the same code produces correct output locally and mojibake in production. Always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8 explicitly. Java 18 changed the default file encoding to UTF-8 (JEP 400), which helps, but explicit is still correct and portable across versions.

Two deeper points. String.length() returns UTF-16 code units, so an emoji or many CJK characters count as 2 — use codePointCount when you mean characters, which matters for validating field lengths. And a multi-byte character can straddle a buffer boundary, so decoding must go through a Reader; decoding fixed-size byte chunks independently corrupts characters at the seams. Also, truncating a UTF-8 byte array to fit a database column can cut a character in half — truncate by code points.

Regex: compile once into a static final Pattern and reuse it. Pattern is thread-safe; Matcher is not, so create one per use. Recompiling inside a request handler is a silent, invisible performance drain.

Catastrophic backtracking is the security-relevant part. Java's engine backtracks, so nested quantifiers over overlapping character classes — (a+)+b, (\d+)*$, or alternations whose branches match the same text — can take exponential time on a non-matching input. A 30-character crafted string can pin a CPU core; if that regex sits in a request path or a log parser, it is a denial-of-service (ReDoS). Mitigate by avoiding nested quantifiers, using possessive quantifiers (a++) or atomic groups ((?>…)) which forbid backtracking, anchoring patterns, and capping input length before matching. For simple work, startsWith, indexOf and split are clearer and immune.

Java
byte[] b = s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);     // never s.getBytes()
String back = new String(b, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

String emoji = "a\uD83D\uDE00";
emoji.length();                                    // 3 - UTF-16 code units
emoji.codePointCount(0, emoji.length());           // 2 - characters

private static final Pattern EMAIL =               // compiled once
        Pattern.compile("^[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.]+$");

Pattern bad  = Pattern.compile("(a+)+b");   // exponential on "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaX"
Pattern safe = Pattern.compile("(a++)+b");  // possessive - no backtracking
Follow-ups they will ask

Where else does an implicit default charset hide?

new FileReader(f), new String(bytes), new PrintWriter(file), InputStreamReader without a charset, and String.format with locale-sensitive formats. Worth a grep in any code review.

How would you spot a ReDoS risk in review?

Look for nested quantifiers, or alternations whose branches can match the same characters, applied to user-controlled input. Then test with a long run of the repeated character followed by one that forces failure — the runtime explodes immediately.

What is the safest general defence?

Cap input length before matching, prefer simple string operations where possible, and for untrusted patterns run the match on a bounded executor with a timeout so a pathological case cannot hold a request thread indefinitely.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Compare them on four axes — uniqueness guarantee, sortability, size, and information leakage — because the choice is almost always driven by database write performance.

UUIDv4 is 128 bits of randomness. Globally unique with no coordination, but random ordering destroys B-tree insert locality: each insert lands in a random leaf page, so the index does not stay in cache, page splits multiply, and write throughput collapses on a large table. It is also 16 bytes (36 as text — never store it as text) versus 8 for a bigint, which inflates every secondary index that references it.

UUIDv7 and ULID fix exactly that by putting a millisecond timestamp in the high bits followed by randomness. They are still uncoordinated and globally unique, but time-ordered, so inserts append to the rightmost page and locality is restored. ULID adds a compact 26-character base32 text form. For most systems today this is the right default.

Snowflake packs timestamp, machine id and a per-millisecond sequence into 64 bits — compact, sortable, and very fast — but it requires coordinated machine ids and is clock-sensitive: NTP moving the clock backwards can produce duplicates, so implementations must refuse to issue ids until the clock catches up. Database sequences are simplest and smallest, but they serialize on one node and, being sequential, leak volume — a competitor can order two accounts and infer how many you created in between.

So: for a primary key, UUIDv7 (or a Snowflake-style id if you already have the infrastructure). Say the reason out loud — insert locality — because that is the answer that shows you have watched a table degrade rather than read a comparison table. And for anything user-facing, never expose a sequential id; use an opaque external identifier so resources are not enumerable.

Comparison
                 unique   sortable  size   coordination  leaks
UUIDv4           yes      NO        16B    none          no
UUIDv7 / ULID    yes      yes       16B    none          timestamp
Snowflake        yes      yes        8B    machine ids   timestamp + rate
DB sequence      yes      yes        8B    single node   volume  <- enumerable

primary key default -> UUIDv7 (locality + no coordination)
public-facing id    -> opaque, non-sequential, separate from the PK
Follow-ups they will ask

Why exactly does UUIDv4 hurt insert performance?

Every insert targets a random leaf page, so the working set of the index is the whole index rather than the right edge. Buffer cache hit rate collapses, page splits increase, and WAL volume grows. On a small table nobody notices; at a hundred million rows it is dramatic.

Does Postgres have a native UUIDv7?

Support has been arriving in recent versions and extensions; until it is available in your version, generate it in the application — which is fine, since the whole point is that it needs no coordination.

How do you handle clock skew in a Snowflake generator?

Detect that the clock moved backwards and either block until it passes the last issued timestamp or fail loudly. Silently continuing issues duplicate ids, which is far worse than a brief unavailability.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Three techniques carry most of the value. First, model state as a discriminated union rather than a bag of optional fields. { status: 'loading' } | { status: 'error', error: Error } | { status: 'success', data: T } makes illegal combinations — loading and errored, or success with no data — fail to compile. Narrowing on status then gives you data as non-optional inside the success branch, so the null checks disappear. Compare that with four booleans and an optional data field, which has sixteen states of which three are legal.

Second, generic components. A <Select<T>> whose options: T[], getLabel: (t: T) => string and onChange: (t: T) => void all share one parameter gives callers full inference — pass User[] and onChange receives a User, with no casts. Write it as a plain function component; React.FC cannot express generics, which is one of several reasons to avoid it.

Third, polymorphic components — a Button that can render as an a or a Link. Use an as prop constrained to ElementType and spread ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T> so the correct DOM props are accepted and typed. Use ComponentPropsWithoutRef rather than ComponentProps for wrappers unless you are forwarding a ref.

The common mistakes: React.FC (no generics, historically an implicit children, awkward with defaults); any in event handlers instead of React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>; optional props everywhere, which pushes runtime checks into every consumer; and typing props by hand when wrapping a DOM element instead of extending its props, which silently drops aria-*, data-* and every other valid attribute.

TypeScript
// discriminated union - illegal states do not compile
type State<T> =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'error'; error: Error }
  | { status: 'success'; data: T };

if (state.status === 'success') {
  state.data.name;          // data is non-optional here, no null check
}

// generic component - full inference at the call site
function Select<T>({ options, getLabel, onChange }: {
  options: T[];
  getLabel: (t: T) => string;
  onChange: (t: T) => void;
}) { /* ... */ }

// wrapping a DOM element - inherit every valid attribute
type ButtonProps = React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> & { variant?: 'primary' };
Follow-ups they will ask

Why avoid React.FC?

It cannot express generic components, it historically added an implicit children prop whether or not the component accepted them, and it complicates defaultProps. A plain function with a typed props parameter does everything it does and more.

How do you type a component that forwards a ref?

forwardRef<HTMLButtonElement, ButtonProps>, and use ComponentPropsWithRef for the prop type. Generic components plus forwardRef need a cast or a helper, which is a known rough edge in the type system.

Where does typing pay off most in a React codebase?

At the API boundary — generate types from OpenAPI or infer them from a Zod schema so server and client cannot drift. Hand-written response interfaces silently rot the moment the backend changes.

Quicksort that only recurses into the side containing the answer. Finds the k-th element without fully sorting.

CostO(n) average, O(n²) worst — randomise the pivotReach for itK-th largest/smallest when you need it once. O(n) beats the heap's O(n log k) if you can accept the worst case.
import random
def quickselect(a, k):            # k-th smallest, 0-indexed
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while True:
        p = random.randint(lo, hi)          # randomise: avoids O(n^2)
        a[p], a[hi] = a[hi], a[p]
        store = lo
        for i in range(lo, hi):
            if a[i] < a[hi]: a[i], a[store] = a[store], a[i]; store += 1
        a[store], a[hi] = a[hi], a[store]
        if   store == k: return a[store]
        elif store < k:  lo = store + 1
        else:            hi = store - 1

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Every Java object has an intrinsic lock (monitor). synchronized on an instance method locks this; on a static method it locks the Class object; a synchronized(obj) block locks whatever you name. Those are different locks — a common bug is assuming a static and an instance synchronized method exclude each other. They do not.

Intrinsic locks are reentrant: the owning thread can re-acquire the same lock, and the JVM keeps an ownership record plus a count. Without reentrancy, a synchronized method calling another synchronized method on the same object would deadlock against itself — so reentrancy is what makes composition possible at all.

What ReentrantLock adds: tryLock() to give up immediately, tryLock(timeout) — the standard deadlock escape — lockInterruptibly(), optional fairness, multiple Conditions on one lock (so a bounded queue can have separate notFull and notEmpty wait sets instead of notifyAll waking everyone), and the ability to acquire in one method and release in another. The cost is that you must unlock() in a finally — forget it and the lock leaks permanently.

Say the honest default: prefer synchronized. It is harder to misuse (no forgotten unlock), reads better, and performs comparably — the JVM optimizes uncontended locks heavily. Reach for ReentrantLock only when you need one of the capabilities above. Fairness in particular sounds attractive but enforces FIFO handoff and roughly halves throughput, so use it only when starvation is a measured problem.

Two practical rules: lock on a private final object, not on this or a public field — locking on this makes your lock part of your public API and any caller can interfere. And never lock on a String literal or a boxed Integer, because they are pooled and shared JVM-wide.

Java
class Counter {
    private final Object lock = new Object();      // private, not `this`
    private int count;
    void inc() { synchronized (lock) { count++; } }

    synchronized void a() { b(); }   // reentrant: b() re-acquires the same monitor
    synchronized void b() { }
}

// tryLock with a timeout: back off instead of blocking forever
if (lock.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
    try { doWork(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }   // finally is mandatory
} else {
    metrics.lockTimeout();
}
Follow-ups they will ask

What does synchronized give you besides mutual exclusion?

Visibility. Releasing a monitor flushes writes and acquiring it invalidates cached reads, establishing a happens-before edge. Mutual exclusion without that memory guarantee would be useless.

Why is a Condition better than wait/notify?

Multiple Conditions on one lock let you signal precisely — wake only the producers, or only the consumers. With a single monitor you must call notifyAll and wake every waiter to re-check its predicate, which is wasteful and can cause missed-signal bugs.

Is synchronized still a problem with virtual threads?

It used to pin the carrier thread if you blocked inside a synchronized block. Recent JDKs largely fixed that, but the safe pattern in code that blocks on IO is still ReentrantLock, which unmounts correctly.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A B-tree index is a balanced tree whose leaves hold sorted key values with pointers to rows. Lookups, range scans and ordered reads are all O(log n). That structure explains what it can and cannot accelerate: equality and range on a prefix of the key, and ordering — but not a function of the column (WHERE lower(email) = ? needs an expression index) and not a leading wildcard (LIKE '%foo').

Composite index column order is governed by the leftmost-prefix rule: an index on (a, b, c) serves queries filtering on a, a,b, or a,b,c — but not on b alone. So order columns by how they are queried: equality predicates first, then the range or sort column last. An index on (status, created_at) serves WHERE status = ? ORDER BY created_at perfectly; reversed, it does not.

Selectivity decides whether the index is used at all. A column where one value covers 60% of rows is a poor leading column — the planner will correctly prefer a sequential scan, because random-access lookups for most of the table cost more than reading it in order. That is why an index on a boolean flag usually does nothing, and why a partial index (WHERE status = 'pending') is often the right answer for a skewed column.

A covering index includes every column the query needs, so the database answers from the index alone — an index-only scan — and never touches the heap. Adding one or two payload columns via INCLUDE can turn a two-step lookup into a single read.

Diagnosis, in order: capture the actual slow statement (pg_stat_statements, or the APM trace), run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), and compare estimated versus actual rows — a large divergence means stale statistics, so ANALYZE first. Look for sequential scans on large tables, nested loops with high row counts, and sorts spilling to disk. Only then consider an index — and remember every index costs write throughput and storage, so check whether an existing one can be extended instead of adding a new one. This is your 30–40% claim; be ready to name the tool and the before/after numbers.

Diagnosis
-- 1. find it
SELECT query, mean_exec_time, calls FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC;

-- 2. explain it (ANALYZE actually runs it)
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ... ;
--    rows=12 (estimated)  vs  actual rows=48000   <- stale stats, run ANALYZE
--    Seq Scan on orders                            <- missing or unusable index
--    Sort ... external merge Disk: 42MB            <- raise work_mem or add an index

-- 3. composite order follows the query, not intuition
CREATE INDEX ON orders (status, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (total);  -- covering
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does adding an index sometimes make things slower?

Every write must update every index, so write throughput and WAL volume grow. A table with a dozen indexes can be write-bound. Indexes also compete for buffer cache, so a rarely-used index can evict pages a hot one needs.

When is a partial index the better answer?

When queries always filter on a skewed predicate — a pending-jobs queue where 99% of rows are complete. The partial index is a fraction of the size, stays in cache, and costs writes only for the rows that match.

What does a high buffers-read versus buffers-hit ratio tell you?

That the query is going to disk rather than the cache — either the working set exceeds shared_buffers, or the access pattern is random (the UUIDv4 problem). It distinguishes 'needs an index' from 'needs more memory or better locality'.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Give the rule as a ladder and climb it only when forced: colocate by default; lift to the lowest common ancestor when two siblings need it; use context for low-frequency values needed widely; use an external store for high-frequency or cross-tree state.

Colocate means the state lives in the component that uses it. This is the default because it keeps re-renders scoped, makes the component self-contained and testable, and means deleting the component deletes its state. Most state should never move.

Lift when two components must agree — a filter input and the list it filters. Move it to their nearest common parent and pass down. The cost is that the parent now re-renders on every change, so keep the lift as low as possible and consider whether the parent can be split so the expensive subtree does not re-render.

Context is for values that are needed almost everywhere and change rarely: theme, locale, the authenticated user, a service client. It is a dependency-injection mechanism, not a state manager. Any context update re-renders every consumer and bypasses React.memo, so high-frequency state in context is the classic cause of an app that re-renders on every keystroke.

External store (Zustand, Redux, or a module store via useSyncExternalStore) when state is high-frequency, needed by distant parts of the tree, or must be readable from non-component code. Its advantage is selector granularity: a component subscribes to a slice and re-renders only when that slice changes.

Then the costs of getting it wrong, in both directions — this is the part that answers the question fully. Too high: unnecessary re-renders across a large subtree, prop drilling through components that do not care, and a parent that becomes a god component. Too low: two sources of truth that drift out of sync, state lost when a component unmounts (a filter resetting on tab switch), and logic duplicated in siblings. Also separate server state from client state — cached server data belongs in a query library with staleness and invalidation, not in a store you hand-synchronise.

Decision ladder
one component uses it            -> useState in that component
two siblings need it             -> lift to the lowest common ancestor
needed everywhere, changes rarely-> context (theme, auth, locale)
high-frequency or cross-tree     -> external store with selectors
cached server data               -> TanStack Query, not a store
URL-shareable (filters, tab, page)-> the URL itself (search params)
Follow-ups they will ask

What state belongs in the URL?

Anything a user should be able to bookmark, share or restore with the back button — the current tab, filters, sort, page, an open detail id. Putting it in component state instead is a subtle bug people report as 'refresh loses my place'.

How do you decide between context and a store?

Update frequency and granularity. If every consumer genuinely needs every change, context is fine and simpler. If consumers need different slices and updates are frequent, a store with selectors avoids the broad re-render.

What is the sign that state was lifted too high?

A parent that re-renders on every keystroke somewhere deep in the tree, or a component whose only job is holding state for children it does not otherwise use. Profile it — if a large subtree re-renders for an unrelated change, the state is in the wrong place.

Linked List III
  • Add Two NumbersMedium
  • Find the Duplicate NumberMedium
  • LRU CacheMedium

When values live in a small known range, count occurrences into buckets and read them back in order. No comparisons at all.

CostO(n + k) time, O(k) spaceReach for itSorting small integers, top-K by frequency in linear time, and 'sort colours' style problems.
def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    from collections import Counter
    cnt = Counter(nums)
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]   # index = frequency
    for v, f in cnt.items(): buckets[f].append(v)
    out = []
    for f in range(len(buckets) - 1, 0, -1):
        out.extend(buckets[f])
        if len(out) >= k: return out[:k]

# O(n) - no sort, because frequency is bounded by n.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The Java Memory Model defines when a write by one thread is guaranteed visible to a read by another. Without it, the compiler, the JIT and the CPU are all free to reorder and cache — and they do. The JMM is not about locks; it is about which reorderings are legal.

The central relation is happens-before: if A happens-before B, A's effects are visible to B. The edges to be able to list: program order within a single thread; monitor unlock → subsequent lock of the same monitor; volatile write → subsequent volatile read of the same field; Thread.start() → everything in that thread; everything in a thread → another thread's successful join(); and the final-field freeze at the end of a constructor → publication of the reference.

Say the thing most candidates miss: without an edge there is no guarantee at all — not "eventually", not "probably within a few milliseconds". A loop reading a non-volatile flag can be hoisted out by the JIT and spin forever. And this is why "it works on my machine" is meaningless for concurrency: x86 has strong ordering and hides bugs that appear immediately on ARM.

volatile gives two things: visibility (the write is pushed out, the read is not served from a cached copy) and ordering (no reordering across the access), which together create that happens-before edge. What it does not give is atomicity of compound operations. i++ is read-modify-write — three steps — so two threads can both read 5, both write 6, and one increment vanishes. volatile makes each individual read and write visible; it does nothing about the gap between them.

So: volatile for a flag or a reference written by one thread and read by others — a shutdown signal, a swapped-in configuration object, the instance field in double-checked locking. For counters use AtomicInteger or LongAdder; for multiple fields that must move together, use a lock.

Java
// broken: no happens-before edge, may never terminate
boolean running = true;
// thread A: while (running) { }      // JIT can hoist the read out of the loop
// thread B: running = false;

volatile boolean running = true;      // fixed - establishes the edge

volatile int count;
count++;                              // STILL a race - not atomic
new AtomicInteger().incrementAndGet();// correct

// a volatile write also publishes everything written before it
config = newConfig;                   // readers see a fully-initialised newConfig
Follow-ups they will ask

Does happens-before mean 'happens earlier in time'?

No. It is a visibility and ordering guarantee, not a timing one. Two actions ordered by happens-before may execute microseconds apart, and unordered actions may happen to be visible — you simply cannot rely on it.

Why must the field in double-checked locking be volatile?

instance = new Registry() is allocate, construct, assign — and the JIT may reorder the assignment before construction completes. Another thread then sees a non-null reference to a half-built object. volatile forbids that reordering.

Is volatile cheaper than synchronized?

A volatile read is nearly free; a volatile write costs a memory fence. Cheaper than locking, but it only solves visibility — using it where you need atomicity is the classic wrong optimization.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Reading a plan: EXPLAIN shows the planner's intent, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) actually runs it and shows reality. Read it inside-out — the innermost nodes execute first. The single most valuable check is estimated versus actual rows: a large divergence means the planner is working from bad statistics, and every downstream join choice is then wrong. Fix the statistics before touching indexes. Then look for sequential scans on large tables, nested loops driving many iterations, sorts spilling to disk, and a poor buffers-hit ratio.

N+1 is one query for the parents followed by one query per parent for a lazy association — 200 orders becomes 201 round trips, each paying network latency. It passes tests with ten rows and dies in production. Diagnose by counting queries, not by inspection: hibernate.generate_statistics, or a datasource proxy asserting query counts in tests. Fix with a JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph for that query, a DTO projection selecting only what you need, or @BatchSize to collapse N queries into N/batch IN queries. Do not fix it by setting the mapping to EAGER — that makes every query everywhere load the association.

Pagination at page 10,000 is the sharpest part. OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 10 still scans and discards 100,000 rows — cost grows linearly with page depth — and it is unstable: if a row is inserted or deleted while the user pages, rows shift and they see duplicates or skips.

Keyset (cursor) pagination fixes both. Carry the sort key of the last row seen and use a row-value comparison: WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 10. With a matching index it seeks directly to the position — O(1) per page regardless of depth — and it is stable under concurrent writes. Include a unique tie-breaker (the id) or rows with equal timestamps are skipped or repeated. The tradeoff to state: no random access to "page 5000" and no total count, which is why UIs that use it show infinite scroll or next/previous rather than numbered pages.

SQL
-- offset: scans and throws away 100k rows, and shifts under concurrent writes
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 10;

-- keyset: seeks straight to the position, stable, O(1) per page
SELECT * FROM orders
 WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id)
 ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
 LIMIT 10;
-- index: (created_at DESC, id DESC)

-- N+1 fix for one use case, without changing the mapping
@Query("select distinct o from Order o join fetch o.lines where o.status = :s")
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does keyset pagination need a unique tie-breaker?

Because created_at is not unique. Without the id in the comparison, rows sharing a timestamp straddle the page boundary and get skipped or duplicated — a bug that only appears with real data.

How do you show a total count with keyset pagination?

You usually do not — an exact count on a large filtered table is itself a full scan. Show an approximate count from statistics, a capped count ('1000+'), or drop it. That is a product conversation, and worth raising as one.

What if the user must jump to an arbitrary page?

Then you need offset, and you bound the damage: cap the maximum page, or precompute page boundaries. Most products that thought they needed deep random access actually needed search and filters instead.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

First make the distinction that reframes the question: server state and client state are different problems. Server state is a cache of something you do not own — it can be stale, needs invalidation, refetching, deduplication and retry. Client state is owned by the UI — a selected tab, an open modal, a draft form. Trying to hold server state in Redux is why so many apps have thousands of lines of loading-flag reducers.

So: server state → TanStack Query or SWR. They give caching by key, staleness, background refetch, deduplication, retries and optimistic updates out of the box. Client state → the smallest thing that works.

Context + useReducer when the state is small, changes rarely, and is needed widely — theme, auth, feature flags. It has no dependency and no selector granularity, so every consumer re-renders on any change. That is fine at low frequency and disastrous at high frequency.

Zustand when you want a store without ceremony: a hook-based API, selector subscriptions so components re-render only for their slice, usable outside React, and a few lines of setup. This is the pragmatic default for most apps today.

Redux Toolkit when you need what it uniquely offers: strict, traceable, serialisable actions with time-travel debugging; complex cross-cutting logic; a large team needing enforced conventions; or middleware for sagas and listeners. It is more boilerplate, and RTK removed most of the historical pain.

Normalization means storing entities by id in a flat map — { users: { byId: {...}, allIds: [...] } } — and referencing them by id elsewhere, exactly like database rows. It exists to guarantee one source of truth per entity: without it, the same user embedded in a list, a detail view and a comment thread must be updated in three places and will drift. It also keeps updates O(1) instead of mapping over nested arrays. The cost is that reads need selectors to denormalise — and note that a query library largely removes the need for it, because the cache is already keyed by query.

JSX
// server state
const { data, isPending, error } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['orders', { page, status }],      // key encodes every input
  queryFn: () => fetchOrders({ page, status }),
  staleTime: 30_000,
});

// client state with selector granularity
const useUi = create(set => ({
  sidebarOpen: false,
  toggle: () => set(s => ({ sidebarOpen: !s.sidebarOpen })),
}));
const open = useUi(s => s.sidebarOpen);   // re-renders only when this slice changes

// normalized shape - one source of truth per entity
{ users: { byId: { u1: {...}, u2: {...} }, allIds: ['u1','u2'] } }
Follow-ups they will ask

Is Redux dead?

No — it is just no longer the default. RTK is a good fit for large apps with complex client-side logic and teams that benefit from enforced structure. It became the wrong tool mainly because people used it to cache server data.

What is the cost of normalization?

Every read needs a selector to reassemble the entity graph, and those selectors must be memoized or you recompute on every render. For small or read-mostly data it is more machinery than it is worth.

How do you avoid duplicating server data into a client store?

Do not copy it — read it from the query cache and store only the client-side additions (selection, draft edits) separately, keyed by entity id. Copying is what creates the sync bug you were trying to avoid.

  • Merge k Sorted ListsHard

Three pointers partition an array into three regions in a single pass. The generalisation of quicksort's partition step.

CostO(n) time, O(1) spaceReach for itSort an array of 0/1/2, move zeroes, partition around a pivot — anything with three categories and one pass.
def sort_colors(a):
    lo, mid, hi = 0, 0, len(a) - 1
    while mid <= hi:
        if   a[mid] == 0: a[lo], a[mid] = a[mid], a[lo]; lo += 1; mid += 1
        elif a[mid] == 1: mid += 1
        else:             a[mid], a[hi] = a[hi], a[mid]; hi -= 1
        # note: no mid++ on the last branch - the swapped-in value is unseen

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Name the six parameters and then the counter-intuitive part, because that is what is being tested. A ThreadPoolExecutor takes corePoolSize, maximumPoolSize, keepAliveTime, the work queue, a thread factory and a rejection policy.

The submission algorithm: if fewer than core threads exist, create one. Otherwise try to queue. Only if the queue is full do you create threads up to maximum. If the queue is full and maximum is reached, reject. The consequence is the trap: with an unbounded queue the queue never fills, so maximumPoolSize is never reached — the pool silently stays at core size while the queue grows until you OOM. That is exactly what Executors.newFixedThreadPool and newSingleThreadExecutor do, which is why the advice is to construct ThreadPoolExecutor directly.

Queue choice encodes the policy: ArrayBlockingQueue (bounded, predictable memory), LinkedBlockingQueue (bounded it if you value your heap), SynchronousQueue (capacity zero — every task needs a free thread immediately, which is how newCachedThreadPool grows without limit). Rejection policies: AbortPolicy throws (the default, and usually correct — it is a visible signal); CallerRunsPolicy executes the task on the submitting thread, which is elegant backpressure because it slows the producer; DiscardPolicy and DiscardOldestPolicy lose work silently and are rarely right.

Sizing: CPU-bound ≈ cores (+1 to cover an occasional stall). IO-bound ≈ cores × (1 + wait/service). But say the systems-level point: the pool is not the only limit — 200 threads in front of a 20-connection database pool just moves the queue. Size the whole chain together.

CompletableFuture composes async steps: thenApply transforms, thenCompose flattens a nested future (the async flatMap), thenCombine joins two, allOf fans in. Two rules: always pass an explicit executor, because the no-arg async methods use the shared common ForkJoinPool where one blocking call starves the whole JVM; and always terminate the chain with an exception handler, because a failed future nobody joins swallows the exception silently.

Java
ExecutorService pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        8, 16, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000),                    // BOUNDED
        new ThreadFactoryBuilder().setNameFormat("orders-%d").build(),
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());        // backpressure

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> client.fetch(id), pool)   // explicit executor
        .thenCompose(u -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> prefs(u), pool))
        .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
        .exceptionally(ex -> { log.warn("degraded", ex); return Profile.empty(); });

pool.shutdown();
if (!pool.awaitTermination(30, SECONDS)) pool.shutdownNow();
Follow-ups they will ask

Why name your threads?

Because a thread dump with 200 threads called pool-3-thread-17 is unreadable. Named pools turn a production stack dump into an immediate diagnosis of which subsystem is stuck.

Should every task type share one pool?

No. Separate pools per dependency is the bulkhead pattern — a slow payment provider then cannot exhaust the threads your health check needs. One shared pool means one slow dependency takes down everything.

thenApply or thenCompose?

thenApply with a function returning a future gives you a nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>. thenCompose flattens it — the same relationship as map versus flatMap.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Leader-follower: all writes go to one leader, which streams its change log to followers that serve reads. It scales reads, provides failover candidates, and keeps a single writer so there are no write conflicts.

Synchronous replication acknowledges the write only after a follower has it — no data loss on leader failure, but write latency now includes the slowest follower, and if that follower stalls, writes stall. Asynchronous acknowledges immediately — fast, but a leader crash loses anything not yet shipped. Semi-synchronous is the usual production compromise: one follower synchronous (bounding data loss), the rest asynchronous. That is the answer to give, with the reasoning.

Replication lag is the gap between leader and follower. Three ways it breaks users, each worth naming with its symptom. Read-your-writes: a user posts a comment, the next read hits a lagging replica, and their own comment is missing — they assume it failed and post again. Monotonic reads: two consecutive reads hit replicas with different lag and time appears to move backwards — a counter decreases, a message disappears and reappears. Consistent prefix: with partitioned replication a reply arrives before the message it answers, so a conversation reads out of order.

The fixes: route a user's reads to the leader for a few seconds after they write; pin a session to one replica (fixes monotonic reads, not read-your-writes); or pass a version/LSN token the replica must have caught up to before serving — the most precise and the one that scales.

Failover is where the real risk lives. Promoting a follower with asynchronous replication loses the un-shipped writes, and if the old leader returns without knowing it was demoted you get split-brain — two leaders accepting conflicting writes. The defence is a consensus-based election plus fencing tokens: a monotonically increasing epoch number that storage checks, so the deposed leader's writes are rejected. Monitor lag as a first-class metric; it is the leading indicator for every symptom above.

Lag mitigations
read-your-writes  -> route reads to leader for N seconds after a write
                     or send an LSN token: WHERE replica_lsn >= :token
monotonic reads   -> pin the session to one replica (sticky by user hash)
consistent prefix -> keep causally related writes in one partition

failover          -> consensus election + fencing token (epoch)
                     async replication => accept a bounded RPO, and say what it is
Follow-ups they will ask

How much data can you lose in an async failover?

Exactly the replication lag at the moment of failure — which is why lag is not just a performance metric, it is your RPO. If lag is 5 seconds, your recovery point objective is 5 seconds of writes.

Why does sticky routing not give read-your-writes?

Because the replica you are pinned to may still be behind the leader. Sticky routing guarantees you see a consistent, non-regressing view, not that you see your own latest write.

When do read replicas not help?

When the load is write-heavy (replicas do the same writes), when queries need the very latest data, or when the problem is a slow query rather than volume — a bad query is equally slow on a replica.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Explain the mental model, not the API. TanStack Query is a cache keyed by query key, with each entry moving through states, plus a subscription mechanism so components using the same key share one entry and one in-flight request.

The query key is the identity. It must encode every input the request depends on — page, filters, sort, id. Get that right and caching, deduplication and refetching are automatic: two components asking for ['orders', {page:2}] trigger one request and share the result; changing a filter is simply a different key, and the previous entry stays cached.

staleTime versus gcTime is the distinction people get wrong. staleTime is how long the data is considered fresh — while fresh, remounting a component triggers no refetch. After it, the data is stale but still shown, and a refetch happens in the background on mount, window focus or reconnect. gcTime is how long an unused entry stays in memory before eviction. Default staleTime is 0, which is why beginners see a request on every mount and assume caching is broken.

Invalidation versus setQueryData. After a mutation, invalidateQueries marks matching entries stale so they refetch — correct and simple, at the cost of a round trip. setQueryData writes the server's response straight into the cache for an instant update with no refetch, which is what you use for optimistic updates and for putting a list item's detail into its own key.

For a paginated, filtered table: put page, filters and sort in the key, and use placeholderData: keepPreviousData so the old page stays on screen while the next loads — no spinner flash, no layout collapse. Prefetch page n+1 on hover or idle. And keep the filter state in the URL, so the query key derives from the URL and the view is shareable and back-button correct.

JSX
const { data, isPending, isPlaceholderData } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['orders', { page, status, sort }],   // every input is in the key
  queryFn: () => fetchOrders({ page, status, sort }),
  staleTime: 30_000,                              // fresh for 30s: no refetch on mount
  placeholderData: keepPreviousData,              // no spinner flash between pages
});

// prefetch the next page while the user reads this one
queryClient.prefetchQuery({ queryKey: ['orders', { page: page + 1, status, sort }],
                           queryFn: ... });

// after a mutation
queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] });   // refetch everything matching
queryClient.setQueryData(['order', id], updated);          // instant, no round trip
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does it refetch on window focus by default?

Because data you fetched before the user switched tabs is probably stale by the time they come back. It is a sensible default for dashboards and a bad one for expensive queries — turn it off per query rather than globally.

How do you handle a dependent query?

enabled: !!userId so it does not run until the input exists. That is also how you avoid the waterfall of firing a request with an undefined parameter and getting a 400.

What does optimistic update look like here?

onMutate cancels in-flight queries, snapshots the current cache, applies the optimistic value with setQueryData; onError restores the snapshot; onSettled invalidates so the server's truth wins. The snapshot-and-rollback is the part people forget.

Heaps I
  • Kth Largest Element in a StreamEasy
  • Last Stone WeightEasy
  • K Closest Points to OriginMedium

Three orders from the same recursion, differing only in when you visit the node: before, between, or after its children.

CostO(n) time, O(h) space for the call stackReach for itPreorder to copy or serialise, inorder to get a BST in sorted order, postorder to compute something from children first.
def inorder(node, out):
    if not node: return
    inorder(node.left, out)
    out.append(node.val)          # BST -> sorted order
    inorder(node.right, out)

# Iterative inorder, when recursion depth is a risk
def inorder_it(root):
    st, cur, out = [], root, []
    while st or cur:
        while cur: st.append(cur); cur = cur.left
        cur = st.pop(); out.append(cur.val); cur = cur.right
    return out
