Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Deadlock requires four conditions simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break any one and it cannot happen — that framing is what turns "add a timeout" into a reasoned answer.

The classic two-lock deadlock is a bank transfer: transfer(a, b) locks a then b, while a concurrent transfer(b, a) locks b then a. Each holds one and waits for the other, forever.

Fix 1 — global lock ordering (breaks circular wait). Always acquire in a consistent order, derived from something stable like the account id. This is the best fix because it eliminates the possibility rather than recovering from it. Handle the equal-id case with System.identityHashCode, and if those collide too, take a third tie-breaker lock first — the standard three-step scheme.

Fix 2 — tryLock with timeout and backoff (breaks hold-and-wait). Attempt both locks; if the second fails, release the first, wait a randomized interval, and retry. Correct, but it converts a hang into livelock risk if the backoff is not randomized, and it needs a bounded retry count.

Fix 3 — remove the need for two locks. Often the best answer in a design discussion: use a single lock over the whole transfer path if contention allows, or push the invariant into the database with a transaction and a consistent update order so the database's deadlock detector handles it — Postgres detects deadlocks and kills one transaction with a clear error.

Detection in production: jstack <pid> or jcmd <pid> Thread.print prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" with both stacks and the lock identities — it is genuinely that explicit. Programmatically, ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() can back a health check. The symptom that leads you there is threads in BLOCKED state that never move across three dumps taken seconds apart, with flat CPU.

Java
// deadlocks when called as transfer(x,y) and transfer(y,x) concurrently
void transfer(Account a, Account b, long amt) {
    synchronized (a) { synchronized (b) { a.debit(amt); b.credit(amt); } }
}

// fix 1: global ordering by id - eliminates circular wait
void transfer(Account a, Account b, long amt) {
    Account first  = a.id() < b.id() ? a : b;
    Account second = a.id() < b.id() ? b : a;
    synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { a.debit(amt); b.credit(amt); } }
}

// fix 2: tryLock with randomized backoff - breaks hold-and-wait
while (true) {
    if (a.lock.tryLock(50, MILLISECONDS)) {
        try { if (b.lock.tryLock(50, MILLISECONDS)) { try { move(); return; }
              finally { b.lock.unlock(); } } }
        finally { a.lock.unlock(); }
    }
    Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(10, 50));   // randomized
}
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you prevent this by construction rather than by discipline?

Funnel every multi-lock acquisition through one helper that sorts the locks before acquiring. Then correctness is a property of one reviewed function rather than of every call site.

What is livelock and how does it differ?

Threads are actively running and responding to each other but making no progress — two retry loops that keep colliding. CPU is high, unlike deadlock where it is flat. Randomized backoff is the standard cure.

What is the general rule that avoids most of this?

Never call foreign or blocking code while holding a lock, and keep lock scopes as small as possible. Most real deadlocks involve a lock held across a call into code the author did not control.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start with why: 5 TB exceeds what one node serves comfortably — the working set no longer fits in memory, index maintenance and vacuum get expensive, and backup and restore times become an availability problem. Before sharding, say what you would try first: archiving cold data to object storage, partitioning by time within one instance, and read replicas. Sharding is the last resort because it costs you cross-shard joins and transactions permanently.

Shard key is the whole design. For a transactions table the natural key is account_id, because the dominant access pattern is "all transactions for this account", which then stays on one shard — a single-shard read, and single-shard transactions for anything that must be atomic per account. Sharding by transaction_id would spread every account's history across every shard and make the common query a scatter-gather. Sharding by time is tempting for an append-only table but creates a hotspot: all writes go to the newest shard while the rest sit idle.

Strategies: range is simple and supports range scans but produces hotspots on skewed keys; hash distributes evenly but destroys range queries; directory-based keeps an explicit lookup table, which is the most flexible and allows targeted rebalancing at the cost of one extra hop and a service to keep available.

Consistent hashing maps both keys and nodes onto a ring, so adding or removing a node remaps only about K/N keys rather than nearly all of them as modulo hashing would. Virtual nodes — many ring positions per physical node — fix the load imbalance that a small number of nodes produces and let you weight heterogeneous machines.

Resharding with zero downtime is a five-step migration, and naming the steps is the answer: dual-write to old and new; backfill historical data in batches; verify by comparing checksums or row counts; cut over reads behind a feature flag, one percentage at a time; then stop writing to the old and drop it. Keep the rollback available until the verification is clean. Finally, state what becomes expensive afterwards: cross-account transfers now span shards and need a saga or two-phase commit, aggregate reporting becomes scatter-gather, and unique constraints across shards must be enforced by a separate service.

Resharding
1. dual-write      app writes old + new (new is not read yet)
2. backfill        batch copy history, throttled, resumable, idempotent
3. verify          row counts + checksums per shard; reconcile drift
4. cut over reads  1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% behind a flag, watch error rate
5. stop old writes then drop  (keep rollback until step 4 is clean for days)
Follow-ups they will ask

What breaks once transactions span shards?

Atomicity. A transfer between accounts on different shards can no longer be one database transaction, so you need a saga with compensations or a two-phase commit — plus an intermediate 'pending' state that reporting must understand.

How do you handle a hot shard after sharding?

Split that key range further, add virtual nodes weighted for it, or introduce a key-splitting scheme for the single hot account. If one account genuinely dominates, it may need dedicated infrastructure.

Do you still need globally unique ids?

Yes, and they should not come from a per-shard sequence or you get collisions on rebalancing. Use UUIDv7 or a Snowflake-style generator so ids are unique and time-ordered independent of placement.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

An optimistic update applies the expected result immediately, before the server confirms, so the interaction feels instant. The whole design is about what happens when you were wrong.

The four-step shape, and you should name all four: cancel any in-flight refetch for the affected key (or it will land later and overwrite you); snapshot the current cache; apply the optimistic change; and on error roll back to the snapshot. Always finish with an invalidate on settle so the server's truth wins regardless of outcome. The snapshot-and-rollback is the part people forget, and without it a failure leaves the UI permanently lying.

A like button is the easy case: the state is a boolean plus a count, the operation is idempotent, and rollback is trivial. A reorderable list is harder — the optimistic state is an entire array order, and the server may reject only part of the change or return a different canonical order. Snapshot the whole list, apply the reorder locally, and on success reconcile with the server's returned order rather than assuming yours was accepted.

The correctness hazards, which is the real question. Concurrent mutations to the same entity: two rapid likes produce two in-flight requests, and the second response may arrive first — mitigate by keying mutations per entity and letting the last one win, or by disabling the control while in flight. The server returns something different from your guess (a computed total, a server-side clamp), so always reconcile with the response rather than keeping your optimistic value. Rollback after the user has moved on — reverting a change three seconds later is confusing, so pair it with a toast explaining what happened. And never use optimistic updates where being wrong is expensive: showing a payment as succeeded before the gateway confirms is not a UX improvement, it is a lie.

JSX
useMutation({
  mutationFn: toggleLike,
  onMutate: async (postId) => {
    await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['post', postId] });   // 1. cancel
    const previous = queryClient.getQueryData(['post', postId]);       // 2. snapshot
    queryClient.setQueryData(['post', postId], p => ({                 // 3. apply
      ...p, liked: !p.liked, likes: p.likes + (p.liked ? -1 : 1),
    }));
    return { previous };
  },
  onError: (err, postId, ctx) =>                                        // 4. roll back
    queryClient.setQueryData(['post', postId], ctx.previous),
  onSettled: (data, err, postId) =>
    queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['post', postId] }),      // server wins
});
Follow-ups they will ask

Why cancel in-flight queries in onMutate?

A refetch started before your optimistic write can resolve after it and overwrite your optimistic state with stale server data — the UI flickers back to the old value and then forward again. Cancelling removes that race.

When should you not be optimistic?

When the operation can fail for reasons the user cannot predict, when the consequence of showing a false success is serious (payments, deletions, permissions), or when the server computes something you cannot guess. Show a pending state instead.

How do you handle rapid repeated clicks?

Either disable the control while a mutation is in flight, or debounce to a single request representing the final state. Firing one request per click and hoping responses arrive in order is the bug.

Heaps II

  • Task SchedulerMedium
  • Design TwitterMedium

A queue visits the tree level by level. Process the whole level at once by reading the queue's length before the loop.

CostO(n) time, O(w) space where w is the widest levelReach for itLevel order output, minimum depth, right-side view, zigzag, and 'nearest' questions in general.
from collections import deque
def level_order(root):
    if not root: return []
    q, out = deque([root]), []
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):        # snapshot the level size FIRST
            node = q.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:  q.append(node.left)
            if node.right: q.append(node.right)
        out.append(level)
    return out

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Compare-and-swap is a single CPU instruction: "if this memory location still holds the value I expect, replace it — atomically". AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet is a loop around it: read the current value, compute the new one, CAS; if the CAS fails because someone else won the race, read again and retry.

That is optimistic concurrency: no locking, no context switch, no scheduler involvement. It wins at low-to-moderate contention. Under heavy contention it loses — threads spin, burning CPU while making no progress, and a lock that parks the thread can actually be faster. Say that tradeoff; "lock-free is always faster" is the wrong answer. Note also that a CAS loop is lock-free but not wait-free: the system always progresses, but an individual thread can starve by losing every race.

The general form is updateAndGet(fn), and it carries a rule people miss: the function may be invoked multiple times if the CAS keeps failing, so it must be pure and free of side effects.

The ABA problem: a CAS checks the value, not the history. If another thread changes A→B→A, your CAS succeeds even though the world changed underneath. It rarely matters for counters, but it breaks lock-free stacks and queues where a node was popped, freed and recycled at the same address. The fix is AtomicStampedReference, which pairs the value with a version counter so you compare both.

LongAdder versus AtomicLong: under heavy write contention every thread CASes the same word, so cache lines ping-pong between cores and most attempts fail. LongAdder stripes — a base value plus per-thread cells — so writes rarely collide; sum() then adds the cells, which makes reads more expensive and non-atomic. So: LongAdder for write-heavy, read-rare counters (metrics); AtomicLong when you read often or need an exact instantaneous value (a sequence generator). Underneath both is false sharing — unrelated variables on the same 64-byte cache line invalidating each other — which is what LongAdder's padded cells and @Contended exist to avoid.

Java
// CAS loop, conceptually
int current;
do { current = value.get(); } while (!value.compareAndSet(current, current + 1));

// the function may run more than once - keep it pure
AtomicReference<Config> ref = new AtomicReference<>(initial);
ref.updateAndGet(c -> c.withRetries(c.retries() + 1));

// ABA-safe
AtomicStampedReference<Node> head = new AtomicStampedReference<>(n, 0);
int[] stamp = new int[1];
Node cur = head.get(stamp);
head.compareAndSet(cur, next, stamp[0], stamp[0] + 1);

LongAdder requests = new LongAdder();   // write-heavy metric
requests.increment();  long total = requests.sum();
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is LongAdder.sum() not exact under concurrency?

It walks the cells without locking, so updates during the walk may or may not be included. That is eventually consistent, which is exactly right for metrics and exactly wrong for a sequence generator.

What is false sharing, concretely?

Two variables written by different cores land in the same cache line. Each write invalidates the other core's copy, so the line bounces between caches even though the variables are unrelated. Padding them a cache line apart removes it.

When would you implement a lock-free structure yourself?

Almost never. Getting the memory ordering and ABA handling right is genuinely hard, and the JDK already provides the useful ones. The value of understanding CAS is diagnosing contention, not hand-rolling a queue.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (the transaction moves the database between valid states, enforcing constraints), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere in ways that break correctness), Durability (committed means survives a crash, via the write-ahead log).

Isolation levels are best explained by the anomaly each one prevents. Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads — seeing another transaction's uncommitted data. Read Committed prevents dirty reads; still allows non-repeatable reads, where the same row read twice differs because another transaction committed in between. Repeatable Read prevents that; classically still allows phantoms, where a range query returns new rows on re-execution. Serializable prevents all of them and behaves as if transactions ran one at a time.

Then the two anomalies not in the textbook list, which is where the interesting discussion is. Lost update: two transactions read a balance of 100, each adds 50, and one write vanishes — read-modify-write in application code is the cause, and the fix is SELECT FOR UPDATE, an atomic UPDATE ... SET x = x + 50, or optimistic locking with a version column. Write skew: two transactions each read a set, each verify an invariant, and each write something that individually looks fine but together violates it — two doctors both going off-call because each sees the other still on. Snapshot isolation does not prevent write skew; only Serializable or explicit locking does.

MVCC is how Postgres implements this without readers blocking writers: an UPDATE writes a new row version rather than modifying in place, each version tagged with the transaction that created and deleted it, and every transaction sees a snapshot consistent with its start. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers.

The operational consequence to volunteer: because old versions must survive while any transaction might still need them, a long-running transaction prevents vacuum from reclaiming dead tuples, causing table and index bloat that persists long after the transaction ends. That is why "never hold a transaction open across a remote call or user think-time" is a hard rule, not a style preference. Postgres defaults to Read Committed, so write skew is possible by default — which most teams never realise.

Anomalies
level             dirty  non-repeat  phantom  lost-update  write-skew
Read Uncommitted   yes      yes        yes       yes          yes
Read Committed     no       yes        yes       yes*         yes    <- PG default
Repeatable Read    no       no         yes**     no           yes
Serializable       no       no         no        no           no

* prevented by SELECT FOR UPDATE / atomic UPDATE / @Version
** Postgres's Repeatable Read (snapshot isolation) does prevent phantoms
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is Serializable not the default?

Cost. Postgres implements it with Serializable Snapshot Isolation, which detects conflicts and aborts transactions — so the application must handle serialization failures and retry. Most workloads do not need it, and paying for it everywhere is wasteful.

How do you prevent a lost update in practice?

Make the update atomic in SQL (SET balance = balance - :amt WHERE balance >= :amt) so the read and write happen in one statement, or use optimistic locking with a version column and retry on conflict. Never read into the application, compute, and write back without one of those.

What does 'Consistency' in ACID actually mean?

Only that the database enforces its declared constraints — foreign keys, unique, check. It is the application's job to define what a valid state is. It is the least interesting letter and often the one people over-explain.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design the wizard around four concerns: where step state lives, how validation spans steps, how autosave works, and how the user resumes. Naming them first is what makes this sound designed rather than improvised.

Step state belongs in the URL, not in component state — /apply/step/3 or ?step=3. That makes refresh, the back button, deep links and analytics all work for free. Holding the step in useState is the single most common wizard bug: the browser back button leaves the wizard entirely instead of going back one step, which users experience as losing their work.

Form data lives in one place above the steps — a reducer or a form library's context — so a value entered in step 1 is still there when the user returns to it. Validate with a schema per step (Zod), composed from one master schema shared with the backend so rules cannot drift. Cross-step validation — a value in step 4 that must be consistent with step 2 — is why you validate the composed schema on final submit as well as validating each step on advance. Do not block the user mid-wizard on a rule they cannot yet satisfy; surface it when they reach the step that owns it, and show a summary of all outstanding errors before submit.

Autosave should target a real server-side draft resource: PATCH /applications/{id}, debounced to roughly a second after typing stops, plus an immediate save on step advance and on visibilitychange (users close tabs, and beforeunload is unreliable on mobile). Send only the changed fields. Track and display a save state — saving, saved, failed — because a silent autosave failure means the user believes their work is safe when it is not. Carry an ETag or version so a second tab cannot silently clobber the first, returning 412 on conflict.

Resumability then falls out: the draft id lives in the URL, the server holds the data, and returning users are dropped at the furthest completed step. Keep an IndexedDB copy as an offline fallback for flaky connections, and reconcile on reconnect. Finally, make the whole thing a state machine — the set of legal transitions between steps, with guards, is exactly what a machine expresses and exactly what a pile of booleans gets wrong.

JSX
// step lives in the URL - back button and refresh just work
const { step } = useParams();
const schema = stepSchemas[step];

const methods = useForm({
  resolver: zodResolver(schema),
  defaultValues: draft,          // loaded from the server draft
  mode: 'onBlur',
});

// debounced autosave with conflict detection
const save = useDebouncedCallback(async values => {
  setSaveState('saving');
  try {
    const res = await patchDraft(id, values, { headers: { 'If-Match': etag } });
    setEtag(res.etag); setSaveState('saved');
  } catch (e) {
    setSaveState(e.status === 412 ? 'conflict' : 'failed');   // never fail silently
  }
}, 1000);

useEffect(() => {
  const onHide = () => { if (document.visibilityState === 'hidden') save.flush(); };
  document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', onHide);
  return () => document.removeEventListener('visibilitychange', onHide);
}, [save]);
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is beforeunload unreliable for the final save?

Mobile browsers frequently do not fire it when an app is backgrounded or killed, and it cannot await an async request. Use visibilitychange plus navigator.sendBeacon or a keepalive fetch, which survive the page going away.

How do you let the user jump back to an earlier step safely?

Allow backward navigation freely — the data is already validated — but guard forward jumps behind the completion of intervening steps. That guard is exactly what a state machine's transition table encodes.

What happens if the schema changes while a user has a half-finished draft?

Version the draft. On load, if the stored version is older, migrate it or drop the fields that no longer exist rather than crashing on validation. Long-lived drafts outlast deploys, and that is a real production case.

Heaps III - two heaps
  • Top K Frequent WordsMedium
  • Find Median from Data StreamHard

Return a value from each subtree on the way back up, and combine it at the parent. Most tree problems are this shape.

CostO(n) time, O(h) spaceReach for itHeight, diameter, balanced check, max path sum. The trick is returning one thing while updating a global answer with another.
def diameter(root):
    best = 0
    def depth(node):
        nonlocal best
        if not node: return 0
        l, r = depth(node.left), depth(node.right)
        best = max(best, l + r)      # path THROUGH this node
        return 1 + max(l, r)         # height, for the parent
    depth(root)
    return best

# Return one value upward, track a different one globally. Very common.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

ThreadLocal gives each thread its own copy of a value. Legitimate uses: per-request context (trace id, tenant, security principal, the logging MDC) and reusing non-thread-safe objects like the old SimpleDateFormat.

In a thread pool it becomes both a leak and a correctness bug. Threads are reused, so a value set during request A is still present for request B — leaking data across requests, which in a multi-tenant system is a security incident, not just a bug. And because the entry is held by the thread's internal map, the value is never collected while the pool lives. The internal keys are weak references, but the values are strongly held until the slot is cleaned, and with a static ThreadLocal the key never dies — so nothing is ever cleaned. Always remove() in a finally.

Virtual threads are the other half. A virtual thread is scheduled by the JVM, not the OS: millions can exist, each a heap object with a growable stack, mounted onto a small pool of OS carrier threads only while running. When it blocks on IO it unmounts, freeing the carrier — so blocking stops being expensive and thread-per-request becomes viable again with ordinary readable code and real stack traces.

What does not change: they give you no extra CPU, so CPU-bound work still needs a bounded pool sized to cores. Do not pool them — they are cheap to create; use newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor. Pinning occurs when a virtual thread blocks inside a synchronized block or a native frame and cannot unmount, holding its carrier; recent JDKs largely fixed the synchronized case, but ReentrantLock is the safe pattern in blocking code.

And the consequence people miss: concurrency is now effectively unbounded, so the thread pool no longer limits load on your dependencies. You must add that limit explicitly — a Semaphore in front of the database or a fragile downstream — or you will simply move the collapse one layer down. On modern JDKs, ScopedValue replaces ThreadLocal for context: bound for the dynamic extent of a call, automatically unbound, immutable, and cheap at virtual-thread scale.

Java
private static final ThreadLocal<String> TRACE = new ThreadLocal<>();
void handle(Request r) {
    TRACE.set(r.traceId());
    try { process(r); }
    finally { TRACE.remove(); }        // MANDATORY in a pooled thread
}

try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (var req : requests) exec.submit(() -> handle(req));   // millions is fine
}

// concurrency is unbounded now - protect the dependency yourself
Semaphore db = new Semaphore(50);

// pinning risk: blocking inside synchronized holds the carrier
ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();   // prefer this in blocking code
Follow-ups they will ask

How would you detect pinning?

Run with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full, which prints a stack trace whenever a virtual thread blocks while pinned. JFR also has events for it. The symptom is throughput that plateaus far below expectation.

Does Loom remove the need for reactive programming?

For most request/response services, yes — it removes the main motivation, which was thread efficiency. Reactive still earns its place for streaming with explicit backpressure and complex event composition.

What replaces ThreadLocal for context propagation?

ScopedValue on recent JDKs: immutable, scoped to a call's dynamic extent, automatically unbound, and designed to be cheap when there are millions of threads. It cannot leak the way ThreadLocal does.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Two-phase commit: a coordinator asks every participant to prepare (do the work, hold locks, promise you can commit), and if all vote yes it tells them to commit. It gives real atomicity across services — and it is rarely the right answer. It is blocking: if the coordinator dies after the prepare phase, participants sit holding locks with no way to decide, indefinitely. It couples availability to the least available participant, it holds database locks across network calls, and it does not scale.

Sagas replace atomicity with a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that semantically undoes it. There is no global lock and no coordinator holding everything hostage. The price is that the system is never atomic — there are intermediate states where the payment succeeded and the inventory has not yet been reserved, and every consumer of that data must understand them.

Choreography: each service listens for events and emits its own. Loosely coupled, no central component — but the flow exists nowhere in the code, so understanding or debugging it means tracing events across services, and cycles are easy to create accidentally. Orchestration: a coordinator explicitly drives the steps as a state machine. The flow is in one readable place, easy to monitor and to add timeouts and retries to, at the cost of a component that must itself be highly available and must not accumulate business logic. For an order flow of any complexity, orchestration is usually the better answer, and saying why — debuggability and explicit timeouts — is the point.

For the order flow: reserve payment → reserve inventory → create shipment. If inventory fails, compensate the payment with a refund or void. And here is the crucial insight: compensations are not rollbacks. They are new forward transactions with their own semantics and their own failure modes. A refund is visible on the customer's statement; an email cannot be unsent; a shipment already dispatched can only be recalled. Some steps are genuinely irreversible, which is why you order the saga to put reversible and risky steps first and irreversible ones last.

Every step must be idempotent, because retries and redeliveries are guaranteed, and every step needs a timeout plus a defined outcome for the timeout case.

Saga (orchestrated)
state machine per order:
  PENDING -> PAYMENT_RESERVED -> INVENTORY_RESERVED -> SHIPPED
                 |                     |
                 v                     v
            (fail) VOID_PAYMENT   (fail) REFUND + RELEASE_INVENTORY

rules:
  - each step idempotent, keyed by orderId
  - each step has a timeout and a defined timeout outcome
  - irreversible steps last
  - persist the state machine; it must survive a restart
Follow-ups they will ask

What if a compensation itself fails?

You retry it with backoff, and if it keeps failing you escalate to a human via a dead-letter queue or an operations dashboard. There is no automatic escape — which is why designs prefer to avoid irreversible steps until the risky ones have succeeded.

When is 2PC actually acceptable?

Within a single database, or between two resources managed by one transaction manager where the participants are co-located and reliable — for example a database and a message broker via XA. Across services over a network, essentially never.

How do you make the intermediate states safe for readers?

Model them explicitly in the domain rather than hiding them. An order in PAYMENT_RESERVED is a real state with defined semantics for the UI and for reporting. Pretending the operation is atomic is what produces the confusing bugs.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Where to split: route boundaries first, because that is where the user's intent changes and the split is natural. Then split heavy leaves regardless of route — a rich text editor, a charting library, a PDF viewer, a date picker with locale data. Those are often larger than the rest of the app combined and are used by a minority of sessions. Do not split small components; each chunk costs a request and a bit of runtime overhead, and dozens of tiny chunks are slower than one.

Prefetching is what removes the cost of splitting. Prefetch a route's chunk on link hover or on focus (typically 200–300 ms of warning, which is usually enough), on viewport entry via IntersectionObserver for links below the fold, and on idle for the one or two most likely next routes. Fetch the data alongside the code — a route whose JavaScript arrives instantly but then starts its query has only moved the wait.

Avoiding a spinner on every navigation is the real question, and there are three parts. Keep the shell persistent — header, nav and layout should never unmount, so only the content region changes. Use transitions (startTransition, or a router that does this for you) so React keeps the current page on screen while the next one loads, showing a subtle pending indicator rather than tearing down to a fallback. And place Suspense boundaries around regions, not around the whole page, so a slow widget shows its own skeleton while everything else renders.

The rule underneath all of it: a fallback should only appear where content has never been shown. Replacing a rendered page with a spinner is a regression in perceived performance even when the measured time is identical. Pair this with skeletons that match the final layout so there is no layout shift when data arrives.

JSX
const Editor = lazy(() => import('./Editor'));       // heavy leaf, not a route

// prefetch on intent - by the time they click, it is already downloaded
<Link to="/reports"

How do you decide what is worth splitting?

Run a bundle analyzer and sort by size. Anything large that is used by a minority of sessions is a candidate. Splitting something used on every page just adds a request.

What is the risk of over-splitting?

Request waterfalls and overhead — chunk A loads chunk B which loads chunk C, so you serialize what should have been parallel. Also more cache entries to invalidate on deploy. Aim for a handful of meaningful chunks.

How do you handle a chunk failing to load after a deploy?

Old clients request hashed filenames that no longer exist and the dynamic import rejects. Catch it in an error boundary and prompt a reload, and keep previous builds' assets available for a grace period so mid-session users are not broken.

def is_valid(node, lo=float('-inf'), hi=float('inf')):

    return (is_valid(node.left,  lo, node.val) and
            is_valid(node.right, node.val, hi))

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

With wait/notify the two rules that matter are: always wait inside a while loop, never an if; and prefer notifyAll over notify when waiters are waiting for different conditions. The while loop exists because of spurious wakeups — a thread can return from wait() without being notified — and, more importantly, because between the notification and reacquiring the monitor another thread may have consumed the item, so the predicate must be re-checked.

The classic bug with a single monitor is the missed signal: with one wait set holding both producers and consumers, notify() may wake a producer when you needed to wake a consumer, and the queue stalls with work available. notifyAll avoids it by waking everyone to re-check, at the cost of a thundering herd on every operation.

ReentrantLock with two Conditions fixes exactly that: notFull and notEmpty are separate wait sets, so a put signals only consumers and a take signals only producers. That is the single strongest argument for ReentrantLock over synchronized, and it is why ArrayBlockingQueue is implemented this way. The cost is that unlock() must be in a finally.

The token bucket has one insight worth stating: do not run a refill thread. Compute tokens lazily from elapsed time on each request — tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed × rate) — which needs no scheduler, no background thread per bucket, and works correctly for buckets that are idle for hours. A bucket is then just two numbers plus a lock, so a limiter for ten thousand keys is trivial.

In an interview, say that in production you would use ArrayBlockingQueue and Guava's RateLimiter or Resilience4j — but be able to write both by hand, because the wait-loop and the lazy-refill are exactly what is being tested.

Java
class BoundedQueue<E> {
    private final Object[] items; private int count, head, tail;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notFull  = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();

    void put(E e) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (count == items.length) notFull.await();   // WHILE, not if
            items[tail] = e; tail = (tail + 1) % items.length; count++;
            notEmpty.signal();                                // wake a consumer only
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

class TokenBucket {                       // no refill thread - compute lazily
    private double tokens; private long lastNanos;
    synchronized boolean tryAcquire(double cost) {
        long now = System.nanoTime();
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - lastNanos) / 1e9 * ratePerSec);
        lastNanos = now;
        if (tokens < cost) return false;
        tokens -= cost; return true;
    }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why while and not if around await?

Spurious wakeups are permitted by the specification, and even without them another thread can win the lock after the signal and consume the item. The predicate must be re-verified after every wake, which is exactly what the loop does.

When is notify() safe instead of notifyAll()?

Only when every waiter is waiting on the same condition and any one of them can proceed — a homogeneous wait set. With mixed producers and consumers on one monitor it can deadlock, which is why two Conditions is the better design.

How would you extend the bucket to a distributed limiter?

Move the two numbers into Redis and do the read-modify-write in a Lua script so it is atomic across nodes. The lazy-refill maths is unchanged; only the storage and atomicity mechanism differ.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Double-entry is the core constraint, so lead with it. Every transaction writes at least two entries — debits and credits — and the sum of every transaction's entries must be exactly zero. Money is never created or destroyed, only moved between accounts. That single invariant is what makes the system auditable and what lets you detect corruption by arithmetic rather than by trust.

The ledger is append-only and immutable. There is no UPDATE and no DELETE on entries — ever. A mistake is corrected by posting a reversing entry, so the history of what you believed and when is preserved. Store amounts as integer minor units, never floating point, with the currency alongside, and reject any transaction whose entries do not balance at the database level via a constraint or a trigger rather than trusting application code.

Balances are a projection, not a column. Summing every entry for an account is O(history) and gets slower forever, so maintain periodic snapshots — a balance as of a sequence number — and compute the current balance as snapshot plus the delta since. Snapshots are derived and can always be rebuilt from the entries, which is the property that makes the design safe.

The idempotent charge API: the client sends an Idempotency-Key. You store the key with a hash of the request body and the eventual response. A repeat with the same key and the same body returns the stored response; the same key with a different body is a 422, because that is a client bug. Crucially, the key insert and the ledger write happen in one transaction with a unique constraint on the key — that is what makes duplicate submission impossible rather than merely unlikely. A timeout is not a failure: the caller must retry with the same key.

Reconciliation is the operational half people forget. Every day you fetch the provider's settlement file and compare it against your ledger, producing three buckets: matched, in our ledger but not theirs, and in theirs but not ours. Both mismatch buckets go to an exceptions queue for human review. Also run an internal check that the sum of all entries across the system is zero — if it is not, you have a bug and you want to know today, not at audit.

Schema
transactions(id, idempotency_key UNIQUE, created_at, status)
entries(id, transaction_id, account_id, amount_minor, currency, seq)
  CONSTRAINT: SUM(amount_minor) per transaction_id = 0     -- enforced in the DB
  no UPDATE, no DELETE - corrections are reversing entries

balance_snapshots(account_id, as_of_seq, balance_minor)
  current = snapshot + SUM(entries WHERE seq > as_of_seq)

BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO transactions(idempotency_key, ...);   -- unique -> duplicate blocked
  INSERT INTO entries(...) x2;                       -- debit + credit, sums to 0
COMMIT;
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you shard something that must balance?

Shard by account so a single account's entries stay together, keeping per-account transactions single-shard. Cross-account transfers between shards need a saga with a pending state, or you keep both sides of a transfer in one shard by routing on a transfer group id.

What if the client never retries after a timeout?

You are left with a transaction whose outcome the client does not know. That is why the charge must be queryable by idempotency key, and why reconciliation exists — the provider's file is the arbiter for anything left ambiguous.

Why not just store a balance column and update it?

Because an update loses history, is vulnerable to lost updates under concurrency, and gives you no way to prove how the balance was reached. The entries are the truth; the balance is a cache of them.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The core problem is that 50 messages/second is not 50 renders/second. Calling setState per message means the main thread does nothing but render, input becomes unresponsive, and React 18's automatic batching only helps within a tick, not across 50 separate socket events.

Buffer and flush on an animation frame. Push incoming messages into a ref-held array — no re-render — and schedule a single requestAnimationFrame that commits the accumulated batch to state. You now render at most once per frame regardless of message rate, which is the maximum the display can show anyway. If a burst arrives, you coalesce it instead of queueing 50 renders.

Keep the socket outside React. Own it in a module-level store subscribed to with useSyncExternalStore, so the connection survives re-renders, is not re-created by effect dependency churn, and can be written to from non-component code. Widgets then select only the slice they display, so a price tick re-renders one widget rather than all eight.

Make the expensive widgets non-blocking. Wrap chart data in useDeferredValue so a heavy re-render is interruptible and typing or clicking stays responsive; virtualize the event log, since an append-only list of thousands of rows is the classic memory and layout killer; and cap retained history explicitly — an unbounded array is a guaranteed leak in a dashboard left open overnight.

Connection lifecycle is the part that separates a demo from something operable: reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter (so a server restart does not bring every client back simultaneously), and on reconnect fetch a snapshot rather than assuming you can resume — you missed messages while disconnected, and replaying deltas onto stale state silently corrupts the display. Show connection state in the UI, and pause updates when the tab is hidden via visibilitychange so a backgrounded dashboard is not burning battery.

JSX
// buffer in a ref, flush once per frame
const buffer = useRef([]);
const frame = useRef(0);

function onMessage(msg) {
  buffer.current.push(msg);                       // no re-render
  if (!frame.current) {
    frame.current = requestAnimationFrame(() => {
      frame.current = 0;
      const batch = buffer.current; buffer.current = [];
      setEvents(prev => [...batch, ...prev].slice(0, 500));   // cap history
    });
  }
}

// reconnect with backoff + jitter, then resync from a snapshot
const delay = Math.min(30_000, 2 ** attempt * 500) * (0.5 + Math.random());

// keep expensive charts interruptible
const deferredSeries = useDeferredValue(series);
Follow-ups they will ask

Why requestAnimationFrame rather than a setTimeout or a debounce?

rAF aligns the flush with the browser's paint cycle, so you never render more often than the screen updates and never render into a frame that will not paint. A timer is either too eager or adds latency.

Why fetch a snapshot on reconnect instead of resuming the stream?

Because you cannot know what you missed while disconnected. Applying deltas onto stale state produces a display that looks fine and is wrong — the worst failure mode for an operations dashboard.

How do you stop the event log from leaking?

Cap the retained array and virtualize the rendering. Both are needed: virtualization fixes the DOM cost, the cap fixes the memory cost. A dashboard is often open for days.

def lca(root, p, q):

    L = lca(root.left,  p, q)

    if L and R: return root      # found one on each side -> this is it

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

ReentrantLock is a plain mutual-exclusion lock with extras — timeout, interruptibility, fairness, multiple Conditions. ReadWriteLock splits it: many concurrent readers or one exclusive writer. StampedLock adds a third mode, optimistic reading, which takes no lock at all.

When a read-write lock performs worse than a plain mutex — this is the real question. It has higher acquisition overhead: acquiring a read lock still involves a CAS on shared state, so with short critical sections that bookkeeping can cost more than the exclusion it replaces. It only pays off when reads are long and writes are rare. If your critical section is incrementing a counter or reading one field, a plain lock — or an atomic — wins. It also risks writer starvation in non-fair mode: a steady stream of readers can keep a writer waiting indefinitely, which is why ReentrantReadWriteLock offers a fair mode that then costs throughput.

Optimistic reading is StampedLock's contribution. tryOptimisticRead() returns a stamp without acquiring anything; you read the fields; then validate(stamp) tells you whether a write intervened. If it did, you fall back to a real read lock and read again. In the common case of no contention you have done zero synchronization — just a volatile read of a counter before and after — which is dramatically cheaper.

The caveats matter and interviewers look for them: StampedLock is not reentrant, so re-acquiring inside a call chain deadlocks; the stamps must not be leaked or reused; and you must copy the fields into locals inside the optimistic block, because the data may be inconsistent while you read it — you only find out afterwards. It also does not support Conditions.

So the ladder: plain synchronized or ReentrantLock by default; ReadWriteLock only when reads are long and demonstrably dominant; StampedLock when you have measured contention on a hot, read-mostly structure and can accept its sharp edges. And note the alternative that often beats all three: an immutable object swapped through a volatile reference, where readers need no lock at all.

Java
private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();
private double x, y;

double distanceFromOrigin() {
    long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();      // no lock acquired
    double cx = x, cy = y;                    // copy into locals - may be torn
    if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {                // a writer intervened
        stamp = sl.readLock();
        try { cx = x; cy = y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
    }
    return Math.hypot(cx, cy);
}

// often better than all of them: immutable snapshot behind a volatile reference
private volatile Config config;               // readers: no lock at all
void update(Config c) { this.config = c; }    // atomic reference swap
Follow-ups they will ask

Why must you copy fields into locals during an optimistic read?

Because a writer may be modifying them while you read, so you can observe a torn, inconsistent combination. Validation afterwards tells you to discard those locals — but only if you read into locals rather than acting on the fields directly.

What is lock striping and when does it help?

Splitting one lock into N locks over disjoint key ranges, so unrelated keys do not contend. It is what ConcurrentHashMap effectively does per bin. It helps when contention is spread across many keys and does nothing for a single hot key.

Which would you reach for first in real code?

Usually none of them — an immutable object behind a volatile reference, an atomic, or a concurrent collection. Explicit locks are for when you must coordinate several fields together, and even then synchronized is the safe default.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

L1 is an in-process cache (Caffeine) giving nanosecond reads with no network hop. L2 is Redis, shared by all instances, giving sub-millisecond reads and a single source of cached truth. The read path is L1 → L2 → database, populating on the way back. This structure is worth it when you have a hot key set small enough to fit in each process and read volume high enough that the Redis round trip itself is the cost.

The hard problem is invalidating L1 across 20 instances. Redis you can simply delete; L1 copies live in 20 separate heaps you cannot reach. Three options, and you should name the tradeoff of each. Short TTL (1–5 seconds) — trivially simple, bounded staleness, no coordination; usually the right answer, and the one to lead with. Pub/sub invalidation — publish the changed key on a Redis channel that every instance subscribes to and evicts locally; near-immediate, but it is fire-and-forget, so an instance that was disconnected during the publish keeps stale data indefinitely unless you also have a TTL as a backstop. Versioned keys — include a version in the key so a write makes the old key unreachable rather than requiring eviction; this sidesteps invalidation entirely at the cost of garbage.

The honest framing: L1 always means accepting some staleness. If you cannot accept it, do not use an L1 cache. Pub/sub narrows the window; it does not close it.

Cache penetration is the third failure: repeated requests for keys that do not exist — a scanner walking random ids, or a legitimate lookup of a deleted record. Every one misses both cache layers and hits the database, so the cache provides no protection at all. Fix with negative caching — store a tombstone with a short TTL, shorter than for real values so a newly created entity appears quickly — or a Bloom filter of existing keys in front, which answers "definitely not present" cheaply and never has false negatives. Add rate limiting on 404s, since a burst of misses from one client is a distinctive signature.

Read path
get(key):
  v = L1.get(key)            # Caffeine, TTL 1-5s, bounded size
  if v != null: return v
  v = redis.get(key)
  if v != null: L1.put(key, v); return v
  v = db.load(key)
  if v == null:
      L1.put(key, TOMBSTONE, 30s)      # negative cache - stops penetration
      redis.setex(key, 30, TOMBSTONE)
      return null
  redis.setex(key, ttl + jitter, v); L1.put(key, v); return v

invalidate(key):  redis.del(key); redis.publish("inval", key)   # L1 evicts on receipt
                  # short L1 TTL remains the backstop for missed messages
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is a short L1 TTL usually better than pub/sub?

Because it needs no coordination and cannot fail silently. Pub/sub adds a component whose failure mode is invisible staleness — the worst kind. Most systems can tolerate a few seconds, and if they cannot, they should not have an L1.

What sizes the L1 cache?

The hot key set, not the total key space. Measure the hit rate at a few candidate sizes; the curve usually flattens sharply, and beyond that point you are spending heap for nothing.

What happens if Redis goes down entirely?

Every request falls through to the database, so a cache outage becomes a database outage. The L1 helps absorb the first seconds; beyond that you need a circuit breaker and load shedding so the database survives to recover.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The scenario: a component fetches when a prop changes. Props go A → B. The request for A is slow, B is fast, B's response lands first, then A's arrives and overwrites it. The UI now shows data for A while the props say B, with no error and nothing in the console. On a fast local connection it never reproduces.

Fix 1 — the ignore flag. Declare let ignore = false in the effect and set it to true in the cleanup; check it before calling setState. Because cleanup runs before the next effect, the previous request is neutralised. Minimal, always correct, no dependencies. Its weakness is that the request still completes — bandwidth, a server connection and a browser connection slot are consumed for a result you discard.

Fix 2 — AbortController. Create one per effect run and call abort() in the cleanup. This cancels the request end to end, so the network work stops too. You must catch and ignore AbortError, or every cancellation looks like a failure and your error state flickers. This is the right hand-rolled answer, and it matters most where requests are frequent — a search-as-you-type firing on every keystroke.

Fix 3 — a query library. TanStack Query or SWR key every request by its inputs and only commit the response belonging to the currently active key, so an out-of-order response for a stale key is discarded structurally. You cannot forget to handle it, and you get deduplication, caching and retries with it.

Which I would ship: fix 3, because races are a class of bug that should be eliminated by the architecture rather than remembered at each call site. Fix 2 is the right answer when you cannot add a dependency. Fix 1 is the right answer inside a small custom hook where cancellation is not worth the complexity.

Worth adding: the sibling pattern is the latest-callback ref. When an effect sets up a long-lived subscription but needs to call a frequently-changing handler, storing the handler in a ref and updating it each render lets the subscription stay stable instead of tearing down and re-subscribing on every render.

JSX
// 1. ignore flag - simplest correct fix
useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;
  fetchUser(id).then(u => { if (!ignore) setUser(u); });
  return () => { ignore = true; };
}, [id]);

// 2. AbortController - also cancels the network work
useEffect(() => {
  const c = new AbortController();
  fetchUser(id, { signal: c.signal })
    .then(setUser)
    .catch(e => { if (e.name !== 'AbortError') setError(e); });   // must filter
  return () => c.abort();
}, [id]);

// 3. structural - the library discards responses for non-active keys
const { data } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['user', id], queryFn: () => fetchUser(id) });
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does the cleanup run before the next effect rather than after?

Because an effect is a synchronization: before syncing to the new value it must un-sync from the old one. That ordering is exactly what makes the ignore flag work — the old run is neutralised before the new one starts.

Does StrictMode's double-mount cause this bug?

No, but it exposes it. The setup-cleanup-setup sequence fires two requests where one is cancelled, which is harmless if you handle cancellation and visibly broken if you do not — which is the point of the double mount.

When is the latest-callback ref pattern the right tool?

When a subscription is expensive to recreate — a WebSocket, an IntersectionObserver, an event listener — but the handler it calls changes every render. Putting the handler in the dependency array would tear down and rebuild the subscription constantly.

A tree keyed by character, so a path from the root spells a prefix. Shared prefixes are stored once.

CostO(L) per operation, where L is the word lengthReach for itAutocomplete, prefix search, word dictionaries, and any problem where 'starts with' is the question.
class Trie:
    def __init__(self): self.root = {}
    def insert(self, w):
        node = self.root
        for ch in w: node = node.setdefault(ch, {})
        node['$'] = True                       # end-of-word marker
    def search(self, w, prefix=False):
        node = self.root
        for ch in w:
            if ch not in node: return False
            node = node[ch]
        return True if prefix else '$' in node

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Fork/Join targets divide-and-conquer: split a task recursively until the pieces are small enough to compute directly, then merge the results. RecursiveTask<V> returns a value; RecursiveAction does not.

Work stealing is the mechanism that makes it efficient. Each worker thread has its own double-ended queue. It pushes and pops its own subtasks from one end — LIFO, which keeps the most recently split, cache-hot data close at hand. Idle workers steal from the other end of a busy worker's deque — FIFO, taking the oldest and therefore largest chunk, which minimizes the number of steals needed to spread the work. There is no central queue to become a bottleneck, and load balances itself without coordination.

The idiomatic shape matters and is frequently got wrong: fork one half, compute the other half on the current thread, then join. Forking both halves and joining both wastes the current thread, which could have been doing work instead of waiting. The recursion threshold is a real tuning parameter — too small and coordination overhead dominates the actual computation.

Why the common pool is dangerous: it is sized to cores − 1 and is shared by the entire JVM — every parallel stream, every CompletableFuture async method with no explicit executor, and any library that uses it internally. One blocking task in that pool occupies a worker that can no longer steal, and enough of them starve everything else in the process, including framework internals you did not write.

So: never do IO or lock acquisition inside a Fork/Join task. If it is unavoidable, wrap it in a ManagedBlocker so the pool can compensate by temporarily adding a thread — or, far more simply, use a dedicated ExecutorService and leave the common pool for CPU-bound work.

Java
class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000;
    private final long[] a; private final int lo, hi;

    @Override protected Long compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
            long s = 0; for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++) s += a[i]; return s;
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        SumTask left = new SumTask(a, lo, mid);
        left.fork();                                     // hand off ONE half
        long right = new SumTask(a, mid, hi).compute();   // do the other half HERE
        return left.join() + right;
    }
}

// isolate from the shared common pool if you must
ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(8);
try { pool.submit(task).get(); } finally { pool.shutdown(); }
Follow-ups they will ask

Why LIFO locally but FIFO for stealing?

LIFO keeps the hottest, most recently split data in the local cache. Stealing from the opposite end takes the oldest and largest remaining task, so one steal transfers a lot of work and steals stay rare.

What does ManagedBlocker actually do?

It tells the pool that a worker is about to block, so the pool can spawn a compensation thread to maintain parallelism. It is the supported escape hatch, but needing it usually means the work belongs in a different executor.

How does this relate to parallel streams?

Parallel streams run on exactly this machinery and the common pool, which is why all the same warnings apply — and why understanding work stealing explains their performance characteristics.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Backpressure is the ability of a slow consumer to make a fast producer slow down. Without it, the producer keeps accepting work the system cannot complete, and the excess accumulates somewhere — a queue, a thread pool, a heap — until it fails.

At each boundary there is a mechanism. Client to service: bounded concurrency plus a rejection response — return 429 or 503 with Retry-After rather than accepting and queueing. Service to service: a bounded connection pool and a concurrency limiter (a semaphore), so a slow downstream causes fast local failures instead of thread exhaustion. Service to queue: a bounded queue with a rejection policy — CallerRunsPolicy is elegant because it makes the submitting thread do the work, which slows the producer automatically. Queue to consumer: consumer-driven pull, which is exactly what Kafka gives you — the consumer asks for records at its own rate, so lag grows visibly instead of memory growing invisibly.

Without backpressure, the failure mode is specific and worth naming: unbounded memory growth followed by a cascading collapse. The queue absorbs the overload and everything looks healthy — latency creeps up, but no errors — until the queue exhausts memory or the latency exceeds every upstream timeout at once. Then every caller retries, tripling the load on a system that is already failing. The insidious part is that the metrics look fine right up to the cliff, because queueing converts an error into latency.

So the design rule: bound every queue, and prefer rejecting early over queueing indefinitely. A fast, explicit failure is more useful than a slow success nobody is waiting for any more — and it lets the caller's circuit breaker do its job. Add load shedding at the edge: when latency or queue depth crosses a threshold, reject low-priority work first so critical paths keep working. And make timeouts shrink down the chain, so a caller has given up before its downstream is still trying.

Mechanisms
client -> gateway    : concurrency limit, 429 + Retry-After, load shedding
gateway -> service   : bounded connection pool, timeout < client timeout
service -> queue     : BOUNDED queue + CallerRunsPolicy (producer slows itself)
queue -> consumer    : pull-based (Kafka) -> lag is visible, memory is not consumed
service -> downstream: semaphore + circuit breaker + timeout

failure without it: latency creeps -> queue grows -> all timeouts fire at once
                    -> everyone retries -> collapse
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is an unbounded queue worse than rejecting requests?

It converts an error you could see and act on into memory growth you cannot. The system stays 'up' while doing progressively less useful work, and the eventual failure is total rather than partial.

What is the difference between load shedding and rate limiting?

Rate limiting is a policy about fairness — this client may send N per minute. Load shedding is a reaction to your own health — I am overloaded, so I am dropping the least important work regardless of who sent it.

How does Kafka provide backpressure if the producer never blocks?

It does not stop the producer, but it makes the imbalance visible and durable as consumer lag rather than as memory pressure. The lag metric is the signal, and acting on it (scaling consumers, shedding upstream) is the backpressure.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Lead with the accessibility requirement, because that is the part that is usually missing: mouse-only drag-and-drop is unusable for keyboard and screen-reader users, and for many motor-impaired users. A compliant implementation needs a full keyboard path, not a drag polyfill.

Pointer events rather than the HTML5 drag-and-drop API: pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup unify mouse, touch and stylus, give you setPointerCapture so the drag survives leaving the element, and avoid the HTML5 API's unfixable styling and touch limitations. Apply a small activation threshold (a few pixels) so a click is not misread as a drag, and use touch-action: none on the handle to stop the browser scrolling instead.

The keyboard path: the item is focusable; Space or Enter picks it up (entering a 'grabbed' mode), arrow keys move it one position, Space drops it, Escape cancels and returns it to its original position. Reflect the state with aria-grabbed or, better, the modern approach of a descriptive aria-roledescription plus live announcements.

Live-region announcements are what make it usable without sight: an aria-live="assertive" region announcing "Picked up Invoice 3. Position 3 of 12." on grab, "Moved to position 2 of 12." on each move, and "Dropped Invoice 3 at position 2 of 12." on drop. Without these a screen-reader user has no idea anything happened.

Optimistic persistence: apply the new order locally on drop, snapshot the previous order, send the mutation, and roll back with an explanatory toast on failure. Reconcile with the server's returned order rather than assuming yours was accepted, since another user may have reordered concurrently. Two more real cases: a drop outside any valid target must cancel cleanly, and an item unmounting mid-drag (because a background refetch removed it) must not leave the drag state stuck — cancel on unmount. In practice use dnd-kit, which is built around exactly this keyboard and announcement model.

JSX
// keyboard path is not optional
function onKeyDown(e, index) {
  if (e.key === ' ' || e.key === 'Enter') {
    e.preventDefault();
    grabbed ? drop() : grab(index);
    announce(grabbed ? `Dropped ${label}. Position ${index + 1} of ${items.length}.`
                     : `Picked up ${label}. Position ${index + 1} of ${items.length}.`);
  }
  if (grabbed && e.key === 'ArrowDown') { move(index + 1); announce(...); }
  if (e.key === 'Escape') { cancel(); announce('Cancelled. Returned to position ...'); }
}

<div aria-live="assertive" className="sr-only">{announcement}</div>

<li tabIndex={0} onKeyDown={e => onKeyDown(e, i)}
    style={{ touchAction: 'none' }} onPointerDown={startDrag}>
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not use the HTML5 drag-and-drop API?

It has almost no styling control, does not work on touch without a polyfill, has inconsistent event behaviour across browsers, and provides no keyboard story. Pointer events give you all of that back at the cost of implementing the movement yourself.

What should the live region announce, exactly?

Position and total on pickup, on every move, and on drop, plus explicit cancellation. Numbers matter — 'moved down' tells a non-sighted user nothing about where the item now is.

How do you handle a concurrent reorder by another user?

Reconcile with the order the server returns rather than keeping your optimistic array, and if the difference is large, surface it rather than silently jumping the list under the user's cursor.

Choose, recurse, un-choose. Build a partial solution, explore deeper, then undo the choice before trying the next one.

CostO(branches^depth) — exponential by natureReach for itEvery 'generate all' or 'find any valid arrangement' question: subsets, permutations, N-Queens, sudoku, word search.
def backtrack(path, options):
    if is_solution(path):
        results.append(path[:])       # COPY - path keeps mutating
        return
    for opt in options:
        if not valid(opt, path): continue
        path.append(opt)              # choose
        backtrack(path, next_options(opt))   # explore
        path.pop()                    # UN-choose  <- the whole technique

# Forgetting path[:] and returning the same mutated list is the #1 bug.

Async error handling and consistency models

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

An exception inside a stage completes the future exceptionally, and that propagates down the chain, short-circuiting the transformation stages. thenApply, thenCompose and thenCombine are all skipped; the failure is carried forward, wrapped in a CompletionException, until something handles it.

The three handlers differ in exactly what they can do. exceptionally(fn) runs only on failure and lets you recover by returning a fallback value — the chain continues normally afterwards. handle(fn) runs on both outcomes, receiving (value, throwable) with one of them null, and returns a new value — so it can both recover and transform. whenComplete(fn) also runs on both outcomes but is a side-effect stage: it cannot change the result, and the original outcome passes through unchanged. Use it for logging and metrics.

The silent killer is a failed future nobody observes. If you create a chain and never call join, get, or attach a handler, an exception inside it simply vanishes — no stack trace, no log, nothing. Unlike an uncaught exception in a thread, there is no default handler that prints it. So the rule is: every chain must terminate in something exception-aware, even if that is just a whenComplete that logs.

Two more details worth having ready. Exceptions are wrapped in CompletionException (or ExecutionException from get), so handlers must unwrap with getCause() to inspect the real type — a common source of confusing instanceof checks that never match. And allOf waits for every future and fails if any fails, but does not cancel the others, so the siblings keep running and consuming resources — which is precisely the gap that structured concurrency closes.

Java
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> client.fetch(id), pool)
    .thenApply(this::transform)                     // SKIPPED on failure
    .exceptionally(ex -> {                          // recovers, chain continues
        log.warn("degraded", ex.getCause());        // unwrap CompletionException
        return Profile.empty();
    })
    .whenComplete((v, ex) -> metrics.record(ex == null));   // side effect only

// silent failure - nothing ever observes this
CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException(); }, pool);

// allOf fails if any fails, but does NOT cancel the siblings
CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b, c).join();
Follow-ups they will ask

handle or exceptionally?

exceptionally when you only care about the failure path and want a fallback. handle when you need to transform both outcomes into a common result type — for example mapping success and failure into a single response object.

Why do exception types not match in a catch?

Because the throwable is wrapped in CompletionException. Call getCause() before testing the type, or use a small unwrap helper — this is one of the most common CompletableFuture bugs.

How does structured concurrency improve on this?

A StructuredTaskScope cancels sibling subtasks automatically when one fails, guarantees nothing outlives the scope, and makes the relationships visible in the stack trace — none of which allOf provides.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Give the catalogue anchored to what a user sees, because the vocabulary alone is cheap and the symptoms are what prove you have operated these systems.

Linearizable (strong): every read returns the most recent committed write, as if there were a single copy. Real systems: a single-primary Postgres, etcd, Spanner. Violation symptom: two people both successfully book the last seat.

Sequential: all operations appear in some total order consistent with each client's own order, but not necessarily real time. Weaker than linearizable and rarely the thing you explicitly choose.

Causal: operations that are causally related appear in order everywhere; concurrent ones may be seen in different orders. Symptom of violation: a reply appears before the message it answers — the classic comment-thread bug, and the one worth naming because it is so recognisable.

Read-your-writes: you always see your own writes. Violation: a user posts a comment, the next read hits a lagging replica, their comment is missing, so they post again — now you have duplicates and an angry user. Fix by routing their reads to the primary for a few seconds, pinning the session, or passing an LSN token the replica must have reached.

Monotonic reads: you never see time move backwards. Violation: consecutive reads hit replicas with different lag, so a counter decreases or a message disappears and reappears. Fix by pinning a session to one replica.

Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop, with no ordering guarantee in the meantime. DNS and S3 listings are the canonical examples. Perfectly fine for a follower count; catastrophic for a balance.

Close with the practical framing: you rarely choose one model globally — you choose per operation. In the same product, the payment write is linearizable, the user's own profile read needs read-your-writes, and the recommendations panel is happily eventual. Saying that is what distinguishes an engineer from someone reciting a hierarchy.

Symptom -> model
"my own comment vanished on refresh"        -> read-your-writes violated
"the count went backwards"                  -> monotonic reads violated
"the reply is above the message"            -> causal order violated
"both users got the last seat"              -> linearizability violated
"the follower count is 2s behind"           -> eventual, and that is fine

choose per operation:
  payment write   -> linearizable
  own profile read-> read-your-writes (sticky-to-primary window or LSN token)
  feed / counts   -> eventual
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you actually implement read-your-writes?

Three practical options: route that user's reads to the primary for N seconds after a write; pin their session to one replica and only serve them from it; or return the write's log sequence number to the client and require the replica to have applied at least that LSN before serving.

Is causal consistency achievable cheaply?

Partially — keeping causally related writes in the same partition gives you it for free within that partition, which is why partitioning a conversation by thread id is such a common design. Cross-partition causality needs vector clocks or a coordination layer and is rarely worth it.

What model does a cache give you?

Eventual, bounded by the TTL, with no ordering guarantee between keys. That is worth stating explicitly when you add a cache, because it silently weakens whatever the database was giving you.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Use IntersectionObserver on a sentinel element rather than listening to scroll. Scroll listeners fire dozens of times per second on the main thread and require you to compute positions yourself; the observer is asynchronous, off the main thread, and simply tells you when a target enters the viewport. Put an empty sentinel div after the last item and load the next page when it becomes visible, with a rootMargin of a few hundred pixels so loading starts before the user reaches the bottom.

Guarding against double-firing is the first real bug: the observer can fire again while a request is in flight, or fire for a stale page number. Gate on isFetchingNextPage and hasNextPage, and key the request by cursor rather than by an incrementing page counter, so a duplicate trigger requests the same cursor and is deduplicated rather than skipping a page.

Deduplication of items is the second: with offset-based paging, new rows inserted while the user scrolls shift everything down, so page 2 repeats rows from page 1. That is exactly the pagination-stability problem — the fix is cursor/keyset pagination, where each page continues from the last item's sort key. If you are stuck with offsets, dedupe by id on merge as a mitigation, but say that it is a mitigation, not a fix.

Error and retry: a failed page load must not kill the list. Show an inline retry affordance at the bottom rather than replacing the loaded content, and stop the observer from retrying automatically in a loop — that is how a failing endpoint gets hammered.

Scroll restoration on back-navigation is the part most implementations get wrong. Returning to a list that has reset to page 1 at scroll position 0 is the most-complained-about behaviour in infinite lists. It needs both halves: the data must still be cached (a query cache keyed by the list query, so the pages are restored without refetching) and the scroll position must be saved and reapplied after the content has its full height — restoring too early lands you at the top. Also provide a keyboard- and screen-reader-accessible "Load more" button as a fallback, because an observer-only list is unreachable without scrolling.

JSX
const { data, fetchNextPage, hasNextPage, isFetchingNextPage } = useInfiniteQuery({
  queryKey: ['feed', filters],
  queryFn: ({ pageParam }) => fetchFeed({ cursor: pageParam, ...filters }),
  getNextPageParam: last => last.nextCursor,      // cursor, not offset
  initialPageParam: null,
});

const sentinel = useRef(null);
useEffect(() => {
  const el = sentinel.current; if (!el) return;
  const io = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting && hasNextPage && !isFetchingNextPage) fetchNextPage();
  }, { rootMargin: '400px' });                    // start early
  io.observe(el);
  return () => io.disconnect();
}, [hasNextPage, isFetchingNextPage, fetchNextPage]);

<div ref={sentinel} />
<button onClick={() => fetchNextPage()} disabled={!hasNextPage}>Load more</button>
Follow-ups they will ask

Why rootMargin instead of loading exactly at the bottom?

So the request starts while the user is still reading, and the next page is usually there by the time they arrive. Loading at the exact bottom guarantees a visible pause on every page.

How do you restore scroll position correctly?

Save scrollTop on navigate-away, restore it only after the cached pages have rendered and the container has its full height — otherwise you set a scroll position larger than the current content and the browser clamps it to the top.

What are the accessibility problems with infinite scroll?

There is no reachable footer, keyboard users cannot trigger loading, and screen readers get no announcement that new content arrived. Provide a real Load more button and announce the number of new items in a live region.

Each element is either in or out, so there are 2ⁿ subsets. Generate by recursion or by treating a bitmask as the membership vector.

CostO(2ⁿ · n) time and output sizeReach for itPower set, subset sum, partitioning. The bitmask form is worth knowing — it is iterative and has no recursion depth limit.
# Recursive
def subsets(nums):
    out = []
    def bt(i, cur):
        if i == len(nums): out.append(cur[:]); return
        bt(i + 1, cur)                   # exclude nums[i]
        cur.append(nums[i]); bt(i + 1, cur); cur.pop()   # include
    bt(0, [])
    return out

# Bitmask - each integer 0..2^n-1 IS a subset
for mask in range(1 << n):
    sub = [nums[i] for i in range(n) if mask >> i & 1]
