Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Name the areas and, crucially, that heap is not the process footprint — that is the operational point the question is really after. The runtime data areas are: the heap (all objects, GC-managed, shared), Metaspace (class metadata, in native memory, unbounded by default), one stack per thread (frames and locals, roughly 1 MB reserved each), the code cache (JIT-compiled native code), and direct/native memory (NIO buffers and native libraries).

So total RSS ≈ heap + metaspace + thread stacks + code cache + direct buffers + GC structures. Setting -Xmx equal to the container limit is therefore a reliable way to get OOMKilled while the heap graph looks perfectly healthy — you left nothing for everything else. Use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage at around 70% instead, and cap Metaspace and direct memory explicitly.

Object layout: every object has a header — a mark word (identity hash, GC age, lock state) plus a class pointer — 12 bytes with compressed oops, padded to 8-byte alignment. So the smallest object is 16 bytes and an Integer spends 16 bytes to hold 4 bytes of data. Compressed oops store 32-bit scaled offsets instead of 64-bit pointers and work up to about a 32 GB heap, which is why a 31 GB heap can hold more objects than a 33 GB one — a genuinely counter-intuitive fact worth having ready.

Escape analysis is the JIT determining whether an object created in a method can be observed outside it. If it cannot, three optimizations become legal: scalar replacement (the object is never allocated — its fields become registers), stack allocation, and lock elision (synchronization on a provably thread-confined object is removed, which is why using a local StringBuffer costs almost nothing).

The practical consequence: "avoid allocation" is often wrong advice for short-lived locals, because the JIT frequently removes them entirely. But it depends on the allocation site being inlined, so it is a best-effort optimization you design for and measure, never assume.

Sizing
# see the real breakdown, not just the heap
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary ...
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary

# container baseline - leave room for non-heap
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m
-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m

# long[1_000_000] ~  8 MB
# Long[1_000_000] ~ 24 MB   (8MB of refs + 16MB of objects)
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does the 32GB compressed-oops threshold exist?

A reference is encoded as a 32-bit value scaled by the 8-byte object alignment, giving 2^32 x 8 = 32GB of addressable heap. Past that the JVM must use full 64-bit pointers, increasing memory use by roughly 20% — so crossing it can make you slower.

Why can you not rely on escape analysis?

It requires the allocation site to be inlined and the analysis to succeed, both of which depend on profile data and inlining budgets that vary at runtime. Design for correctness, measure, and treat it as a bonus.

What is the first thing you check when RSS exceeds the heap by a lot?

Thread count times stack size, then Metaspace, then direct buffers — in that order. Native Memory Tracking gives you all three, and one of them is nearly always the answer.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start with the problem it solves. With hash(key) % N, changing N remaps almost every key — go from 4 nodes to 5 and roughly 80% of keys move. For a cache that means a near-total miss storm and a database that suddenly receives full traffic; for a sharded store it means moving nearly all the data. Consistent hashing exists to bound that blast radius.

The mechanism: map the output of the hash function onto a conceptual ring (0 to 2³²−1). Hash each node onto the ring too. A key belongs to the first node encountered walking clockwise from the key's position. Adding a node captures only the keys between it and its predecessor; removing one hands its keys to its successor. So a change remaps roughly K/N keys instead of nearly all of them.

Virtual nodes fix the two weaknesses of the naive ring. With a small number of physical nodes, random placement produces very uneven arc lengths, so load is imbalanced — one node may own three times its share. Giving each physical node many ring positions (typically 100–200) makes the distribution converge to uniform by the law of large numbers. It also makes removal smooth: a departing node's keys spread across many successors rather than dumping entirely onto one, and it lets you weight heterogeneous machines by giving bigger ones more virtual nodes.

Where it is used: cache client sharding (Memcached, Redis Cluster's slot mapping is a variant), Cassandra and DynamoDB partitioning, and load balancers doing session or cache affinity.

What it does not solve — worth volunteering — is a hot key. Consistent hashing distributes keys evenly, not traffic. One celebrity key still lands on one node and saturates it, and no amount of ring tuning helps. That needs key splitting or a local cache. Two refinements to name: bounded-load consistent hashing caps how much above average any node may take, spilling overflow to the next node; and rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing achieves the same minimal-disruption property with simpler code and no ring.

Ring
ring position = hash(node_id + ":" + vnode_index)     # 100-200 vnodes per node
key owner     = first vnode clockwise from hash(key)

add a node    -> only keys between it and its predecessor move  (~K/N)
modulo hashing-> nearly every key moves                          (~K)

virtual nodes give:  even load, smooth removal, weighting by capacity
does NOT give:       protection from a hot key (that needs key splitting)
Follow-ups they will ask

How many virtual nodes should you use?

Enough that load variance is acceptable — 100 to 200 per physical node is typical. More means smoother distribution but a bigger ring to store and search, and the returns flatten quickly.

What is bounded-load consistent hashing?

A variant that caps each node at a small factor above the average load; when a node is at capacity the key spills to the next node on the ring. It trades a little locality for a hard guarantee against imbalance.

Why might you use rendezvous hashing instead?

It computes hash(key, node) for each node and picks the highest score. It gives the same minimal-disruption property, distributes evenly without virtual nodes, and is far simpler to implement — at O(N) per lookup, which is fine for small N.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Test behaviour, not implementation. React Testing Library's guiding principle is that tests should resemble how users interact with the software — so query by accessible role and name (getByRole('button', { name: /save/i })) rather than by test id or class. The side benefit is real: a test that can only find your button by role is also asserting the button is accessible.

What to test: user-visible behaviour and the contract of a component — does submitting an invalid form show the errors, does clicking Save call the API and show a success state, does the empty state appear when there are no rows. What never to test: internal state values, whether a specific hook ran, implementation details like class names, and large snapshot trees — a snapshot that changes on every refactor gets regenerated without being read, so it asserts nothing while costing review noise.

Network: use MSW (Mock Service Worker) to intercept at the network layer rather than mocking your fetch wrapper or the query client. That way tests exercise the real data-fetching code path, survive a refactor from fetch to axios, and let you assert loading, error and empty states by returning the corresponding responses. Mocking the module under test's own dependency is how you end up with tests that pass while the app is broken.

Shape of the pyramid for React specifically: more integration tests than isolated unit tests — a component rendered with its real children and a mocked network is far more valuable than each child tested alone with everything stubbed. Extract genuinely pure logic (formatting, validation, reducers) into plain functions and unit-test those directly, since they need no DOM at all. Then a small number of E2E tests through Playwright for the critical journeys.

Two practical rules: use userEvent rather than fireEvent, because it simulates the full sequence a real user generates (pointer, focus, keydown, input) and catches bugs a synthetic change event misses; and prefer findBy* queries over manual waits, since they retry until the element appears and give a readable failure when it does not.

JSX
// MSW: intercept the network, not your own module
const server = setupServer(
  http.get('/api/orders', () => HttpResponse.json({ items: [] }))
);

test('shows the empty state when there are no orders', async () => {
  render(<Orders />);
  expect(await screen.findByText(/no orders yet/i)).toBeInTheDocument();
});

test('submits the form', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<OrderForm />);
  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: /reference/i }), 'INV-1');
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /save/i }));
  expect(await screen.findByText(/saved/i)).toBeInTheDocument();
});
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is getByRole preferred over getByTestId?

Because it asserts the accessible tree, which is what assistive technology uses. A component that cannot be queried by role is usually one a screen reader cannot operate either — so the query choice doubles as an accessibility check.

When is a test id acceptable?

When there is genuinely no accessible way to identify the element — a decorative container you need to scope a query to. It should be the exception, and reaching for it often signals missing semantics in the markup.

How do you test a hook?

Prefer testing it through a component that uses it. If it is complex enough to warrant direct testing, use renderHook — but first check whether the logic could be a plain function outside React, which is easier to test and reason about.

Every ordering of the input. Swap-based generation avoids a 'used' array; sorting first plus a skip rule handles duplicates.

CostO(n! · n) timeReach for itArrangement problems, and the duplicate-handling rule generalises to combinations and subsets with repeats.
def permute_unique(nums):
    nums.sort()                       # required for the dedupe rule
    out, used, cur = [], [False]*len(nums), []
    def bt():
        if len(cur) == len(nums): out.append(cur[:]); return
        for i, v in enumerate(nums):
            if used[i]: continue
            # skip a duplicate unless its identical predecessor is in use
            if i and v == nums[i-1] and not used[i-1]: continue
            used[i] = True; cur.append(v)
            bt()
            cur.pop(); used[i] = False
    bt()
    return out

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Serial — one thread, stop-the-world; correct for tiny heaps and single-CPU containers, where the coordination cost of a parallel collector is not repaid. Parallel — multi-threaded stop-the-world, maximum throughput, long pauses; the right choice for batch jobs where total wall time matters and a two-second pause does not. CMS — the historic concurrent old-gen collector, removed in JDK 14; know the name and that fragmentation was its undoing.

G1 is the default since Java 9. The heap is divided into equal-sized regions, each dynamically assigned as Eden, Survivor or Old. It marks liveness concurrently, then collects the regions containing the most garbage first — hence Garbage-First — choosing how many regions to include in order to meet your MaxGCPauseMillis target. That target is a goal, not a guarantee, which is worth saying explicitly.

ZGC and Shenandoah are the low-latency collectors: they compact concurrently using load and store barriers, giving sub-millisecond pauses largely independent of heap size — ZGC handles terabytes. You pay a few percent of throughput and some extra memory for pause times that stop appearing in your latency graphs.

Choosing: throughput and batch → Parallel; balanced default → G1; a strict tail-latency SLO on a large heap → ZGC. Never switch on intuition — compare pause histograms under real load.

Reading a GC log is the actual skill. Enable -Xlog:gc* and look at four things: pause durations and their distribution; collection frequency; how much the heap drops at each collection — if the post-GC floor keeps rising you have a leak, not a tuning problem; and promotion and allocation rates. Then map symptoms: frequent young collections with a low promotion rate is usually healthy, just high allocation. Frequent full GCs or a monotonically rising live set is a leak. "To-space exhausted" or promotion failures mean the young generation or survivor spaces are mis-sized for your object lifetimes. Long pauses on a big heap is the signal to evaluate ZGC.

Finally, prove causation before tuning: correlate the GC pause timestamps against your p99 latency timeline. If they do not line up, GC is not your problem — and that is a very common false lead.

GC log
-Xlog:gc*,gc+heap=debug,safepoint:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20M

read for:
  "Pause Young"     frequency + duration distribution
  "Pause Full"      should be ~zero in a healthy service
  heap after each GC -> a rising floor means a LEAK, not a tuning problem
  "to-space exhausted" / promotion failure -> young gen or survivors mis-sized

-XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200      # balanced default
-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational             # strict tail latency
-XX:+UseParallelGC                          # batch throughput
Follow-ups they will ask

Which single flag matters most?

-Xmx, or MaxRAMPercentage in a container. Almost every GC problem is really a heap-sizing problem or a leak, and no collector choice fixes either of those.

Does a bigger heap always mean fewer pauses?

Fewer collections, but with a non-concurrent collector each old-gen collection traces a larger live set, so pauses grow. That inversion is exactly the problem ZGC's concurrent compaction solves.

What is a humongous allocation in G1?

An object larger than half a region, which is allocated directly into contiguous old-gen regions rather than Eden. Many of them fragment the heap and trigger more full collections — a reason to avoid very large arrays or to raise the region size.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Compare them on burst behaviour and memory cost, since those are the two axes that decide the choice.

Fixed window: one counter per key per window. Memory O(1) per key, trivially cheap. The flaw is a 2x burst at the boundary — 1,000 requests at 11:59:59 and another 1,000 at 12:00:00 is 2,000 in one second while never breaching the stated limit of 1,000 per minute. That is the derivation to state out loud.

Sliding window log: store the timestamp of every request and count those inside the window. Perfectly accurate with no boundary effect — but memory is O(requests per window) per key, so 10,000 keys at 1,000 requests each is ten million timestamps. Unacceptable at scale, and the reason it is mostly a teaching example.

Sliding window counter: keep the current and previous window counts and interpolate by how far into the current window you are — count = current + previous × (1 − elapsed_fraction). Memory O(1) per key, no boundary burst, and the approximation error is small and bounded. This is the industry default, and knowing the interpolation formula is a strong signal.

Token bucket: tokens accumulate at a fixed rate up to a cap; each request consumes one. Memory is two numbers per key. It deliberately permits bursts up to the bucket capacity, which is the right model when bursts are legitimate — a client that has been idle should be allowed to catch up. Tune the cap to the largest burst you want to allow. Leaky bucket is its mirror image: requests queue and drain at a constant rate, so output is perfectly smooth and bursts are delayed rather than allowed — the right model when the thing you are protecting cannot absorb bursts at all.

So the selection rule: token bucket when bursts are acceptable, leaky bucket when the downstream needs a smooth rate, sliding window counter when you want a simple accurate limit. And in all cases compute state lazily from elapsed time rather than running refill timers, and make the check-and-update atomic — a Redis Lua script — or two nodes will both read 999 and both allow.

Derivations
fixed window        mem O(1)/key   burst 2x at the boundary
sliding log         mem O(reqs)    burst none, exact          <- too much memory
sliding counter     mem O(1)/key   burst ~none, approximate   <- default
token bucket        mem O(1)/key   burst up to capacity       <- bursts allowed
leaky bucket        mem O(queue)   burst none, output smoothed

sliding counter:
  count = current + previous * (1 - elapsed_fraction_of_window)
token bucket:
  tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed_seconds * rate)
Follow-ups they will ask

Which would you pick for a public API?

Token bucket, with the capacity set to the burst you are willing to absorb and the rate set to the sustained limit. It is the most forgiving to well-behaved clients while still bounding sustained load, and clients understand it.

How do you communicate the limit to clients?

Return 429 with Retry-After, plus X-RateLimit-Limit, -Remaining and -Reset headers so a well-written client can pace itself rather than hammering and backing off blindly.

Fail open or fail closed when the limiter store is down?

It depends on what the limiter protects. Guarding a fragile backend from abuse: fail closed. Preventing accidental over-use of a robust service: fail open, because taking the whole API down to enforce a rate limit is the worse outcome. State the choice explicitly.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Work through the five things a modal must do, because missing any one of them makes it unusable for keyboard or screen-reader users.

Semantics: role="dialog" with aria-modal="true", plus aria-labelledby pointing at the title (and aria-describedby for supporting text). Without aria-modal, assistive technology does not know the rest of the page is inert.

Initial focus: move focus into the dialog on open — but to the first meaningful element, not blindly the first focusable one. For a confirmation dialog that is often the least destructive action or the dialog container itself; focusing a Delete button by default is how people delete things by pressing Enter. For a form, focus the first field.

Focus trap: Tab and Shift+Tab must cycle within the dialog. Implement it by finding the focusable elements and wrapping at the ends, and make the background genuinely unreachable — the modern way is the inert attribute on the rest of the page, which removes it from the tab order and the accessibility tree in one step. Before inert was available this required aria-hidden plus manual tabindex management, which was easy to get wrong.

Restore focus: on close, return focus to the element that opened it. Losing focus to document.body dumps a keyboard user back at the top of the page with no context — one of the most common and most disorienting bugs.

Escape and scroll lock: Escape closes; lock background scrolling while open (and compensate for the scrollbar width, or the page visibly shifts). Also render through a portal so the dialog escapes any ancestor's overflow: hidden or transform-created stacking context.

Worth saying at the end: the native <dialog> element with showModal() now provides the trap, the inert background, Escape handling and the top layer for free, and is the right default in new code. Reach for a hand-rolled implementation only when you need behaviour it does not support.

JSX
function Modal({ open, onClose, titleId, children }) {
  const ref = useRef(null);
  const opener = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!open) return;
    opener.current = document.activeElement;           // remember the trigger
    document.getElementById('root').inert = true;      // background unreachable
    ref.current?.querySelector('[data-autofocus]')?.focus();

    const onKey = e => { if (e.key === 'Escape') onClose(); };
    document.addEventListener('keydown', onKey);
    return () => {
      document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey);
      document.getElementById('root').inert = false;
      opener.current?.focus();                         // RESTORE focus
    };
  }, [open, onClose]);

  return open ? createPortal(
    <div role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby={titleId} ref={ref}>
      {children}
    </div>, document.body) : null;
}
Follow-ups they will ask

What exactly does the inert attribute do?

It removes an element and its subtree from the tab order, from hit testing, and from the accessibility tree. It replaces the old combination of aria-hidden plus setting tabindex=-1 on every focusable descendant, which was error-prone and easy to leave inconsistent.

Where should focus go on open?

The first element that makes sense for the task — usually the first form field, or the safest action in a confirmation. Never a destructive button, and never leave focus behind on the page, which makes the dialog invisible to keyboard users.

Why is the native dialog element preferable now?

It provides the focus trap, background inertness, Escape handling and rendering in the browser's top layer natively, so you inherit correct behaviour instead of reimplementing it. It also avoids z-index fights entirely.

Binary Search Trees
  • Validate Binary Search TreeMedium
  • Kth Smallest Element in a BSTMedium
  • Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder TraversalMedium

Backtracking where an element may be reused. Passing the same index allows reuse; passing i+1 forbids it — that one character is the whole difference.

CostO(n^(target/min)) — bounded by pruningReach for itCoin combinations, target sums, and any 'pick items to reach exactly X' where order does not matter.
def combination_sum(cands, target):
    cands.sort()                          # enables the break below
    out = []
    def bt(start, cur, remain):
        if remain == 0: out.append(cur[:]); return
        for i in range(start, len(cands)):
            if cands[i] > remain: break   # sorted -> everything after is worse
            cur.append(cands[i])
            bt(i, cur, remain - cands[i])  # i (reuse) vs i+1 (no reuse)
            cur.pop()
    bt(0, [], target)
    return out

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Frame it as unintended reachability — in a garbage-collected language there are no leaks, only objects you forgot you were still referencing. Then name the five classics, since interviewers want the list.

Static collections that only ever grow — a cache with no eviction, a registry nobody unregisters from. Listeners and callbacks never removed, which also pins whatever they close over. ThreadLocals in pooled threads without remove(), where the value is held by the long-lived thread. Classloader leaks on redeploy, where a static field or running thread outside the app pins the app's loader and every class it loaded — this shows as Metaspace growth, not heap. Inner class instances pinning their outer object through the synthetic this$0 reference.

The workflow is the same every time, and stating it in order is the answer. Take two heap dumps separated by time under load — one snapshot tells you what is big, two tell you what is growing, which is what a leak is. Open them in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM. Compare histograms to find the class whose instance count is climbing. Then open the dominator tree and sort by retained size — not shallow size — because retained size is what would actually be freed if that object went away.

Finally, on the biggest growing object, run "path to GC roots, excluding weak and soft references". That gives you the exact chain of strong references keeping it alive, and it is almost always immediately obvious once you see it — a static map, a thread, a listener list.

Say "retained size" and "path to GC roots" explicitly; those two phrases demonstrate you have actually done this rather than read about it. And in production, always run with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError and a writable path — an OOM without a dump is a lost investigation, and the next occurrence is another outage.

Workflow
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/dump1.hprof
# ... run under load for a while ...
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/dump2.hprof

Eclipse MAT:
  1. Histogram -> compare the two dumps -> which class is GROWING
  2. Dominator Tree -> sort by RETAINED heap (not shallow)
  3. right-click -> Path to GC Roots -> exclude weak/soft references
  4. the chain terminates at a static field, a live thread, or a listener list

# always on in production:
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
Follow-ups they will ask

Shallow versus retained size?

Shallow is the object itself. Retained is the object plus everything only it keeps alive. A HashMap has a tiny shallow size and an enormous retained size — retained is the number that tells you where the memory actually went.

Why exclude weak and soft references when finding the path?

Because those do not prevent collection — following them leads you to a reference that is not the problem. You want the strong chain, which is the one actually keeping the object alive.

Is a soft-reference cache a good idea?

Rarely. Clearing is at the GC's discretion, so behaviour is unpredictable: entries are cleared too late to prevent pressure or too eagerly to be useful, and it interacts badly with tuning. An explicitly bounded cache like Caffeine is almost always better.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design it as layered defences, each with a distinct job, and the ordering matters because each one only works if the ones before it are present.

Timeouts first, because nothing else works without them. Every call needs one, and the budget must shrink down the chain: if the client waits 3 s, the gateway waits 2.5 s and the service 2 s. Without that, the client has given up while every layer below still holds threads and connections — resources consumed for a response nobody will read.

Retries, carefully. Only for idempotent operations, with exponential backoff and jitter, and a hard cap on attempts. Backoff without jitter is the classic amplification bug: every client retries at the same instant, producing a synchronized retry storm that keeps a recovering service down. And retries at multiple layers multiply — 3 at the gateway times 3 at the service is 9 requests for one user action, which turns a brownout into an outage. Retry at one layer only.

Circuit breakers stop you from sending traffic to something that is clearly failing. Three states: closed (normal), open (fail immediately without calling), half-open (let a trial request through to test recovery). It trips on an error-rate or slow-call-rate threshold over a rolling window — not on a single failure. The value is twofold: your threads are not held waiting on a dead dependency, and the failing service gets breathing room to recover instead of being hammered.

Bulkheads isolate the blast radius: a separate connection pool or semaphore per dependency, so a slow payment provider cannot consume every thread and take down your health check. This is the difference between one degraded feature and a total outage.

Graceful degradation is the product half: for each dependency, decide in advance what happens when it is unavailable. Recommendations → show a popularity-based list. Avatar service → show initials. Payment provider → fail the request honestly. The design point is that a fallback must never fabricate data that looks authoritative — degrading a balance to a cached value without saying so is worse than an error.

Per dependency
payments:      timeout 2s   retries 0 (not idempotent)  breaker on  bulkhead 20
recommendations: timeout 300ms retries 1 + jitter      breaker on  bulkhead 10
                 fallback: popularity list
avatars:       timeout 200ms  retries 1                breaker on  bulkhead 5
                 fallback: initials

retry backoff: base * 2^attempt * random(0.5, 1.5), capped, max 3 attempts
retry at ONE layer only - nested retries multiply
Follow-ups they will ask

When should you not retry at all?

Non-idempotent operations without an idempotency key, and any 4xx — a 400 or 422 will fail identically every time, so retrying just wastes capacity. Retry 429, 503 and timeouts; do not retry validation errors.

What trips a circuit breaker?

An error rate or slow-call rate above a threshold across a rolling window with a minimum call volume, so one failure among three calls does not trip it. Slow-call rate matters as much as errors — a dependency answering in 10 s is failing even if it returns 200.

How do you test that any of this works?

Fault injection: add latency and errors to a dependency in a staging environment or a small production slice and verify the breaker opens, the fallback appears, and the rest of the page still works. Untested resilience config is usually misconfigured.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

First establish which of three problems you have, because the fixes are entirely different: too many renders, renders that are individually too slow, or a blocked main thread that is not React's fault at all. Guessing here is why most performance work achieves nothing.

Use the React DevTools Profiler. Record the interaction, then read the commit list: the flame graph shows what rendered and how long each took, the ranked chart sorts by duration. For each expensive component, DevTools tells you why it rendered — props changed, state changed, parent re-rendered, or a hook changed. That single piece of information usually points straight at the fix.

Too many renders → the cause is almost always identity: an inline object or function prop defeating React.memo, a context whose value is recreated each render, or state placed too high so an unrelated change re-renders a large subtree. Fix by stabilizing identities, splitting context, moving state down, or adopting selector-based subscriptions. Renders too slow → the component is doing too much work: virtualize long lists, memoize expensive derivations, or move the computation off the render path. Main thread blocked → the cost is not React: a long task parsing JSON, a synchronous layout thrash, or a heavy third-party script. Use the browser Performance panel, not the React profiler, and consider a Web Worker.

Core Web Vitals for interactivity: INP (Interaction to Next Paint) replaced FID and measures the full latency from interaction to the next painted frame — input delay, processing, and presentation — so long tasks and expensive renders both show up in it. LCP is usually an image, font, or render-blocking resource problem rather than a React problem. CLS comes from unsized media and content injected above existing content.

Close with the discipline: measure in the field, not just the lab. Lab profiling on a fast laptop hides the p75 experience on a mid-range Android. Ship RUM (web-vitals library) and set your targets on the field percentiles, because that is what users actually have.

Diagnosis
React DevTools Profiler -> record interaction
  many small renders        -> identity problem (memo defeated, context, state too high)
  one long render           -> virtualize / memoize the derivation
  nothing renders, still slow-> not React: Performance panel, look for long tasks

web-vitals in production:
  onINP(send)   # interactivity - long tasks + heavy renders
  onLCP(send)   # usually image/font/render-blocking, not React
  onCLS(send)   # unsized media, injected content
Follow-ups they will ask

Why did INP replace FID?

FID measured only the delay before the handler started, so a page could score well while the handler itself took 500ms and the UI froze. INP measures the whole interaction through to the next paint, which is what the user actually experiences.

What is the first thing to check on a slow list?

Whether every row re-renders when one item changes. If so it is an identity or state-placement problem, not a rendering-cost problem — and virtualizing will not fix it, it will just render fewer wrong things.

How do you stop a fixed regression from coming back?

A performance budget in CI on bundle size, and RUM alerts on the INP and LCP p75. Without a guard, the fix decays within a few sprints.

Trees - hard
  • Binary Tree Maximum Path SumHard
  • Serialize and Deserialize Binary TreeHard

Place one queen per row, tracking which columns and diagonals are taken in sets so each placement check is O(1).

CostO(n!) worst, far less with pruningReach for itConstraint satisfaction: sudoku, graph colouring, scheduling. The diagonal encoding is the reusable idea.
def solve_n_queens(n):
    cols, diag, anti = set(), set(), set()
    out, pos = [], []
    def bt(r):
        if r == n: out.append(pos[:]); return
        for c in range(n):
            if c in cols or r-c in diag or r+c in anti: continue
            cols.add(c); diag.add(r-c); anti.add(r+c); pos.append(c)
            bt(r + 1)
            cols.discard(c); diag.discard(r-c); anti.discard(r+c); pos.pop()
    bt(0)
    return out

# r-c is constant along one diagonal, r+c along the other. Memorise that.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The delegation model: loaders form a hierarchy — bootstrap (core JDK), platform (JDK modules), application (your classpath) — and each asks its parent first, loading the class itself only if the parent cannot. That is what stops you replacing java.lang.String with your own, and it is the security foundation of the whole model.

Application servers and plugin systems deliberately invert this (child-first) so each deployment can carry its own library versions. That is also where the pain comes from: the same class name loaded by two loaders is two distinct runtime classes, so casting between them throws a ClassCastException that reads like nonsense — "cannot cast Foo to Foo". Class identity is (name, loader), not name alone.

Static initialization order: static fields and static blocks run top to bottom in source order, once, lazily, on first active use — creating an instance, calling a static method, or reading a non-constant static field. Reading a static final compile-time constant does not trigger initialization, because javac inlines the value into the caller; that catches people debugging why a class never initialized. The JVM guards initialization with a per-class lock, which is exactly what the holder idiom exploits for a lazy thread-safe singleton with no synchronization in your code.

One trap: if a static initializer throws, the class is marked erroneous and every subsequent use throws NoClassDefFoundError — with the original ExceptionInInitializerError visible only in the first stack trace. In production that means the real cause is in a log line from hours earlier.

Why reflection is slow: access checks on every call, arguments boxed into an Object[], and — most importantly — the JIT cannot inline through a reflective call, so all the downstream optimizations that inlining unlocks are lost. It has improved a lot, but when it is genuinely hot, use MethodHandles or LambdaMetafactory to generate a call site the JIT can treat like a normal invocation. That is precisely what modern frameworks do internally.

Java
// holder idiom - lazy + thread-safe via the class-init lock, no synchronized
class Config {
    private Config() {}
    private static class Holder { static final Config INSTANCE = new Config(); }
    static Config get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }
}

class A { static final int X = 42; }   // compile-time constant
// int y = A.X;  does NOT initialize A - javac inlines the 42

// diagnosing a classloader leak (shows as Metaspace growth, not heap)
// jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats
// jcmd <pid> GC.class_stats
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does a classloader leak show as Metaspace rather than heap?

Class metadata lives in Metaspace (native memory since Java 8). A pinned loader keeps every class it loaded alive, so you get OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace after a few redeploys while the heap graph looks entirely healthy.

What typically pins a classloader?

Something with a longer lifetime than the app holding a reference into it: a static field in a parent-loaded class, a running thread, a ThreadLocal, a registered JDBC driver, or a shutdown hook. Deregistering drivers and stopping threads in a context-destroyed listener is the standard fix.

What is the bytecode verifier protecting against?

Hand-crafted or corrupted bytecode that would violate memory safety — bad casts, stack underflow, jumps into the middle of an instruction. It is why the JVM can run untrusted bytecode at all.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Three signals, three jobs. Metrics are cheap aggregated numbers — good for dashboards and alerts, bad for asking "what happened to this request". Logs are detailed per-event records — good for forensics, expensive at volume, and useless without structure. Traces tie one request's spans together across services — the only signal that answers "which hop was slow". You need all three, and the mistake is trying to make one do another's job (metrics with unbounded labels, or logs used as metrics).

RED for request-driven services: Rate, Errors, Duration — the three graphs that describe a service's health from the caller's perspective. USE for resources: Utilization, Saturation, Errors — for CPU, memory, connection pools, queues. Saturation is the one people omit and it is usually the leading indicator: a connection pool at 100% utilization with a growing wait queue predicts the latency spike before it appears.

SLI, SLO, error budget. The SLI is the measurement — "proportion of requests served in under 300 ms without a 5xx". The SLO is the target you choose, deliberately stricter than any contractual SLA. The error budget is the allowance the SLO implies: 99.9% over 30 days is 43 minutes. It turns reliability into a spendable resource — budget intact, ship faster; budget burned, freeze features and spend on reliability. That converts an argument into arithmetic.

Alert on symptoms, not causes. Alerting on high CPU wakes someone for a condition users may not notice; alerting on SLO burn rate — "at this rate we exhaust the month's budget in six hours" — wakes them only when it matters, and multi-window burn-rate alerts catch both fast outages and slow bleeds.

Cardinality is what kills metric systems. Every unique label combination is a separate time series, so putting a user id, request id or raw URL in a label multiplies series into the millions and takes the metrics backend down. Keep labels bounded — status code, endpoint template, region — and push high-cardinality detail into traces and logs, which are designed for it. And for traces across Kafka, remember context must be propagated in message headers, or the trace breaks at every async boundary.

Signals
RED (per service):  rate, errors, duration(p50/p95/p99)
USE (per resource): utilization, saturation(queue depth/wait), errors

SLI  = good_requests / total_requests           (measured)
SLO  = 99.9% over 30 days                       (chosen, stricter than the SLA)
budget = 43m 12s;  alert on BURN RATE, not on CPU

cardinality: labels must be bounded
  good: {endpoint="/orders/{id}", status="500", region="ap-south-1"}
  fatal: {user_id=..., request_id=..., url="/orders/12345"}
Follow-ups they will ask

What are the four golden signals?

Latency, traffic, errors, saturation — Google's formulation, essentially RED plus saturation. Either framing is fine as long as you include saturation, which is the leading indicator the others miss.

How does trace context survive a queue?

You inject the trace and span ids into the message headers on publish and extract them on consume. Without that, every asynchronous boundary starts a new disconnected trace, and you lose exactly the end-to-end view you built tracing for.

What is the cheapest useful observability to add first?

Structured logs with a correlation id propagated through every hop, plus RED metrics per endpoint. That combination answers most incidents. Full distributed tracing is more valuable but more work, so it usually comes second.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Analyze before changing anything. Run source-map-explorer, rollup-plugin-visualizer or webpack-bundle-analyzer and look at the treemap. Almost always two or three dependencies dominate, and guessing wastes days on the wrong ones.

Tree shaking is dead-code elimination that relies on ES modules, because their imports and exports are statically analysable — CommonJS require is not, so a CJS-only dependency cannot be shaken at all. It also relies on "sideEffects": false in package.json: without it the bundler must assume importing a module might do something observable and keeps it. If a package genuinely has side effects (a CSS import, a polyfill), list those files rather than omitting the field.

The usual wins, in order of how often they apply. Moment.js → date-fns or Temporal, since moment bundles every locale and is not tree-shakeable. Barrel-file imports: import { Button } from '@/components' pulls the entire index and everything it re-exports; import the file directly. Icon libraries imported as a namespace instead of per-icon. Duplicate React or a duplicate library version from mismatched transitive dependencies — visible as the same package appearing twice in the treemap, fixed with a resolution or by aligning versions. Polyfills for browsers you do not support — check your browserslist, since a stale one can add hundreds of kilobytes for IE11.

Dynamic import boundaries handle what remains: split at route boundaries first, then split heavy leaves regardless of route — an editor, a charting library, a PDF viewer. Anything large used by a minority of sessions is a candidate. Do not over-split: dozens of tiny chunks create request waterfalls and are slower than a few well-chosen ones.

Then guard it: a bundle-size budget in CI failing on a delta against the base branch, so the 3 MB does not silently return over the next two quarters. Also measure what matters — total bytes is less important than what is on the critical path for first render, and compressed size is what users actually download.

Diagnosis
npx source-map-explorer 'dist/assets/*.js'      # look at the treemap FIRST

// barrel import pulls the whole index and its re-exports
import { Button } from '@/components';          // bad
import { Button } from '@/components/Button';   // good

// package.json - lets the bundler drop unused modules
{ "sideEffects": ["*.css"] }

// split the heavy leaf, not every component
const Editor = lazy(() => import('./Editor'));

# CI budget: fail on a delta, not an absolute number
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does a CommonJS dependency defeat tree shaking?

Because require is dynamic — it can be conditional or computed — so the bundler cannot statically prove which exports are unused. Prefer packages that ship an ESM build, and check the module/exports fields.

How do you find a duplicated dependency?

The analyzer shows the same package at two paths with different versions. Fix by aligning the version range, adding an npm overrides/yarn resolutions entry, or deduping. Duplicate React specifically causes hook errors, not just size.

Is total bundle size the right metric?

No — the right metric is compressed bytes on the critical path for first render, plus INP and LCP in the field. A large lazily-loaded chunk that nobody on the landing page downloads costs nothing.

Tries
  • Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)Medium
  • Design Add and Search Words Data StructureMedium
  • Word Search IIHard

DFS across a grid, marking cells visited on the way in and unmarking on the way out so other paths can reuse them.

CostO(4^L) where L is the path lengthReach for itWord search, path counting, island shapes with revisits. Mutating the grid in place avoids a separate visited set.
def exist(board, word):
    R, C = len(board), len(board[0])
    def bt(r, c, i):
        if i == len(word): return True
        if not (0 <= r < R and 0 <= c < C) or board[r][c] != word[i]:
            return False
        board[r][c] = '#'                       # mark visited
        found = any(bt(r+dr, c+dc, i+1)
                    for dr, dc in ((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)))
        board[r][c] = word[i]                   # RESTORE - this is the key
        return found
    return any(bt(r, c, 0) for r in range(R) for c in range(C))

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Java serialization turns an object graph into bytes with almost no code, and that convenience is exactly the problem. Deserialization constructs objects without running their constructors, so every invariant your constructor enforces is bypassed — an object can come back in a state it could never legally reach.

Worse, the byte stream decides which classes get instantiated. A crafted stream can drive a chain of readObject calls through classes already on your classpath — "gadget chains" — into arbitrary code execution. That is the root of a long line of critical CVEs in widely used libraries. The rule is absolute: never deserialize untrusted input. If you must, install an ObjectInputFilter that allowlists classes.

serialVersionUID is the compatibility contract. If you do not declare it, the compiler derives one from the class structure — so adding a field, changing a method signature, or even a compiler version change can alter it and break deserialization of previously written data with InvalidClassException. Declare it explicitly on anything you serialize. transient excludes a field from the default form, which is how you keep secrets and caches out — though it does nothing about the security problem.

Prefer an explicit format: JSON for APIs, Protobuf or Avro for internal messaging with a schema registry. All three have a visible, versioned schema, defined compatibility rules, and cannot be tricked into constructing arbitrary types.

Jackson pitfalls worth naming, since that is what you actually use: a missing no-arg constructor on a non-record type; LocalDateTime failing without JavaTimeModule registered; FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES breaking you the moment a producer adds a field — turn it off for consumers so you can evolve independently; and Lombok's @Builder quietly breaking deserialization unless you add @Jacksonized. Most importantly, never enable default polymorphic typing — it reintroduces exactly the arbitrary-instantiation vulnerability, and has produced multiple RCEs.

Java
class Session implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;   // declare it explicitly
    private transient String password;                  // never written
}

// if you truly must deserialize, allowlist
ois.setObjectInputFilter(ObjectInputFilter.Config.createFilter(
        "com.acme.dto.*;java.base/*;!*"));

// Jackson: tolerate new fields from producers, keep types safe
mapper.configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false);
mapper.registerModule(new JavaTimeModule());
// NEVER: mapper.activateDefaultTyping(...)
Follow-ups they will ask

What is a gadget chain?

A sequence of classes already present on your classpath whose readObject or field-setting behaviour can be composed to reach a dangerous operation. You did not write it and you cannot audit for it easily — which is why the defence is not deserializing untrusted data at all.

Does making a class Serializable have a design cost?

Yes — the serialized form becomes part of your public API. Every field name and type is now something external data depends on, which severely constrains refactoring. Effective Java treats implementing Serializable as a long-term commitment.

How do you evolve a JSON contract safely?

Additive changes only: new optional fields, never removing or repurposing existing ones. Consumers ignore unknown fields, producers never rely on a consumer understanding a new field immediately. That is the same expand-contract discipline as database migrations.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Deploy strategies first. Rolling replaces instances gradually — the default, cheap, but old and new run simultaneously so both must be compatible. Blue/green runs two full environments and switches traffic at once — instant rollback, but double the infrastructure and the database is still shared. Canary sends a small percentage to the new version and watches error rate and latency before proceeding — the safest for risky changes, and the one to name, because it detects problems with a fraction of users affected. Automate the rollback on a metric threshold; a canary a human must watch is a canary that ships at 2 a.m. unattended.

Feature flags are the crucial complement: they decouple deploy from release. Code ships dark, is enabled for internal users, then a percentage, then everyone — and disabling is instant with no deploy. That turns a rollback from a fifteen-minute pipeline into a config change. The discipline is that flags need an owner and an expiry, or you accumulate hundreds and the combinatorial state space becomes untestable.

Schema migrations are the hard half, because you cannot roll back data the way you roll back code. The pattern is expand-contract, and the point is that every step is independently deployable and backward compatible: expand — add the new nullable column, deploy; dual-write — write both old and new, deploy; backfill — populate historical rows in throttled, resumable batches; switch reads to the new column, deploy, verify; contract — stop writing the old column, then drop it, in a later release.

The rules that make it safe: never rename in one step (add, dual-write, backfill, switch, drop), every migration is forward-only and additive within a release, and the previous version of the application must run against the new schema — because during a rolling deploy it will. Adding a NOT NULL column with a default, or an index without CONCURRENTLY, takes a lock that stalls writes on a large table — those are the migrations that cause outages.

With Flyway, migrations are versioned, checksummed and immutable once applied; never edit an applied migration, add a new one. Long backfills belong in application code or a job, not in a migration that blocks startup.

Expand-contract
release 1: ADD COLUMN new_email TEXT NULL            -- expand (safe, additive)
release 2: write BOTH old_email and new_email       -- dual write
           backfill in batches (throttled, resumable, idempotent)
release 3: read from new_email, verify parity        -- switch reads
release 4: stop writing old_email
release 5: DROP COLUMN old_email                     -- contract

rules: old app version must run against the new schema (rolling deploy)
       CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on large tables (no write lock)
       never edit an applied Flyway migration - add a new one
Follow-ups they will ask

Why can you not just rename the column?

Because during a rolling deploy both versions run at once: the old code queries a column that no longer exists. A rename is a delete plus a create from the old code's perspective, and it fails instantly.

What makes a backfill safe?

Batched with a bounded size, throttled so it does not saturate IO, resumable from a checkpoint, and idempotent so a retry is harmless. Running it as a single UPDATE over ten million rows takes a long lock and cannot be interrupted.

How do you verify a canary automatically?

Compare error rate, latency percentiles and a couple of business metrics between the canary and the baseline over a fixed window, and roll back automatically if any breach a threshold. Comparing against the baseline rather than an absolute number handles normal traffic variation.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

CSR ships an empty shell and renders in the browser — simple, cheap to host, but poor first paint and poor SEO. SSR renders HTML per request on the server — good first paint and SEO, at the cost of server compute and TTFB dependent on your data. SSG renders at build time — fastest possible and CDN-cacheable, but content is fixed until the next build. ISR is SSG plus background regeneration after a TTL, giving static performance with periodically fresh content. Streaming SSR sends the shell immediately and streams slower regions as their data resolves, so LCP no longer waits for the slowest query.

Choose by content, not by fashion: marketing pages → SSG; a dashboard behind a login → CSR or SSR without much SEO concern; a product catalogue → ISR; anything where first paint matters and data is slow → streaming SSR.

Hydration is the client re-running the component tree over the server-rendered HTML to attach event handlers and rebuild internal state. The cost is that it is O(entire tree), not O(interactive parts) — so a page can be visible but unresponsive while hydration runs, which is precisely what INP measures. A hydration mismatch — server and client rendering different output, usually from Date.now(), Math.random(), locale differences or reading window during render — makes React discard the server HTML and re-render on the client, silently throwing away the entire benefit of SSR.

React Server Components attack the root cause. RSCs run only on the server, can access the database directly, and ship zero JavaScript — their output is a serialized description of the UI, not code. So the bundle contains only the interactive client components, and hydration cost scales with interactivity rather than with page size.

The constraints to state: props crossing the server-to-client boundary must be serializable (no functions, no class instances), client components cannot import server components as children except by composition, and pushing the 'use client' boundary as deep as possible is the main optimization — a client component high in the tree makes everything beneath it client too.

Choosing
marketing page          -> SSG (or ISR if content changes)
logged-in dashboard     -> CSR / SSR, SEO irrelevant
product catalogue       -> ISR (static speed, periodic freshness)
slow-data page, SEO     -> streaming SSR + Suspense per region

hydration mismatch causes:
  Date.now() / Math.random() during render
  reading window/localStorage during render
  locale or timezone differences between server and client
  -> React discards the server HTML and re-renders: SSR benefit lost
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you fix a hydration mismatch legitimately?

Render the deterministic version on both sides and apply the client-only value in an effect after mount, or use suppressHydrationWarning for genuinely unavoidable cases like a timestamp. Never leave it unresolved — the cost is a full client re-render.

Do RSCs replace SSR?

No, they compose with it. SSR is about producing HTML for the initial response; RSCs are about which components ever ship JavaScript. You typically use both.

What is the practical downside of RSCs?

A more complex mental model and a harder debugging story — the server/client boundary is a new thing to reason about, serialization constraints surprise people, and the ecosystem is still catching up. It is worth it when bundle size is a real problem.

Write the obvious recursion, then cache results by arguments. You get dynamic programming without designing a table or an iteration order.

CostTurns exponential into O(states × work per state)Reach for itYour first move on any DP problem. Get the recursion right, add a cache, and only convert to bottom-up if you need the space or speed.
from functools import cache

@cache                              # that is the entire optimisation
def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)

# Manual version, when arguments are unhashable
memo = {}
def solve(i, j):
    if (i, j) in memo: return memo[(i, j)]
    memo[(i, j)] = ...   # compute
    return memo[(i, j)]

# Design rule: the cache key IS your DP state. If the key is wrong,
# the DP is wrong.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Run the contracts as a list, since that is what the question wants, then the modern types.

equals — reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and false for null. hashCode — equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal ones may collide. compareTo — a total order that should be consistent with equals; when it is not, sorted collections misbehave, because TreeSet decides membership by compare, never by equals, and silently treats two distinct elements as duplicates. clone — the broken one: Cloneable is a marker with no clone method, the default is a shallow field copy that bypasses constructors, and it fights final fields. Prefer a copy constructor or static copy factory. toString — cheap to write, valuable in every log line, and must never contain secrets, because it ends up in logs you do not control.

Records generate a canonical constructor, component accessors, and correct equals, hashCode and toString from all components. They are implicitly final and cannot extend a class. What they do not give you is deep immutability — record Order(String id, List<Item> items) holds the caller's list, which the caller can still mutate. A compact constructor is where you validate and defensively copy.

Sealed classes name exactly which types may implement them, and each permitted subtype must itself be final, sealed, or explicitly non-sealed. The payoff is exhaustiveness: a switch expression covering every permitted subtype needs no default, and adding a new variant later breaks the build at every such switch — a compile-time checklist instead of a runtime surprise.

Together, sealed + records + pattern matching is Java's answer to algebraic data types, and the right tool for a closed domain: payment outcomes, order states, parse results. Use an enum when the variants are constants with the same shape; use a sealed hierarchy when each variant carries different data — an enum cannot give Approved an auth code and Declined a reason.

Java
sealed interface PaymentResult permits Approved, Declined, Pending {}
record Approved(String authCode) implements PaymentResult {}
record Declined(String reason, boolean retryable) implements PaymentResult {}
record Pending(Instant checkAfter) implements PaymentResult {}

String describe(PaymentResult r) {
    return switch (r) {                         // no default needed
        case Approved a -> "ok " + a.authCode();
        case Declined d when d.retryable() -> "retry: " + d.reason();
        case Declined d -> "final: " + d.reason();
        case Pending p  -> "check after " + p.checkAfter();
    };   // adding a 4th variant breaks the build HERE
}

record Order(String id, List<Item> items) {
    Order { items = List.copyOf(items); }        // compact ctor: validate + copy
}
Follow-ups they will ask

When is a record the wrong choice?

JPA entities (they need a no-arg constructor and mutable identity), anything with meaningful behaviour beyond its data, and anything needing inheritance. Records are for transparent data carriers — DTOs, value objects, sealed-hierarchy variants.

Why is clone considered broken?

It creates an object without running a constructor, so invariants and final fields are bypassed; Cloneable declares no method so the contract is untyped; and deep versus shallow is left implicit. A copy constructor is ordinary, typed, explicit code.

What does non-sealed mean?

It deliberately reopens one branch of an otherwise closed hierarchy for extension. It also means switches over that hierarchy again require a default, since the compiler can no longer enumerate the possibilities.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The inverted index is the whole idea: instead of documents → terms, store term → posting list of document ids (with positions and frequencies). A query for two terms then intersects two posting lists rather than scanning 100M documents. That is why search is a different system from your database, and why a LIKE '%term%' on Postgres does not scale.

Analysis happens at both index and query time and must match: tokenize, lowercase, strip punctuation, remove stop words, then stem or lemmatize so "running" matches "run". Language matters here, and getting the analyzer wrong is the most common cause of "why doesn't this match".

Ranking: BM25 is the modern default (TF-IDF's successor) — term frequency with saturation, inverse document frequency, and length normalization so a long document does not win by repetition alone. Real systems layer business signals on top: recency, popularity, click-through, and increasingly a vector/semantic score blended with the lexical one.

Elasticsearch sharding: an index is split into primary shards (fixed at creation — you cannot change the count without reindexing, which is the single most important operational fact) and each has replicas for availability and read throughput. A search fans out to one copy of every shard, each returns its top K, and the coordinating node merges. That fan-out is why over-sharding hurts: a query to 200 shards pays 200 round trips and merges 200 result sets.

Two more things to volunteer. Elasticsearch is near-real-time, not real-time: documents become searchable only after a refresh, by default once a second — so a write-then-immediately-search flow will miss. And it should not be your source of truth: index from your database via CDC or an outbox so you can always rebuild, because reindexing is a routine operation, not an emergency.

For typeahead specifically, do not use the full search path — use a completion suggester (an FST in memory) or a prefix trie, which are built for latency rather than relevance.

Inverted index
docs:  1 "fast payment gateway"   2 "payment ledger"   3 "gateway timeout"

index: payment -> [1, 2]
       gateway -> [1, 3]
       ledger  -> [2]

query "payment gateway" -> intersect [1,2] and [1,3] -> doc 1, then rank by BM25

Elasticsearch:
  primary shards  fixed at index creation (reindex to change)
  search fans out to every shard -> over-sharding costs latency
  near-real-time: visible only after refresh (~1s)
  NOT the source of truth - index from the DB via CDC/outbox, rebuildable
Follow-ups they will ask

How many shards should an index have?

Enough that each shard is a manageable size (tens of GB) and no more, because every query touches every shard. Start small — over-sharding a small index is the more common mistake and it is expensive to undo.

How do you reindex without downtime?

Write to a new index, then flip an alias atomically once it is caught up. Applications query the alias, never the concrete index name, which makes reindexing a routine operation with instant rollback.

Why is typeahead a different problem from search?

It has a much tighter latency budget, needs prefix matching rather than relevance ranking, and benefits from a purpose-built structure — a trie or FST held in memory — rather than the general query path.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Define it precisely first: independently deployable frontend applications composed into one product, usually split by team ownership. The point is deployment independence, not code splitting — if one team can ship without coordinating with another, you have micro-frontends; if you just have lazy-loaded routes, you have a modular monolith, which is usually better.

When it is worth it: multiple teams (realistically five or more) whose release cadences genuinely conflict, a large legacy application being strangled incrementally, or acquired products that must appear as one. The benefit is organisational, so if the pain you have is technical, this is the wrong tool.

What breaks. Shared dependencies: without care every micro-frontend ships its own React and you download it three times — Module Federation's shared-singleton config fixes this, but then version skew becomes a coordination problem, and two Reacts on a page break hooks outright. Routing: the host must own a contract for how children register routes and handle deep links and the back button. Shared state: cross-application state is the hardest part — the workable answer is a narrow, versioned event bus or a shared store exposed as a contract, not shared imports. Design consistency: a shared design system package is mandatory, and it becomes another versioned dependency everyone must upgrade. Performance: each boundary is a chunk load, and independent bundles duplicate common code.

The honest closing position: the costs are real and permanent, and most teams reaching for micro-frontends actually need clear module boundaries, ownership rules and a good CI pipeline in a single repo. Say that. If you do adopt them, keep the boundaries aligned to business domains rather than technical layers, so a feature change lives inside one micro-frontend rather than spanning three — otherwise you have distributed the deployment without distributing the work.

Module Federation
// host
new ModuleFederationPlugin({
  remotes: { checkout: 'checkout@https://cdn/checkout/remoteEntry.js' },
  shared: {
    react:       { singleton: true, requiredVersion: '^18.2.0' },
    'react-dom': { singleton: true, requiredVersion: '^18.2.0' },
  },
});
// singleton: true is mandatory - two Reacts on a page breaks hooks

// boundaries follow business domains, not layers:
//   good: checkout, catalogue, account
//   bad:  header, forms, tables
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the smallest team size where this makes sense?

Rarely below about five independent teams. Below that, the coordination cost you remove is smaller than the operational cost you add — versioning, shared deps, cross-app debugging and a more complex deploy story.

How do micro-frontends communicate?

Through a narrow, versioned contract: custom events on a shared bus, URL state, or a small explicitly-exposed store. Never by importing each other's internals, which recreates the coupling you split to avoid.

What is the alternative you would usually recommend?

A monorepo with enforced module boundaries, package-level ownership, and a CI pipeline that only builds and deploys what changed. You get most of the independence with far less runtime complexity.

Each state depends on a few earlier ones. Fill an array left to right, and usually you only need the last one or two values.

CostO(n) time, O(1) space after rollingReach for itClimbing stairs, house robber, decode ways, min cost to reach the end. The gateway DP pattern.
def rob(nums):
    prev, cur = 0, 0
    for v in nums:
        prev, cur = cur, max(cur, prev + v)   # skip this house, or take it
    return cur

# The full table version is:
#   dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i])
# Only two values are ever needed -> two variables, O(1) space.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Walk the toolchain in order, because the sequence is what is being scored — anyone can name jstack.

1. Which threads are burning CPU? top -H -p <pid> shows per-thread CPU. Take the hot thread's id, convert to hex (printf '%x\n' 12345), then jcmd <pid> Thread.print and find the matching nid=0x.... Now you know exactly what that thread is executing. Take three dumps a few seconds apart: a thread stuck in the same frame is a lock or an infinite loop; threads spread across many frames is genuine work.

2. Rule out GC. Check the GC log and correlate pause timestamps against the latency spikes. A GC death spiral — near-continuous collection recovering almost nothing — presents exactly as 100% CPU with terrible latency, and no amount of profiling application code will explain it. If it lines up, the problem is a leak or an undersized heap.

3. Check for lock contention. The thread dump shows BLOCKED threads and the owner of the monitor they are waiting on. Many threads blocked on one monitor is a serialization bottleneck; it also usually shows as low CPU with high latency, which is a useful discriminator.

4. The trap worth naming: pool exhaustion looks like a slow application. If threads are parked in HikariPool.getConnection or waiting on a bounded executor queue, CPU is low, the database looks idle, and p99 explodes. Check HikariCP's pending connection metric. The cause is usually a leaked connection (a transaction never committed) or one slow query holding connections, not an undersized pool.

5. Profile properly. JFR.start is built in, low overhead and safe in production; async-profiler gives a flame graph including native frames and avoids safepoint bias — the systematic error where a profiler can only sample at safepoints and therefore misses tight loops. The flame graph's widest frame is your answer.

Say the discriminator explicitly: high CPU with threads in application code is a hot code path or an infinite loop; high CPU with GC threads dominating is memory; low CPU with high latency is blocking — a lock, a pool, or a slow downstream.

Sequence
top -H -p $PID                     # 1. hottest threads
printf '%x\n' 12345                #    TID -> hex nid
jcmd $PID Thread.print | grep -A 30 'nid=0x3039'
#    take 3 dumps ~5s apart: same frame = stuck; different = working

grep 'Pause' gc.log                # 2. does GC correlate with the p99 spikes?
jcmd $PID GC.heap_info

#                                  # 3. BLOCKED threads + monitor owner
#                                  # 4. hikaricp_connections_pending > 0 ?
./profiler.sh -d 30 -f flame.html $PID   # 5. flame graph, no safepoint bias
Follow-ups they will ask

What is safepoint bias?

Many profilers can only sample when threads reach a safepoint, so they systematically attribute time to safepoint-reachable code and miss tight loops that never reach one. async-profiler uses OS-level perf events plus AsyncGetCallTrace, so its samples are unbiased.

High CPU but all threads show SocketRead — what does that mean?

That you are not actually CPU-bound in application code, so the CPU is going somewhere else — most likely GC. It also hints at a downstream slowdown causing threads to pile up. Check the GC log next.

How do you get a profile without shell access to the container?

JFR can be started at launch or triggered remotely via JMX, and the recording file can be pulled out or shipped to a collector. Many teams run continuous low-overhead JFR precisely so the data already exists when an incident starts.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Requirements first. Channels: push, email, SMS, in-app. 10M users. Per-user, per-channel, per-category preferences (including quiet hours and timezone). Deduplication so one event never produces two notifications. Rate caps so a user is not spammed. Delivery tracking for sent/delivered/opened/failed. Estimate before designing: if 10% of users get 3 notifications a day, that is 3M/day ≈ 35/s average and perhaps 350/s at peak — modest, but the fan-out cases (a broadcast to all users) are what actually size the system.

Architecture: producers publish a domain event to Kafka. A notification service consumes it, resolves recipients, checks preferences and rate limits, renders content from a template service, and publishes one message per channel to a per-channel topic. Channel workers (push/email/SMS) consume their topic and call the provider. Splitting per channel matters because their latency, failure modes and throughput are completely different — an SMS provider outage must not back up push notifications.

Idempotency keyed by (user_id, event_id, channel), enforced with a unique constraint. Delivery is at-least-once, so this is what stops a redelivery becoming a second push at 3 a.m. Dedupe also needs a semantic layer — collapsing ten "new message" events in a minute into one — which is where digesting comes in: batch low-priority notifications into a periodic summary, which serves both the rate cap and the user experience.

Reliability per channel: retries with exponential backoff and jitter, a DLQ per channel, and provider failover — two SMS providers behind an interface, with a circuit breaker so a failing one is bypassed. Respect provider rate limits with a token bucket per provider, not per user.

Tracking: providers report delivery asynchronously via webhooks, so the notification record has a state machine — queued → sent → delivered → opened, or failed — updated by webhook and reconciled by polling for providers whose webhooks are unreliable. Store this because it drives both product analytics and the decision to suppress a channel for users who never engage.

The fan-out case is worth raising unprompted: a broadcast to 10M users cannot be one synchronous job. Chunk it, spread it over a window, respect per-user quiet hours in their local timezone, and make it resumable — a broadcast that dies halfway must not restart from zero.

Pipeline
domain event -> Kafka "events"
   |
   v  notification-service (consumer)
      resolve recipients -> preferences -> quiet hours (user tz) -> rate cap
      dedupe on (user_id, event_id, channel)   UNIQUE
      render from template
   |
   +-> topic "notify.push"  -> push worker  -> FCM/APNs
   +-> topic "notify.email" -> email worker -> SES  (+ DLQ, breaker, failover)
   +-> topic "notify.sms"   -> sms worker   -> Twilio
            |
            v webhooks -> state machine: queued -> sent -> delivered -> opened
Follow-ups they will ask

Why one topic per channel rather than one shared topic?

Isolation. Channels have different throughput, latency and failure characteristics; a backed-up SMS provider would otherwise create lag that delays push notifications. It also lets you scale and tune consumers independently.

How do you honour quiet hours correctly?

Store the user's timezone, not an offset, and evaluate quiet hours in their local time at send time. Scheduled sends must be re-evaluated at delivery, because a user may have travelled or the rules may have changed since queueing.

What is the hardest correctness problem here?

Deduplication across retries and across semantically duplicate events. The unique constraint handles redelivery; collapsing genuinely distinct events that mean the same thing to the user requires a product decision about digesting, and that decision has to be in the design.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start by refusing the naive answer. A Table with props for sorting, selection, pagination, expansion and sticky columns becomes a forty-prop god component that every team fights. The API you actually want is a headless core plus composable subcomponents.

Headless core: a useTable hook owns the logic — sort state, selection set, pagination, column sizing — and returns state plus prop-getters. It renders nothing, so it is testable in isolation and reusable across completely different visual designs. This is the TanStack Table model and it is the right one to name.

Composition for markup: expose Table.Root, Table.Header, Table.Row, Table.Cell and let consumers assemble them, with a context inside Root sharing state. Consumers who need a custom cell write JSX instead of passing a renderCell prop through three layers. The tradeoff to acknowledge: composition makes the API implicit and harder to document and type than a flat prop list, and it is easier for consumers to assemble incorrectly.

Dual controlled/uncontrolled support per feature. Each feature takes an optional value plus onChange; if value is provided the consumer controls it, otherwise the component manages it internally. That way a simple table needs no state at all, and a table whose sort lives in the URL is equally supported — without two components or a mode flag.

Accessibility is part of the API, not an add-on: real semantics (role="grid" when interactive, aria-sort on sortable headers, aria-selected on rows), roving tabindex for keyboard grid navigation rather than 400 tab stops, and sort controls that are actual buttons. Building this into the core is the main argument for a shared component — every team reimplementing it will get it wrong.

Versioning: semver with a written breaking-change policy, deprecation warnings in development pointing at a migration note, codemods for mechanical renames, and a support window. Prefer additive changes with sensible defaults over a new major version — and track adoption so you know when the old path can actually be deleted.

JSX
// headless core: logic only, no markup
const table = useTable({
  data, columns,
  sorting,  onSortingChange,        // controlled if provided...
  // ...uncontrolled if omitted
  getRowId: row => row.id,
});

// composition instead of 40 props
<Table.Root {...table.getTableProps()}>
  <Table.Header>
    {table.headers.map(h => (
      <Table.HeaderCell key={h.id} {...h.getSortProps()} aria-sort={h.ariaSort}>
        {h.label}
      </Table.HeaderCell>
    ))}
  </Table.Header>
  <Table.Body>
    {table.rows.map(row => (
      <Table.Row key={row.id} aria-selected={row.isSelected}>
        {row.cells.map(c => <Table.Cell key={c.id}>{c.render()}</Table.Cell>)}
      </Table.Row>
    ))}
  </Table.Body>
</Table.Root>
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the cost of the headless approach?

Consumers write more markup, so simple cases are more verbose, and the API is implicit rather than discoverable from a props table. Mitigate with a thin opinionated wrapper for the common case, built on the same core.

How do you keep sorting and pagination server-side without changing the API?

Make them controlled: the consumer passes the current sort and page, and handles the change by refetching. The component does not care whether the data was sorted locally or by the server — which is exactly why controlled/uncontrolled duality matters.

How do you handle a breaking change across 40 teams?

Deprecate with a dev-time warning and a migration link, ship a codemod for the mechanical part, support both paths for a defined window, and track adoption via telemetry or a dependency scan. Removing before adoption reaches ~100% is how you lose your consumers' trust.
