  • Word Search IIHard

Trie + backtracking together. If you cannot finish, get the trie built and state the search plan.

Each item is taken once or not at all. State is (items considered, capacity used); iterate capacity downward to prevent reuse.

CostO(n · W) time, O(W) space rolledReach for itSubset sum, equal partition, target sum, and any 'pick a subset within a budget' problem.
def knapsack(weights, values, W):
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)
    for w, v in zip(weights, values):
        for c in range(W, w - 1, -1):    # DOWNWARD: each item used once
            dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - w] + v)
    return dp[W]

# Iterating upward instead makes it UNBOUNDED knapsack (reuse allowed).
# The loop direction is the only difference between the two problems.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode while collecting a profile — which methods are hot, which branches are taken, which receiver types appear at each call site. Tiered compilation then escalates: C1 compiles quickly with instrumentation still in place, and once a method is hot enough C2 compiles it aggressively using the profile C1 gathered.

Inlining is the enabling optimization — pasting a callee's body into the caller, which then unlocks constant folding, escape analysis and lock elision. Methods above a bytecode-size threshold are not inlined, which is a genuine argument for keeping hot methods small. Virtual calls are devirtualized when the profile shows only one or two receiver types; a megamorphic call site with three or more types stays an indirect jump and blocks all downstream optimization.

Deoptimization is the flip side: these optimizations are speculative, guarded by cheap runtime checks. If a new class breaks a monomorphic assumption, or an "uncommon" branch is finally taken, the JVM discards the compiled code, falls back to the interpreter, and recompiles with the corrected profile. That is why performance can visibly change minutes into a run.

Warmup is therefore real and operationally significant. A freshly started JVM is genuinely slower — interpreted, unprofiled, with a cold code cache. The consequences: ramp traffic gradually to new instances (slow-start on the load balancer) or pre-warm them with synthetic requests, because sending full production traffic to a cold JVM produces a latency spike that can cascade into upstream timeouts. During a rolling deploy, that means every replacement instance is a small brownout unless you handle it.

For benchmarking the same fact is why a naive microbenchmark lies: without warmup you measure the interpreter. JMH exists to handle this — warmup iterations, forking a fresh JVM per trial so one benchmark's profile does not pollute another's, and Blackhole plus @State to defeat dead-code elimination and constant folding.

Observing it
-XX:+PrintCompilation                                   # what gets compiled, when
-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining       # inlining decisions

consequences:
  new pod  -> slow start on the LB, or pre-warm with synthetic traffic
  hot path -> keep methods small enough to inline (~35 bytes for hot inlining)
  bench    -> JMH: @Warmup, @Fork, Blackhole, @State (or you measure the interpreter)

megamorphic call site (3+ receiver types) -> no devirtualization, no inlining
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does a megamorphic call site hurt so much?

It is not just the indirect jump — it blocks inlining, and inlining is what unlocks escape analysis, constant folding and lock elision. One polymorphic call in a hot loop can cost far more than the dispatch itself.

How does this affect canary deployments?

A canary instance is cold, so its latency will look worse than the baseline for the first minute purely from warmup. Compare after a warmup window, or you will roll back healthy deploys.

Can you avoid warmup entirely?

GraalVM native image compiles ahead of time, giving near-instant startup at peak-ish speed — at the cost of a closed-world assumption, long builds, and reflection needing explicit configuration. It is a real option for serverless and CLI, less so for a dynamic Spring app.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Capacity planning starts from the SLO, not from current usage. Work out peak QPS (average × peak multiplier, plus known events), the per-request cost in CPU and memory, and then how many instances that needs with headroom. Headroom is the part people skip: you size for peak plus the loss of one instance or availability zone, plus the queueing cliff.

That cliff is the reasoning to state: queueing delay grows roughly as 1/(1−ρ), so at 50% utilization you wait about one service time, at 90% about nine, at 95% about nineteen. A system "efficiently" running at 85% CPU is one traffic bump from a latency collapse. Target 50–70% for latency-sensitive services; batch systems can safely run much hotter because queueing does not hurt them.

Why CPU is usually the wrong autoscaling metric. For an IO-bound service, threads are blocked waiting rather than computing, so CPU stays low while latency climbs and the queue grows — you scale far too late, or never. CPU also lags: by the time the average rises above a threshold, requests have already been queueing. And in containers, cgroup throttling makes CPU readings misleading.

Scale on what actually saturates: in-flight request concurrency, queue depth or consumer lag, or request latency against the SLO. Those are leading indicators. Kafka consumers should scale on lag; a worker pool on queue depth; an HTTP service on concurrency or p99 latency. Use CPU only when the work is genuinely CPU-bound.

Finally, account for scale-up lag — image pull, container start, JVM warmup, cache fill, connection pool establishment. That can be one to three minutes, which is often longer than the traffic spike you are scaling for. So combine reactive autoscaling with predictive/scheduled scaling for known patterns (market open, a marketing send, month-end), keep a warm buffer, and make scale-down slow and hysteretic so you do not flap. And remember autoscaling the stateless tier just moves the bottleneck to the database — scale the whole chain or you have merely made the collapse faster.

Signals
scale on:            because
  in-flight concurrency  leading indicator, works for IO-bound work
  queue depth / lag      directly measures "falling behind"
  p99 latency vs SLO     measures what users experience
  CPU                    ONLY when genuinely CPU-bound

headroom: size for peak + loss of one AZ, target 50-70% utilization
  rho=0.90 -> ~10x service time queueing;  rho=0.95 -> ~20x

scale-up lag (pull + start + JVM warmup + cache fill) is often 1-3 min
  -> add scheduled scaling for known spikes; scale down slowly
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the danger of aggressive scale-down?

Flapping: you remove capacity, latency rises, you scale back up, and each new instance is cold. Use a long cool-down and a lower scale-down threshold than scale-up so the system is hysteretic rather than oscillating.

How do you find the per-request cost?

Load test a single instance to saturation and divide. Do it against realistic data volumes — a query that is fast on 10k rows and slow on 10M invalidates the whole model.

What breaks when you autoscale the app tier only?

The database. Ten new instances each open connections, and you exhaust the connection limit or overload the primary. Connection pool sizing and database capacity must be part of the plan, or scaling makes the outage arrive faster.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

LCP measures when the largest content element in the viewport renders — usually a hero image, a heading, or a large text block. Target is 2.5 s at the 75th percentile of field data. Almost always the fix is not React at all, which is the first thing to say.

Order of impact. 1. The LCP resource itself. If it is an image: preload it, set fetchpriority="high", and never lazy-load above the fold — loading="lazy" on the hero image is one of the most common self-inflicted LCP regressions. Serve modern formats (AVIF/WebP), correctly sized with srcset, and always set width and height so it reserves space (which also fixes CLS).

2. Remove render-blocking resources. Synchronous scripts and non-critical CSS in <head> delay first paint. Inline critical CSS, defer the rest, and add defer or async to scripts. A third-party tag manager in the head is frequently the single largest cost on the page.

3. Fonts. font-display: swap so text renders immediately in a fallback rather than being invisible (FOIT) — because if your LCP element is text, an invisible font is your LCP delay. Preload the woff2 you actually use, subset it, and self-host rather than adding a third-party connection.

4. Server and network. LCP cannot be faster than TTFB, so a slow server response or a missing CDN caps everything else. Use preconnect for essential third-party origins, and consider streaming SSR so the shell paints before the slowest query resolves.

Measure in the field, not the lab. Lab profiling on a fast laptop hides the p75 experience on a mid-range Android over 4G. Ship the web-vitals library, report to your analytics, and set the target on the field p75 — Chrome's own CrUX data is what search ranking uses, so it is the number that counts.

HTML
<!-- the LCP image: preload, prioritise, size it, never lazy-load it -->
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">
<img src="/hero.avif" width="1200" height="600" fetchpriority="high" alt="...">

<!-- fonts: swap avoids invisible text, preload the one you use -->
<link rel="preload" as="font" type="font/woff2" href="/inter.woff2" crossorigin>
<style>@font-face { font-family: Inter; src: url(/inter.woff2); font-display: swap; }</style>

<script defer src="/app.js"></script>   <!-- not render-blocking -->

// field measurement, not lab
import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS } from 'web-vitals';
onLCP(m => beacon('lcp', m.value));
Follow-ups they will ask

What if the LCP element is text rather than an image?

Then fonts and render-blocking CSS dominate. font-display: swap plus preloading the font, and inlining the critical CSS, are the whole fix — the text can paint as soon as the CSS is parsed.

Why is lazy-loading the hero image so damaging?

Lazy loading defers the request until layout determines the image is near the viewport, adding a full round trip after CSS and layout. For an above-the-fold image that delay lands squarely on LCP.

How do lab and field numbers differ, and which do you act on?

Lab (Lighthouse) is a controlled single run on your hardware; field (CrUX/RUM) is real users on real devices and networks. Act on field p75 — lab is for diagnosing a cause once the field data tells you there is a problem.

Items can be reused any number of times. Same table as 0/1, with the capacity loop running forward.

CostO(n · W) time, O(W) spaceReach for itCoin change (min coins and number of ways), rod cutting, integer break. Loop order decides combinations vs permutations.
def coin_change(coins, amount):
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [0] + [INF] * amount
    for c in coins:
        for x in range(c, amount + 1):    # FORWARD: reuse allowed
            dp[x] = min(dp[x], dp[x - c] + 1)
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] < INF else -1

# Counting WAYS: coins outer, amount inner -> combinations (order ignored)
#                amount outer, coins inner -> permutations (order counts)

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Direct ByteBuffers allocate outside the Java heap, in native memory. The advantage is that IO can read and write them without copying through the heap — the kernel can DMA straight into that memory — which is why NIO and Netty use them heavily. The cost is that allocation is expensive and, critically, they are freed only when the referencing Java object is collected, via a Cleaner. So if GC is infrequent (a healthy heap!), native memory can grow unbounded while your heap graph looks perfect.

Memory-mapped files (FileChannel.map) map a file region into the process address space, so reads and writes become memory accesses and the OS page cache does the work. Excellent for large read-mostly files and index structures; the caveats are that a mapping is not unmapped deterministically, page faults can produce unpredictable latency spikes, and on 32-bit or huge files address space becomes a constraint.

Zero-copy is FileChannel.transferTo / sendfile: data moves from the page cache to the socket without being copied into user space and back. That is exactly how Kafka serves consumers so cheaply — the broker does not deserialize or copy messages to send them, which is a large part of why it is fast.

Where it shows up in monitoring — and why it causes an OOM the heap graph cannot explain. Direct memory does not appear in heap metrics at all. The symptoms are: RSS far exceeding heap, or OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory, or in a container the kernel OOM-killing you (exit 137) with no Java error at all. Track it with Native Memory Tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then jcmd VM.native_memory), and always set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize explicitly so the failure is a diagnosable Java error rather than a silent kill.

The practical rule: direct buffers should be pooled and reused, not allocated per request — which is precisely what Netty's pooled allocator does — and the pool should be bounded.

Java
ByteBuffer direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024);  // native, off-heap
// freed only when this object is collected -> pool and reuse, do not allocate per request

// zero-copy: page cache -> socket, never through user space (how Kafka serves)
fileChannel.transferTo(position, count, socketChannel);

// diagnosing: heap looks fine, RSS does not
// -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m
// jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
// symptoms: OOM "Direct buffer memory", or exit code 137 with no Java error
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does a healthy heap make direct-memory leaks worse?

Direct buffers are reclaimed only when their Java wrapper is collected. If the heap is comfortable, GC runs rarely, so the native memory those objects hold is not released — good heap behaviour actively delays the cleanup.

When is a heap ByteBuffer the better choice?

For small, short-lived buffers and for data you will manipulate in Java anyway. Direct buffers pay an allocation cost that only repays itself when the buffer is reused and actually used for IO.

How is zero-copy defeated?

By touching the data — TLS encryption, compression, or any transformation forces it through user space. That is one reason enabling TLS on a Kafka broker measurably increases CPU.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Estimate first: 10 TB/day is roughly 116 MB/s sustained, and log traffic is spiky, so peak may be 3–5× that. At an average 1 KB per line that is ~120,000 lines/second. Seven days hot means ~70 TB of hot storage before replication. Those numbers immediately tell you this is a streaming problem with tiered storage, not a database problem.

Pipeline: an agent on each host (Fluent Bit, Vector) tails and ships; a buffer — Kafka — absorbs spikes and decouples producers from the index, which is the single most important component because it means an indexing outage does not lose logs or back-pressure into the application; an indexer writes to the hot store; and a lifecycle policy tiers older data to object storage.

The key design decision is what you index. Indexing every field of every line is what makes log platforms ruinously expensive. Index only the fields you search on — timestamp, service, level, trace id, a handful of dimensions — and store the raw message as an unindexed blob. That alone often cuts cost several-fold.

Structured logging is a precondition, not a nice-to-have: JSON with consistent field names, so you can query rather than regex. Include a correlation/trace id in every line, because the single most common query is "show me everything for this request", and that only works if the id was propagated through every hop including across queues.

Retention and tiering: time-based indices (one per day, or per hour at this volume) so expiring data is a drop, not a delete — deleting rows from an index at this scale is prohibitively expensive. Hot for 7 days in the search cluster, then warm, then to S3/Glacier queryable by Athena for the compliance tail.

Cost control is the honest closing point: sampling (keep 100% of errors, 1–10% of debug), per-service quotas so one misbehaving service cannot consume the whole budget, and alerting on ingest volume growth. Log volume grows silently until the bill arrives, and a runaway debug log in a hot loop is the classic cause.

Pipeline
app (structured JSON + trace_id)
  -> agent (Fluent Bit / Vector)  sampling, per-service quota
  -> Kafka                        buffer: absorbs spikes, decouples indexing
  -> indexer                      index ONLY searchable fields; message as blob
  -> hot index  (7d, time-based indices -> expiry is a DROP, not a DELETE)
  -> warm -> S3/Glacier (queryable via Athena for the compliance tail)

10 TB/day = 116 MB/s sustained, 3-5x at peak, ~120k lines/s
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is Kafka in the middle rather than shipping straight to the index?

It decouples the producers from the indexer. If the search cluster is down or reindexing, logs queue durably instead of being dropped or back-pressuring into application threads. It also lets multiple consumers — search, metrics extraction, archival — read the same stream.

What is the single biggest cost lever?

What you index. After that, sampling and retention. Teams usually discover this after the first large bill, and the fix is a schema conversation, not an infrastructure one.

How do you find a specific request's logs across ten services?

A correlation id generated at the edge and propagated through every HTTP header and message header, written on every log line. Without it you are correlating by timestamp, which does not work at 120k lines/second.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A single-page app never reloads, so anything you fail to clean up accumulates for the whole session — which for a dashboard can be days. That is the framing: in an SPA, a leak is not a slow crash, it is a slow degradation nobody attributes to memory.

What leaks, in order of frequency. Event listeners added to window, document or a DOM node without a matching removal in the effect cleanup. Timers — setInterval especially — that keep running after unmount, holding their closure and everything it captured. Subscriptions: WebSocket handlers, store subscriptions, IntersectionObserver/ResizeObserver/MutationObserver never disconnected. Detached DOM nodes held alive by a closure or a ref you stored in a module-level variable. Unbounded caches and arrays — an event log appended to forever, or a query cache with no gcTime.

Detection workflow, and this is the part worth rehearsing: open Chrome DevTools → Memory, take a heap snapshot, perform the suspect interaction several times (mount and unmount the component, navigate away and back), force garbage collection, take a second snapshot, then use Comparison view to see which constructors grew. Filter by Detached to find DOM nodes that are unreachable from the document but still referenced by JavaScript — the retainers panel then shows you exactly what is holding them.

The Performance panel's memory timeline is the quicker first check: run the interaction in a loop and see whether the sawtooth's floor rises. A rising floor after GC means a leak; a rising peak that returns to the same floor is just allocation churn.

The prevention rule is simple and worth stating as a rule: every addEventListener, setInterval, subscribe and observe must have its counterpart in the same effect's cleanup. StrictMode's double-mount in development exists precisely to make an asymmetric effect visible immediately. And cap anything unbounded — retained history, cached entries, accumulated log lines.

JSX
// every subscribe needs its unsubscribe, in the same effect
useEffect(() => {
  const onResize = () => setWidth(window.innerWidth);
  window.addEventListener('resize', onResize);
  const id = setInterval(poll, 5000);
  const obs = new ResizeObserver(measure); obs.observe(el.current);

  return () => {
    window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize);
    clearInterval(id);
    obs.disconnect();
  };
}, []);

// cap anything unbounded
setEvents(prev => [...batch, ...prev].slice(0, 500));

// DevTools -> Memory -> snapshot, interact, GC, snapshot, Comparison
//                    -> filter "Detached" for leaked DOM nodes
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is a rising floor the signal rather than a rising peak?

Peaks are normal allocation churn that GC reclaims. The floor after a forced collection is the live set — if that grows monotonically across identical cycles, something is retaining memory that should have been freed.

What is a detached DOM node?

An element removed from the document but still referenced by JavaScript — typically captured in a closure or stored in a module-level array. It keeps itself and its entire subtree alive. Filtering snapshots by 'Detached' finds them immediately.

Do query libraries leak?

They can if gcTime is set very high or infinite, because inactive query data is retained. The defaults are sensible; the leak comes from someone raising them to 'avoid refetching' without considering a long-lived session.

Two-dimensional DP over the two strings. Characters match, so take the diagonal plus one; otherwise take the better of dropping one character from either.

CostO(n · m) time, O(min(n,m)) space rolledReach for itDiff tools, edit distance, longest palindromic subsequence (LCS of the string and its reverse).
def lcs(a, b):
    dp = [[0]*(len(b)+1) for _ in range(len(a)+1)]
    for i in range(1, len(a)+1):
        for j in range(1, len(b)+1):
            if a[i-1] == b[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1
            else:                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
    return dp[-1][-1]

# dp[i][j] = LCS of the first i chars of a and first j of b.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

JPMS adds a layer above packages: a module-info.java declares what a module exports and what it requires. Without an export, even a public class is inaccessible from outside the module — strong encapsulation that packages alone never gave you. The gain is a genuinely enforced API surface and better dependency hygiene; the loss is that reflective libraries break unless you open packages, which is why most Spring Boot applications still run on the classpath as an unnamed module.

jlink builds a custom runtime image containing only the modules you need, so a container image ships perhaps 40 MB of JDK instead of 300 MB. That is a real deployment win and it works even for modest applications.

GraalVM native image compiles ahead of time to a native executable. The gains are dramatic where they matter: startup in tens of milliseconds instead of seconds, and much lower memory, because there is no interpreter, no JIT, and no class loading at runtime. That makes it compelling for serverless functions, CLI tools, and any workload that scales to zero.

What you give up is the honest half. It assumes a closed world — everything reachable must be known at build time — so reflection, dynamic proxies, resource loading and serialization all need explicit configuration (or an agent run to generate it). Build times go from seconds to minutes, which slows the inner loop. You lose the JIT's profile-guided optimizations, so peak throughput is often lower than a warmed-up JVM. And debugging and profiling tooling is less mature.

So the tradeoff to state: native image trades peak throughput and developer flexibility for startup time and memory. For a long-running Spring service handling steady traffic, the JVM usually wins. For serverless, CLI, or a service that scales frequently from zero, native image wins. Spring Boot's AOT processing and the Spring Native support have made the second case much more practical than it used to be.

module-info / native
module com.acme.payments {
    requires java.sql;
    requires transitive com.acme.core;
    exports com.acme.payments.api;      // internal packages stay inaccessible
}

# jlink: ship only the modules you use (~40MB runtime instead of ~300MB)
jlink --add-modules java.base,java.sql --output runtime

# native image tradeoff
#   +  startup ~50ms, low memory, small container
#   -  closed world: reflection/proxies/resources need explicit config
#   -  long builds, lower peak throughput, weaker tooling
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does reflection break under native image?

The compiler must know at build time which classes and members can be reached, in order to include them. Anything looked up by a string at runtime is invisible to that analysis, so it must be declared in reachability metadata or discovered by running the tracing agent.

What is Spring Boot AOT processing?

A build-time step that evaluates the bean configuration ahead of time and generates the reachability metadata and code needed for native image, removing much of the manual configuration that made this painful before.

When would you use JPMS in an application?

Rarely — the benefit is strongest for library and platform authors who need a genuinely enforced API boundary. For most services the cost of fighting reflective libraries is not repaid.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start with why the split exists. OLTP is optimized for many small, indexed, latency-sensitive transactions — row-oriented, heavily indexed, tuned for concurrency. OLAP is optimized for scanning and aggregating huge volumes — column-oriented, compressed, tuned for throughput. Running an analyst's GROUP BY over three years of transactions on your production primary competes for the same buffer cache, CPU and locks as the checkout path. That is the failure to prevent.

The naive solutions and why they fail: a read replica helps with load but the schema and storage format are still wrong for scans, and a long analytical query on a Postgres replica delays WAL replay and can cause replication lag or query cancellation. Nightly batch SELECT * exports put a heavy periodic load on the primary, miss deletes, and give you data that is up to a day stale.

Change Data Capture is the right answer. CDC reads the database's write-ahead log — the same stream replication uses — via a tool like Debezium, and emits an event per row change into Kafka. Three properties make it superior: it adds no query load on the primary; it captures deletes and every intermediate update, which polling by updated_at cannot; and it preserves commit order, so downstream consumers see a consistent sequence.

From there the stream feeds the warehouse or lakehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, Iceberg), a search index, a cache invalidator, and any other derived system — all from one pipeline, all rebuildable by replaying from the log.

The operational realities to name: the WAL slot must be consumed or the primary's disk fills up — an unconsumed replication slot is a genuine way to take down a database. Schema changes must be handled (a schema registry with compatibility rules). Initial snapshots of large tables need care. And the pipeline is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent — usually an upsert keyed by primary key, which is naturally idempotent.

CDC
Postgres WAL --> Debezium --> Kafka topic per table --> consumers
                                                          |- warehouse (upsert by PK)
                                                          |- search index
                                                          |- cache invalidation

why not polling by updated_at?
  - adds query load to the primary
  - misses DELETEs entirely
  - misses intermediate updates between polls
  - clock/ordering issues on concurrent writes

watch: an unconsumed replication slot fills the primary's disk
Follow-ups they will ask

Is CDC exactly-once?

No — at-least-once. Consumers must be idempotent, which for a warehouse means upserting by primary key rather than appending. That is naturally idempotent, which is why the pattern works so well.

How do you handle schema changes in the stream?

A schema registry with compatibility rules (backward-compatible additive changes), and consumers written to tolerate unknown fields. A breaking change requires a coordinated migration, exactly as it would in the database.

What if you also need real-time aggregates, not just a warehouse?

Add a stream processor — Kafka Streams or Flink — consuming the same CDC topics to maintain windowed aggregates in a low-latency store. That is the standard shape for near-real-time dashboards without touching the primary.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The premise to state first: performance regresses by default. Every sprint adds a dependency, a chart, a tracking script. Without an automated guard, a page you optimized returns to its previous state within a quarter and nobody notices because each change is individually small.

What to measure in CI. Bundle size per entry and per route chunk, compressed — that is what users download. Lighthouse CI on a handful of representative pages for LCP, CLS and total blocking time. Dependency count and size deltas, so adding a 300 KB library is a visible, discussed decision rather than an invisible one.

What fails a build. Fail on the delta against the base branch, not an absolute number. An absolute budget is either so loose it never fires or so tight it blocks unrelated work, and either way people start ignoring it. A delta budget — "this PR adds more than 10 KB to the main chunk" — is specific, attributable and actionable, and the PR author is the one person who can explain it. Make the check comment on the PR with the before/after breakdown so the conversation happens in review.

Lab metrics are noisy, so treat Lighthouse in CI as a coarse guard: run it multiple times and use the median, set generous thresholds, and never block on a two-point score change. Bundle size, by contrast, is deterministic and is the metric worth enforcing strictly.

The field is the real signal. Ship the web-vitals library reporting INP, LCP and CLS to your analytics, chart the p75, and alert on regressions there. That catches what CI cannot: real devices, real networks, real third-party scripts, and interactions that only occur in production. Set the SLO on the field number and use CI to prevent the obvious regressions from ever getting there.

Finally, make it owned. A dashboard nobody looks at is not a guard — put the chart in the team's regular review and give someone responsibility for the trend.

CI
# per PR - deterministic, attributable, blocks on a DELTA
- name: bundle budget
  run: npx bundlesize          # or size-limit; comment the diff on the PR
  # fail if main chunk grows > 10KB gzipped vs base branch

- name: lighthouse
  run: lhci autorun --collect.numberOfRuns=3   # median, generous thresholds

# nightly - fuller matrix
- full E2E, visual regression, Lighthouse on more routes

// production - the signal that matters
import { onINP, onLCP, onCLS } from 'web-vitals';
onINP(m => beacon({ metric: 'INP', value: m.value, route }));
// alert on p75 regression, not on individual samples
Follow-ups they will ask

Why block on a delta rather than an absolute budget?

Because a delta is attributable — this PR caused it, and its author can explain or fix it. An absolute budget fails on whichever PR happens to cross the line, which is often unrelated to the cause, so teams learn to bypass it.

Why is Lighthouse in CI unreliable?

Runner CPU contention makes scores vary by several points run to run. Use the median of several runs, set wide thresholds, and treat it as a smoke test — bundle size is the metric to enforce precisely.

What do you do when a necessary feature blows the budget?

Raise the budget deliberately, in the PR, with the reason recorded. The point of the guard is to make the cost visible and intentional, not to forbid growth.

The minimum insert/delete/replace operations to turn one string into another. Same grid as LCS, minimising instead of maximising.

CostO(n · m) time, O(min(n,m)) space rolledReach for itSpell check, fuzzy matching, DNA alignment, and 'one edit away' variants.
def edit_distance(a, b):
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    dp = [[0]*(n+1) for _ in range(m+1)]
    for i in range(m+1): dp[i][0] = i        # delete everything
    for j in range(n+1): dp[0][j] = j        # insert everything
    for i in range(1, m+1):
        for j in range(1, n+1):
            if a[i-1] == b[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]
            else: dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j],    # delete
                                     dp[i][j-1],    # insert
                                     dp[i-1][j-1])  # replace
    return dp[m][n]

Must coverThree-level cache of singletons enables setter/field circular refs; constructor injection cannot because the object does not exist yet - and that is a feature, it surfaces a design smell. Know @Primary/@Qualifier, @Lazy, and why field injection hurts testability.

StudySpring Framework — Core / IoC container →

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

IoC means the container creates and wires your objects instead of each class constructing its own dependencies; DI is how they arrive. The payoff is testability and swappability — your service depends on a PaymentGateway interface and neither knows nor cares which implementation the container supplies.

Bean lifecycle: instantiate → inject dependencies → BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization → @PostConstruct/afterPropertiesSet → postProcessAfterInitialization — which is where AOP proxies are created — then the bean is ready. On shutdown, @PreDestroy, for singletons only. Knowing that proxies are created in the post-processing step is what explains every @Transactional and @Cacheable surprise.

Scopes: singleton (one per container — so it must be stateless or thread-safe), prototype (a new instance per injection, and Spring does not manage its destruction), plus the web scopes. The classic bug is injecting a prototype or request-scoped bean into a singleton: injection happens once, so the singleton keeps the first instance forever. Fix with a scoped proxy or by injecting an ObjectProvider.

@Configuration CGLIB proxying: Spring subclasses your configuration class so that calling one @Bean method from another returns the existing singleton rather than executing the method again. Without that interception, @Bean A a(){ return new A(b()); } would create a second, container-unknown B. Setting proxyBeanMethods = false skips the subclass for faster startup — correct only when your @Bean methods never call each other, which is why Spring Boot's own auto-configurations use it.

Circular dependencies: Spring resolves them for setter/field injection using a three-level cache — it instantiates A, exposes an early reference to the half-built A, creates B with that reference, then finishes A. It cannot for constructor injection, because neither object can be constructed without the other. Since Boot 2.6 that fails at startup by default, and that is correct: a cycle almost always means a shared responsibility belongs in a third bean. Fix by extracting it, or by breaking the cycle with an event — @Lazy works but hides the problem.

Java
@Service
class PaymentService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;      // final, explicit, testable
    PaymentService(PaymentGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; }  // no @Autowired
}
var svc = new PaymentService(new FakeGateway());   // unit test needs no Spring

@Configuration                       // proxied: a() gets the singleton b()
class AppConfig {
    @Bean A a() { return new A(b()); }
    @Bean B b() { return new B(); }
}

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)   // faster; take deps as parameters instead
class Lite { @Bean A a(B b) { return new A(b); } @Bean B b() { return new B(); } }
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is constructor injection the right default?

Dependencies are explicit and mandatory, fields can be final (so the object is immutable and safely publishable), missing beans fail at startup rather than at first use, and the class can be instantiated in a test with plain new. It also makes a bloated constructor visibly painful, which pressures you to split the class.

Why can a @Configuration class not be final?

CGLIB creates a subclass to intercept the bean methods, and you cannot subclass a final class. The same applies to any class Spring needs to proxy for AOP — a real gotcha in Kotlin, where classes are final by default.

What are the three levels of the singleton cache?

singletonObjects (fully initialised), earlySingletonObjects (instantiated but not fully injected), and singletonFactories (factories producing an early reference, which is also where a proxy is created if AOP applies).

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The two models. Fan-out on write (push): when a user posts, write that post id into every follower's precomputed feed list. Reads are then a single fast lookup — ideal, because reads vastly outnumber writes. Fan-out on read (pull): store posts once and, at read time, query the people you follow and merge. Writes are cheap; reads are expensive.

The arithmetic decides it. A typical user with 200 followers costs 200 small writes per post — fine. A celebrity with 50 million followers costs 50 million writes per post, which is not a spike you can absorb, and by the time it completes the post is old. So pure fan-out on write breaks precisely on the accounts that matter most.

The hybrid is the answer, and it is what real systems do. Fan out on write for normal accounts; for accounts above a follower threshold, do not fan out — instead, at read time, take the reader's precomputed feed and merge in the recent posts of the few celebrities they follow. Reads stay fast because the celebrity set per reader is tiny and their recent posts are hot in cache, and writes stay bounded because the expensive fan-out never happens.

Storage: the feed itself is a capped list per user — a Redis sorted set of post ids scored by time, holding a few hundred entries — not the post content. Hydrate content from a separate store or cache at read time, so one post edit does not require rewriting 50 million feed entries. Only materialize feeds for active users; computing feeds for accounts that have not opened the app in a year is pure waste, so materialize lazily on login for dormant users.

Ranking and pagination: once the feed is ranked rather than chronological, pagination by offset breaks as new items arrive. Use a cursor anchored to a position in the ranked set, and consider snapshotting the ranked feed for the duration of a session so scrolling is stable. Finally, mention cache warming and the thundering herd on a popular post — and that the fan-out job must be idempotent, since it will be retried.

Hybrid
on write:
  if author.followers < THRESHOLD (say 10k):
      for each follower: ZADD feed:{follower} score=ts member=post_id   # push
  else:
      skip fan-out                                                      # celebrity

on read:
  ids = ZREVRANGE feed:{user} cursor..limit                # precomputed
  ids += recent posts of the celebrities this user follows # merged at read time
  merge by score, then hydrate content from cache

feed holds IDs only, capped (~500) - never the post content
Follow-ups they will ask

Where do you set the celebrity threshold?

Wherever the write amplification becomes unacceptable for your infrastructure — often somewhere between 10k and 100k followers. It is a tunable operational number, not a product concept, and it should be adjustable without a deploy.

What happens when a user follows someone new?

You do not backfill their whole history into the feed — that is expensive and rarely wanted. New posts arrive through the normal path, and the merge step naturally picks up recent activity. Some systems backfill a small window.

How do you handle deletes and blocks?

Filter at read time rather than trying to remove entries from millions of precomputed feeds. The feed is a list of candidate ids; visibility and blocking are applied during hydration, which also keeps the fan-out write path simple.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Compound components share implicit state through context so consumers assemble the markup themselves: <Select> holds the state and <Select.Trigger>, <Select.Option> read it. The consumer controls structure, ordering and styling without the parent exposing a prop for every variation.

Headless components go further: a hook owns behaviour, state and accessibility and returns state plus prop-getters, rendering nothing. The consumer owns 100% of the markup. That is the TanStack/Radix-primitives model, and it is what lets one behavioural implementation serve completely different visual designs.

Refactoring a 25-prop Select: identify which props exist purely to customise rendering (renderOption, optionClassName, showIcon, emptyMessage) — those become composition. Which describe behaviour (multiple, searchable, disabled) — those stay as props on the root. Which are state (value, onChange) — those stay, with controlled/uncontrolled duality so simple cases need no state.

The result is a small root with maybe six props, plus subcomponents. Adding a badge inside an option becomes writing JSX rather than requesting a new prop from the design-system team — which is the actual organisational win, and worth saying out loud: the goal is to stop being the bottleneck for every visual variation.

The tradeoffs, honestly. Composition makes the API implicit: there is no props table listing what is possible, so documentation and examples matter far more. It is harder to type well, and consumers can assemble it incorrectly — a Select.Option outside a Select must fail with a clear error, which means your context hook should throw a helpful message rather than returning undefined. And the flexibility can undermine consistency, which is usually addressed by shipping a thin opinionated wrapper over the compound API for the common case.

JSX
// compound: consumer owns structure, parent owns state via context
<Select value={v} onChange={setV}>
  <Select.Trigger placeholder="Choose" />
  <Select.Options>
    {items.map(i => (
      <Select.Option key={i.id} value={i.id}>
        {i.label} {i.isNew && <Badge>New</Badge>}   {/* no new prop needed */}
      </Select.Option>
    ))}
  </Select.Options>
</Select>

// the context hook must fail loudly when used outside
function useSelectContext() {
  const ctx = useContext(SelectContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('Select.Option must be used inside <Select>');
  return ctx;
}
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you keep consistency if consumers own the markup?

Ship a thin opinionated wrapper over the compound API covering the common case, and let teams drop to the primitives only when they need to. Most usage goes through the wrapper, so consistency holds by default.

What is the typing difficulty with compound components?

Relating child props to the parent's generic type parameter — Select.Option's value should be typed by Select's item type, and TypeScript cannot infer that across a static property. Usually solved with a generic factory function or by accepting a small loss of inference.

When is a plain props API still better?

For genuinely simple components with a small, stable surface — a Button, a Badge. Compound composition adds ceremony that only pays off when the number of visual variations is large and growing.

Topological Sort
  • Course ScheduleMedium
  • Course Schedule IIMedium
  • Graph Valid TreeMedium

The O(n²) DP is easy; the O(n log n) version keeps an array of the smallest possible tail for each length and binary searches it.

CostO(n log n) time, O(n) spaceReach for itLIS itself, Russian doll envelopes, box stacking, and 'longest chain' problems after sorting.
from bisect import bisect_left
def lis(a):
    tails = []                        # tails[k] = smallest tail of an
    for v in a:                       #            increasing subseq of length k+1
        i = bisect_left(tails, v)
        if i == len(tails): tails.append(v)
        else:               tails[i] = v
    return len(tails)

# tails is NOT the actual subsequence - only its LENGTH is meaningful.
# Use bisect_right for a non-decreasing (allows equal) variant.

Studyreact.dev — Escape hatches →
Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Everything surprising about @Transactional follows from one fact: it is implemented by an AOP proxy. Spring wraps your bean in a proxy that begins a transaction before the method and commits or rolls back after. Lead with that and the rest is derivation.

Self-invocation does not work. If a() calls this.b(), the call goes straight to the target object and never through the proxy — so @Transactional on b() is silently ignored. No error, no warning. The same reason it does nothing on private, final or static methods, and why a final class cannot be proxied at all (a Kotlin gotcha, since classes are final by default). Fixes: move the method to another bean, self-inject, or use AopContext.currentProxy() — the first is the only good one.

Rollback rules catch people out: Spring rolls back on RuntimeException and Error only. A checked exception commits unless you write rollbackFor = Exception.class. That default surprises almost everyone and is worth stating explicitly.

Propagation: REQUIRED (default) joins an existing transaction, so an inner failure marks the whole thing rollback-only — which produces the confusing "Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only" error. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the current transaction and opens a second one on a different connection, so it can deadlock against the first if both touch the same rows, and it consumes two pool connections for one request. NESTED uses savepoints. MANDATORY and SUPPORTS are for enforcing caller contracts.

Isolation defaults to the database's (Read Committed in Postgres), and raising it per-method is rarely the right tool — prefer explicit locking or an atomic UPDATE for the specific invariant.

The operational rule to close on: never make a remote call inside a transaction. You hold a database connection and its locks for the duration of someone else's outage, which converts a slow dependency into connection-pool exhaustion. Keep transactions short and confined to database work.

Java
@Service
class OrderService {
    @Transactional
    public void place(Order o) {
        save(o);
        audit(o);          // self-invocation: @Transactional on audit() is IGNORED
        gateway.charge(o); // NEVER: holds a DB connection across a remote call
    }
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void audit(Order o) { }
}

// checked exceptions COMMIT by default
@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
public void risky() throws IOException { }

// survive a rollback of the main transaction:
@TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you write an audit record that survives a rollback?

Either a separate bean with REQUIRES_NEW so it commits independently, or publish an event and handle it with @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT). Writing it in the same transaction guarantees it disappears with the rollback.

What does readOnly = true actually do?

Hibernate skips dirty checking and can avoid snapshotting loaded entities, and some setups route to a read replica. It is a real optimization on read-heavy endpoints and it documents intent.

Why does REQUIRES_NEW risk a deadlock?

It runs on a second connection while the first still holds its locks. If the inner transaction needs a row the outer one has locked, neither can proceed — a self-deadlock resolved only by the lock timeout.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Requirements: 1-1 and group chat, online presence, delivery and read receipts, correct ordering, and offline sync. Then the number that drives everything: chat is connection-bound, not request-bound — 10M concurrent users means 10M open WebSocket connections, which is a fleet-sizing problem (roughly 100k connections per node, so ~100 nodes) rather than a QPS problem.

Connection layer: WebSocket to a gateway tier, with a connection registry in Redis mapping user → the gateway node currently holding their socket. To deliver a message you look up the recipient's node and forward to it (via Redis pub/sub or direct RPC). This is the key structural decision: the gateway tier is stateful in exactly one way — which socket lives where — and everything else stays stateless.

Ordering: do not use client timestamps — clocks are wrong and adversarial. Assign a monotonic per-conversation sequence number server-side; clients sort by it and can detect gaps. Partitioning by conversation id in Kafka keeps a conversation's messages ordered while different conversations process in parallel.

Delivery guarantees: persist the message before acknowledging the sender, so a crash after the ack never loses it. Then receipts are a small state machine — sent (server persisted), delivered (recipient's device acked), read (recipient opened) — each a small update propagated back to the sender. Receipts are high-volume and low-value, so batch them.

Presence is the classic scaling trap: naive presence is O(users × contacts) updates. Use a heartbeat with a TTL key in Redis (online = key exists), fan out changes only to users who currently have that contact on screen, and accept coarse granularity — "last seen recently" rather than second-accurate.

Offline sync: the client stores the last sequence number it has per conversation and, on reconnect, asks for everything after it. That single design makes reconnection, multi-device and message history the same mechanism. Cap the catch-up window and fall back to a full snapshot beyond it. Group chat changes the fan-out arithmetic — for large groups, do not write per-member copies; keep one message log per conversation and track a per-member read cursor.

Architecture
client --WS--> gateway node (holds socket)
                 registry: Redis  user_id -> node_id   (TTL, heartbeat)

send:
  1. persist message with per-conversation seq (monotonic, server-assigned)
  2. ack the sender          <- only AFTER persistence
  3. look up recipient node -> forward -> push over its socket
  4. recipient device acks  -> delivered; opens -> read (batched receipts)

reconnect:
  client sends last_seq per conversation -> server streams everything after it

presence: heartbeat -> Redis key with TTL; fan out only to watchers
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not just use timestamps for ordering?

Client clocks are unsynchronised and can be manipulated; even server clocks skew across nodes. A per-conversation sequence assigned by a single authority gives a total order within the conversation and lets clients detect missing messages.

How do you handle a user with several devices?

Track connections per (user, device) and keep a read cursor per device, delivering to all of them. Read state is usually reconciled to the furthest-read position, and the sequence-number sync handles each device catching up independently.

What is the hardest part to scale?

Presence and receipts, because both are high-frequency, low-value fan-out that grows with the square of social connectivity. The answer is always to reduce granularity and batch, not to make the fan-out faster.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Frame it historically — each pattern solved the same problem, sharing stateful logic between components, and each failed differently.

HOCs wrap a component and inject props: withUser(Profile). Problems: wrapper hell (five HOCs deep in the DevTools tree), prop collisions where two HOCs both inject data and one silently wins, no static typing of what is injected, and you cannot easily use values from one HOC in another's configuration.

Render props pass a function as a child: <Mouse>{pos => …}</Mouse>. This fixed collisions — the consumer names the value — but produced callback nesting: three render props means three levels of indentation, and the JSX becomes unreadable.

Hooks won because they compose linearly rather than by nesting. Three hooks are three lines, not three levels; each names its own values, so collisions are impossible; there is no wrapper component, so the tree stays flat and the DevTools output is readable; and the types flow naturally. Crucially, hooks share logic without dictating structure, which is what both earlier patterns inevitably did.

Where a HOC is still right: cross-cutting concerns applied at a boundary rather than inside a component — withErrorBoundary (error boundaries must still be classes, so a hook cannot express it), route guards, instrumentation and profiling wrappers, and framework integrations like React.memo and forwardRef, which are themselves HOCs. The distinguishing test: if you are wrapping to add behaviour around a component, a HOC fits; if you are sharing logic inside it, use a hook.

Render props still have a narrow niche too — when the consumer must control where in the markup something renders, which is the same problem compound components solve more ergonomically.

JSX
// HOC: wrapper hell + prop collisions
export default withRouter(withUser(withTheme(Profile)));

// render props: callback nesting
<User>{user => <Theme>{theme => <Router>{r => <Profile .../>}</Router>}</Theme>}</User>

// hooks: linear, named, flat
function Profile() {
  const user  = useUser();
  const theme = useTheme();
  const nav   = useNavigate();
}

// HOC still correct at a boundary - error boundaries must be classes
export default withErrorBoundary(Widget, { fallback: <WidgetError /> });
Follow-ups they will ask

Why can an error boundary not be a hook?

There is no hook equivalent of componentDidCatch/getDerivedStateFromError — React has not exposed one. So catching render errors still requires a class, which is why react-error-boundary ships a class plus a HOC wrapper.

Do hooks have a downside compared with HOCs?

Yes — a hook cannot wrap the render output, so anything requiring an extra element or intercepting rendering must be a component or HOC. Hooks also cannot be called conditionally, which occasionally forces awkward structure.

What replaced render props for layout control?

Compound components with context: the consumer places <Select.Option> exactly where they want it and the parent shares state implicitly, giving the same control without nesting callbacks.

Union-Find

  • Redundant ConnectionMedium
  • Accounts MergeMedium

An adjacency list — a map from node to its neighbours — is the right default. Adjacency matrices only pay off on dense graphs.

CostList: O(V+E) space. Matrix: O(V²)Reach for itEvery graph problem starts here. Building the list correctly (and remembering both directions when undirected) is half the bugs.

g = defaultdict(list)
for u, v in edges:

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The persistence context is the EntityManager for one transaction — a first-level cache and a unit of work. Entities are transient (new), managed (tracked), detached (context closed) or removed. Within one context, loading the same row twice returns the same object instance, which is why == works for entities inside a transaction.

Dirty checking is the consequence people forget: while an entity is managed, changing a field is enough — Hibernate compares against the snapshot taken at load and issues an UPDATE at flush. You never call save(). Powerful, and also a trap: an accidental setter inside a transaction writes to the database.

Flush is not commit. Hibernate flushes before a query that might be affected by pending changes, and at commit. That explains why your INSERT appears at a surprising point, and why a batch loop needs flush() then clear() — otherwise the context accumulates every entity and dirty-checks all of them on each flush, making the job quadratic.

N+1: one query for parents, then one per parent for a lazy association — 200 orders becomes 201 round trips. Diagnose by counting queries (hibernate.generate_statistics, or asserting query counts in tests), never by inspection. Fix per query with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, a DTO projection, or @BatchSize to collapse N queries into N/batch. Do not set the mapping to EAGER — that is a global decision for a local problem, and it makes every query everywhere load the association.

LazyInitializationException means you touched a lazy proxy after the context closed — usually during JSON serialization in the controller. OSIV (open-in-view, on by default in Spring Boot) hides it by holding the session for the whole request, and it is a bad fix: it holds a database connection through view rendering and any remote call, so under load the pool is exhausted by requests doing no database work, and it silently reintroduces N+1 during serialization where your service tests will never see it. Set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false, decide the fetch plan explicitly inside the transaction, and map to a DTO.

Java
@Transactional
void rename(Long id, String name) {
    Order o = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
    o.setName(name);              // dirty checking issues the UPDATE - no save()
}

// batch: without flush+clear the context grows and dirty-checking goes quadratic
for (int i = 0; i < rows.size(); i++) {
    em.persist(rows.get(i));
    if (i % 50 == 0) { em.flush(); em.clear(); }
}

// N+1 fixed for this query only
@Query("select distinct o from Order o join fetch o.lines where o.status = :s")
List<Order> findWithLines(@Param("s") Status s);

# application.yml
spring.jpa.open-in-view: false
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is EAGER fetching an anti-pattern?

It is a global decision made for one use case. Every query touching the entity now joins or issues extra selects, including the many that never need the association — and you cannot switch it off per query, whereas LAZY can always be fetched on demand.

What is MultipleBagFetchException?

Fetch-joining two List collections at once produces a cartesian product Hibernate refuses to build. Make them Sets, or fetch one collection per query.

Why does JOIN FETCH break pagination?

The join multiplies rows, so the database cannot apply LIMIT correctly to entities. Hibernate warns and paginates in memory after loading everything — which silently turns a paged query into a full load. Use a two-query approach: page the ids, then fetch.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The structural decision is the metadata/blob split: a database holds file metadata (path, size, version, owner, chunk list) and an object store holds immutable content. Never put multi-gigabyte blobs in the relational database — it destroys backup times, replication and buffer cache.

1 GB uploads mean chunking, not streaming. Split client-side into fixed-size chunks (4–8 MB), hash each one, and upload chunks independently and in parallel — which both saturates the connection far better than a single stream and makes retries cheap, since a failed chunk costs 8 MB, not 1 GB. Resumability then falls out for free: on resume the client asks which chunk hashes the server already has and uploads only the missing ones. Bytes go directly to storage via presigned URLs, never through your API servers, or a single upload occupies an application thread for minutes.

Deduplication works at two levels. Whole-file dedup by content hash: if the hash already exists, the upload is instant — the metadata row simply points at the existing blob with a reference count. Chunk-level dedup is what makes sync efficient: editing 1 MB of a 1 GB file changes a handful of chunks, so only those are uploaded and stored. That is delta sync, and it is the difference between a usable sync product and an unusable one.

Note the tradeoff you should raise unprompted: content-addressed dedup across users saves enormous storage but leaks information — an attacker can test whether a file exists by observing that its upload completed instantly. Mitigations are per-user dedup scopes or convergent encryption, and the honest answer is that it is a security/cost tradeoff to be made deliberately.

Sync across devices: each file has a version, and clients hold a cursor into a per-user change journal. On reconnect a client asks for changes since its cursor. Conflicts are inevitable with offline edits — the pragmatic answer used by real products is not automatic merge but keep both versions ("file (conflicted copy from a second laptop)"), because silently losing a user's edit is far worse than showing them two files. Finally, durability: replication for hot data, erasure coding for cold — the same durability at roughly 1.5× storage rather than 3×.

Upload + sync
upload:
  client: split into 8MB chunks, hash each (SHA-256)
  POST /files  -> server returns which chunk hashes it ALREADY has
  client uploads only the missing chunks, in parallel, via presigned URLs
  POST /files/{id}/complete -> metadata row: [chunk hashes], size, version

resume: repeat the "which do you have" call - already-uploaded chunks are skipped
edit 1MB of a 1GB file -> only the changed chunks move  (delta sync)

sync: per-user change journal + client cursor
conflict: keep BOTH versions, do not auto-merge, do not silently overwrite
Follow-ups they will ask

Fixed-size or content-defined chunking?

Fixed-size is simple but an insertion near the start shifts every subsequent boundary, so nothing dedupes. Content-defined chunking (rolling hash, Rabin fingerprint) picks boundaries from the content, so an insertion changes only the local chunks — meaningfully better for documents that get edited.

How do you garbage-collect unreferenced chunks?

Reference counting on the blob, decremented when a version is deleted, with a delayed sweep so a race between a delete and a concurrent upload referencing the same hash cannot delete live data. Delayed deletion is the safe pattern.

What if the client dies mid-upload?

The metadata row stays incomplete and a reaper cleans it up after a timeout, along with the orphaned chunks. Creating the metadata row first is what makes those bytes findable — otherwise you have data nobody can reference or delete.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start with the arithmetic that makes the case. A checkout flow modelled with booleans — isLoading, hasError, isPaid, isRetrying, isConfirmed — has 2⁵ = 32 combinations, of which perhaps six are legal. The other 26 are reachable by a mistimed update, and each is a bug someone will eventually report as "the button was disabled and the spinner ran forever".

A state machine inverts that: you enumerate the legal states and the legal transitions between them. idle → collecting → authorizing → (succeeded | declined) → retrying → authorizing. Anything not in the transition table simply cannot happen, so illegal states become unrepresentable rather than merely unlikely.

Why that is better in practice, concretely. An event that arrives in the wrong state is ignored by definition — a late payment webhook arriving after the user cancelled cannot resurrect the flow, because cancelled has no transition for it. Double submission is impossible, because authorizing has no SUBMIT transition. Those are two of the most common real bugs in payment UIs and the machine eliminates both structurally rather than with guard flags.

It is also testable and diagrammable. The transition table is a pure function you can unit-test exhaustively with no rendering, and it can be drawn — so a designer, a QA engineer and a backend developer can look at the same diagram and agree on what the flow does. That shared artefact is worth as much as the bug prevention.

The practical shape: useReducer is enough for most flows — a switch on (state, event) returning the next state. Reach for XState when you need hierarchical or parallel states, delayed transitions, or the visualizer. Keep side effects out of the reducer: the machine decides what state we are in, and effects are triggered by entering a state, which keeps it pure. And model the wait states explicitly — authorizing needs a timeout transition, because a payment gateway that never responds is a real state your UI must handle.

JSX
// legal states and transitions - everything else is impossible
const machine = {
  idle:        { SUBMIT: 'authorizing' },
  authorizing: { OK: 'succeeded', FAIL: 'declined', TIMEOUT: 'unknown' },
  declined:    { RETRY: 'authorizing', CANCEL: 'cancelled' },
  unknown:     { POLL_OK: 'succeeded', POLL_FAIL: 'declined' },
  succeeded:   {},                       // terminal
  cancelled:   {},                       // terminal - a late webhook cannot revive it
};

function reducer(state, event) {
  const next = machine[state.name][event.type];
  return next ? { ...state, name: next, ctx: apply(state.ctx, event) } : state;
}                                        // unknown event in this state -> ignored

// double-submit is structurally impossible: 'authorizing' has no SUBMIT
Follow-ups they will ask

Where do the side effects go?

Triggered on entering a state, not inside the reducer — an effect keyed on state.name, or XState's invoke/actions. Keeping the reducer pure is what makes the transition table exhaustively testable.

Is this overkill for a simple form?

Yes for two states. The threshold is roughly four or more states with non-trivial transitions, or any flow involving money, external systems, or retries — where an illegal state has real consequences.

What does XState add over useReducer?

Hierarchical and parallel states, delayed and guarded transitions, invoked services with cancellation, and a visualizer that generates the diagram from the code. For a flat flow, useReducer is enough and has no dependency.

Shortest Path
  • Network Delay TimeMedium
  • Cheapest Flights Within K StopsMedium
  • Swim in Rising WaterHard

Depth-first search from every unvisited node; each launch discovers exactly one component.

CostO(V + E) time, O(V) spaceReach for itCounting islands or components, flood fill, detecting reachability, and computing something per component.
def count_components(n, g):
    seen, count = set(), 0
    def dfs(u):
        seen.add(u)
        for v in g[u]:
            if v not in seen: dfs(v)
    for u in range(n):
        if u not in seen:
            dfs(u); count += 1        # each launch = one new component
    return count

# Deep graphs overflow the recursion stack. Either raise the limit or
# use an explicit stack: st=[start]; while st: u=st.pop() ...
