Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters, which sits before the DispatcherServlet. That single fact explains why @ControllerAdvice cannot handle security failures — they go to the AuthenticationEntryPoint (401) and AccessDeniedHandler (403) instead. Authentication establishes who you are and puts an Authentication into the SecurityContextHolder (a ThreadLocal); authorization decides what you may do, via URL rules or method-level @PreAuthorize.

Because the context is a ThreadLocal, it does not propagate to threads you spawn — async work runs unauthenticated unless you use DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor or pass the principal explicitly. That catches people constantly.

Authorization code flow with PKCE: the client redirects to the authorization server with a code_challenge (a hash of a random code_verifier); the user authenticates there; the server redirects back with a short-lived code; the client exchanges that code plus the original verifier for tokens. PKCE exists so an intercepted code is useless without the verifier — which is why the implicit flow is deprecated for everything, not just mobile.

Validating a JWT means: verify the signature against the JWKS (selecting the key by kid), and check iss, aud, exp and nbf. Critically, reject alg: none and pin the expected algorithm — accepting whatever the token's header claims is the classic algorithm-confusion vulnerability, where an attacker signs with HMAC using the public RSA key as the secret. Spring's resource server does all of this correctly; hand-rolled validation is where it goes wrong.

Revocation is the hard part, and the honest answer is that a JWT is valid until it expires — by design. The practical scheme is short-lived access tokens (5–15 minutes) plus a longer refresh token with rotation and reuse detection: each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, and if an already-used token is presented again you revoke the whole family, because that means one was stolen. Keep a denylist by jti only for emergencies, and remember that rotating the signing key via JWKS (with overlapping keys) is what limits the blast radius of a key compromise.

Java
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .csrf(c -> c.disable())                       // stateless API, bearer tokens
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
            .requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())            // deny by default
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(withDefaults()))
        .build();
}

spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri: https://issuer
// signature (via JWKS + kid), iss, aud, exp all validated for you
Follow-ups they will ask

When is disabling CSRF correct?

Only for a stateless API authenticated by a bearer token in a header, since a browser cannot be induced to add that header cross-site. If you authenticate with cookies, CSRF protection is mandatory.

What is refresh token reuse detection?

Each refresh rotates the token. If a previously-used refresh token is presented again, it means someone replayed a stolen one, so you revoke the entire token family and force re-authentication. It converts theft from unlimited access into a single use plus an alert.

Why anyRequest().authenticated() at the end?

Deny by default. A newly added endpoint is then secure until someone deliberately opens it. The reverse ordering fails open, which is how endpoints ship unprotected.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Sessions versus JWT is the first decision and it is a real tradeoff, not a fashion. Server-side sessions: the token is an opaque id, all state lives server-side, so revocation is instant and you can change permissions immediately — at the cost of a lookup on every request and a shared session store that must be highly available. JWTs: self-contained and verifiable without a lookup, so they scale statelessly across services — but they are not revocable before expiry, and any permission change is invisible until the token refreshes.

The practical resolution is the hybrid nearly everyone lands on: short-lived access JWTs (5–15 min) plus a long-lived, revocable refresh token stored server-side with rotation and reuse detection. You get stateless verification on the hot path and a genuine revocation point.

SSO via OIDC: a central identity provider issues an id_token (about the user) and an access_token (about permissions). Every product becomes a relying party, so account lifecycle, MFA and password policy live in one place. Federate to enterprise IdPs via SAML or OIDC for B2B customers.

RBAC versus ABAC: roles are simple and auditable but combinatorially explode — once you need "admin, but only for their own region, and only during business hours" you are inventing roles per combination, and past roughly fifty roles it becomes unmaintainable. ABAC evaluates a policy over attributes of the subject, resource, action and environment, which expresses those rules directly. The usual architecture is a policy engine (OPA, Cedar) with policies as versioned, testable code, evaluated locally in each service from a distributed policy bundle so authorization is not a network hop.

Token lifetimes and blast radius is where to finish. Access token minutes, refresh token days-to-weeks with rotation, and signing keys rotated regularly via JWKS with overlapping validity so rotation causes no downtime. If a signing key leaks, an attacker can mint tokens for any user until it is rotated and every issued token expires — which is precisely the argument for short access-token lifetimes and for keeping keys in a KMS or HSM rather than in configuration.

Architecture
login -> IdP (OIDC) -> access JWT (10 min) + refresh token (14 days, rotating)

request -> service verifies JWT locally (JWKS, kid, iss/aud/exp)   # no lookup
        -> authorization: OPA policy evaluated in-process from a policy bundle

refresh -> auth service: rotate, detect reuse (reuse => revoke the whole family)
logout  -> revoke the refresh token; access token dies within 10 min

blast radius of a leaked signing key = until rotation + max token lifetime
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not just use long-lived JWTs and skip refresh tokens?

Because you lose revocation entirely — a compromised token is valid for its whole lifetime and logout becomes cosmetic. The refresh token is what gives you a revocation point without a lookup on every request.

Where should permissions live — in the token or looked up?

Coarse claims (roles, tenant) in the token; fine-grained decisions evaluated at request time against current policy. Embedding detailed permissions makes them stale for the token's lifetime, which is exactly the wrong property for a permission revocation.

How do you handle logout across many services?

Revoke the refresh token centrally and accept that access tokens remain valid for their (short) remaining lifetime. For immediate global logout you need a denylist checked by every service, which reintroduces the lookup you were avoiding — so it is reserved for security incidents.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Token storage is the decision that matters, and there is no free option — say the tradeoff explicitly. localStorage is convenient and works across tabs, but it is readable by any JavaScript, so a single XSS anywhere on your origin — including in a third-party script — exfiltrates the token. httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie is invisible to JavaScript, so XSS cannot read it — but it is sent automatically, which reintroduces CSRF, handled with SameSite=Lax or Strict plus a double-submit token for cross-site cases. In-memory only is the most secure and loses the session on refresh, so it is paired with a refresh cookie.

The common production answer is a refresh token in an httpOnly cookie plus an access token held in memory: XSS cannot steal the long-lived credential, and the short-lived one dies with the tab.

Silent refresh needs a single-flight interceptor, and this is the part that is usually implemented wrong. When a 401 arrives, the first request triggers the refresh and every other concurrent 401 must queue on that same promise rather than each firing its own refresh — otherwise ten parallel requests trigger ten refreshes, and with rotation enabled nine of them present an already-used token and trip reuse detection, logging the user out. Queue, refresh once, then retry all the queued requests with the new token.

Route guards without flashing protected content is the second classic bug. On first load you do not yet know whether the user is authenticated, so rendering the protected page and redirecting on failure flashes private UI, and rendering the login page and redirecting flashes the wrong screen. The fix is an explicit three-state auth status — loading, authenticated, unauthenticated — and rendering a neutral shell or skeleton while loading. Never render-then-redirect.

Two more: capture the attempted URL and redirect back after login, and handle multi-tab logout by listening to the storage event or a BroadcastChannel so signing out in one tab does not leave another tab in a stale authenticated state.

JSX
// single-flight refresh: concurrent 401s queue on ONE refresh
let refreshing = null;
api.interceptors.response.use(null, async err => {
  if (err.response?.status !== 401 || err.config._retry) throw err;
  err.config._retry = true;
  refreshing ??= refresh().finally(() => { refreshing = null; });
  await refreshing;                      // all callers await the same promise
  return api(err.config);
});

// three-state guard - no flash of protected content
function Protected({ children }) {
  const { status } = useAuth();          // 'loading' | 'authed' | 'anon'
  if (status === 'loading') return <AppSkeleton />;   // neutral, not the page
  if (status === 'anon') return <Navigate to="/login" state={{ from: location }} replace />;
  return children;
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does the refresh have to be single-flight?

With rotating refresh tokens, a second concurrent refresh presents a token the first has already consumed. Reuse detection treats that as theft and revokes the family — so a naive implementation logs users out whenever two requests fail at once.

Is localStorage ever acceptable?

For low-risk internal tools where the XSS surface is small and understood, yes — but you must say that you are accepting the risk. For anything holding real user data or money, use httpOnly cookies and take on the CSRF work.

How do you keep tabs in sync on logout?

Broadcast the logout via the storage event or a BroadcastChannel and have every tab clear its in-memory state. Otherwise a second tab keeps making requests with a revoked session and shows confusing errors.

Advanced Graphs
  • Min Cost to Connect All PointsMedium
  • Reconstruct ItineraryHard
  • Alien DictionaryHard

BFS visits nodes in order of distance, so the first time you reach a node is via a shortest path. Only true when every edge costs the same.

CostO(V + E) time, O(V) spaceReach for itShortest path in a grid or unweighted graph, word ladder, minimum moves puzzles. Multi-source: seed the queue with all starts.
from collections import deque
def shortest(start, target, g):
    q, dist = deque([start]), {start: 0}
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        if u == target: return dist[u]
        for v in g[u]:
            if v not in dist:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1     # mark on ENQUEUE, not dequeue
                q.append(v)
    return -1

# MULTI-SOURCE: start with q = deque(all_sources) and dist for each at 0.
# 'Rotting oranges' and 'nearest 0' are exactly this.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design it as a contract you will have to keep for years — that framing is what separates this from listing HTTP verbs.

Versioning: URI versioning (/v1/orders) is the pragmatic default — visible, cacheable, trivially routable, easy to reason about in logs. Header or media-type versioning is purer but harder to debug and to cache. The more important discipline is to avoid needing a new version: additive, backward-compatible changes (new optional fields, new endpoints) cost nothing, and consumers must ignore unknown fields.

Pagination: cursor-based by default (?cursor=&limit=), because offset pagination degrades linearly with depth and is unstable under concurrent writes. Cap limit server-side; an uncapped page size is a denial-of-service vector. Return the next cursor in the body or a Link header.

Error contract: RFC 9457 application/problem+json — type, title, status, detail, instance, plus your own extension members such as a stable machine-readable code and a list of field errors. The two rules: return all validation failures at once, not just the first, and never leak stack traces, SQL or internal hostnames — log those server-side with a correlation id and return the id.

Idempotency: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST is not, so any POST that creates or moves money takes an Idempotency-Key header. Store the key with a hash of the request and the response, return the stored response on a repeat, and reject the same key with a different body as a client error.

Partial updates: PATCH with JSON Merge Patch is the usual choice — simple, but it cannot distinguish "set to null" from "leave alone" for nullable fields, so say that limitation; JSON Patch is more expressive and less ergonomic.

HATEOAS in reality: the theory is that responses carry links driving discoverable state transitions. In practice almost no client is written to follow them, so it adds payload and complexity for little benefit. Include links where they genuinely help (pagination, a next action in a workflow) and skip the rest — being able to say that with a reason is better than reciting the Richardson maturity model.

HTTP
POST /v1/payments
Idempotency-Key: 8f3c...             # required for money-moving POSTs

409 Conflict
Content-Type: application/problem+json
{
  "type":"https://api.acme.com/errors/insufficient-funds",
  "title":"Insufficient funds",
  "status":409,
  "code":"INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS",       # stable, machine-readable
  "detail":"Balance 250 is below the requested 400",
  "instance":"/v1/payments/abc",
  "traceId":"7c1f..."                # correlate without leaking internals
}

GET /v1/orders?cursor=eyJ...&limit=50     # cursor, and limit is capped server-side
Follow-ups they will ask

When would you choose gRPC or GraphQL over REST?

gRPC for internal service-to-service calls where you want a schema, code generation, streaming and lower overhead. GraphQL when many diverse clients need different shapes of the same graph and over-fetching is the real problem — at the cost of caching complexity and query-cost control.

How do you deprecate an endpoint?

Announce it, add a Deprecation and Sunset header, monitor which clients still call it, contact them, and only then remove it. Removing on a schedule without measuring usage is how you break a customer you did not know existed.

Why return all validation errors at once?

So a user fixes the form in one pass instead of discovering errors one at a time. It is a small server-side change that materially improves every client's UX, and clients cannot work around its absence.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Separate the three by who owns them and what concern they serve, because that is the distinction that actually matters.

API gateway — the edge, owned by the platform team. It handles cross-cutting concerns that must happen once, at the boundary: TLS termination, authentication, coarse rate limiting, routing, request/response logging, and IP allow-listing. The critical rule: no business logic. A gateway that starts aggregating and transforming domain data becomes a distributed monolith that every team must change together.

BFF (backend-for-frontend) — one per client type, owned by that client's team. Its job is aggregation and shaping: a mobile app on a slow connection wants one call returning exactly the fields it renders, not seven calls returning full entities. Because the web and mobile clients have genuinely different needs, giving each its own BFF avoids the compromise API that serves neither well — and, importantly, lets the client team change their own contract without cross-team coordination.

Service mesh — a sidecar per service, for service-to-service concerns: mTLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, traffic splitting for canaries, and uniform telemetry. It is infrastructure, not an edge component, and its value is that these behaviours become consistent and configurable without every team implementing them per language.

For the three client types: web and mobile each get a BFF behind the gateway; the partner API gets something different — a stable, versioned, thoroughly documented public contract with its own stricter rate limits, quotas and deprecation policy, because external consumers cannot be redeployed by you. Do not let partners consume a BFF; a BFF's contract is meant to change with its client.

Service discovery is the plumbing beneath all of it — usually the platform's DNS or the mesh's registry rather than something you build. The failure mode to name: a gateway or BFF that accretes logic becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure, so keep them thin and keep ownership clear.

Edge
                 +-- web BFF    --+
internet -> gateway |               |--> services (mesh: mTLS, retries, breakers)
  TLS, authN,    +-- mobile BFF --+
  rate limit,    |
  routing        +-- partner API (versioned, documented, stricter quotas)

gateway : platform-owned, NO business logic
BFF     : client-team-owned, aggregation + shaping, changes with its client
mesh    : service-to-service concerns, sidecar, language-agnostic
partner : external contract - cannot be redeployed by you, so version it strictly
Follow-ups they will ask

When is a BFF not worth it?

When you have one client, or when clients genuinely need the same data shape. It is another deployable to own, and premature BFFs add a hop and a team boundary for no benefit.

Do you need a service mesh?

Below roughly a dozen services, usually not — libraries (Resilience4j, an HTTP client with sane defaults) give you most of it with far less operational complexity. A mesh earns its keep when you have many services in multiple languages and need uniform mTLS and telemetry.

What belongs in the gateway versus the BFF?

If it applies to every client identically and must happen before anything else — authentication, TLS, coarse rate limiting — it is gateway. If it is about what one client needs to render — aggregation, field shaping, client-specific caching — it is BFF.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The goal is that components speak domain language and know nothing about transport. If swapping REST for GraphQL, or adding a retry policy, requires touching fifty components, the layer is missing.

One client at the base. A single configured fetch/axios instance with interceptors for authentication (inject the token, single-flight refresh on 401), tracing (propagate a correlation id), and error normalization — convert every failure into one ApiError type carrying status, a stable machine-readable code, field errors and the trace id. Without normalization every component invents its own error handling and the UX is inconsistent.

Typed by generation, not by hand. Generate types from OpenAPI or a GraphQL schema, or infer them from a Zod schema validated at runtime. Hand-written response interfaces silently rot the moment the backend changes a field, and TypeScript will happily agree with a lie. Validating at the boundary also means a malformed response fails at the seam with a clear message rather than as undefined is not a function deep in a component.

Domain hooks on top. Components call useInvoice(id) or useCreatePayment() — never fetch directly. Those hooks wrap the query library, own the query keys, and expose exactly what the UI needs. That is what makes the transport swappable: the hook's signature is the contract, and the component never sees a URL.

Cancellation and retries belong here too: the client passes an AbortSignal through, and the retry policy is defined once — retry idempotent requests on 5xx and network errors with backoff and jitter, never retry 4xx, and cap attempts. Defining that per call site is how you get accidental retry storms.

The test for whether the layer is right: a component file should contain no URL, no HTTP status code and no catch block full of transport concerns.

TypeScript
// base client: auth, tracing, normalized errors - configured once
api.interceptors.response.use(r => r, err => {
  throw new ApiError({
    status: err.response?.status,
    code:   err.response?.data?.code ?? 'UNKNOWN',
    fields: err.response?.data?.errors,
    traceId: err.response?.headers['x-trace-id'],
  });
});

// domain hook - components never see a URL
export function useInvoice(id: string) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: ['invoice', id],
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => api.get<Invoice>(`/v1/invoices/${id}`, { signal }),
    retry: (n, e) => n < 2 && e.status >= 500,     // policy defined ONCE
  });
}

// component
const { data: invoice, error } = useInvoice(id);   // domain language only
Follow-ups they will ask

Why validate responses at runtime if you already have types?

TypeScript types are erased at compile time and describe what you believe. A schema check at the boundary catches an actual contract break immediately, with a message naming the field, instead of a confusing crash three components deep.

Where should retry policy live?

In the client or the query configuration, once. Per-call-site retries multiply when layered with server-side retries and produce storms, and they are impossible to audit when scattered.

How does this help testing?

Components depend on domain hooks, which are trivial to mock, and integration tests can intercept at the network layer with MSW so the real client code runs. Both levels stay meaningful because the seam is explicit.

Order a DAG so every edge points forward. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes a node with no remaining incoming edges.

CostO(V + E) timeReach for itBuild order, course prerequisites, task scheduling. It also detects cycles — if you cannot emit every node, one exists.
from collections import deque
def topo(n, edges):
    g = [[] for _ in range(n)]; indeg = [0]*n
    for u, v in edges:
        g[u].append(v); indeg[v] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
    out = []
    while q:
        u = q.popleft(); out.append(u)
        for v in g[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0: q.append(v)
    return out if len(out) == n else []    # short -> there is a cycle

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Spring's cache abstraction is annotation-driven and backed by a pluggable CacheManager — Caffeine locally, Redis when it must be shared. @Cacheable returns from cache or computes and stores; @CachePut always computes and updates; @CacheEvict removes.

It is proxy-based, exactly like @Transactional, so it has the identical self-invocation trap: a call to this.cachedMethod() bypasses the proxy and the cache does nothing at all. Same for private and final methods. This is the single most common reason people say "caching isn't working", and naming it immediately is the strong answer.

Key generation is the next trap. The default key generator uses all parameters, so overloads and irrelevant parameters silently fragment the cache into entries that never hit. Specify key explicitly with SpEL. Also, @Cacheable caches null by default, which can pin a negative result — use unless = "#result == null" when that is wrong.

sync = true is the one to volunteer. Without it, N concurrent misses for the same key all execute the method — a cache stampede straight into your database, which is exactly the failure that turns a cache expiry into an outage. sync = true gives single-flight behaviour: one caller computes, the rest wait.

Redis-specific pitfalls: there is no per-annotation TTL — it is configured on the CacheManager, per cache name. Do not use JDK serialization for values: it locks entries to exact class versions, so adding a field breaks every cached entry across a rolling deploy, and it carries the deserialization attack surface — configure a JSON serializer and treat the cache format as a versioned contract. And decide what happens when Redis is down: by default an error propagates, so wrap with a CacheErrorHandler that logs and falls through to the method, because a cache outage should degrade performance, not availability.

For the 96% latency win, be ready to name the TTL, the invalidation strategy, and the worst-case staleness you accepted.

Java
@Cacheable(cacheNames = "rates",
           key = "#from + ':' + #to",     // explicit key - not all parameters
           sync = true,                    // single-flight: prevents the stampede
           unless = "#result == null")     // do not cache negatives
public Rate lookup(String from, String to) { return client.fetch(from, to); }

@CacheEvict(cacheNames = "rates", key = "#rate.from + ':' + #rate.to")
public void update(Rate rate) { repo.save(rate); }

// TTL lives on the CacheManager, not the annotation
RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig()
    .entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
    .serializeValuesWith(fromSerializer(new GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer()));
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is JDK serialization wrong for Redis cache values?

It ties the payload to exact class versions, so a field addition breaks every cached entry during a rolling deploy while both versions are live. It is also a deserialization attack surface. JSON keeps the format inspectable and evolvable.

What happens when Redis is unavailable?

By default the exception propagates and requests fail — a cache outage becomes an application outage. Install a CacheErrorHandler that logs and falls through to the underlying method, and add a circuit breaker so the database is not overwhelmed by the sudden miss storm.

Why does the self-invocation trap exist at all?

Because the proxy wraps the bean, and an internal this call never leaves the object. AspectJ weaving would intercept it, but it requires build or load-time weaving — so in practice the answer is to move the method to another bean.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Data structures are the point of Redis — treating it as a string cache wastes most of its value. Strings for cached values and counters (INCR is atomic). Hashes for objects, so you can update one field without rewriting the whole value. Sorted sets are the workhorse: leaderboards, rate limiters (score = timestamp, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to expire), delayed queues (score = due time), and time-ordered feeds. Sets for membership and unique counts. Lists for simple queues. Streams for a lightweight append-only log with consumer groups. HyperLogLog for cardinality at ~12 KB regardless of volume. Bitmaps for daily-active-user style flags.

Persistence: RDB is a point-in-time fork-and-snapshot — compact, fast to restore, but you lose everything since the last snapshot. AOF appends every write, with fsync policy deciding durability (everysec is the usual compromise, so worst case one second of writes). Most production setups run both. Say the honest framing: Redis is not a database of record — durability is best-effort, and designs that assume otherwise eventually lose data.

Cluster mode shards by hash slot (16,384 slots mapped to nodes). The consequence that catches people: multi-key operations only work if the keys are in the same slot, so transactions, Lua scripts and MGET across arbitrary keys fail. The fix is hash tags — user:{123}:profile and user:{123}:settings hash on the braced part and land together. Design key names for this from the start; retrofitting it is painful.

Distributed locking is the deliberately contentious part. SET key value NX PX ttl with a unique value, released only by a Lua script that checks the value first (so you never release someone else's lock), is fine for coordination. Redlock extends this across independent nodes, and Martin Kleppmann's critique is the one to cite: it assumes bounded clock drift and bounded process pauses, and a GC pause longer than the TTL means you believe you hold a lock you have lost. If correctness depends on it, you need fencing tokens — a monotonically increasing number the protected resource checks and rejects if stale. Redis locks are fine for "only one worker should do this job", not for guarding money.

Redis
# sorted set as a delayed queue
ZADD jobs <due_epoch> job_id
ZRANGEBYSCORE jobs -inf <now> LIMIT 0 100      # due jobs

# safe lock: unique value, released only by its owner
SET lock:order:42 <uuid> NX PX 30000
# release (Lua, atomic):
#   if redis.call('get',KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del',KEYS[1]) end

# cluster: hash tags keep related keys in one slot
user:{123}:profile   user:{123}:settings      # same slot -> MGET/Lua/txn work

# correctness-critical? use a fencing token, not just a lock
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is Redlock controversial?

It relies on assumptions distributed systems do not guarantee: bounded clock drift and bounded pauses. A stop-the-world GC pause longer than the lock TTL means another client acquires it while you still think you hold it. For mutual exclusion that must be correct, a fencing token checked by the resource is the only sound answer.

When would you use Redis Streams over Kafka?

When you already run Redis, the volume is modest, and you want consumer groups without operating another system. Kafka wins on retention, throughput, durability and ecosystem — Streams is the pragmatic small-scale option.

What is the memory risk with Redis?

There is no built-in bound unless you set maxmemory and an eviction policy. Without them Redis grows until the OOM killer intervenes. With allkeys-lru it behaves as a cache; with noeviction writes start failing, which is what you want if it holds queue state.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Choose by size, access pattern and consequence of loss — that is the framework, and each mechanism has one job it is genuinely good at.

localStorage: small key-value strings, synchronous — and that is the decisive fact. Every read and write blocks the main thread, so storing anything sizeable in it directly costs you INP. Use it for a theme preference, a collapsed-sidebar flag, a draft under a few kilobytes. Roughly 5 MB, string-only, so anything structured needs JSON round-tripping.

IndexedDB: asynchronous, transactional, indexed, and gigabytes of capacity. This is where structured data belongs — cached API responses, offline documents, a queue of pending mutations. The raw API is unpleasant, so use idb or Dexie. It is also the only option that will not block rendering.

Service worker Cache API: HTTP request/response pairs, so it caches at the network layer. It is what makes the app shell load offline, and it composes with strategies — cache-first for hashed assets, stale-while-revalidate for semi-static data, network-first for anything that must be fresh.

An offline-capable read path combines them: the service worker serves the shell and assets from cache instantly; the app reads data from IndexedDB and renders immediately; a background fetch updates IndexedDB and the UI re-renders when it lands. The user sees content instantly, online or off — which is the actual goal, not offline as a feature.

The hard part is writes, and you should name it unprompted: queue mutations in IndexedDB with a client-generated id, apply them optimistically, and replay on reconnect (Background Sync where available). Then conflict resolution — last-writer-wins silently loses data, so either version the entity and surface the conflict, or keep both versions. And never present stale data as authoritative: show when it was last synced. A cached balance displayed as current is worse than showing nothing.

Finally: all of this is per-origin and evictable — browsers clear storage under pressure, and Safari has aggressive limits — so it is a cache, never the system of record.

JSX
// localStorage: small, synchronous, main-thread blocking -> preferences only
localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark');

// IndexedDB: structured, async, large -> cached data and a mutation queue
await db.put('invoices', invoice);
await db.add('outbox', { id: crypto.randomUUID(), op: 'update', payload });

// service worker: network-layer caching for the shell
registerRoute(({request}) => request.destination === 'document',
              new NetworkFirst());
registerRoute(({url}) => url.pathname.startsWith('/static/'),
              new CacheFirst());     // hashed assets: safe forever

// read path: render from IndexedDB immediately, revalidate in the background
// write path: optimistic + outbox + replay on reconnect + explicit conflict handling
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is localStorage's synchronous API such a problem?

It blocks the main thread on every access, including during rendering. A few hundred kilobytes of JSON parsed on startup is a measurable delay before first paint, and it shows up directly in INP for anything reading it in a handler.

How do you replay the outbox safely?

Each queued mutation carries a client-generated idempotency key, so replaying one the server already applied is harmless. Replay in order, stop on a conflict rather than plowing through, and surface conflicts to the user.

Can you rely on this storage persisting?

No. Browsers evict under storage pressure and Safari caps and expires it aggressively. Request persistent storage where supported, but design for the cache being empty on any load — it is an optimization, not durability.

In a directed graph, use three colours and look for an edge back into the current recursion path. In an undirected graph, any edge to a visited non-parent node is a cycle.

CostO(V + E) timeReach for itDeadlock detection, dependency validation, and 'is this a valid tree' (connected with exactly n-1 edges).
# DIRECTED: white 0 / grey 1 (on the current path) / black 2 (done)
def has_cycle_directed(n, g):
    color = [0]*n
    def dfs(u):
        color[u] = 1
        for v in g[u]:
            if color[v] == 1: return True      # back edge -> cycle
            if color[v] == 0 and dfs(v): return True
        color[u] = 2
        return False
    return any(color[u] == 0 and dfs(u) for u in range(n))

# UNDIRECTED: track the parent; an edge to a seen node that is not the
# parent is a cycle. Union-Find also works and is often shorter.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design the API first, out loud: get(key), set(key, value), delete(key), plus begin(), commit(), rollback() — with nested transactions, so begin can be called inside an open transaction.

The core insight is a stack of change-sets. The committed data lives in a base map. Each begin pushes a new empty overlay map onto a stack. A set writes into the top overlay only. A get walks the stack from the top down, returning the first overlay that contains the key, and falls through to the base map if none do. rollback pops the top overlay and discards it. commit merges the top overlay down one level — into the overlay beneath it, or into the base map if it was the outermost.

That merge-down-one-level detail is what makes nesting correct: committing an inner transaction must not make its changes durable, only visible to the enclosing transaction. Getting that wrong is the most common failure in this exercise.

Deletion needs a tombstone. If delete simply removes the key from the overlay, get falls through and finds the old value in the base map — so a delete inside a transaction appears not to work. Store an explicit sentinel meaning "deleted here", and treat it as absent on read.

Complexity: set, delete and begin are O(1); get is O(depth), which is fine since transaction nesting is shallow; commit is O(size of the merged overlay). Error cases: commit or rollback with no open transaction should throw rather than silently succeed.

Then answer the follow-up before it is asked: making it thread-safe is not just wrapping it in a lock. A single global lock serializes everything and gives you serializable isolation trivially. Per-key locking is faster but reintroduces deadlock, needing lock ordering. And be precise about what you have actually built — this is read-committed within your own transaction only, with no isolation between concurrent transactions and no durability. Saying that shows you understand what a real database provides.

Java
class TxStore {
    private static final Object TOMBSTONE = new Object();
    private final Map<String,Object> base = new HashMap<>();
    private final Deque<Map<String,Object>> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    void begin() { stack.push(new HashMap<>()); }

    String get(String k) {
        for (Map<String,Object> layer : stack)          // top-down
            if (layer.containsKey(k)) {
                Object v = layer.get(k);
                return v == TOMBSTONE ? null : (String) v;   // tombstone = deleted
            }
        return (String) base.get(k);
    }
    void set(String k, String v)  { current().put(k, v); }
    void delete(String k)         { current().put(k, TOMBSTONE); }

    void rollback() { require(); stack.pop(); }

    void commit() {
        require();
        Map<String,Object> top = stack.pop();
        Map<String,Object> target = stack.isEmpty() ? base : stack.peek();
        target.putAll(top);                              // merge DOWN ONE LEVEL
    }
    private Map<String,Object> current() { return stack.isEmpty() ? base : stack.peek(); }
    private void require() { if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("no transaction"); }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

What isolation level have you actually implemented?

None between concurrent transactions — the stack is per-instance and single-threaded. Within one transaction you see your own uncommitted writes, which is read-committed-like from your own perspective. Real isolation needs locking or MVCC.

How would you add MVCC?

Store a list of versions per key, each tagged with the transaction id that created it, and give every transaction a snapshot timestamp so it reads the newest version visible at that timestamp. That is roughly how Postgres works, and it lets readers proceed without blocking writers.

Why does deletion need a tombstone rather than a removal?

Because get falls through to lower layers. Removing the key from the overlay makes the base map's old value visible again, so the delete silently appears to have no effect inside the transaction.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design it as the pipeline you actually built, and lead with the decisions rather than the boxes. Producers publish domain events; Kafka is the buffer and the integration point; consumers process into stores and downstream systems.

Topic and partition design is the first real decision. One topic per event type or per aggregate, not one giant topic. Partition count sets your maximum consumer parallelism and cannot be reduced, and increasing it changes key-to-partition mapping and therefore breaks ordering for in-flight keys — so size it with headroom (a few times current need). The partition key is the design decision that matters most: keying by account or entity id gives per-entity ordering while different entities process in parallel. A null key round-robins and gives no ordering at all.

Producer settings: acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 for durability, enable.idempotence=true so retries do not duplicate, and linger.ms/batch.size tuned to trade a little latency for throughput. If the event must be consistent with a database write, use the transactional outbox — write the row and the event in one local transaction and let a relay publish — because you cannot atomically write to Postgres and Kafka.

Consumers: enable.auto.commit=false and commit after processing, giving at-least-once — so every handler must be idempotent, typically an upsert or a dedupe table keyed by event id. Keep processing well under max.poll.interval.ms, or the broker assumes the consumer died and rebalances mid-batch, which produces a loop of reprocessing. Errors: classify them — a deserialization or validation failure will never succeed, so send it straight to a DLQ; a downstream timeout deserves bounded retries via retry topics with increasing delays, rather than blocking the partition.

Schema evolution: a schema registry with backward compatibility, additive fields only, consumers tolerating unknown fields.

Monitoring: consumer lag is the primary SLI — alert on lag and its growth rate, because growth predicts a breach long before latency alarms fire. Also watch DLQ depth and rebalance frequency.

Scaling to 100×: the first thing that breaks is consumer parallelism capped by partition count; then the downstream database write path; then rebalance storms as the consumer group grows. Say that explicitly — naming what breaks first is the senior half of the answer.

Config + limits
producer: acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, enable.idempotence=true
          key = accountId        # ordering per account, parallel across accounts
          outbox pattern if the event must match a DB write

consumer: enable.auto.commit=false; commit AFTER processing (at-least-once)
          handler idempotent (upsert / dedupe on event_id)
          max.poll.records tuned so a poll cycle < max.poll.interval.ms
          errors: deserialization -> DLQ immediately
                  transient       -> retry topics with increasing delay

at 100x, what breaks first:
  1. consumers capped by partition count   2. downstream DB writes
  3. rebalance storms as the group grows   4. retention vs lag (data loss)
Follow-ups they will ask

What actually happens if lag exceeds retention?

The consumer's offset falls off the beginning of the log and those messages are gone permanently — the one genuinely unrecoverable failure in this design. That is why lag alerting must fire long before retention is at risk.

Why is increasing partitions not a free scaling lever?

Key-to-partition mapping changes, so a key that lived on partition 3 may move to partition 7 and its messages can be processed out of order across the transition. Treat repartitioning as a planned migration, not a scaling reflex.

How do you reprocess history after a bug?

Reset the consumer group's offsets to an earlier point and replay — which works precisely because the log is retained and handlers are idempotent. That replay capability is the main argument for a log over a queue.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Do not start by refactoring. Start by making change safe: write characterization tests at the component's boundary — render it, drive the main user flows, assert the visible outcomes. You are capturing current behaviour, bugs included, because your goal in this phase is that behaviour does not change. Without this you cannot tell a refactor from a rewrite.

Then extract pure logic. Formatting, validation, derivation, sorting — move it into plain functions outside the component. This is the highest-value, lowest-risk step: those functions are trivially unit-testable, the component shrinks immediately, and nothing about the React tree changes.

Then collapse related state. Thirty useState calls almost always contain clusters that change together — a form's data/errors/touched/submitting, a modal's open/target/mode. Replace each cluster with one useReducer. This is where most of the actual bugs disappear, because the illegal combinations stop being representable.

Then split by responsibility. With state consolidated, the seams are visible: this reducer plus this JSX is the filter panel, that group is the results table. Extract components, passing state and dispatch down. Then extract custom hooks for stateful logic that is reused or that isolates an external system.

Only then memoize, and only where the Profiler proves it is needed. Memoizing before splitting is optimizing a structure you are about to delete.

How you avoid regressions is the part the question is really asking. Three rules. Never refactor and change behaviour in the same commit — if a bug surfaces, you must be able to say which commit could possibly have caused it. Ship in small, independently revertable steps rather than one heroic pull request that nobody can review. And keep the public props stable until the end, so callers are untouched and the blast radius stays inside the file. If the component is genuinely business-critical, add feature-flagged parallel rendering or visual regression snapshots before starting.

Order of operations
1. characterization tests at the boundary   (capture behaviour, bugs included)
2. extract pure functions                   (format, validate, derive, sort)
3. collapse state clusters into useReducer  (illegal states stop existing)
4. split by responsibility into components  (seams are now visible)
5. extract custom hooks                     (reused or external-system logic)
6. memoize ONLY where the Profiler proves it

rules:
  never refactor + change behaviour in one commit
  small, independently revertable steps
  keep the public props stable until the end
Follow-ups they will ask

What if there are no tests and the component is business-critical?

Write the characterization tests first — that is the price of touching it. If that is genuinely impossible in the time available, add visual regression snapshots and feature-flag the new implementation so you can run both and compare in production.

How do you know when to stop?

When the component fits on a screen or two, each extracted piece has one responsibility, and adding the next feature no longer requires reading the whole file. Refactoring to an abstract ideal past that point is unpaid risk.

What is the most common mistake in this refactor?

Starting with component extraction before consolidating state. You end up threading fifteen props and five callbacks through the new boundaries, which is worse than what you started with — collapse the state first and the seams reveal themselves.

MOCK - 45 min, two mediums
  • Course Schedule IIMedium
  • Cheapest Flights Within K StopsMedium

Graph round. Say which traversal you are choosing and why before you write it.

Track which set each element belongs to. Union merges two sets; find returns a set's representative. With path compression it is effectively constant time.

CostO(α(n)) ≈ O(1) amortised per operationReach for itConnected components with incremental edges, Kruskal's MST, cycle detection, and 'are these two related' queries.
class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.p = list(range(n)); self.sz = [1]*n; self.count = n
    def find(self, x):
        while self.p[x] != x:
            self.p[x] = self.p[self.p[x]]      # path compression
            x = self.p[x]
        return x
    def union(self, a, b):
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if ra == rb: return False              # already together -> a cycle
        if self.sz[ra] < self.sz[rb]: ra, rb = rb, ra   # union by size
        self.p[rb] = ra; self.sz[ra] += self.sz[rb]; self.count -= 1
        return True

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Trace the path: the request passes the servlet filter chain, reaches the DispatcherServlet, which consults HandlerMapping to find the controller method; a HandlerAdapter invokes it after argument resolvers build the parameters (@RequestBody via an HttpMessageConverter, @PathVariable, @RequestParam); the return value goes back through a message converter; then the response unwinds through the filters.

Filters versus interceptors is the crux. Filters are servlet-level: they see every request including static resources and error dispatches, they run outside Spring's exception handling, and they can wrap the request and response objects. Spring Security lives here — which is exactly why @ControllerAdvice cannot handle authentication failures. Interceptors are Spring MVC-level: they run after handler mapping, so they know which controller method will handle the request, and they have preHandle/postHandle/afterCompletion hooks.

So the selection rule: filter for anything that must cover every request — correlation ids, request logging, CORS, security. Interceptor for handler-aware concerns — per-endpoint auditing, timing a specific controller, injecting model attributes. Put the correlation id in a filter and into the MDC, so it is present before anything else logs.

@ControllerAdvice centralizes exception handling. Map each exception type to a status and a stable error contract — RFC 9457 application/problem+json with a machine-readable code and the trace id. Two rules: return all validation failures at once, not just the first; and never let internal detail reach the client — log the stack trace server-side against the trace id and return something safe.

Bean validation plugs in here: @Valid on the parameter, constraints on the DTO, and a MethodArgumentNotValidException handler that flattens the binding result into field errors. Validate DTOs at the boundary rather than entities, so failures surface with a good message before anything reaches the persistence layer.

Java
// filter: sees EVERY request, runs before Spring's exception handling
@Component
class TraceFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws  IOException, ServletException {
        MDC.put("traceId", Optional.ofNullable(req.getHeader("X-Trace-Id"))
                                   .orElse(UUID.randomUUID().toString()));
        try { chain.doFilter(req, res); } finally { MDC.clear(); }
    }
}

@RestControllerAdvice
class ApiErrors {
    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    ProblemDetail invalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException e) {
        var errors = e.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
                .map(f -> Map.of("field", f.getField(), "message", f.getDefaultMessage()))
                .toList();                                  // ALL failures, not the first
        var p = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
        p.setProperty("errors", errors);
        p.setProperty("traceId", MDC.get("traceId"));
        return p;
    }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why can @ControllerAdvice not handle a security exception?

Because Spring Security's filters run before the DispatcherServlet, so the exception never reaches Spring MVC's exception resolvers. Authentication and authorization failures go to the AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler instead.

Where should request logging live?

A filter, so it covers requests that never reach a controller — 404s, security rejections, malformed bodies. Those are precisely the requests you most want logged, and an interceptor would miss them.

What is OncePerRequestFilter for?

It guarantees the filter body runs a single time per request even when the container performs internal forwards or error dispatches, which would otherwise re-run a plain filter and duplicate logging or MDC setup.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Requirements come from compliance, not from product, and saying that first frames the whole design: who changed what, when, from what value to what value; immutable; queryable by actor, subject and time range; retained seven years; and tamper-evident, because an audit log an insider can edit is worthless.

Schema: (event_id, occurred_at, actor_id, actor_type, action, subject_type, subject_id, before, after, trace_id, source_service, ip, user_agent). Store before/after as JSON, and store the changed fields only for large entities. The trace_id is what lets you tie an audit entry back to the request that caused it, which is the first thing an investigation needs.

Immutability and tamper evidence: append-only, with no UPDATE or DELETE grants for the application role. For genuine tamper evidence, hash-chain the records — each row stores the hash of its own content plus the previous row's hash — so altering any historical row invalidates every hash after it. Periodically publish the chain head somewhere independent (a separate account, a WORM bucket, or timestamped externally). Cheaper alternative: write to object storage with an object-lock/WORM policy, where the storage layer itself forbids modification.

Ingestion: audit must never block the business transaction, but it also must not be lost. The resolution is the transactional outbox — write the domain change and the audit record in the same local transaction, then a relay ships it asynchronously to the audit store. That gives durability without coupling latency, and it is the correct answer to "async or sync?".

Storage and retention: this is append-only, time-ranged, and enormous — so partition by time (monthly), keep 90 days hot in the database for interactive queries, and tier older partitions to object storage queryable via Athena or BigQuery. Expiry is then dropping a partition rather than deleting rows, which at this volume is the difference between instant and impossible.

Access control on the audit log itself deserves a sentence: reads are privileged and — this is the detail auditors look for — reading the audit log is itself an auditable event.

Schema + chain
audit(event_id, occurred_at, actor_id, action, subject_type, subject_id,
      before jsonb, after jsonb, trace_id, source_service, ip,
      prev_hash, hash)                       -- hash = H(content || prev_hash)

  PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at)           -- monthly; expiry = DROP PARTITION
  app role: INSERT + SELECT only, no UPDATE/DELETE

write path (never lose it, never block on it):
  BEGIN; update domain row; insert into outbox; COMMIT;
  relay -> audit store (at-least-once, dedupe on event_id)

hot 90d in Postgres -> tiered to S3/Glacier, queried via Athena for the 7-year tail
Follow-ups they will ask

Why hash-chain rather than just restricting permissions?

Permissions stop the application; they do not stop someone with database access. The chain makes tampering detectable after the fact, which is what an auditor actually requires — and publishing the chain head externally is what makes it credible.

Should audit writes be synchronous with the business transaction?

The audit record should be written in the same transaction (via the outbox), so it cannot be lost if the transaction commits. The shipping to the audit store is asynchronous, so audit-store latency never affects the business path.

What about PII in before/after values?

Redact or tokenize sensitive fields before writing, and be prepared for erasure requests — which conflict directly with immutability. The usual resolution is storing a reference to a separately-erasable PII vault, so the audit trail survives while the personal data can be deleted.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The problem being solved is the request waterfall. With fetch-on-render, a parent mounts, fetches, renders, and only then does the child mount and start its fetch. Three nested components with a 300 ms API is a 900 ms page. Route-level loading fixes this by starting every request for a route when navigation begins, before any component renders.

Nested layouts map to nested routes, and each segment gets its own loader. Because the router knows the whole matched route tree up front, it can fire every segment's loader in parallel — the shell, the sidebar and the detail panel all start at once rather than in sequence. That parallelism is the entire point.

Pending UI then has two levels. For a navigation, keep the current page on screen and show a subtle global indicator (a top progress bar) rather than tearing down to a spinner — because replacing rendered content with a fallback is a perceived-performance regression even when the measured time is identical. For a segment that is slow, show a skeleton in that region only, so a slow sidebar does not blank the page.

Error isolation per segment is the third piece: each route segment declares its own error boundary, so a failing recommendations panel renders an error card while the rest of the route is fine. Without per-segment boundaries a single failure takes down the whole page.

Deferred data is the refinement worth naming: split a loader's data into critical (awaited, so the route does not render without it) and non-critical (returned as a promise, streamed in behind a Suspense boundary). The order detail renders immediately while the slow "related items" query resolves separately — you no longer let the slowest query set the page's time to content.

One caution: loaders mean data fetching lives outside components, so a component is no longer self-contained. That is a deliberate trade — you gain parallelism and lose colocation — and it is worth acknowledging rather than presenting the pattern as free.

JSX
// nested routes: all matched loaders run in PARALLEL on navigation
{ path: 'orders', element: <OrdersLayout />, loader: ordersLoader,
  errorElement: <OrdersError />,
  children: [
    { path: ':id', element: <OrderDetail />, loader: orderLoader,
      errorElement: <DetailError /> },        // isolated per segment
  ]}

// defer the slow part - critical data awaited, the rest streamed
async function orderLoader({ params }) {
  const order = await getOrder(params.id);        // critical: awaited
  return defer({ order, related: getRelated(params.id) });   // streamed
}

<Await resolve={related} errorElement={<RelatedError />}>
  {items => <Related items={items} />}
</Await>

// navigation pending: keep the old page, show a progress bar
const nav = useNavigation();
{nav.state === 'loading' && <TopProgressBar />}
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the cost of moving fetching out of components?

Colocation. The component no longer declares its own data needs, so a refactor that moves it to another route can silently break it. Mitigate by exporting the loader alongside the component and keeping them in the same module.

How does this compare with React Server Components?

RSCs achieve the same goal differently — data access happens during server rendering, so there is no client waterfall and no data-fetching JavaScript in the bundle. Loaders are the client-router answer; RSCs are the framework answer.

When is a spinner actually correct?

On first load, where there is no previous content to keep. On subsequent navigations, keeping the old page with a pending indicator is almost always better — the exception is when the new route is so different that stale content would be misleading.

1-D DP III
  • Coin ChangeMedium
  • Maximum Product SubarrayMedium
  • Word BreakMedium

Sort every edge by weight and add it if it connects two different components. Union-Find makes the check cheap.

CostO(E log E) time, dominated by the sortReach for itMinimum spanning tree, clustering, and 'connect all points at minimum cost' problems.
def kruskal(n, edges):            # edges = [(w, u, v), ...]
    edges.sort()
    dsu, total, used = DSU(n), 0, 0
    for w, u, v in edges:
        if dsu.union(u, v):       # False means it would create a cycle
            total += w; used += 1
            if used == n - 1: break
    return total if used == n - 1 else -1     # -1: graph is disconnected

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Spring Data generates implementations from interfaces. Derived queries parse the method name — findByStatusAndCreatedAtAfter — which is convenient and becomes unreadable past three or four conditions; at that point switch to @Query (JPQL) or a Specification.

Projections are the highest-value feature and the one people underuse. Returning a full entity to render three fields loads every column, puts the entity in the persistence context, and dirty-checks it at flush. An interface projection generates a narrow SELECT of just those columns. A DTO/constructor projection returns a plain object with no persistence-context involvement at all. On a wide table, switching to a projection is frequently a larger win than adding an index — and it is a one-line change.

Specifications build type-safe dynamic predicates with the Criteria API, composable with and/or. They are the right tool for a filter or search endpoint where the predicate set is combinatorial, instead of concatenating JPQL strings. The cost is verbosity and poor readability — use them where the dynamism is real, not everywhere.

Native queries for database-specific features JPQL cannot express: window functions, CTEs, JSONB operators, INSERT … ON CONFLICT. Accept that you lose portability and must map results explicitly.

Pagination has a cost people miss: returning Page issues an additional COUNT query on every call, and on a large filtered table that count can dominate the request. Use Slice when the UI only needs "is there a next page" — it fetches limit + 1 rows and skips the count entirely. And for deep pages, offset pagination degrades linearly and is unstable under concurrent writes, so use keyset pagination.

One guard rule for search endpoints: require at least one selective filter, cap the page size server-side, and make sure the specification's predicates match an index — an unbounded dynamic query endpoint is a denial-of-service vector.

Java
// interface projection -> narrow SELECT, no entity in the persistence context
interface OrderSummary { Long getId(); BigDecimal getTotal(); String getStatus(); }
List<OrderSummary> findByCustomerId(String id);

// constructor projection
@Query("select new com.acme.OrderDto(o.id, o.total) from Order o where o.status = :s")
List<OrderDto> summaries(@Param("s") Status s);

// Slice: no COUNT query
Slice<Order> findByStatus(Status s, Pageable p);

// dynamic filters without string concatenation
Specification<Order> spec = Specification.where(hasStatus(status))
                                         .and(createdAfter(from));
Follow-ups they will ask

When is a full entity the right return type?

When you are going to modify it — you need it managed so dirty checking works. For read-only endpoints, a projection is almost always better and it also makes the query's cost obvious from the signature.

Why can @Query with JOIN FETCH not paginate properly?

The join multiplies rows, so the database cannot apply LIMIT to entities correctly. Hibernate warns and paginates in memory after loading everything — silently turning a paged query into a full table load. Page the ids first, then fetch.

How do you keep derived query names maintainable?

Set a limit — roughly three conditions — and move beyond that to @Query or a Specification. A method called findByStatusAndCreatedAtAfterAndCustomerIdOrderByTotalDesc is a signal, not a feature.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design the cache as a service, not as a library — the interesting questions are placement, replication, eviction and failure.

Partitioning: consistent hashing with virtual nodes so adding or removing a node remaps only K/N keys rather than nearly all of them, and so load is even across heterogeneous machines. Clients compute placement locally from a cluster topology they subscribe to, which avoids a routing hop on every request.

Replication: a cache is derived data, so replication is for availability and read throughput, not durability. One replica per partition is usually enough — asynchronous, because paying synchronous replication latency for data you can recompute is a poor trade. On a node loss, promote the replica; if there is none, those keys simply become misses.

Eviction: a hard maxmemory per node with LRU (or W-TinyLFU, which resists a scan flushing the hot set) plus per-entry TTL. Both are needed — TTL bounds staleness, size bounds memory. And every TTL needs jitter, or entries populated together expire together and manufacture a stampede on a schedule.

Consistency with the source of truth is the real design question. Cache-aside with TTL is the default, accepting bounded staleness. If that is not acceptable, invalidate explicitly on write — with the caveat that there is a race where a concurrent read repopulates the old value just after the delete, which is why versioned keys (embedding a version so the old key becomes unreachable) are sometimes cleaner. State the staleness window you are accepting; that is the answer interviewers want.

Cold start is the failure to volunteer. After a deploy or a mass eviction, every request is a miss and the entire read load lands on the database simultaneously — a cache outage becoming a database outage. Defences: single-flight so N misses for one key produce one load, a small in-process L1 to absorb the first seconds, request-level load shedding, and where possible warm the cache before taking traffic — bring the node up, populate the hot key set, then add it to the pool.

Design
placement:   consistent hashing + ~150 vnodes/node; client-side routing
replication: 1 async replica per partition (availability, not durability)
eviction:    maxmemory + LRU/W-TinyLFU, per-entry TTL + JITTER
consistency: cache-aside + TTL (bounded staleness), or versioned keys

node loss -> promote replica, else those keys become misses
cold start-> single-flight + L1 + load shedding + warm before joining the pool

never let a cache outage become a database outage
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is asynchronous replication acceptable here when it is not for a database?

Because the data is derived and recomputable. Losing a few recently-written cache entries costs a handful of misses; paying synchronous replication latency on every write costs you the very speed you built the cache for.

How do you handle a hot key that saturates one partition?

Consistent hashing distributes keys, not traffic, so it cannot help. Split the key into key#0..key#N with readers picking a random suffix, or put a short-TTL in-process L1 in front so most reads never reach the cache tier.

What should the client do when the cache is unreachable?

Fail open — treat it as a miss and go to the source — with a circuit breaker and load shedding so the database is not overwhelmed. A cache that returns errors instead of misses turns an optimization into a dependency.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Two-axis virtualization is the base: window rows and columns, so a 100-column grid renders only the ~15 columns in view. Row virtualization is the standard windowing maths; column virtualization needs per-column widths and a prefix-sum of offsets so you can binary-search from scrollLeft to the first visible column. With variable widths you need a measurement cache exactly as with variable row heights.

Sticky headers and columns fight virtualization, and this is the part worth explaining. A sticky column must remain rendered even when scrolled far right, but it is not in the virtualized window — so it is rendered in a separate pinned layer outside the virtualized region, synchronized to the same vertical scroll offset. That is why pinned columns are the feature that most often breaks in hand-rolled grids: two independently scrolling layers that must stay in lockstep, and any rounding difference shows as a one-pixel drift.

Resize and reorder should be controlled state persisted per user — column widths, order and visibility saved to localStorage or, better, the server so it follows the user across devices. Persist a version with it, because columns get added and removed by deploys and a stale saved layout referencing a deleted column must degrade gracefully rather than crash.

Keyboard grid navigation follows the ARIA grid pattern and is the accessibility requirement most grids fail: role="grid", and a roving tabindex so the grid is a single tab stop rather than 4,000. Arrow keys move the focused cell, Home/End and PageUp/PageDown jump, and moving focus must scroll the target cell into view — which with virtualization means rendering it first, then focusing it, or focus lands on nothing.

Finally, the performance rule that ties it together: keep the row data out of React state and isolate re-renders to the cell level, so editing one cell does not re-render the grid. Memoize rows on their data identity, and derive cell content rather than storing it.

JSX
// column windowing: prefix-sum offsets, binary search from scrollLeft
const offsets = useMemo(() => prefixSum(columnWidths), [columnWidths]);
const firstCol = binarySearch(offsets, scrollLeft);
const lastCol  = binarySearch(offsets, scrollLeft + viewportWidth);

// pinned columns live OUTSIDE the virtualized region, synced to scrollTop
<div className="pinned" style={{ transform: `translateY(${-scrollTop}px)` }}>

// roving tabindex: one tab stop for the whole grid
<div role="grid" aria-rowcount={rows.length} aria-colcount={cols.length}>
  <div role="row" aria-rowindex={r + 1}>
    <div role="gridcell" tabIndex={isFocused ? 0 : -1} aria-colindex={c + 1}>

// focus must scroll the cell into view BEFORE focusing it (it may not be rendered)
scrollToCell(r, c); requestAnimationFrame(() => cellRef.current?.focus());
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is a roving tabindex necessary?

Without it every cell is a tab stop, so reaching the content after a 4,000-cell grid takes 4,000 tab presses. The roving pattern makes the grid one stop and delegates internal movement to the arrow keys, which is what the ARIA grid pattern specifies.

How do you handle inline editing without re-rendering the grid?

Keep edit state per cell rather than in a grid-level object, and memoize rows on their data identity. A single cell entering edit mode should re-render one cell, which the Profiler can confirm.

What breaks when a saved column layout references a removed column?

Everything, if you apply it blindly. Version the saved layout and reconcile on load — drop unknown columns, append newly added ones with defaults — so a deploy never leaves users with a broken grid they cannot reset.

1-D DP IV
  • Longest Increasing SubsequenceMedium
  • Partition Equal Subset SumMedium
  • Combination Sum IVMedium

Grow one tree outward, always taking the cheapest edge leaving it. A heap supplies that edge.

CostO(E log V) with a binary heapReach for itMST on dense graphs, where Prim beats Kruskal by avoiding the full edge sort.
import heapq
def prim(n, g):                    # g[u] = [(weight, v), ...]
    seen, h, total = {0}, list(g[0]), 0
    heapq.heapify(h)
    while h and len(seen) < n:
        w, v = heapq.heappop(h)
        if v in seen: continue     # stale entry - skip it
        seen.add(v); total += w
        for nw, nv in g[v]:
            if nv not in seen: heapq.heappush(h, (nw, nv))
    return total if len(seen) == n else -1
