Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Actuator exposes operational endpoints — /health, /metrics, /info, /env, /loggers (which lets you change a log level at runtime without a restart — genuinely useful during an incident). Expose only what you need and secure the rest; /env and /heapdump leak configuration and memory contents.

Liveness versus readiness is the part that causes real outages. Liveness answers "is this process broken beyond recovery" — failing it makes the orchestrator restart the pod. Readiness answers "should this instance receive traffic right now" — failing it removes it from the load balancer without killing it. Conflating them is the classic incident: you put a database check in liveness, the database blips, every pod fails liveness simultaneously, Kubernetes restarts the entire fleet, and now you have a cold fleet on top of a database problem.

So the rule: liveness should check almost nothing — is the process responsive — while readiness checks the dependencies you cannot serve without. Spring Boot exposes these separately as /health/liveness and /health/readiness, with readiness automatically reporting false during startup and shutdown.

Graceful shutdown is the other half. On SIGTERM the sequence must be: fail readiness first so the load balancer stops sending new requests; keep serving in-flight requests until they complete or a timeout expires; stop Kafka consumers cleanly, committing offsets; then exit. Skip the readiness step and every deploy drops live requests — and with Kubernetes the pod is removed from endpoints asynchronously, so you need a small preStop sleep to cover the propagation delay.

For Kafka specifically, an abrupt kill means uncommitted offsets are reprocessed, which is safe only because your consumers are idempotent — but it also triggers a rebalance, so clean shutdown genuinely matters.

Configuration refresh: Spring Cloud Config plus /actuator/refresh can rebind @ConfigurationProperties at runtime. Useful for feature toggles and log levels; be cautious with anything that would need to rebuild a connection pool.

Config
management:
  endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true
  health.livenessState.enabled: true
  health.readinessState.enabled: true
server:
  shutdown: graceful                  # finish in-flight requests
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s

# k8s
livenessProbe:  { path: /actuator/health/liveness }    # almost nothing: is it alive
readinessProbe: { path: /actuator/health/readiness }   # deps: should it get traffic
lifecycle: { preStop: sleep 5 }        # cover endpoint-removal propagation

# SIGTERM -> fail readiness -> drain -> stop consumers -> exit
Follow-ups they will ask

What exactly goes wrong if the database check is in liveness?

A transient database failure fails liveness on every pod at once. The orchestrator restarts them all, they come up cold, the database is still down so they fail again — a restart loop that turns a partial degradation into a total outage.

Why is a preStop sleep needed if shutdown is graceful?

Removing a pod from the service endpoints is eventually consistent — the kubelet may deliver SIGTERM before every proxy has stopped routing to it. A few seconds of sleep before shutdown begins covers that window.

What should readiness actually check?

Only dependencies you genuinely cannot serve without — usually the database and, during startup, that caches and pools are initialised. Checking every downstream makes your availability the product of all of theirs.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Estimate first: a billion pages at, say, 30 days of recrawl is roughly 385 pages/second sustained, and at 100 KB average that is ~100 TB of raw content. Those numbers say this is a distributed, storage-heavy pipeline with a coordination problem at its centre.

The URL frontier is the core component. It is not a simple queue — it must enforce two things at once: priority (crawl important pages more often) and politeness (never hammer one host). The standard design is two levels: front queues by priority, and back queues partitioned by host, where each host queue has a next-allowed-fetch timestamp derived from robots.txt crawl-delay or a default. A worker takes the host whose timestamp has passed. That structure is what makes politeness a property of the data structure rather than of every worker remembering to be polite.

Politeness also means fetching and honouring robots.txt per host with caching, identifying yourself in the User-Agent, and respecting rate limits — a crawler that ignores this gets blocked and is, reasonably, treated as an attack.

Deduplication happens at two levels. URL dedup after normalization (lowercase host, strip default ports, sort or strip tracking query parameters, resolve relative paths) — at a billion URLs a Bloom filter in front of the store keeps the membership check cheap. Content dedup matters more, because the same page is reachable at many URLs: hash the content for exact duplicates, and use simhash or minhash shingling for near-duplicates, which is what catches boilerplate-heavy templated pages.

Freshness scheduling: do not recrawl uniformly. Estimate each page's change rate from observed history and schedule proportionally — a news homepage hourly, a static documentation page monthly. That is where most of the crawl budget saving comes from.

Traps are the operational reality: infinite calendars, session ids in URLs generating unbounded unique pages, faceted-search parameter explosions, and deliberate spider traps. Defences are a per-host page cap, a maximum URL depth and length, parameter allow-listing during normalization, and detecting hosts producing unusually many near-duplicate pages.

Frontier
front queues (by priority)  ->  router  ->  back queues (one per host)
                                             each with next_fetch_at

worker: pick the host whose next_fetch_at <= now
        fetch -> parse -> extract links -> normalize -> dedupe -> enqueue
        set next_fetch_at = now + crawl_delay(host)

dedupe: URL  -> normalize + Bloom filter (1B URLs)
        content -> exact hash, plus simhash for near-duplicates

traps: per-host page cap, max depth, strip session/tracking params,
       flag hosts producing many near-duplicates
Follow-ups they will ask

Why partition back queues by host rather than by worker?

Because politeness is a per-host constraint. If two workers can hold URLs for the same host, they must coordinate on rate — partitioning by host makes the constraint structural and lock-free.

How do you decide crawl priority?

A combination of link-based importance (PageRank-like), observed change rate, and business value. The frontier's front queues encode it, and the scheduler blends priority with the freshness estimate.

What is the hardest part operationally?

Politeness and traps — the parts that make you a good citizen and stop you wasting the entire crawl budget on one pathological site. The distributed fetching itself is comparatively routine.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The mental model: Server Components run only on the server, during rendering, and ship zero JavaScript to the browser. What crosses the wire is a serialized description of the UI, not code. Client Components — marked with 'use client' — are the ones that ship JavaScript and hydrate.

What runs where. Server: data fetching (query the database directly, no API layer needed), secrets and API keys, heavy dependencies like a markdown or syntax-highlighting library, and anything that would otherwise bloat the bundle. Client: state, effects, event handlers, browser APIs, and anything using useState, useEffect or context.

The boundary rule that matters most: 'use client' is infectious downward — everything imported by a client component becomes part of the client bundle. So push the boundary as deep as possible. A common mistake is marking a whole page as client because one button needs onClick; instead keep the page a server component and make just the button a client component.

Props crossing the boundary must be serializable: primitives, plain objects, arrays, dates, and — importantly — JSX. Functions and class instances cannot cross. The exception that makes composition work is passing server components as children to a client component: the server renders them and passes the resulting element, so a client-side layout wrapper can contain server-rendered content without making it client. That pattern is the answer to "how do I put server content inside an interactive shell".

Interleaving follows from that: server → client → server is possible via children, but a client component cannot import a server component.

The honest tradeoff: it is a genuinely new mental model, the serialization constraints surprise people, and debugging across the boundary is harder. It pays off when bundle size and data-fetching waterfalls are real problems — a content-heavy app — and is less compelling for a highly interactive dashboard where almost everything is client anyway.

JSX
// server component (default) - queries the DB directly, ships no JS
async function OrderPage({ params }) {
  const order = await db.order.findUnique({ where: { id: params.id } });
  return (
    <Layout>
      <OrderSummary order={order} />         {/* server: static, no JS */}
      <ActionsPanel orderId={order.id}>     {/* client: needs onClick */}
        <OrderTimeline order={order} />     {/* server, passed as children! */}
      </ActionsPanel>
    </Layout>
  );
}

'use client';
function ActionsPanel({ orderId, children }) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);   // client state
  return <div>{children}<button onClick={...}>Refund</button></div>;
}
// children were rendered on the server - they stay out of the client bundle
Follow-ups they will ask

Why can a client component not import a server component?

Because the import would have to be resolved in the browser, where the server component's code and its database access cannot exist. Passing it as children works because the server has already rendered it to an element before the client component receives it.

Do Server Components replace SSR?

No — they compose with it. SSR produces HTML for the initial response; RSCs determine which components ever ship JavaScript. You typically use both, plus streaming to send the shell before slow data resolves.

What is the most common mistake adopting them?

Putting 'use client' at the top of a page because something deep inside needs interactivity. That pulls the entire subtree into the bundle and forfeits the whole benefit — push the directive down to the smallest interactive leaf.

2-D DP I - grids
  • Unique PathsMedium
  • Minimum Path SumMedium
  • Longest Common SubsequenceMedium

Shortest paths from one source with non-negative weights. Always expand the closest unfinished node; a heap supplies it.

CostO((V + E) log V) with a heapReach for itWeighted shortest path, network latency, cheapest route. Breaks silently on negative edges — check before using it.
import heapq
def dijkstra(src, n, g):           # g[u] = [(v, weight), ...]
    dist = [float('inf')]*n; dist[src] = 0
    h = [(0, src)]
    while h:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(h)
        if d > dist[u]: continue   # stale entry
        for v, w in g[u]:
            nd = d + w
            if nd < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = nd
                heapq.heappush(h, (nd, v))
    return dist

# NEGATIVE EDGES break this - not slowly, but with a WRONG answer.
# Use Bellman-Ford instead.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

WebFlux is Reactive Streams on Spring: Mono<T> (0 or 1) and Flux<T> (0..N), composed with operators (map, flatMap, zip, retryWhen) and executed on a small event-loop pool rather than thread-per-request. Nothing runs until you subscribe.

Schedulers control where work executes: Schedulers.parallel() for CPU work, boundedElastic() for unavoidable blocking calls, and — the rule that matters — never block on the event loop. One blocking JDBC call on a Netty event-loop thread stalls every request that thread is multiplexing, which is the failure mode that makes reactive systems fall over in a way thread-per-request never does.

Backpressure is the genuine differentiator: the subscriber signals demand with request(n), so a slow consumer propagates that pressure upstream instead of accumulating an unbounded buffer. Operators like onBackpressureBuffer, onBackpressureDrop and limitRate let you choose the policy explicitly. That is something imperative code has to construct by hand with bounded queues.

Detecting blocking calls: BlockHound instruments the JVM and throws when a blocking call happens on a non-blocking thread — run it in tests, because this is exactly the bug that passes code review and only appears under load.

When is WebFlux genuinely right post-Loom? Be direct: virtual threads deliver most of the throughput benefit with ordinary blocking code, readable stack traces, working debuggers, and ThreadLocal/MDC that behave normally. So the reason most teams adopted reactive — thread efficiency for IO-bound work — is largely gone. What remains genuinely reactive territory is streaming (server-sent events, long-lived subscriptions, WebSocket fan-out), explicit backpressure across a pipeline, and complex asynchronous composition where the operator vocabulary is a real expressive win.

The operational costs are why this matters: stack traces that do not show your call path, debuggers that cannot step through an operator chain, context propagation needing Context instead of ThreadLocal, and a steep learning curve for the whole team. Choosing reactive for a CRUD service is a cost with no remaining benefit.

Java
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
Mono<OrderDto> get(@PathVariable String id) {
    return repo.findById(id)                       // reactive all the way down
        .flatMap(o -> pricing.quote(o).map(q -> OrderDto.of(o, q)))
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> Mono.just(OrderDto.degraded()));
}

// unavoidable blocking call: get it OFF the event loop
Mono.fromCallable(() -> legacyJdbc.load(id))
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());

// tests: fail fast when something blocks a non-blocking thread
BlockHound.install();

// backpressure made explicit
flux.limitRate(100).onBackpressureBuffer(1000, dropped -> metrics.dropped());
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the single most common WebFlux bug?

A blocking call — JDBC, a synchronous HTTP client, Thread.sleep — on an event-loop thread. Throughput collapses under load in a way that looks like a capacity problem rather than a code problem. BlockHound in tests catches it.

Does reactive give better latency?

Not usually — it gives better throughput per thread for IO-bound work. Per-request latency is often slightly worse due to operator overhead. The win is handling many concurrent connections with few threads.

What would you tell a team choosing today?

Default to virtual threads with ordinary blocking code. Reach for reactive when you have streaming, genuine backpressure requirements, or an existing reactive ecosystem — and be honest that the operational cost is real.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Two distinct problems, and separating them is the answer. The first is load: 500,000 people arriving at once for 50,000 seats. The second is correctness: never sell the same seat twice. Load is solved by admission control; correctness is solved in the database. Conflating them is how systems oversell.

Admission control first. A virtual waiting room at the edge issues queue tokens and admits users to the real system at a rate it can serve — say a few thousand concurrent. This is the highest-leverage decision: 450,000 people waiting politely is a far better outcome than 500,000 people getting timeouts, and it protects every downstream component. Give the queue position and estimated wait so it is a tolerable experience.

Seat holds, not optimistic checks. Selecting a seat creates a hold with a short TTL (typically 5–10 minutes) — a row in the database with a state and expiry, or a Redis key with a fencing token. The critical part is that acquiring the hold must be atomic: a conditional update (UPDATE seats SET held_by=?, held_until=? WHERE seat_id=? AND (held_by IS NULL OR held_until < now())) that affects zero or one row. Zero rows means someone else got it. Never read-then-write in application code.

Overselling is a correctness bug, so state exactly where the invariant lives: in the database, as a unique constraint on (seat, event) for confirmed bookings plus the conditional hold update. Not in application logic, not in the cache, not in a distributed lock — those can all be wrong under partition or GC pause.

Payment timeout is the subtle case. A hold expires while the payment is in flight, someone else takes the seat, and then the payment succeeds. You must decide this in advance: either extend the hold for the duration of the payment and make the release idempotent, or accept it and issue an automatic refund with a clear message. The one unacceptable outcome is charging someone for a seat they do not have — so the payment must be reconciled against the booking state, not assumed.

Add: expire holds with a sweeper and lazily on read, so a dead sweeper does not lock inventory permanently.

Atomic hold
-- affects 0 or 1 rows; no read-then-write, no application-level check
UPDATE seats
   SET held_by = :user, held_until = now() + interval '8 minutes'
 WHERE seat_id = :seat
   AND (held_by IS NULL OR held_until < now());
-- 0 rows -> someone else holds it, tell the user immediately

-- confirmation: the invariant is a DB constraint, not application logic
ALTER TABLE bookings ADD CONSTRAINT one_booking_per_seat UNIQUE (event_id, seat_id);

admission: virtual waiting room admits N concurrent users at a serviceable rate
expiry:    background sweeper AND lazy expiry on read
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not a distributed lock in Redis?

Because a GC pause or clock skew longer than the lock TTL means two clients believe they hold it, and you oversell. The database's conditional update and unique constraint are the only mechanisms that cannot be wrong here.

How do you handle general admission rather than assigned seats?

Then it is a counter, not per-seat rows — an atomic decrement with a floor (UPDATE ... SET remaining = remaining - 1 WHERE remaining > 0). Same principle: the check and the decrement must be one statement.

What does the user see when their hold expires during payment?

That is a product decision you must raise: either the hold is extended for the payment window (preferred), or you refund automatically and tell them clearly. Silently failing after taking payment is the outcome to design out.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

What breaks under interruption is the frame for this. Concurrent rendering lets React start rendering, pause, abandon or resume, and render the same component multiple times before committing — so anything that assumes "render runs once and always commits" is now wrong.

The specific hazards. Mutating during render: incrementing a module-level counter, pushing to an array outside the component, generating an id — these run an unpredictable number of times. Reading mutable module state during render, which can change between the paused and resumed halves of a render. Side effects in render — a fetch, an analytics call, a subscription — which may fire for renders that never commit. Deriving state from a ref during render, since refs are not tracked and can be stale or torn.

Tearing is the specific external-store failure: two components reading the same mutable store during one render can see different values if the store changes mid-render, so a single committed UI shows two inconsistent versions of the same state. React state cannot tear, because React controls when it changes.

The fixes. Keep render pure — a function of props, state and context, with no mutation and no side effects. Use useSyncExternalStore for anything outside React, which forces a consistent snapshot and re-renders synchronously if the store changed mid-render. Put side effects in effects or event handlers. For a third-party library that mutates its own state (a chart instance, a map, an editor), wrap it: hold the instance in a ref, create it in an effect, and drive it imperatively from effects — never touch it during render.

StrictMode is the detector. Its double-render and double effect mount in development exist precisely to surface impurity and missing cleanup, which are the two things concurrent rendering punishes. If double-invocation breaks your component, concurrent React will too — so the correct response is to fix the component, never to disable StrictMode.

JSX
// unsafe under concurrent rendering: runs an unpredictable number of times
let counter = 0;
function Row() { const id = ++counter; }          // impure render

// safe: derive deterministically, or use useId
const id = useId();

// external store: consistent snapshot, no tearing
const value = useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, store.getSnapshot);

// third-party imperative library: ref + effect, never touched during render
const chartRef = useRef(null);
useEffect(() => {
  chartRef.current = new Chart(el.current, config);
  return () => chartRef.current.destroy();
}, []);
useEffect(() => { chartRef.current.setData(data); }, [data]);
Follow-ups they will ask

Is tearing a real problem or a theoretical one?

Real, but only with concurrent features (transitions, Suspense-driven updates) plus an external mutable store updated outside React. That combination is exactly why useSyncExternalStore was added and why every major store library adopted it.

How do you make a legacy class component safe?

The same rules apply — no side effects in render, no mutation of shared state. The legacy lifecycles that were removed (componentWillMount and friends) were removed precisely because they were unsafe under interruption.

Why does StrictMode double-invoke updater functions too?

Because a reducer or state updater must be pure — React may call it more than once to verify or to recompute. An updater with a side effect produces different results depending on how many times it runs.

2-D DP II - state machines
  • Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with CooldownMedium
  • Target SumMedium
  • Interleaving StringMedium

Relax every edge V-1 times. Slower than Dijkstra, but it handles negative weights and detects negative cycles.

CostO(V · E) time, O(V) spaceReach for itNegative edge weights, currency arbitrage, and 'shortest path using at most k edges'.
def bellman_ford(src, n, edges):
    dist = [float('inf')]*n; dist[src] = 0
    for _ in range(n - 1):                  # V-1 rounds is always enough
        changed = False
        for u, v, w in edges:
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w; changed = True
        if not changed: break
    # one more round: anything still improving is on a negative cycle
    for u, v, w in edges:
        if dist[u] + w < dist[v]: return None
    return dist

Patterns and service boundaries

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The value here is pointing at patterns in code you already use — that is what separates fluency from recitation.

In the JDK: Decorator throughout java.io (new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(in)) — each wrapper adds behaviour behind the same interface). Strategy in Comparator, passed in to vary the sorting algorithm's behaviour. Factory Method in Collection.iterator() and the List.of/Optional.of family. Builder in StringBuilder and HttpRequest.newBuilder(). Adapter in Arrays.asList, which adapts an array to the List interface. Singleton done correctly as an enum. Observer in java.util.concurrent.Flow.

In Spring: Proxy is the big one — @Transactional, @Cacheable and @Async are all proxies, and understanding that explains every self-invocation surprise. Template Method in JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate and KafkaTemplate: the framework owns the algorithm — acquire connection, execute, handle exceptions, release — and you supply the varying step as a RowMapper or callback. Being able to say "JdbcTemplate is Template Method, and that is why you pass a RowMapper" lands much better than a definition. Strategy in PlatformTransactionManager and CacheManager, swapped by configuration. Chain of Responsibility in the Spring Security filter chain. Factory in BeanFactory. Observer in ApplicationEventPublisher.

The patterns you actually write in a service: Strategy for pluggable business rules (pricing, fraud checks), Builder for objects with many optional fields, Factory for choosing an implementation by type, Decorator for cross-cutting behaviour like retry or caching around a client, and Observer via application events to decouple side effects from the main flow.

The one to criticise — and volunteering a criticism is a good signal — is Singleton: usually a global mutable variable in disguise, which destroys testability. In Spring you almost never need it, because a singleton-scoped bean gives you one instance with dependency injection and no static state.

Java
// Decorator - java.io
var in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(socket.getInputStream(), UTF_8));

// Template Method - JdbcTemplate owns the algorithm, you supply the mapping step
List<Order> orders = jdbc.query("select * from orders where status = ?",
        (rs, i) -> new Order(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getBigDecimal("total")), status);

// Strategy registry - Spring injects every implementation, keyed by bean name
@Service
class Dispatcher {
    private final Map<String, PricingStrategy> strategies;   // injected by Spring
    BigDecimal price(String plan, Cart c) { return strategies.get(plan).price(c); }
}
// adding a strategy = adding a class. The dispatcher never changes.
Follow-ups they will ask

Which pattern is most over-applied?

Singleton, and after that an interface with exactly one implementation created 'for flexibility'. Both add indirection without buying anything, and the second makes navigation harder for every future reader.

How does the strategy registry pattern work in Spring?

Inject Map<String, Handler> and Spring populates it with every Handler bean keyed by bean name — or List<Handler> and each declares what it supports. Adding a strategy becomes adding a class with no change to the dispatcher, which is Open/Closed done for real.

Why does knowing Proxy matter practically?

Because it explains the behaviour that confuses everyone: why @Transactional does nothing on a self-call, on a private method, or on a final class. One mechanism, three symptoms.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start from the organisation, not the code. Service boundaries exist to let teams deploy independently; if a boundary does not reduce coordination, it is only adding network calls. That is the frame the rest follows from.

Bounded contexts are the DDD tool: a bounded context is where a term has one unambiguous meaning. "Customer" means something different to Billing (a payment method and an address) than to Support (a ticket history) than to Marketing (a segment). Forcing one shared Customer model across all three produces a bloated entity every team must coordinate on — the classic distributed monolith. Each context owns its own model and they integrate through explicit contracts.

The heuristics for drawing a boundary: it should own its data exclusively (no other service reads its tables), it should be cohesive around a business capability rather than a technical layer, and — the practical test — a typical feature should be implementable inside one service. Boundaries drawn along technical layers (a "database service", a "validation service") fail this immediately.

Three signs a service should not have been split — this is the part to be concrete about. One: almost every feature requires a coordinated change and deploy across two or three services; that is a boundary drawn through the middle of a capability. Two: you need distributed transactions or sagas for ordinary operations; if a routine business action spans services, the invariant that action protects lives in one place and the split cut through it. Three: chatty synchronous call chains — service A calls B calls C on every request — which multiplies latency, couples availability (three services at 99.9% give 99.7%), and means you have distributed a function call.

A fourth worth naming: a shared database. If two services write the same tables, they are one service with two deployables and all the costs of both.

The recommendation to state: start with a modular monolith — clear module boundaries, no shared internals, separate schemas — and extract a service only when a module has a genuinely different scaling profile, deploy cadence, or team. Extraction from a well-modularised monolith is straightforward; recombining prematurely split services is not.

Tests
good boundary:
  [ ] owns its data exclusively (nobody else reads its tables)
  [ ] cohesive around a business capability, not a technical layer
  [ ] a typical feature ships from ONE service
  [ ] can be deployed without coordinating with another team

signs the split was wrong:
  - most features need changes in 2-3 services
  - routine operations need a saga or 2PC
  - synchronous A -> B -> C on every request
  - shared database tables

default: modular monolith -> extract when scaling/cadence/team genuinely differ
Follow-ups they will ask

How do services share data if each owns its own?

Through explicit contracts: synchronous APIs for queries you need now, or events for propagating state changes so each context keeps its own read model. Duplicating the fields you need is correct here — it is not denormalization, it is each context holding its own view.

When is extraction genuinely justified?

A different scaling profile (one module needs 50 instances and the rest need 3), a different deploy cadence, a different team, or a different compliance boundary. Those are real forces; 'microservices are best practice' is not.

What is the migration path out of a monolith?

The strangler pattern: put a facade in front, extract one bounded context at a time behind it, migrate its data, and cut traffic over incrementally. Never a rewrite — the monolith's behaviour is not fully documented anywhere but in the monolith.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

These are the three escape hatches from React's declarative model, and the interesting part of the answer is the discipline that keeps them from becoming architecture.

Portals render a subtree into a different DOM node while keeping it in the React tree. Use them for anything that must escape a parent's overflow: hidden, z-index stacking context, or transform — modals, dropdowns, tooltips, toasts. The behaviour to know: events bubble through the React tree, not the DOM tree, so a click inside a portal still reaches the React parent that rendered it. Usually convenient (a form's onChange still fires), occasionally surprising (a click-outside handler on the parent fires for clicks inside the modal).

Refs are for values that must survive renders without triggering one, and for DOM access. Two legitimate uses: holding a DOM node, and holding mutable non-render state — a timer id, a WebSocket, a previous value, the latest-callback pattern. The rule is never read or write a ref during render; it belongs in effects and event handlers, because refs are invisible to React's rendering and a render-time read can be stale or torn under concurrent rendering.

useImperativeHandle exposes a deliberately narrow imperative API from a component to its parent via a ref — focus(), scrollIntoView(), play(), reset(). It exists because some actions genuinely are imperative: you cannot express "focus this now" declaratively without inventing a shouldFocus prop that then needs resetting.

The discipline is three rules. Expose actions, never state — a handle with setValue() is a second source of truth and will drift from props. Keep the surface tiny and named, so it is documentable and greppable. And prefer declarative first: if a prop can express it, use the prop. The test is whether the operation is a moment in time (imperative) or a state of the world (declarative) — focus is a moment, visibility is a state.

JSX
// portal: escapes overflow/stacking, still bubbles through the React tree
function Modal({ children }) {
  return createPortal(<div className="modal">{children}</div>, document.body);
}

// imperative handle: ACTIONS only, never state
const VideoPlayer = forwardRef(function VideoPlayer(props, ref) {
  const el = useRef(null);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
    play:  () => el.current.play(),
    pause: () => el.current.pause(),
    seek:  (t) => { el.current.currentTime = t; },
    // NOT: setVolume/getState - that belongs in props
  }), []);
  return <video ref={el} {...props} />;
});

playerRef.current.seek(30);   // a moment in time -> imperative is correct
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does event bubbling through the React tree surprise people?

Because a modal portalled into document.body is visually and structurally separate, yet a click inside it triggers handlers on the React ancestor that rendered it. Click-outside logic must therefore check containment against the portal node, not rely on DOM ancestry.

When is a ref the only correct option?

When the value must persist across renders and must not cause one — an interval id, a WebSocket, a mutable third-party instance. Putting a timer id in state re-renders on every tick for no reason.

How do you decide imperative versus declarative?

Ask whether it is a moment or a state. "Focus this input now" and "play the video" are moments and fit an imperative handle. "Is this open" and "which item is selected" are states and belong in props.

All-pairs shortest paths in three nested loops. The intermediate node k must be the outermost loop — that ordering is the algorithm.

CostO(V³) time, O(V²) spaceReach for itAll-pairs distances when V ≤ ~500, transitive closure, and finding the graph's diameter.
def floyd_warshall(n, dist):       # dist[i][j] preloaded, inf if no edge
    for k in range(n):             # k OUTERMOST - this is not optional
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                if dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] < dist[i][j]:
                    dist[i][j] = dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]
    return dist

# Meaning: after iteration k, dist[i][j] is the best path using only
# nodes 0..k as intermediates. Putting k inside gives a wrong answer.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Take the classic offender: a service that validates, persists and notifies. Three responsibilities, three reasons to change, and a test that needs the database and a mail server to check a validation rule.

SRP — split it: a validator, a repository, a notifier, and a service that orchestrates them. Now the validation rule is unit-testable in microseconds. DIP — the service depends on interfaces it owns (OrderRepository, OrderNotifier), implemented by JPA and email adapters. The direction matters: the high-level policy defines the interface, the low-level detail implements it, which is what makes the detail swappable.

LSP shows up as the rule that a subtype must be usable wherever the supertype is — Square extends Rectangle fails because code setting width and height independently breaks. ISP — do not force a client to depend on methods it does not use; a fat Repository interface with twenty methods makes every fake implementation painful. OCP — new behaviour by adding a class rather than editing a switch; the Spring strategy-registry pattern (Map<String, Handler>) is OCP done for real.

Which earns its keep: SRP and DIP, constantly. SRP is the one that makes tests fast and code navigable; DIP is what makes the code testable at all and lets you defer infrastructure decisions.

Which is most over-applied: OCP and ISP. An interface with exactly one implementation, created "for flexibility", is pure indirection — an extra file, an extra hop when navigating, and you will change both together anyway. Likewise a Strategy plus enum plus factory built for a rule that has never varied in three years, where a plain if would have been clearer. The senior move is knowing when not to apply a principle, and being able to give a concrete example of over-application is what distinguishes a real answer from a memorized one.

The rule of thumb: introduce the abstraction when the second implementation arrives, or when you need a genuine test seam at an external boundary — not in anticipation.

Java
// before: three reasons to change; testing validation needs a DB and a mailer
class OrderService {
    void place(Order o) { validate(o); jpaRepo.save(o); mailer.send(o); }
}

// after: SRP + DIP - interfaces owned by this layer, implemented at the edges
class OrderService {
    private final OrderValidator validator;
    private final OrderRepository repository;   // interface here, JPA impl outside
    private final OrderNotifier notifier;       // interface here, email impl outside

    void place(Order o) {
        validator.check(o);
        repository.save(o);
        notifier.placed(o);
    }
}
new OrderService(new RealValidator(), new InMemoryRepo(), new NoopNotifier());  // fast test
Follow-ups they will ask

Give a concrete example of over-applying OCP.

A DiscountStrategyFactory with an enum, an interface and one implementation, for a discount rule that has not changed since it was written. Four files and an indirection to follow one branch that a single if would have expressed.

Does DIP mean every class needs an interface?

No — only at boundaries you want to swap or fake: external systems, infrastructure, and genuinely pluggable policy. An interface over your own domain logic with one implementation adds a file and hides the code you are trying to read.

How does SRP relate to test speed?

Directly. A class with one responsibility has few collaborators, so its tests need few fakes and run in memory. If a test requires six mocks to set up, the class has six responsibilities and the mocks are telling you so.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

CQRS separates the write model from the read model. Writes go through commands into a normalized model enforcing invariants; reads come from one or more projections shaped for specific queries. The motivation is that the shape that protects invariants and the shape that answers queries fast are usually different, and forcing one model to do both compromises each. Note that CQRS does not require event sourcing — a read replica with denormalized views is CQRS, and it is often the right dose.

Event sourcing goes further: the events are the source of truth, and current state is a fold over them. You never store "balance = 500"; you store every credit and debit and derive the balance. For an audit-critical system that is powerful — you get the complete history for free, you can answer "what did we believe on this date", and you can build a new projection retroactively over data you already have because you kept the facts rather than just the conclusions.

The three costs, which is where the answer earns its marks. One: eventual consistency between write and read models. A user submits a form and immediately queries — the projection has not caught up, so their own change is missing. You must design for it: return the command result directly, use client-side optimistic updates, or expose the projection's version so the client can wait.

Two: schema evolution of stored events. Events are immutable and kept forever, so version one of your event will still be in the store in five years. You cannot migrate them the way you migrate a table; you need upcasters that transform old event versions on read, and every one is permanent code. This is the cost people underestimate most.

Three: replay time. Rebuilding a projection means folding millions of events, which grows without bound. The mitigation is snapshots — periodically persist the aggregate state at a version and replay only from there — which is now another artefact to version and invalidate.

So the recommendation: use event sourcing where the history is the product — ledgers, audit, regulatory systems — and CQRS without event sourcing for most read-scaling problems.

Shapes
CQRS only (common, cheap):
  writes -> normalized model (invariants) -> replicate/derive -> read views

CQRS + event sourcing (audit-critical):
  command -> validate against aggregate -> append EVENT (immutable, forever)
         -> projections fold events into read models
  current state = fold(events)   |   balance is derived, never stored

costs: eventual consistency write->read
       event schema evolution forever (upcasters)
       replay time grows -> snapshots (another versioned artefact)
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you handle a user reading immediately after writing?

Return the result of the command directly rather than re-querying, apply it optimistically on the client, or return the projection version the write reached and have the client wait for the read model to reach it. Pretending it is synchronous is what produces the 'my change disappeared' bug.

What happens when you need to change an event's shape?

You add a new version and write an upcaster that transforms old events into the new shape on read. You cannot edit history — that is the whole point — so every schema change leaves permanent translation code behind.

When is event sourcing clearly wrong?

When history has no business value and you just want read scaling — then plain CQRS or a read replica gives you the benefit without the permanent costs. Adopting it for fashion is one of the most expensive architectural mistakes available.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

All three exist to stop expensive work from blocking the user, and they do it by making rendering interruptible.

startTransition marks an update as non-urgent. React renders it at lower priority and will abandon and restart it if an urgent update — typing, clicking — arrives. The canonical case: a search input filtering a list of 10,000 rows. Without it, every keystroke blocks on the filter render and typing feels laggy. Wrapping the filter update in a transition keeps the input responsive because the character update is urgent and the list update is not. isPending lets you show a subtle indicator rather than a jarring spinner.

useDeferredValue is the same idea when you do not own the update site — you receive a value as a prop and want a lagging copy to feed expensive children. It renders the old value at normal priority and the new one at low priority. Use it when you cannot wrap the setter; use startTransition when you can.

Streaming SSR with Suspense applies interruptibility to the server. The server sends the shell immediately and streams each Suspense boundary's HTML as its data resolves, so LCP no longer waits for the slowest query. Previously one slow database call delayed the entire document; now the page paints, the fast regions fill in, and the slow one arrives with its skeleton replaced in place — no client-side waterfall and no layout shift if the skeleton matches.

The visible improvement for each: transitions keep typing smooth while a heavy list re-renders; useDeferredValue keeps a chart's parent responsive when the chart is expensive to redraw; streaming SSR turns a 2-second blank page into a 300 ms shell with progressively filling content.

One caution worth adding: transitions do not make the work faster, they make it interruptible — if the render genuinely takes 800 ms, the result still arrives in 800 ms, it just no longer blocks input. If the work is that expensive, virtualize or memoize it as well.

JSX
// I own the setter -> startTransition
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
function onChange(e) {
  setQuery(e.target.value);                    // urgent: the input updates instantly
  startTransition(() => setFilter(e.target.value));  // non-urgent: interruptible
}
{isPending && <Spinner subtle />}

// I only receive the value -> useDeferredValue
function Chart({ data }) {
  const deferred = useDeferredValue(data);     // expensive redraw at low priority
  return <ExpensiveChart data={deferred} />;
}

// streaming SSR: shell first, slow regions stream in
<Suspense fallback={<FeedSkeleton />}>
  <Feed />        {/* its query does not delay the shell's paint */}
</Suspense>
Follow-ups they will ask

Does a transition make rendering faster?

No — it makes it interruptible and lower priority, so urgent updates preempt it. The total work is unchanged, which is why you still need memoization or virtualization if the render itself is genuinely slow.

startTransition or useDeferredValue?

Use startTransition when you control the state update. Use useDeferredValue when the value arrives as a prop and you cannot wrap the setter. They achieve the same effect from different sides.

What is the risk with streaming SSR?

Layout shift if the skeleton does not match the final content, and a more complex error story — a boundary that fails after the shell has been sent cannot change the HTTP status. Design skeletons to match, and pair each Suspense boundary with an error boundary.

Greedy I
  • Maximum SubarrayMedium
  • Jump GameMedium
  • Jump Game IIMedium

When every edge weighs 0 or 1, a deque replaces the heap: push 0-weight edges to the front and 1-weight edges to the back.

CostO(V + E) — better than Dijkstra's log factorReach for itGrids where some moves are free, minimum obstacle removal, minimum flips to reach a target.
from collections import deque
def zero_one_bfs(src, n, g):       # g[u] = [(v, 0 or 1), ...]
    dist = [float('inf')]*n; dist[src] = 0
    dq = deque([src])
    while dq:
        u = dq.popleft()
        for v, w in g[u]:
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
                if w == 0: dq.appendleft(v)   # free move -> front
                else:      dq.append(v)       # costly move -> back
    return dist

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Answer by matching each primitive to the shape of the coordination problem, because that is the actual skill.

CountDownLatch — one-shot, asymmetric: one set of threads waits for a different set to finish. Initialize to N, each worker calls countDown(), waiters block in await(). It cannot be reset. Scenario: the application must not accept traffic until three subsystems have initialized — latch of 3, readiness waits on it. Also the standard way to start N threads simultaneously in a test.

CyclicBarrier — reusable, symmetric: the same N threads rendezvous repeatedly, and all are released together, optionally running a barrier action first. Scenario: an iterative parallel simulation where every worker must finish phase K before any starts K+1. Note the fail-fast semantics: if one waiter is interrupted or times out, the barrier is broken and all others get BrokenBarrierException.

Semaphore — bounds concurrent access to a resource with a permit count. Scenario: limit concurrent calls to a fragile downstream to 20 regardless of how many threads exist. This is also the primitive you pair with virtual threads, since unbounded cheap threads mean the pool no longer limits load on your dependencies. Always release in a finally.

Phaser — a barrier with dynamic party registration, so threads can join and leave between phases. Scenario: a phased pipeline where the number of workers changes. Rarely needed; if a CyclicBarrier fits, use it.

CompletableFuture.allOf — for asynchronous composition rather than thread coordination. Scenario: fan out to three services and continue when all complete, without blocking a thread waiting. Prefer this to a latch whenever the work is already async, because a latch blocks a thread purely to wait.

Exchanger swaps objects between exactly two threads — genuinely rare.

The selection rule to state: latch for one-shot waiting, barrier for repeated rendezvous, semaphore for bounding concurrency, CompletableFuture for async composition. And prefer the higher-level construct — most "coordinate these threads" problems are better expressed as an executor plus futures than as hand-managed latches.

Java
// latch: one-shot, wait for N one-time initializations
CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(3);
for (var s : subsystems) pool.submit(() -> { s.init(); ready.countDown(); });
ready.await(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

// semaphore: bound concurrency against a fragile dependency
Semaphore limit = new Semaphore(20);
limit.acquire();
try { downstream.call(); } finally { limit.release(); }   // finally is mandatory

// async composition - no thread blocked waiting
CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b, c)
    .thenApply(v -> combine(a.join(), b.join(), c.join()));
Follow-ups they will ask

Latch or barrier — the one-line difference?

A latch is one-shot and asymmetric (waiters differ from the counters-down). A barrier is reusable and symmetric (the same parties meet repeatedly). If you find yourself wanting to reset a latch, you wanted a barrier.

Why pair a semaphore with virtual threads?

Because virtual threads remove the thread pool as an implicit concurrency limit. A million virtual threads will all call your database at once unless something bounds them — the semaphore becomes the explicit limiter the pool used to be implicitly.

When would you use a Phaser?

When the number of participating threads changes between phases, which a CyclicBarrier cannot express. It is powerful and rarely necessary — reaching for it when a barrier suffices adds complexity for nothing.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Frame it correctly first: consensus is how a set of nodes agree on a value despite failures. It underpins leader election, configuration, and anything requiring exactly one authoritative answer. And the practical position to state up front — you use a consensus system, you do not implement one.

Raft's intuition, which is what is actually being asked. Nodes are follower, candidate or leader. Time is divided into terms, each with at most one leader. A follower that hears nothing from a leader for a randomized election timeout becomes a candidate, increments the term, and requests votes; a node votes once per term, so a candidate winning a majority becomes leader. Randomized timeouts are what prevent perpetual split votes.

Log replication: all writes go to the leader, which appends to its log and replicates to followers. Once a majority have acknowledged, the entry is committed and applied to the state machine. That majority quorum is why you need an odd number of nodes — five nodes tolerate two failures, six also tolerate only two, so the sixth adds cost and no availability.

Safety comes from the election restriction: a candidate cannot win unless its log is at least as up to date as the voter's, which guarantees a committed entry can never be lost by a leader change. That single rule is the heart of Raft's correctness, and mentioning it shows you have read past the diagram.

Real uses: ZooKeeper (ZAB, Raft-like) and etcd are used for coordination, not data — service discovery, distributed configuration, distributed locks and leases, leader election for singleton jobs, and cluster membership. Kubernetes stores all its state in etcd; Kafka's KRaft mode replaced ZooKeeper with Raft.

The limits to name: consensus requires a majority to be reachable, so it sacrifices availability under partition — it is CP. Every write costs at least one round trip to a majority, so throughput is bounded and latency is a function of your slowest quorum member. Never put high-volume application data in it; keep it for small, critical, rarely-changing state.

Raft
roles: follower -> (election timeout) -> candidate -> (majority votes) -> leader
terms: monotonically increasing; at most one leader per term

write: client -> leader -> append to log -> replicate
       majority ack -> COMMIT -> apply to state machine -> reply

quorum: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure; 5 tolerate 2; use ODD counts
safety: a candidate needs an up-to-date log to win -> committed entries survive

use for: leader election, config, locks/leases, membership   (small, critical state)
not for: application data volume - every write is a majority round trip
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does a distributed lock need a fencing token even with consensus?

Because the lock holder can be paused (GC, VM suspend) past its lease expiry while another node legitimately acquires it. The token — a monotonically increasing number checked by the protected resource — makes the stale holder's writes rejected.

What happens to a minority partition?

It cannot elect a leader or commit writes, so it becomes read-only or unavailable. That is the deliberate CP choice: consensus systems refuse to serve rather than risk divergence.

Raft or Paxos?

Practically the same guarantees; Raft was designed to be understandable and decomposes into leader election, log replication and safety. Almost every modern system chose Raft for that reason.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start with the reason to consider it: JavaScript is single-threaded, so any task over about 50 ms blocks input handling, rendering and animation. That is measured directly by INP. A Web Worker runs on a separate thread, so the main thread stays free.

The cost is the message boundary, and this is the part that decides whether it is worth it. Data passed to a worker is structured-cloned — deep-copied — so the transfer cost is proportional to payload size. For small payloads that copy can exceed the compute you moved off the main thread, making the worker a net loss. Two escapes: transferable objects (an ArrayBuffer is moved, not copied, in O(1) — but the sender loses access to it) and SharedArrayBuffer for genuinely shared memory, which requires cross-origin isolation headers (COOP/COEP) and so is often impractical.

Good candidates are large-payload, high-compute tasks: parsing a multi-megabyte JSON or CSV file, image or video processing, cryptography, compression, diffing large datasets, search indexing, and running a WASM module. Poor candidates: anything touching the DOM (workers cannot), anything needing frequent small round trips (the messaging overhead dominates), and anything already fast.

The ergonomics problem is real — raw postMessage with a message-type switch and manual correlation of responses becomes unpleasant quickly. Comlink wraps it in a proxy so worker functions are called with await as if they were local, which removes most of the friction and is worth naming.

Two practical notes: workers have startup cost, so pool and reuse them rather than creating one per task; and always provide a main-thread fallback plus a timeout, because a worker that fails to load or hangs should degrade rather than leave the feature dead.

The alternative worth mentioning: for work that is bursty rather than heavy, scheduler.yield() or chunking with requestIdleCallback can keep the main thread responsive without a worker at all.

JS
// transferable: O(1) move, not a copy - sender loses access
worker.postMessage({ buffer }, [buffer]);

// Comlink removes the postMessage ceremony
import * as Comlink from 'comlink';
const api = Comlink.wrap(new Worker(new URL('./parser.js', import.meta.url)));
const rows = await api.parseCsv(file);      // called like a local async function

// worker.js
Comlink.expose({ parseCsv(file) { /* heavy work, off the main thread */ } });

// pool + fallback + timeout
const result = await Promise.race([
  api.parseCsv(file),
  timeout(5000).then(() => parseOnMainThread(file)),   // degrade, never hang
]);
Follow-ups they will ask

When is a worker a net loss?

When the structured-clone cost of the payload exceeds the compute you moved. Measure both sides — a 50 ms computation on a 20 MB payload may spend more than 50 ms just copying it across the boundary.

Why is SharedArrayBuffer hard to use?

It requires cross-origin isolation (COOP and COEP headers), which breaks embedded third-party content — ads, analytics iframes, some payment widgets. Many production sites cannot enable it without losing functionality.

What is the alternative for bursty work?

Chunk the work and yield to the main thread between chunks using scheduler.yield() or requestIdleCallback. It keeps input responsive without a worker, and it is far simpler when the total work is moderate.

  • Gas StationMedium
  • Hand of StraightsMedium

Two-colour the graph with BFS or DFS. If an edge ever joins two nodes of the same colour, it is not bipartite.

CostO(V + E) timeReach for itCan this group be split in two, is there an odd cycle, conflict scheduling, and 'possible bipartition' questions.
from collections import deque
def is_bipartite(n, g):
    color = [0]*n                             # 0 unvisited, 1 and -1 the sides
    for s in range(n):
        if color[s]: continue
        color[s] = 1; q = deque([s])
        while q:
            u = q.popleft()
            for v in g[u]:
                if color[v] == color[u]: return False   # same side -> odd cycle
                if not color[v]:
                    color[v] = -color[u]; q.append(v)
    return True

Structure it as a pyramid with a specific shape for Spring. Most tests should be plain unit tests — new the class, pass fakes, assert. No Spring context, milliseconds each. That speed is what keeps the suite usable, and constructor injection is what makes it possible.

Slices in the middle: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer with MockMvc; @DataJpaTest only JPA with a transactional rollback per test. Full @SpringBootTest for a handful of end-to-end paths only — it starts the whole context, and its context caching is easily defeated by inconsistent configuration, so a suite full of slightly-different @SpringBootTest variants starts a new context for each and takes minutes.

Mocks, stubs, fakes — the distinction matters. A stub returns canned answers. A mock also asserts on interactions. A fake is a working lightweight implementation (an in-memory repository). Prefer fakes: they exercise real behaviour and survive refactoring, whereas interaction-heavy mocks assert how the code works and break on every restructuring even when behaviour is unchanged. And the rule: do not mock what you do not own — mocking a third-party client encodes your assumption about it, so if the assumption is wrong the test still passes. Wrap it in your own interface, fake that, and cover the real thing with one integration test.

Note @MockBean's hidden cost: each distinct set of mocked beans produces a different application context, and Spring caches contexts by configuration — ten variations means ten context startups.

Async and Kafka: never Thread.sleep. Use Awaitility to poll a condition with a timeout — faster and non-flaky. For Kafka, assert on the consumed side reaching a state rather than on timing.

Testcontainers changes the calculus because it makes the real dependency cheap: a real Postgres, Kafka or Redis in Docker per test class. Testing against H2 when production runs Postgres hides dialect differences, missing JSONB, different locking semantics and different constraint behaviour — bugs that pass locally and fail in production. Use a static container reused across classes to keep it fast.

Java
@Testcontainers @SpringBootTest
class OrderIT {
    @Container static PostgreSQLContainer<?> db =
            new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16");   // static = reused, fast

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void props(DynamicPropertyRegistry r) {
        r.add("spring.datasource.url", db::getJdbcUrl);
    }

    @Test void publishesEvent() {
        service.place(order);
        await().atMost(5, SECONDS)                       // Awaitility, not sleep
               .untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(consumed()).hasSize(1));
    }
}

// most tests need no Spring at all
var svc = new OrderService(new RealValidator(), new InMemoryRepo(), new NoopNotifier());
Follow-ups they will ask

Why prefer fakes over mocks?

Mocks assert on interactions, so they encode how the code works and break on refactoring even when behaviour is unchanged. A fake asserts on outcomes and keeps passing through a restructure — which is the behaviour you actually want from a regression suite.

What should you never mock?

Types you do not own. The mock encodes your belief about the library's behaviour; if that belief is wrong, the test passes and production fails. Wrap it behind your own interface and verify the real thing once with Testcontainers.

How do you keep an integration suite fast?

Reuse containers across test classes (static, or Testcontainers reuse mode), minimise distinct Spring context configurations so caching works, and keep the number of full @SpringBootTest classes small and deliberate.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Be honest about the ordering: most systems do not need multi-region, and the ones that do usually need it for latency or compliance rather than availability. Multi-AZ within one region already survives a datacentre failure and costs a fraction as much.

Active-passive: one region serves traffic, the other replicates asynchronously and stands ready. Simple, cheap, no conflict resolution — but failover is a real operation with real risk, your RPO equals the replication lag, and the passive region is untested unless you exercise it regularly. The failure mode to name: a standby you have never failed over to does not work.

Active-active: both regions accept writes. Excellent latency and true regional resilience — and it forces you to solve write conflicts, which is the hard part. Options: last-writer-wins (simple, and it silently discards data — unacceptable for anything transactional), CRDTs (converge without coordination, but only for data types that fit — counters, sets, sequences), or application-level merge (correct and expensive to build).

The design most teams should actually choose is the middle path worth naming explicitly: region-pinned users. Each user's writes are routed to their home region, so there are no concurrent conflicting writes for a given entity, with asynchronous cross-region replication for disaster recovery and cross-region reads. You get active-active's latency and utilization without the conflict problem.

Data residency (GDPR and similar) can make this mandatory rather than optional: EU users' personal data must stay in the EU. That means partitioning by jurisdiction, keeping PII in a region-local store with only non-personal references crossing borders, and being able to prove it. Compliance frequently dictates the topology before performance does.

RTO and RPO must be defined before the architecture, because they determine it. RPO of zero requires synchronous cross-region replication and its 100 ms+ write latency. RPO of five minutes allows asynchronous replication. RTO of minutes needs automated failover with health checks and DNS or anycast; RTO of hours can be a runbook. State them, then design — and test the failover on a schedule, because an untested one is a plan, not a capability.

Choosing
RPO = 0        -> synchronous cross-region  -> +100ms on every write
RPO = minutes  -> async replication         -> lose the replication lag on failover
RTO = minutes  -> automated failover, health-checked DNS/anycast
RTO = hours    -> documented runbook, tested quarterly

active-passive : simple, cheap, untested standby is the risk
active-active  : must solve write conflicts (LWW loses data; CRDT limited)
region-pinned  : <- usually the right answer. No conflicts, good latency, async DR

GDPR: PII stays in-region; only non-personal references cross borders
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is last-writer-wins usually unacceptable?

Because it silently discards a concurrent write with no record that it happened. For a shopping cart or a document that is a lost update the user will notice; for financial data it is a correctness failure.

What breaks first when you go active-active?

The database. Application servers are easy to run in two regions; a single-writer database is not, and moving to multi-master introduces exactly the conflict resolution you were trying to avoid.

How do you keep the passive region trustworthy?

Fail over to it on a schedule — a planned regional failover exercise. Anything less means discovering during an incident that a certificate expired, a secret was never replicated, or capacity was never provisioned.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Split it by what runs per pull request versus nightly, driven by one constraint: PR feedback must be fast enough that people wait for it. Past roughly ten minutes, developers context-switch and the value collapses.

Per PR: typecheck, lint, unit and integration tests (React Testing Library plus MSW), the affected E2E subset, and a bundle-size budget checked as a delta against the base branch. Bundle size is the one to enforce strictly because it is deterministic and attributable — this PR added 40 KB, and its author is the person who can explain why.

Nightly or on merge to main: the full E2E matrix across browsers and viewports, visual regression, Lighthouse on key routes, and accessibility scans (axe). These are slower and noisier, so they inform rather than block.

Visual regression deserves care: it catches CSS changes nothing else can, and it is the most likely to produce noise from font rendering and animation timing. Make it deterministic — freeze time, disable animations, wait for fonts, use a consistent container — and review diffs as a normal part of code review rather than auto-approving them, which is how the whole tool becomes decorative.

Flaky E2E is the main failure mode, and the answer is a process, not a flag. Blind retries hide real race conditions and let flakiness compound. Quarantine instead: move a flaky test out of the blocking suite, file it with an owner, and fix or delete it within a fixed window. A suite people routinely re-run until it passes has stopped being a signal — that is the point to make.

Prevention matters more than detection: prefer role-based queries and findBy* auto-retrying assertions over fixed waits, seed deterministic data per test, and avoid tests that depend on shared mutable state or on each other's ordering.

Finally, publish the trends — suite duration, flake rate, bundle size — somewhere the team sees weekly, or all of it silently degrades.

CI
# per PR - must finish in <10 min or people stop waiting
typecheck | lint | unit + integration (RTL + MSW) | affected E2E
bundle budget: fail on DELTA vs base branch, comment the diff on the PR

# nightly / on main - slower, informational
full E2E matrix (browsers x viewports) | visual regression | Lighthouse | axe

# flaky tests
quarantine (out of the blocking suite) -> owner -> fixed or deleted in 2 weeks
NEVER: blanket retries - they hide real races and let flakiness compound

# publish weekly: suite duration, flake rate, bundle size trend
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not just retry flaky tests?

Because a flaky test is usually a real race condition in the application or the test's synchronization. Retrying hides it until it appears in production, and it removes the pressure to fix the underlying cause.

How do you make visual regression usable?

Determinism: freeze the clock, disable animations and transitions, wait for web fonts, pin the viewport and device pixel ratio. Without those, every run produces diffs and the team learns to approve them without looking.

What if the E2E suite is genuinely slow?

Run only the tests affected by the change on PRs (by dependency graph or tagging), parallelise across shards, and keep the full matrix nightly. Most E2E suites are also testing too much — push coverage down to integration tests where it is faster and more stable.

Treat an integer as an array of bits. Four operations cover almost everything: test, set, clear, and toggle.

CostO(1) per operationReach for itCompact sets, flags, parity tricks, and the prerequisite for bitmask DP.
x >> i & 1          # test bit i
x |=  1 << i        # set bit i
x &= ~(1 << i)      # clear bit i
x ^=  1 << i        # toggle bit i

x & (x - 1)         # clear the LOWEST set bit
x & -x              # ISOLATE the lowest set bit
x & (x - 1) == 0    # is x a power of two?
bin(x).count('1')   # popcount  (int.bit_count() in Python 3.10+)

# Count set bits by repeatedly clearing the lowest one:
while x: x &= x - 1; count += 1
