Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Both resolve transitive dependencies, but with different conflict rules — and that difference causes real, confusing bugs. Maven uses nearest-wins: the version at the shallowest depth in the dependency tree, with declaration order breaking ties. Gradle uses highest-wins: the newest version anyone requested. The same dependency graph can therefore produce different runtime versions in the two tools, which is why a project that builds fine in one fails in the other.

Diagnosis: mvn dependency:tree and gradle dependencyInsight. Learn to read them, because NoSuchMethodError or NoClassDefFoundError at runtime is almost always "I compiled against one version and am running against another" — a resolution problem, not a code problem. mvn dependency:analyze additionally finds dependencies you use but do not declare (fragile — they can vanish when a transitive dependency changes) and ones you declare but never use.

The fix is centralization: a BOM (dependencyManagement with scope=import in Maven, a platform in Gradle) pins versions in one place. The Spring Boot BOM exists precisely so the dozens of libraries it pulls in remain mutually compatible — you should almost never specify a version for anything the BOM manages. For a multi-module build, one parent or version catalogue keeps modules aligned.

Shading (relocating a dependency's packages into your own namespace at build time, via the Maven Shade plugin or Gradle Shadow) solves the case where you and a dependency need genuinely incompatible versions of the same library. It is a library author's tool: it makes your artifact self-contained at the cost of a larger jar, duplicated classes across the ecosystem, and broken debugging. Using it in an application almost always means the dependency graph needs cleaning instead.

Two practical additions: keep an allowlist for scope — provided and test scopes prevent leaking build-only dependencies into runtime — and run a vulnerability scanner in CI, since most real-world Java breaches arrive through a known CVE in a transitive dependency rather than through code anyone wrote.

Diagnosing
mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind
mvn dependency:analyze          # used-but-undeclared / declared-but-unused
gradle dependencyInsight --dependency jackson-databind

<!-- pin transitively in ONE place -->
<dependencyManagement><dependencies><dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
  <version>3.3.0</version><type>pom</type><scope>import</scope>
</dependency></dependencies></dependencyManagement>

# Maven: nearest-wins   Gradle: highest-wins   <- same graph, different result
Follow-ups they will ask

What does NoSuchMethodError actually tell you?

That the class was found but the method signature was not — you compiled against one version and are running against another. It is a dependency-resolution problem essentially every time.

When is shading legitimate?

When you publish a library that must not impose its dependency versions on consumers — for example bundling a specific Guava version. In an application it is a workaround for a graph you should fix instead.

How do you keep the dependency graph healthy over time?

Use the BOM, run dependency:analyze in CI to catch undeclared transitive usage, enable Dependabot or Renovate for updates, and scan for CVEs. Left alone, a graph degrades silently until an upgrade becomes a multi-week project.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

B-tree: updates are made in place. A write finds the leaf page, modifies it, and the change is made durable through a write-ahead log. Reads are excellent — a point lookup is a handful of page reads, and range scans follow the leaf ordering. The cost is that writes are random IO: each one touches a specific page, plus the WAL write, so write amplification is roughly the page size divided by the row size, and it does not batch well.

LSM tree: writes go to an in-memory memtable and a sequential commit log. When the memtable fills, it is flushed to an immutable, sorted SSTable on disk. So every write is sequential — dramatically faster on both spinning disks and SSDs, and it batches naturally. The cost is on the read side: a key may live in any of several SSTables, so a read may probe many files. Bloom filters per SSTable make "definitely not here" cheap, and compaction merges SSTables in the background to bound their number.

The amplification trade is the crisp summary: B-tree has lower read amplification and higher write amplification; LSM has lower write amplification at write time but higher read amplification, and compaction moves the write cost into the background where it competes for IO. That background IO is the operational surprise — an LSM store can be fast until compaction falls behind, and then latency degrades sharply.

Cassandra over Postgres, honestly: when you need multi-region writes with no single primary, very high write throughput, linear scalability by adding nodes, and you can model every query in advance — because Cassandra makes you design tables per access pattern, with no joins and no ad-hoc queries. Its tunable consistency (quorum reads and writes) lets you choose per operation.

When not to: if you need transactions, joins, ad-hoc queries, or strong consistency by default, Postgres wins and it scales further than most teams assume. The failure mode is choosing Cassandra for scale you do not have, then discovering you need a query you did not model — which means a new table, a backfill, and dual writes. Say that: the cost of Cassandra is paid at design time, in query inflexibility.

Trade
B-tree (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB)
  write: random IO, in-place, + WAL      -> higher write amplification
  read : few page reads, ordered scans   -> low read amplification

LSM (Cassandra, RocksDB, ScyllaDB)
  write: append to memtable + seq log    -> sequential, very fast
  read : may probe N SSTables            -> bloom filters + compaction
  compaction: moves the write cost to background IO  <- the operational surprise

Cassandra when: multi-region writes, huge write volume, all queries known upfront
Postgres when:  transactions, joins, ad-hoc queries, strong consistency (most cases)
Follow-ups they will ask

What is read amplification in an LSM tree, concretely?

A point lookup checks the memtable, then each SSTable that might contain the key. Bloom filters eliminate most misses cheaply, but a key updated many times across levels still costs several file reads — which is why compaction strategy matters so much.

What goes wrong when compaction falls behind?

SSTable count grows, so reads probe more files and latency climbs; disk usage grows because superseded data is not yet merged away. It presents as a gradual degradation rather than a failure, which makes it easy to miss until it is severe.

Can Postgres handle write-heavy workloads?

Considerably more than people assume — with partitioning, appropriate indexes, and attention to autovacuum. The genuine limits are single-primary write throughput and multi-region writes, not raw volume.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

OT (Operational Transformation) works by transforming operations against concurrent ones. If I insert at position 5 and you concurrently insert at position 2, my operation must be transformed to position 6 before being applied to your document. It converges, and it produces compact operations — but it requires a central server to establish a canonical order, and the transformation functions are notoriously difficult to get right for every operation pair. Google Docs uses it.

CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are designed so that concurrent operations commute — apply them in any order and every replica converges to the same state, with no central coordinator and no transformation. For text this is usually a sequence CRDT where each character gets a unique, densely-ordered identifier, so an insertion never needs to renumber anything. The cost is metadata overhead — identifiers and tombstones for deleted characters — which historically made documents grow without bound, though modern implementations (Yjs, Automerge) compress this well.

The tradeoff to state: OT is compact but needs a server and is hard to implement correctly; CRDTs are simpler to reason about, work peer-to-peer and offline, and cost memory and bandwidth in metadata.

Now the honest answer for the diary approval workflow, which is the point of the question. That feature is not concurrent free-form editing — it is a propose-and-approve flow. The simpler and more correct design is explicit diffs: an editor submits a proposed change as a diff against a specific version, the owner sees the diff and approves or rejects, and the system rejects the proposal if the base version has moved. That is optimistic concurrency with a version check — the same model as a pull request.

Why that is better here: the product requires an explicit review step, so automatic merging actively defeats the feature. A CRDT would silently converge changes the owner never approved. Document-level locking ("someone is editing this page") is an even simpler variant if concurrent proposals are rare. Choosing the weaker mechanism because the product does not need the stronger one is the senior answer — reaching for a CRDT here would be an expensive solution to a problem you do not have.

For the approval workflow
PROPOSE:
  POST /pages/{id}/proposals { baseVersion: 42, diff: [...] }
  -> 409 if the page has moved past version 42 (rebase or reject)

REVIEW:
  owner sees the rendered diff -> approve -> apply atomically, version -> 43
                               -> reject  -> proposal closed, page untouched

why not a CRDT here:
  CRDTs converge automatically - which SKIPS the approval step the product requires
  the review gate IS the feature; automatic merge defeats it

if concurrent proposals are rare: document-level lock is simpler still
Follow-ups they will ask

When would a CRDT genuinely be right for this product?

If you added a live co-editing mode where two people type in the same page simultaneously and expect to see each other's cursors. That is a different feature with different requirements, and Yjs would be the pragmatic choice.

What is the hardest part of a sequence CRDT?

Identifier allocation and tombstones. Identifiers must be densely orderable so insertion between two characters never requires renumbering, and deleted characters must be retained as tombstones so concurrent operations referencing them still apply — which is where the memory growth comes from.

Why is a version check enough here?

Because proposals are discrete and reviewed. Optimistic concurrency detects that the base moved and asks the proposer to rebase — exactly how code review works, and users already understand that model.

Bit Manipulation I
  • Single NumberEasy
  • Number of 1 BitsEasy
  • Counting BitsEasy
  • Missing NumberEasy

XOR is its own inverse: a^a = 0 and a^0 = a. So XORing everything cancels every value that appears an even number of times.

CostO(n) time, O(1) spaceReach for itSingle number among pairs, finding two singles, missing number, and any 'everything appears twice except' problem.
def single_number(nums):
    r = 0
    for v in nums: r ^= v      # pairs cancel; the loner survives
    return r

# TWO singles: XOR everything, then split by any set bit in the result
def two_singles(nums):
    x = 0
    for v in nums: x ^= v      # x = a ^ b
    bit = x & -x               # a bit where a and b differ
    a = b = 0
    for v in nums:
        if v & bit: a ^= v
        else:       b ^= v
    return a, b

# XOR prefix: xor[i..j] = pre[j] ^ pre[i-1]  (like prefix sums)

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Walk the ones that actually appear in a Spring service rather than reciting all ten.

Injection. In Java this is almost always SQL built by string concatenation. The fix is parameter binding — PreparedStatement, JPQL parameters, Spring Data. The case that catches people is that you cannot parameterize SQL structure: a dynamic ORDER BY or table name must be validated against an allowlist of known column names, never interpolated from user input. Allowlist rather than escaping, because escaping requires anticipating every encoding and an attacker only needs one you missed.

Mass assignment. Binding @RequestBody directly to a JPA entity lets a caller set any field the entity exposes — role, balance, isVerified. Always bind to a request DTO containing only the fields a client may legitimately set, and map explicitly. This is a one-line vulnerability that is trivially exploitable and extremely common.

SSRF. Any feature that fetches a user-supplied URL — webhook registration, image import, link preview — lets an attacker reach your internal network and cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254) to steal credentials. Defend with a host allowlist, blocking private and link-local address ranges after DNS resolution (to defeat rebinding), and disabling redirects.

Deserialization. Never deserialize untrusted Java-serialized data — it constructs objects without constructors and the stream chooses the classes. With Jackson, never enable default polymorphic typing, which reintroduces the same arbitrary-instantiation hole and has produced multiple RCEs.

Secrets. From environment variables or a vault, never in committed YAML, never in logs, never in toString(). Rotate them, and scan git history — a secret committed once is compromised even after removal.

Close with the one that matters most statistically: most real Java breaches arrive through a known CVE in a transitive dependency, not through code anyone wrote. Dependency scanning in CI and a fast patch process outrank most code-level hardening.

Java
// injection-safe including the dynamic sort
private static final Set<String> SORTABLE = Set.of("created_at","amount","status");
String sort = SORTABLE.contains(req.sort()) ? req.sort() : "created_at";  // allowlist
jdbc.query("select * from orders where account_id = ? order by " + sort,
           mapper, accountId);                              // value is bound

// mass assignment: bind to a DTO, never to the entity
record UpdateProfile(String displayName, String avatarUrl) {}   // no `role` field

// SSRF: resolve first, then check the resolved address
InetAddress addr = InetAddress.getByName(uri.getHost());
if (addr.isSiteLocalAddress() || addr.isLoopbackAddress() || addr.isLinkLocalAddress())
    throw new SecurityException("blocked");
Follow-ups they will ask

Why allowlist rather than blocklist or escaping?

A blocklist must anticipate every attack encoding and an attacker needs only one you missed. An allowlist enumerates what is permitted, so anything unforeseen is rejected by default — it fails safe rather than failing open.

Why check the resolved address for SSRF rather than the hostname?

Because DNS rebinding lets an attacker point a public hostname at an internal address, and the hostname check passes. Resolve first, validate the actual IP, and ideally pin the connection to that resolved address.

What is the highest-leverage security work in a Java service?

Dependency scanning with a fast patch process, followed by input validation at the boundary and secrets management. Those three cover the overwhelming majority of real incidents.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Requirements set the architecture: a decision in under 200 ms in the authorization path, so this is a synchronous scoring service backed by asynchronously computed features. You cannot compute aggregates at request time; you can only look them up.

Feature computation is streaming. Transactions flow through Kafka into a stream processor (Kafka Streams or Flink) that maintains windowed aggregates — transactions in the last 5 minutes, hour, day for this card; distinct merchants in the last hour; distance from the previous transaction location over elapsed time (the classic impossible-travel signal); deviation from the account's normal amount. Those are written to a low-latency feature store (Redis or similar) keyed by card and account, so the scoring path is a handful of key lookups.

Two layers in the decision. A rules engine for hard blocks — deterministic, explainable, changeable in minutes without a model retrain, and legally defensible when a customer asks why they were declined. Then a model score for the grey area. The rules exist not because models are worse but because explainability and fast response to a new attack pattern are operational requirements.

Shadow mode is the deployment answer and you should volunteer it: run a new rule or model in parallel, log what it would have done, compare against actual outcomes for days or weeks, then enable enforcement. Deploying a fraud rule straight to blocking is how you decline thousands of legitimate customers before anyone notices.

The feedback loop is slow, and this is the part interviewers probe. Ground truth comes from chargebacks, which arrive 30 to 90 days later. So your labels lag by months, the model you are training reflects attack patterns that have already changed, and you cannot measure a change quickly. Mitigate with faster proxy signals — customer-reported fraud, manual review outcomes, step-up authentication failures — but state the constraint honestly.

Fail-open or fail-closed is a business decision, not a technical one: if the scoring service is down, do you decline everything (losing revenue and angering customers) or approve everything (accepting fraud)? Most payment systems fail open with a conservative fallback rule set, because declining all transactions is usually the larger loss — but that must be an explicit, documented decision with a monitored fallback path.

Pipeline
transactions -> Kafka -> Flink/Kafka Streams (windowed aggregates)
                              |
                              v  feature store (Redis) keyed by card/account

authorization (<200ms):
  fetch features (few key lookups) -> RULES (hard blocks, explainable)
                                   -> MODEL score -> approve / review / decline

rollout: shadow mode -> compare vs outcomes -> enforce
labels:  chargebacks arrive 30-90 days later  <- the feedback loop is months long
outage:  fail-open with conservative fallback rules (an explicit business decision)
Follow-ups they will ask

Why keep a rules engine if you have a model?

Explainability and speed of response. A regulator or a customer can be told exactly which rule fired; and when a new attack pattern appears on Monday you can block it on Monday, not after the next retraining cycle.

What is the hardest data problem here?

Label lag. Chargebacks define truth and arrive months later, so you are always training on stale attack patterns and cannot quickly measure whether a change helped. Proxy labels help but are biased — a declined transaction never produces a chargeback, so you never learn whether it was fraud.

How do you avoid blocking legitimate customers?

Shadow mode before enforcement, a step-up path (challenge rather than decline) for the uncertain band, tight monitoring of decline rates by segment, and a fast manual-review queue with a feedback path into the rules.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

XSS in React: JSX escapes interpolated values by default, so {userInput} is safe — which lulls people into thinking React is XSS-proof. It is not. Three real vectors: dangerouslySetInnerHTML with unsanitized input; URL attributes — href={userInput} or src accepts javascript: and data: URLs, which execute on click; and props spread onto DOM elements from server data, which can inject event handlers.

So: sanitize with DOMPurify whenever you must render HTML, and validate URL schemes against an allowlist (https:, mailto:) rather than blocking javascript:, since encodings defeat blocklists.

CSP is the defence-in-depth layer, and the important point is that it only works if you avoid unsafe-inline. A CSP with script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' provides almost no protection, because injected inline script is exactly what XSS produces. Use nonces or hashes for the inline scripts you genuinely need, and add object-src 'none', base-uri 'self' (which blocks base-tag injection) and frame-ancestors to prevent clickjacking. Deploy in Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first and collect violation reports, or you will break your own site.

CSRF matters only with cookie authentication — this is the distinction people miss. If you send a bearer token in an Authorization header, a cross-site form post cannot add that header, so CSRF is structurally impossible. With cookies, the browser attaches them automatically, so you need SameSite=Lax (which blocks cross-site POSTs while allowing normal top-level navigation) or Strict, plus a double-submit token for the cases SameSite does not cover. Mark cookies httpOnly and Secure so XSS cannot read them.

The relationship to state clearly: httpOnly cookies defend against XSS stealing the token but require CSRF protection; localStorage avoids CSRF but is readable by any XSS. There is no option without a tradeoff — pick one and defend it.

Two more: keep third-party scripts to a minimum and use Subresource Integrity, since a compromised analytics tag runs with your origin's full privileges; and never put secrets in client-side code, because everything shipped to the browser is public.

JSX
// URL scheme allowlist - blocklists lose to encoding
const SAFE = /^(https?:|mailto:)/i;
<a href={SAFE.test(url) ? url : '#'}>{label}</a>

// must render HTML? sanitize
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';
<div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(html) }} />

# CSP - nonces, not unsafe-inline
Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'self';
  script-src 'self' 'nonce-{random}';
  object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none';

# cookie auth -> CSRF applies
Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does a bearer token in a header remove CSRF risk?

Because a cross-site request cannot set custom headers — the browser will not attach your Authorization header to a forged form post. Cookies are attached automatically, which is precisely what makes CSRF possible.

What makes a CSP actually effective?

Removing unsafe-inline from script-src. Everything else is secondary, because injected inline script is the primary XSS payload. Nonces or hashes are the way to keep the inline scripts you need.

Is React's escaping enough on its own?

No. It covers text interpolation, which is the most common case, but not dangerouslySetInnerHTML, URL attributes, or props spread onto DOM elements. Those three are where React XSS actually happens.

Bit Manipulation II
  • Reverse BitsEasy
  • Single Number IIMedium
  • Sum of Two IntegersMedium

Use an integer's bits as a subset, so dp[mask] means 'the best result having used exactly this set'. Only feasible while n ≤ about 20.

CostO(2ⁿ · n) time, O(2ⁿ) spaceReach for itTravelling salesman, assignment problems, minimum set cover. The constraint n ≤ 20 is effectively a label for this technique.
def tsp(n, cost):
    FULL = (1 << n) - 1
    dp = [[float('inf')]*n for _ in range(1 << n)]
    dp[1][0] = 0                             # started at 0, only 0 visited
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        for u in range(n):
            if dp[mask][u] == float('inf') or not mask >> u & 1: continue
            for v in range(n):
                if mask >> v & 1: continue   # already visited
                nm = mask | 1 << v
                dp[nm][v] = min(dp[nm][v], dp[mask][u] + cost[u][v])
    return min(dp[FULL])

# Enumerate SUBMASKS of m:  s = m; while s: ...; s = (s-1) & m

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design the API first: submit(task, delay), and the scheduler owns retry policy, attempt counting and the dead-letter path. Then the data structure.

Use a DelayQueue or a PriorityQueue ordered by next-run time, with one or more worker threads taking from the head. DelayQueue is the cleanest — take() blocks until the head element's delay has elapsed, so there is no polling loop and no busy-waiting. Each queued item implements getDelay and compareTo against its scheduled instant.

Backoff: delay = min(cap, base × 2^attempt) with full jitter — multiply by a random factor rather than adding a fixed one. Jitter is not cosmetic: without it, a thousand jobs that failed together retry at exactly the same instant, producing a synchronized thundering herd against a dependency that is already struggling. That is the detail worth stating.

Attempt limit and dead-lettering: carry the attempt count on the task; when it exceeds the maximum, move the task to a dead-letter store with the last exception, the attempt history and a timestamp. A DLQ nobody monitors is just deleting data, so alert on its depth and have a documented replay path.

Classify failures before retrying — a validation error or a 400 will never succeed, so retry only transient failures (timeouts, 5xx, connection resets) and dead-letter the rest immediately. Blind retries on permanent failures waste capacity and delay the real signal.

Thread safety: DelayQueue is already concurrent, so multiple workers can take safely; the attempt counter lives on the immutable task record, and re-submission creates a new instance rather than mutating.

Then answer the two follow-ups before they are asked. Surviving a restart: this is entirely in-memory, so a crash loses every pending job — persistence means a table with next_run_at and a status, polled with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Running on many nodes: an in-memory scheduler runs the job N times, so you need a lease — claim the row with an owner and expiry so a crashed worker's job is redelivered — which in turn requires the handler to be idempotent. Naming those two limits is what separates the exercise from a production answer.

Java
record Task(String id, Runnable body, int attempt, long runAtNanos)
        implements Delayed {
    public long getDelay(TimeUnit u) {
        return u.convert(runAtNanos - System.nanoTime(), NANOSECONDS);
    }
    public int compareTo(Delayed o) { return Long.compare(runAtNanos, ((Task)o).runAtNanos); }
}

private final DelayQueue<Task> queue = new DelayQueue<>();

void worker() throws InterruptedException {
    while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
        Task t = queue.take();                       // blocks until due
        try { t.body().run(); }
        catch (Exception e) {
            if (!isTransient(e) || t.attempt() >= MAX) { deadLetter(t, e); continue; }
            long base = 500L, cap = 60_000L;
            long backoff = Math.min(cap, base * (1L << t.attempt()));
            long jittered = (long)(backoff * (0.5 + ThreadLocalRandom.current()
                                                     .nextDouble() * 0.5));   // full jitter
            queue.put(new Task(t.id(), t.body(), t.attempt() + 1,
                               System.nanoTime() + MILLISECONDS.toNanos(jittered)));
        }
    }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why DelayQueue rather than a ScheduledExecutorService?

ScheduledExecutorService is fine and simpler for straightforward scheduling. DelayQueue gives you the queue explicitly, so you can inspect it, size it, and implement custom retry and priority logic — which is what the exercise is testing.

What is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for?

It lets many workers poll the same jobs table without contending: each claims rows nobody else has locked, skipping over locked ones instead of blocking. It is the standard pattern for a database-backed queue.

Why must the handler be idempotent once this is distributed?

Because leases expire. If a worker pauses (GC, network) past its lease, another worker legitimately takes the job and both may run it. At-least-once is the only achievable guarantee, so the handler must tolerate a repeat.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The core problem is proximity search over moving points: given a rider's location, find nearby available drivers, fast, while millions of drivers update their position every few seconds.

Geospatial indexing. A naive bounding-box query over latitude and longitude scans badly and handles the poles and antimeridian poorly. Use a grid of cells — geohash, S2 or H3 — which maps a 2-D coordinate to a single sortable cell id. Then "drivers near me" becomes "drivers in my cell plus its neighbours", which is a set of exact key lookups rather than a range scan. H3's hexagons are the nicest for this because every neighbour is equidistant, whereas square cells have diagonal neighbours that are further away — which matters when you are ranking by distance.

Location updates are high-write and low-value, and this is the key design decision to state: a driver's position five seconds ago is worthless, so do not put it in Postgres. Keep the current position in Redis — a hash per driver plus a set per cell, or Redis's own geospatial commands — with a TTL so a driver who stops reporting simply disappears. Write the historical trail asynchronously to a separate store if you need it for analytics or billing.

Matching runs per cell: gather candidate drivers from the rider's cell and its ring of neighbours, filter by availability and vehicle type, then rank by estimated time of arrival (not straight-line distance — road network matters) plus fairness and acceptance-rate signals. Expand the ring if there are too few candidates.

The race to name unprompted is double assignment: two riders matched to the same driver simultaneously. Solve it with an atomic claim — a conditional update or a Redis SET NX on the driver id — so exactly one match succeeds and the loser re-matches. Never rely on "check then assign" in application code.

Surge is computed per cell from the ratio of open requests to available drivers over a short window, smoothed to avoid oscillation, with the price locked at request time so it cannot change under the rider mid-flow.

Matching
driver ping (every ~4s) -> Redis:
  HSET driver:{id} lat lng cell status   EX 30      # TTL: stale drivers vanish
  SADD cell:{h3}  {driver_id}

match(rider):
  cells = h3.kRing(rider_cell, 1)        # hexagons: neighbours are equidistant
  candidates = union(SMEMBERS cell:{c} for c in cells)
  filter available + vehicle type -> rank by ETA (road network), not straight line
  expand kRing if too few

claim (prevents double assignment):
  SET assign:{driver_id} {ride_id} NX EX 30    -> only one rider wins
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not store driver locations in Postgres with PostGIS?

Write volume. Millions of drivers updating every few seconds is a punishing write load for a relational primary, and the data is worthless within seconds. Redis absorbs the churn; PostGIS is the right tool for static geospatial data like service areas.

Why hexagons rather than square cells?

Every hexagon neighbour is the same distance from the centre, so a k-ring is a clean approximation of a circle. With squares, diagonal neighbours are 1.41x further, which distorts distance-based ranking and makes ring expansion uneven.

How do you handle a rider in a sparse area?

Expand the k-ring progressively and widen the ETA threshold, with a timeout after which you tell the rider no driver is available. Silently searching forever is worse than an honest failure.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Lead with the constraint that shapes everything: 100,000 rows cannot be in React state. Holding them in state means every update diffs the whole array, and any state change re-renders a component holding 100k items. Keep the dataset in a ref, a store outside React, or the query cache, and let the grid read slices from it.

Virtualize both axes so only the ~30 visible rows and ~15 visible columns are in the DOM. That is what makes 100k rows possible at all — the rest is about keeping updates surgical.

Inline editing must be isolated per cell. Keep edit state keyed by (rowId, columnId) rather than in a grid-level object, and memoize rows on their data identity, so entering edit mode on one cell re-renders one cell. The common failure is storing editingCell at the grid level, which re-renders every visible row on every keystroke.

Sorting and filtering have a threshold. Below roughly 10,000 rows, sort client-side — it is instant and avoids a round trip. Above that, sort server-side, because sorting 100k objects on the main thread blocks for hundreds of milliseconds. Multi-column sort is a composed comparator; the important part is that the sort must be stable, or adding a second sort key visibly reshuffles rows that should have kept their relative order.

CSV export is the classic main-thread killer: serializing 100k rows blocks the UI for seconds. Do it in a Web Worker and stream the result to a Blob, showing progress — or, better for very large exports, generate it server-side and hand back a download link, since the browser should not be assembling a 50 MB file at all.

Responsive for a data grid does not mean shrinking columns to unreadable widths — it means changing the presentation: prioritise columns by importance and hide the rest behind an expandable row, or switch to a card layout below a breakpoint. And the accessibility floor still applies: role="grid" with a roving tabindex so the grid is one tab stop, not 100,000.

JSX
// data lives OUTSIDE React state
const rowsRef = useRef(data);                  // 100k rows, never in setState

// edit state keyed per cell -> one cell re-renders, not the grid
const [editing, setEditing] = useState/*<{rowId,colId}|null>*/(null);
const Row = memo(function Row({ row, editingColId }) { /* ... */ },
                 (a, b) => a.row === b.row && a.editingColId === b.editingColId);

// stable multi-column sort
const cmp = (a, b) => sorts.reduce((acc, s) =>
    acc !== 0 ? acc : s.dir * compare(a[s.id], b[s.id]), 0);

// export off the main thread
const worker = new Worker(new URL('./csv-worker.js', import.meta.url));
worker.postMessage({ rows: rowsRef.current, columns });
worker.onmessage = e => download(new Blob([e.data], { type: 'text/csv' }));
Follow-ups they will ask

What is your re-render isolation strategy in one sentence?

Data outside React state, rows memoized on data identity, and per-cell edit state — so a keystroke re-renders one cell, a row update re-renders one row, and a scroll re-renders only the newly visible window.

When do you move sorting to the server?

Around ten thousand rows, or as soon as sorting blocks long enough to be felt (roughly 50 ms). Measure rather than guess — the threshold depends on row width and comparator cost.

Why does sort stability matter here?

Because users apply a second sort expecting the first to act as a tie-breaker. An unstable sort reshuffles equal rows arbitrarily, which reads as a bug and destroys trust in the grid.

MOCK - 45 min, 1 medium + 1 hard

DP round. Write the recurrence on the board before writing any code - that is what is being scored.

Repeatedly replace the larger number with its remainder. It terminates fast, and the extended form solves modular inverses.

CostO(log min(a,b)) timeReach for itFraction reduction, LCM, and the extended version for modular inverses and linear Diophantine equations.
def gcd(a, b):
    while b: a, b = b, a % b
    return a

def lcm(a, b): return a // gcd(a, b) * b   # divide FIRST to avoid overflow

# Extended: finds x, y with a*x + b*y = gcd(a, b)
def egcd(a, b):
    if not b: return a, 1, 0
    g, x, y = egcd(b, a % b)
    return g, y, x - (a // b) * y

# Modular inverse of a mod m (when gcd(a,m)==1): egcd(a, m)[1] % m

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Data-oriented programming is the framing: when the data shapes are fixed and the operations vary, model the data as a closed set of immutable records and write operations as functions over them. That is the opposite of classic OO, where types vary and operations are fixed.

The construction: a sealed interface names exactly which types implement it, each implementation is a record carrying its own data, and operations are switch expressions with record patterns that destructure in the case label. The payoff is compile-time exhaustiveness — no default needed, and adding a variant breaks the build at every switch until it is handled. That converts a runtime surprise into a build-time checklist.

What it replaces: the visitor pattern, which existed precisely because Java could not do this — visitor gets you exhaustiveness at the cost of a large amount of ceremony and an inversion that makes the code hard to read. It also replaces the enum-plus-nullable-fields hack, where every variant carries every possible field and most are null.

Where it beats polymorphism: when operations vary and types do not. If you keep adding new operations over the same fixed set of shapes — validate, price, serialize, audit, render — polymorphism forces you to add a method to every class each time, spreading one concern across N files. A switch keeps the whole operation in one readable place.

Where classic polymorphism still wins: when types vary and operations do not — an open plugin set where third parties add implementations. There, adding a class must not require editing existing code, which is exactly what a sealed switch prevents. This is the expression problem, and naming it is a strong signal: OO makes adding types easy and adding operations hard; sealed types plus pattern matching make adding operations easy and adding types deliberate.

Choose by asking which axis actually changes in your domain. For payment outcomes, order states and parse results, the variants are fixed and the operations multiply — so sealed plus records is right.

Java
sealed interface Instruction permits Transfer, Refund, Reversal {}
record Transfer(String from, String to, Money amount) implements Instruction {}
record Refund(String original, Money amount, String reason) implements Instruction {}
record Reversal(String original, Instant at) implements Instruction {}

// record patterns destructure in the case label
String describe(Instruction i) {
    return switch (i) {
        case Transfer(var from, var to, var amt) -> amt + " from " + from + " to " + to;
        case Refund(var orig, var amt, var why)  -> "refund " + amt + " (" + why + ")";
        case Reversal(var orig, var at)          -> "reversal of " + orig;
    };   // exhaustive: adding a 4th variant breaks the build HERE
}
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the expression problem?

The observation that OO makes it easy to add new types and hard to add new operations, while functional/pattern-matching styles make it easy to add operations and hard to add types. Neither is universally better — you choose based on which axis your domain actually varies along.

When is an enum better than a sealed hierarchy?

When every variant has the same shape and carries no distinct data. An enum cannot give Refund a reason and Reversal a timestamp, which is exactly when you move to sealed records.

Do you lose anything by making the hierarchy sealed?

Extensibility by outside code — which is the point. If a third party must add a variant, sealed is the wrong choice; use an open interface. Sealing is a deliberate statement that the set is closed.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Lead with the tension: the dashboard wants counts within seconds and can tolerate approximation, while billing needs an exact number that reconciles to the penny. Those are different systems with different guarantees, and trying to serve both from one path is the mistake. That is the lambda architecture shape — a fast approximate path and a slow exact path.

Ingestion: 1M events/sec into Kafka, partitioned by a key that keeps a campaign's events together (campaign or ad id) so per-key aggregation is local to a partition. Producers batch aggressively; at this volume the network and serialization cost dominates.

Fast path: a stream processor (Flink or Kafka Streams) maintains windowed aggregates — per-minute and per-hour tumbling windows keyed by campaign — written to a low-latency store for the dashboard. The two things that make windowing correct are watermarks and an allowed lateness: events arrive out of order, so the watermark declares "we believe we have seen everything up to time T", the window closes then, and events arriving after that within the lateness bound update the result while later ones go to a side output rather than being silently dropped.

Deduplication is essential because delivery is at-least-once and clicks are money. Dedupe by event_id within a bounded window — a state store keyed by id with a TTL matching your maximum redelivery window. Beyond that window you accept the risk, and you should say so explicitly rather than implying perfect dedup.

Exact path: the same raw events land in object storage (partitioned by hour), and a batch job recomputes authoritative counts for billing — able to see all late data, apply full fraud filtering, and be rerun deterministically if a bug is found. The batch result is the source of truth; the streaming numbers are an estimate the dashboard displays.

Reconciliation closes the loop: compare streaming and batch totals daily, alert when they diverge beyond a threshold, and correct the served numbers. And note the fraud dimension — a meaningful fraction of raw clicks are invalid, so "exact" means exact after filtering, which is another reason billing cannot use the streaming number.

Two paths
events (1M/s) -> Kafka (partition by campaign_id)
   |
   +-- FAST: Flink windowed aggregates (1m/1h tumbling)
   |     watermarks + allowed lateness; dedupe on event_id (TTL state)
   |     -> low-latency store -> dashboard  (APPROXIMATE, seconds)
   |
   +-- EXACT: raw events -> object storage (partitioned by hour)
         -> batch recompute: all late data + fraud filtering, deterministic, rerunnable
         -> billing  (SOURCE OF TRUTH, hours)

reconcile daily: |fast - batch| > threshold -> alert + correct
Follow-ups they will ask

Why can billing not use the streaming numbers?

Because streaming closes windows on a watermark, so genuinely late events may be excluded, dedup is bounded by a window, and full fraud filtering needs a global view. Billing must be recomputable and defensible, which means batch over retained raw events.

What is a watermark, in one sentence?

A declaration by the stream processor that it believes all events up to time T have arrived, which is what allows a time window to close and emit a result despite out-of-order data.

Could you use one path instead of two?

Increasingly yes — the kappa architecture keeps only the streaming path and reprocesses from the retained log when you need to correct. It is simpler operationally; the reason to keep batch is when billing demands a separately-auditable computation.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Animate only transform and opacity. Those two are handled by the compositor and never trigger layout or paint, so they run at 60fps even when the main thread is busy. Animating width, top, margin or height forces layout on every frame and is the single most common cause of janky animation.

That creates the layout-animation problem: the things you most want to animate — an item moving to a new position in a reordered list, a card expanding — are layout changes. FLIP is the technique that resolves it. First: measure the element's position before the change. Last: apply the change and measure again. Invert: apply a transform that visually puts it back where it started. Play: remove the transform with a transition, so the browser animates a pure transform from the old position to the new one. You get a layout animation that never triggers layout during the animation.

Enter and exit transitions have a specific React difficulty: React removes an element from the DOM immediately on unmount, so there is nothing left to animate out. The solution is to keep the element mounted until the exit animation completes — which is what AnimatePresence in Framer Motion does, and what any hand-rolled version must do by tracking an "exiting" state and removing on transitionend.

Interruption is what separates a good implementation: an animation that cannot be reversed mid-flight feels broken. Spring-based animation handles this naturally because it animates from the current velocity and position; CSS transitions restart from wherever they are, which is usually acceptable but can jump.

prefers-reduced-motion is a hard requirement, not a nicety. Vestibular disorders make large motion genuinely painful, and the OS-level setting is an explicit user request. Respect it in CSS with a media query and in JS by checking matchMedia. The right response is usually not removing feedback entirely but replacing motion with a cross-fade — the user still gets the state-change signal without the movement.

JSX
// FLIP: animate a layout change using only transform
const first = el.getBoundingClientRect();     // First
reorder();                                     // DOM changes
const last = el.getBoundingClientRect();      // Last
const dx = first.left - last.left, dy = first.top - last.top;

el.style.transform = `translate(${dx}px, ${dy}px)`;   // Invert
el.style.transition = 'none';
requestAnimationFrame(() => {                          // Play
  el.style.transition = 'transform 250ms ease';
  el.style.transform = '';
});

/* reduced motion is a requirement, not an option */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * { animation-duration: .01ms !important; transition-duration: .01ms !important; }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does animating width cause jank?

It changes layout, so the browser must recompute geometry for the element and potentially its siblings and ancestors on every frame, then repaint. Transform and opacity skip layout and paint entirely and are handled on the compositor thread.

How do you animate an element out when React unmounts it immediately?

Delay the unmount: track an exiting state, keep rendering the element with an exit class, and remove it after transitionend or a timeout. That is precisely what AnimatePresence encapsulates.

What should reduced motion do — remove the animation entirely?

Usually not. Replace movement with a cross-fade or an instant change, so the user still perceives that state changed. Removing all feedback can make the interface feel broken rather than calm.

Math & Geometry I

Mark multiples of each prime as composite. Storing the smallest prime factor instead of a boolean lets you factorise any number instantly afterwards.

CostO(n log log n) time, O(n) spaceReach for itAll primes up to n, fast repeated factorisation, counting divisors. Single-number factorisation only needs trial division to √n.
def sieve(n):
    spf = list(range(n + 1))            # smallest prime factor
    for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if spf[i] == i:                 # i is prime
            for j in range(i*i, n + 1, i):
                if spf[j] == j: spf[j] = i
    return spf

def factorise(x, spf):                  # O(log x) after the sieve
    f = {}
    while x > 1:
        p = spf[x]; f[p] = f.get(p, 0) + 1; x //= p
    return f

Persistent (immutable) data structures return a new version on every modification while sharing structure with the previous version — so a "copy with one change" costs O(log n) rather than O(n), because only the path from the root to the changed node is rebuilt and everything else is shared by reference.

What Java gives you out of the box is not this. List.of, Map.of and List.copyOf are immutable but copy-on-write with full copies — creating a modified version is O(n). CopyOnWriteArrayList is the same: every write copies the whole array, which is why N sequential adds allocate N arrays. So Java's built-in immutability is cheap to read and expensive to modify.

Real persistent structures — Vavr's List and HashMap, or Clojure's — use a trie (typically a 32-way HAMT) so both reads and modifications are effectively O(log₃₂ n), which is near-constant for practical sizes.

Where I would use one in a service. Versioned configuration: hold config in an immutable structure behind a volatile reference, so readers need no lock at all and an update is a single atomic reference swap — with structure sharing, producing the new version is cheap even for a large config. Undo stacks and audit trails, where you want to retain every intermediate version without paying a full copy each time. Snapshot isolation: hand a request a consistent view that cannot change underneath it, while writers continue.

The honest comparison to close on: for a small collection, List.copyOf is simpler and fast enough — do not add a dependency for a ten-element list. Persistent structures earn their place when the collection is large and modified often and you need old versions to remain valid. Otherwise the immutable-snapshot-behind-a-volatile-reference pattern gives you most of the benefit with no library at all.

Java
// Java built-in: immutable, but modification is O(n) - a full copy
List<String> a = List.of("x", "y");
List<String> b = Stream.concat(a.stream(), Stream.of("z")).toList();   // copies

// lock-free readers via an immutable snapshot behind a volatile reference
private volatile Config config;                 // readers: no lock, no copy
void update(UnaryOperator<Config> f) { config = f.apply(config); }  // atomic swap

// persistent structure (Vavr): structure sharing, O(log32 n) modification
io.vavr.collection.List<String> v1 = io.vavr.collection.List.of("x","y");
io.vavr.collection.List<String> v2 = v1.append("z");   // v1 still valid, shares nodes
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is CopyOnWriteArrayList not a persistent data structure?

Because it copies the entire backing array on every write with no structure sharing — O(n) per modification. It is a concurrency tool for read-dominant listener lists, not an efficient immutable collection.

What is a HAMT?

A hash array mapped trie — a 32-way branching trie used to implement persistent maps. Depth is log₃₂ of the size, so even a million entries is four levels deep, making lookups and updates effectively constant time in practice.

Would you add Vavr to a Spring service for this?

Rarely. The volatile-immutable-snapshot pattern covers the common case with no dependency. Vavr earns its place if you are doing a lot of functional transformation and want persistent collections throughout — but it is a team-wide style decision, not a local one.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The whole design is driven by a 100 ms budget over millions of items, so state the shape immediately: you cannot score everything, so it is a funnel — cheap retrieval narrowing millions to hundreds, then expensive ranking over that small set.

Stage 1 — candidate generation (~10 ms). Retrieve a few hundred candidates cheaply from several sources in parallel: collaborative-filtering co-occurrence ("users who liked X also liked Y", precomputed offline), an approximate nearest neighbour index over embeddings (HNSW or IVF in a vector store), recently trending items, and items from followed creators or categories. Union and de-duplicate. Nothing here scores individual items with a model — it is all precomputed lookups.

Stage 2 — feature lookup (~20 ms). Fetch features for those few hundred candidates from a low-latency feature store: user features (long-term preferences, recent activity), item features (quality, age, engagement rate), and cross features (has the user seen this, interacted with this creator). This must be a small number of batched multi-get calls, not one call per candidate — the classic mistake that turns 20 ms into 2 seconds.

Stage 3 — ranking (~40 ms). A model scores the few hundred candidates. Because the set is small, you can afford a real model here — that is the entire reason for the funnel. Then apply business rules: diversity (do not return ten items from one creator), freshness, and any hard exclusions.

The fallbacks are the part interviewers wait for. If the model service is slow or down, return a popularity-based or recently-trending list rather than a spinner — a slightly worse recommendation is vastly better than an empty panel. Cache the previous result per user with a short TTL so a blip is invisible. And the cold-start case: a new user has no features, so fall back to popularity within their locale or a lightweight onboarding signal.

Finally, log the candidates, features and scores for every served request — that log is your training data and your only way to debug why something was recommended.

Funnel
millions -> ~500 candidates -> ~500 scored -> top 20

1. candidate generation  ~10ms  (parallel, all precomputed)
     co-occurrence | ANN over embeddings | trending | followed creators
2. feature lookup        ~20ms  BATCHED multi-get, not per candidate
3. ranking               ~40ms  model over ~500 items + diversity/business rules
4. serve + LOG candidates, features, scores   <- training data and debuggability

model down -> trending/popularity fallback, never a spinner
new user   -> popularity by locale, onboarding signals
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not just score everything with the model?

Because scoring millions of items per request is impossible in 100 ms at any reasonable cost. The funnel exists so the expensive model only ever sees a few hundred candidates — retrieval trades a little recall for three orders of magnitude less compute.

What is the most common latency bug in this design?

Fetching features per candidate instead of in a batch. Five hundred sequential lookups at 1 ms each is 500 ms; one batched multi-get is a few milliseconds. The same applies to calling the model once per item.

How do you evaluate whether a change helped?

Offline replay against logged data for a sanity check, then an online A/B test on engagement metrics — because offline metrics routinely fail to predict online behaviour. That is why logging candidates and scores matters.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start from the constraint: forty teams means you cannot coordinate a synchronised upgrade. Every decision follows from the fact that consumers upgrade on their own schedule, and some will not upgrade for a year.

Semver with a written policy defining what counts as breaking. Be explicit, because it is not obvious: removing or renaming a prop, changing a default value, changing rendered DOM structure that consumers style against, tightening a type, and changing visual output enough to break visual regression tests are all breaking. Adding an optional prop is not. Publish that list so "is this breaking?" is not re-litigated per PR.

Prefer additive change with sensible defaults over a major version. Most "we need a breaking change" situations can be expressed as a new optional prop whose default preserves current behaviour, with the old path deprecated. Majors are expensive for everyone; spend them rarely.

Deprecate with a runtime warning in development only — naming the deprecated API, the replacement, and a link to the migration guide — plus a JSDoc @deprecated tag so editors surface it inline. Warn once per component per session, not per render, or the console becomes unusable and people stop reading it.

Ship a codemod for anything mechanical: renamed props, moved imports, changed call signatures. A jscodeshift script turns a forty-team migration from a quarter of nagging into a pull request each team runs in a minute. If you cannot codemod it, reconsider whether the change is worth it.

Track adoption — via a dependency scan across repos, or telemetry from the dev-mode warning — so you know the real number rather than guessing. Support both paths for a defined window (typically two minors or a quarter), and only remove when adoption is effectively complete. Removing early breaks a team who had good reasons to be behind, and you lose the trust that makes future migrations possible.

One more: keep a changelog written for consumers rather than for you — what changed, why, and what to do — and run a canary release with two or three friendly teams before a wide rollout.

Deprecation
// dev-only, once per component, names the replacement
if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' && props.variant === 'legacy') {
  warnOnce('Table', '`variant="legacy"` is deprecated; use `appearance="plain"`. ' +
                    'Migration: https://ds.acme.com/migrate/table-v3');
}

/** @deprecated Use `appearance` instead. Removed in v4. */
variant?: 'legacy' | 'modern';

# mechanical change -> ship a codemod, not a request
npx @acme/ds-codemod table-variant-to-appearance src/

# timeline
v3.4 add new API + deprecate old   -> both work
v3.x support window (a quarter), track adoption
v4.0 remove old API                -> only when adoption is ~complete
Follow-ups they will ask

What if a team refuses to migrate?

Find out why — it is usually a genuine gap in the new API, or a deadline. Fix the gap or extend the window. Forcing removal on schedule against a real blocker damages the relationship and makes the next migration harder.

How do you version a design system's visual changes?

Treat visually-breaking changes as breaking, because consumers have visual regression tests and design sign-off. Ship them behind an opt-in prop or a theme flag first, then flip the default in a major.

What makes a codemod worth writing?

Any rename or signature change affecting more than a handful of call sites. The cost is an afternoon; the alternative is weeks of chasing teams and a long tail that never completes.

Math & Geometry II
  • Happy NumberEasy
  • Pow(x, n)Medium
  • Multiply StringsMedium

Keep every intermediate under a modulus so nothing overflows. Exponentiate by squaring to raise to huge powers in log time.

CostO(log n) for the powerReach for itCounting problems modulo 1e9+7, hashing, modular inverses via Fermat's little theorem.
MOD = 10**9 + 7

def power(b, e, m=MOD):
    r = 1; b %= m
    while e:
        if e & 1: r = r * b % m
        b = b * b % m
        e >>= 1
    return r

# Modular inverse when m is PRIME (Fermat): a^(m-2) mod m
inv = power(a, MOD - 2)

# Precompute factorials once for nCr
fact = [1]*(N+1)
for i in range(1, N+1): fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % MOD
def nCr(n, r): return fact[n] * power(fact[r]*fact[n-r] % MOD, MOD-2) % MOD

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

javap -c -p disassembles a class file, and reading it settles arguments that are otherwise speculation. Three things are worth being able to explain.

Lambdas do not compile to anonymous classes. The compiler emits an invokedynamic instruction plus a private static (or synthetic) method holding the body. At first execution, the JVM calls a bootstrap method — LambdaMetafactory — which spins up the implementing class at runtime and links the call site permanently. The consequences are concrete: no class file per lambda (so startup and jar size do not degrade with lambda count), a non-capturing lambda is a singleton reused on every call, and the JIT can inline through the linked call site more readily than through a virtual call. An anonymous class, by contrast, produces Outer$1.class, a new instance per evaluation, and — if non-static — an implicit reference to the enclosing instance.

String concatenation changed in Java 9. It used to compile to an explicit StringBuilder chain — new StringBuilder().append(a).append(b).toString() — visible in the bytecode. Now it compiles to invokedynamic against StringConcatFactory, which generates an optimal concatenation strategy at runtime, typically sizing the buffer exactly in one pass. That is why a + b + c in a single expression is fine and needs no manual StringBuilder — but a concatenation across loop iterations still allocates per iteration and is still O(n²), because each iteration is a separate expression.

Why this is worth knowing: it lets you answer performance questions with evidence rather than folklore. When someone claims lambdas are slow because "they create a class every time", javap settles it. It also explains stack traces containing lambda$method$0 and LambdaMetafactory frames, which otherwise look like framework noise.

Related: records generate their equals, hashCode and toString through invokedynamic against ObjectMethods, which is why they do not bloat the class file either.

Bytecode
javap -c -p MyClass.class

// lambda -> invokedynamic + a synthetic method, NOT an inner class
  invokedynamic #2, 0   // InvokeDynamic #0:apply:()Ljava/util/function/Function;
  private static java.lang.String lambda$main$0(java.lang.String);

// anonymous class -> a real class file + a new instance each evaluation
  new  #3   // class MyClass$1

// string concat (Java 9+) -> invokedynamic against StringConcatFactory
  invokedynamic #5, 0   // makeConcatWithConstants

// a + b + c in ONE expression: fine
// s += x inside a LOOP: still O(n^2) - each iteration is a separate expression
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is a non-capturing lambda a singleton?

Because it holds no state, so the same instance is valid for every call. LambdaMetafactory caches it at the call site, which means list.forEach(System.out::println) allocates nothing per invocation — unlike an anonymous class.

Does this mean lambdas are always faster than anonymous classes?

In allocation and class-loading terms, generally yes, and they inline better. The difference is rarely the bottleneck, but it does mean the common advice to avoid lambdas in hot paths is outdated.

What does a lambda in a stack trace look like?

Frames such as MyClass.lambda$process$2 plus synthetic LambdaMetafactory or generated-class frames. Knowing that lets you read past them to your real code instead of assuming the framework is at fault.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The pipeline shape: upload → object storage → transcode fan-out → segmented output → CDN. Say it, then defend each decision.

Upload: chunked and resumable, straight to object storage via presigned URLs, so a 4 GB file never passes through your API servers. On completion, publish an event to start processing and set the video's state to processing — the state machine matters because the uploader needs honest progress and the video must not be publishable until it is ready.

Transcoding is the expensive part and it fans out. One source produces multiple renditions — 240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, each at a target bitrate. Each rendition is an independent job on a queue, so they process in parallel across a worker fleet. Prioritise the lowest rendition first: as soon as 240p exists the video is playable, so publish it and let higher qualities arrive afterwards. That single ordering decision transforms perceived turnaround.

Adaptive bitrate is why the output is segmented: each rendition is cut into 2–10 second segments (HLS or DASH) and described by a manifest. The player measures throughput and buffer level and switches rendition at segment boundaries, so a viewer on a degrading connection drops to a lower quality instead of stalling. The server does nothing clever — all the adaptation logic is client-side, which is what makes it scale.

Delivery: segments are immutable and content-hashed, so they are ideal CDN objects with a long TTL; the manifest gets a short TTL because it changes as renditions become available or for live streams.

Reliability: transcoding jobs must be idempotent — keyed by (video id, rendition) and writing to a deterministic output path — because at-least-once delivery means retries, and a partially written output must be overwritten cleanly. Keep the source file so any rendition can be regenerated when a codec or preset changes. Failures go to a DLQ with the ffmpeg stderr attached, because "transcode failed" without the log is unactionable.

Progress feedback comes from workers emitting progress events per rendition, aggregated into an overall percentage the client polls or receives over a WebSocket.

Pipeline
upload (chunked, presigned) -> object storage -> event: video.uploaded
   |
   v  fan-out: one job per rendition (240p first!)
   [240p] [480p] [720p] [1080p]   parallel workers, idempotent per (video, rendition)
   |
   v  segment (2-10s) + manifest (HLS/DASH) -> object storage -> CDN

player: measures bandwidth + buffer -> switches rendition AT SEGMENT BOUNDARIES

segments: immutable, long TTL   |   manifest: short TTL (renditions appear over time)
keep the source forever -> re-encode when codecs/presets change
Follow-ups they will ask

Why transcode the lowest rendition first?

Because the video becomes playable as soon as one rendition exists. Publishing 240p in two minutes and adding 1080p later is a far better experience than waiting fifteen minutes for everything.

How does the player decide when to switch quality?

From measured segment download throughput and current buffer level, switching only at segment boundaries so the decoder is not disrupted. Conservative switching up and aggressive switching down avoids the oscillation that feels worse than a steady lower quality.

What makes transcoding jobs idempotent?

Keying by (video id, rendition) and writing to a deterministic output path, so a retry overwrites rather than duplicating. Combined with a completion marker, a partially-written output is never mistaken for a finished one.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The document model comes first, because undo quality depends on it. Store the document as a structured tree (ProseMirror or Slate style nodes), never as an HTML string. With a structured model, operations are well defined — insert text at a position, toggle a mark over a range, split a block — and each one has a computable inverse.

Undo is a stack of invertible operations, not a stack of document snapshots. Snapshots are simple but memory-heavy for a long session, and they lose intent — you cannot tell whether the user changed a word or reformatted a paragraph. Operations give you compact history and, later, the basis for collaboration.

Coalescing is what makes undo feel right, and it is the detail worth leading with. Undo must not be per-character, or a user presses Ctrl+Z fifteen times to remove one word. Merge consecutive operations into one history entry when they are the same type, contiguous in position, and within a short time window (roughly 500–1000 ms). Break the coalescing group on a pause, on a caret move, on a different operation type, and on a save — those boundaries are what match user intent.

Selection must be part of the history entry. Undoing should restore the caret to where it was before the change, otherwise the user loses their place, which is disorienting even when the text is correct.

Autosave: debounce roughly a second after typing stops, plus an immediate flush on visibilitychange (mobile browsers often do not fire beforeunload) and on blur. Send a diff or the operations rather than the whole document once documents get large. Always show save state — saving, saved, failed — because a silent failure means the user believes their work is safe when it is not.

Conflict with a concurrent edit: send the base version with each save and let the server return 412 if it has moved. Then either rebase your operations onto the new version (possible precisely because you stored operations, not snapshots) or, when that is ambiguous, surface it — never silently overwrite. If the product genuinely needs simultaneous editing, that is when a CRDT (Yjs) becomes the right answer rather than version checks.

JSX
// operations, not snapshots - each has an inverse
type Op = { type: 'insert'; at: number; text: string }
        | { type: 'delete'; at: number; text: string }   // stores the deleted text
        | { type: 'mark';   from: number; to: number; mark: string; on: boolean };

// coalesce: same type, contiguous, within the time window
function shouldMerge(prev, next, now) {
  return prev.type === 'insert' && next.type === 'insert'
      && next.at === prev.at + prev.text.length
      && now - prev.at_time < 800;
}

// history entry carries selection so undo restores the caret
history.push({ ops, selectionBefore, selectionAfter, at_time: Date.now() });

// autosave: debounce + flush on visibilitychange (beforeunload is unreliable)
document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === 'hidden') save.flush();
});
Follow-ups they will ask

Why store operations rather than document snapshots?

Compact history, the ability to rebase onto a concurrent change, and preserved intent. Snapshots grow with document size times history length and give you no way to merge with someone else's edit.

What breaks if selection is not in the history?

Undo restores the correct text but drops the caret somewhere unrelated — often the start of the document. Users perceive that as the editor losing their place, which feels worse than the original mistake.

When do you move from version checks to a CRDT?

When the product requires genuine simultaneous editing with live cursors. For a propose-and-review or single-editor-at-a-time flow, optimistic version checks are simpler, correct, and preserve the review step a CRDT would silently bypass.

  • Implement Queue using StacksEasy
  • Design HashMapEasy

Spiral order, rotation, and transposition. All of them are index bookkeeping, and all are easier with a named trick than with careful loops.

CostO(R · C) timeReach for itRotate an image, spiral print, set matrix zeroes, diagonal traversal. Common in interviews precisely because they are fiddly.
# Rotate 90 clockwise IN PLACE: transpose, then reverse each row
def rotate(m):
    n = len(m)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n): m[i][j], m[j][i] = m[j][i], m[i][j]
    for row in m: row.reverse()

# Spiral order: shrink four boundaries inward
def spiral(m):
    out = []
    top, bot, left, right = 0, len(m)-1, 0, len(m[0])-1
    while top <= bot and left <= right:
        for c in range(left, right+1): out.append(m[top][c])
        top += 1
        for r in range(top, bot+1): out.append(m[r][right])
        right -= 1
        if top <= bot:
            for c in range(right, left-1, -1): out.append(m[bot][c])
            bot -= 1
        if left <= right:
            for r in range(bot, top-1, -1): out.append(m[r][left])
            left += 1
    return out
610/4
