Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Leave the JVM only when you must, and be able to name the legitimate cases: a native cryptography or codec library you cannot reimplement, direct hardware or OS access, an existing C/C++ library representing years of work, or a numerical kernel where hand-tuned SIMD genuinely beats the JIT.

JNI is the old mechanism: you write C glue code, compile it per platform, and load it with System.loadLibrary. The problems are all operational — you ship platform-specific binaries, mistakes crash the JVM rather than throwing, memory management across the boundary is manual and leak-prone, and the glue code is a second build system.

Panama's Foreign Function & Memory API replaces it with pure Java: MemorySegment for off-heap memory with explicit lifetimes via an Arena, and Linker/MethodHandle to call native functions directly with no C glue at all. jextract generates the bindings from a header file. It is safer (segments are bounds-checked and have scoped lifetimes, so use-after-free becomes an exception rather than a crash), faster (the JIT can intrinsify the downcall), and there is no separate native build.

The cost model of crossing the boundary is the part worth stating precisely. A downcall is not free: the JIT cannot inline through it, so all the optimizations inlining unlocks are lost at that point; arguments must be marshalled; and if you pass on-heap data the GC may need it pinned or copied off-heap, because a moving collector cannot let native code hold a raw pointer into the heap. So the rule is coarse-grained calls: one call processing a megabyte beats a million calls processing a byte each.

Upcalls — native code calling back into Java — are considerably more expensive still, and worth avoiding in a hot path.

So the summary: Panama over JNI for anything new, keep the boundary crossings few and chunky, and be honest that the right answer for most services is not to cross it at all — the JIT is very good, and native interop is a source of crashes, platform-specific builds and debugging pain that pure Java does not have.

Java
// Panama: no C glue, explicit lifetimes, bounds-checked
try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
    MemorySegment buf = arena.allocate(1024);          // off-heap, freed on close

    Linker linker = Linker.nativeLinker();
    MethodHandle strlen = linker.downcallHandle(
            linker.defaultLookup().find("strlen").orElseThrow(),
            FunctionDescriptor.of(JAVA_LONG, ADDRESS));

    long len = (long) strlen.invoke(buf);              // direct call, no JNI glue
}   // arena closed -> segment invalid -> use-after-free is an exception, not a crash

// rule: ONE call over a large buffer, not many calls over small ones
// (no inlining across the boundary; marshalling and possible pinning per call)
Follow-ups they will ask

Why can the JIT not inline through a native call?

Because it has no bytecode for the native side to inline — it is opaque machine code. The call becomes an optimization barrier, so surrounding code loses escape analysis, constant folding and everything else inlining enables.

What does an Arena give you over JNI's manual memory management?

A scoped, deterministic lifetime. When the arena closes, every segment allocated from it becomes invalid, and touching one throws instead of corrupting memory. Confined arenas additionally restrict access to the creating thread, catching cross-thread misuse.

When is native interop clearly the wrong choice?

When the motivation is a guess that Java is slow. Profile first — the JIT usually closes the gap, and you would be trading a crash-free, portable deployment for platform-specific binaries and a whole class of memory bugs.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Model it as a state machine per application, because the domain is genuinely a workflow with regulatory obligations at each step. States: submitted → screening → manual_review → approved | rejected, plus expired and resubmission_required. Every transition is recorded with actor, timestamp and reason — that audit trail is the compliance deliverable, not a byproduct.

The transitions are forward-only. You never mutate an application's decision in place; a reversal is a new transition with its own justification. That is the same discipline as an append-only ledger and for the same reason: an auditor must be able to reconstruct what you knew and when.

External vendor calls are asynchronous and unreliable, which drives the integration design. Document verification, sanctions and PEP screening, and liveness checks are third-party APIs that take seconds to hours. So: fire the request, persist a pending record, and consume the result via webhook with a polling fallback — because webhooks are lost, delayed and delivered out of order. Verify webhook signatures, treat delivery as at-least-once (dedupe on the vendor's reference), and reconcile anything still pending after an SLA window.

The manual review queue is where the system meets people: prioritise by risk score and age, assign with a lease so two reviewers cannot work the same case, capture the reviewer's decision and rationale, and sample approved cases for quality control. Reviewer throughput is the real capacity constraint, so the automated tiers exist to keep that queue small.

SLAs are per-state, not end-to-end: screening completes in minutes, manual review within a business day. Track time-in-state and alert on breaches, because a regulator asks about turnaround.

PII is the design constraint that colours everything. Encrypt documents at rest with per-tenant or per-subject keys, store them in a separate vault referenced by id so the workflow database holds no raw personal data, log every read of a document (access to PII is itself an auditable event), enforce retention — delete after the statutory period — and be ready for erasure requests, which conflict with immutability and are resolved by deleting the vault contents while the audit trail retains only references.

State machine
submitted -> screening -> (auto_pass) -> approved
                       -> (uncertain) -> manual_review -> approved | rejected
                       -> (auto_fail) -> rejected
              any state -> expired (SLA breach) | resubmission_required

every transition: actor, timestamp, reason, evidence refs   -> append-only audit

vendor calls: async + webhook (signed, at-least-once, dedupe on vendor ref)
              + polling fallback + reconciliation of stuck pendings

PII: documents in an encrypted vault, referenced by id from the workflow DB
     reads are logged; retention enforced; erasure deletes vault, keeps references
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is a polling fallback needed if the vendor sends webhooks?

Because webhooks are lost, delayed, and sometimes never sent for edge-case outcomes. Without polling, an application sits in screening forever and nobody notices until a customer complains. Reconciliation of stale pendings is mandatory.

How do you handle an erasure request against an immutable audit trail?

Keep personal data in a separately-erasable vault and store only references in the audit records. Erasure empties the vault; the trail still shows that a decision was made, by whom and when, without retaining the personal data itself.

What is the capacity bottleneck?

Human reviewers. Automated tiers exist to keep the manual queue small, so the metric that matters is the proportion of applications requiring review — a small increase there translates directly into hiring or backlog.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Chunk client-side and treat each chunk as an independent unit of work. Split into 5–10 MB parts, hash each one, upload them in parallel with a concurrency limit of three or four. That concurrency limit matters in both directions — too few and you never saturate the connection, too many and you starve every other request on the page, including the ones keeping the UI responsive.

Resume is then trivial by construction: before uploading, ask the server which chunk hashes it already holds and skip those. That single design makes pause, resume, a dropped connection and a page reload all the same code path — which is the point worth making, because implementations that treat them separately end up with three half-working mechanisms.

Retry per chunk with exponential backoff and jitter, not per file. A failed 8 MB chunk costs 8 MB to retry; a failed 1 GB upload costs the whole thing. Cap attempts per chunk and surface a per-file error only when a chunk exhausts them.

Progress must be honest. Report per-file progress from bytes actually acknowledged by the server, not from bytes handed to fetch — the browser buffers, so naive progress hits 100% while the upload is still in flight, then appears to hang. Aggregate per-file progress into an overall figure weighted by file size, not by file count, or one large file among ten small ones makes the bar lie.

Queueing multiple files needs a small scheduler: a queue with a global concurrency cap across files, per-file state (queued, uploading, paused, failed, complete), and the ability to reorder or cancel. Cancelling must abort in-flight chunk requests via AbortController, not just stop scheduling new ones.

The tab-close case deserves honesty: you cannot reliably finish an upload during unload. Persist the upload id and the completed chunk list to IndexedDB as you go, so returning to the page offers to resume rather than starting over. And warn on unload only when an upload is genuinely in progress — a blanket beforeunload handler is an antipattern users learn to dismiss.

Accessibility: progress needs role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow, and status changes should be announced in a polite live region rather than only shown visually.

JSX
const CHUNK = 8 * 1024 * 1024, CONCURRENCY = 4;

// 1. ask what the server already has -> resume, reload and reconnect are one path
const { have } = await api.post(`/uploads/${id}/status`, { hashes });
const todo = chunks.filter((c, i) => !have.includes(hashes[i]));

// 2. bounded parallelism, per-chunk retry, abortable
await pool(CONCURRENCY, todo, async (chunk, i) => {
  await retry(() => api.put(urls[i], chunk, {
    signal: controller.signal,
    onUploadProgress: e => bump(i, e.loaded),      // per-chunk, aggregated
  }), { attempts: 5, backoff: 'jitter' });
});

// 3. persist progress so a reload can resume
await idb.put('uploads', { id, hashes, done: [...doneSet] });
Follow-ups they will ask

Why report progress from server acknowledgement rather than fetch's upload events?

Because the browser buffers what you hand it, so the progress event reaches 100% while bytes are still on the wire. The user then sees a full bar that does nothing for thirty seconds, which reads as a hang.

What concurrency should you use?

Three or four chunks in flight is the usual sweet spot: enough to saturate a typical connection and hide per-request latency, few enough to leave headroom for the rest of the application's requests.

How do you handle the user closing the tab mid-upload?

You cannot complete it — so persist the upload id and completed chunks to IndexedDB continuously and offer to resume on return. Warn on unload only while an upload is actually running.

Precompute cumulative sums over a grid so any submatrix total is four array lookups.

CostO(R·C) build, O(1) per queryReach for itRepeated submatrix sum queries, counting rectangles, and image-style region aggregates.
def build(mat):
    R, C = len(mat), len(mat[0])
    p = [[0]*(C+1) for _ in range(R+1)]
    for r in range(R):
        for c in range(C):
            p[r+1][c+1] = mat[r][c] + p[r][c+1] + p[r+1][c] - p[r][c]
    return p

def region(p, r1, c1, r2, c2):        # inclusive corners
    return (p[r2+1][c2+1] - p[r1][c2+1] - p[r2+1][c1] + p[r1][c1])

# Inclusion-exclusion on four corners. Draw it once and it sticks.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Both solve the same problem — not blocking an OS thread while waiting on IO — but they pay for it differently.

Reactive makes non-blocking explicit in the programming model: you compose a pipeline of operators, nothing runs until subscription, and a small event-loop pool multiplexes thousands of connections. Virtual threads make it invisible: you write ordinary blocking code, and when it blocks the JVM unmounts the virtual thread from its carrier, freeing the OS thread. Same outcome — high concurrency with few OS threads — but one restructures your code and the other does not.

Why reactive is harder to operate, which is the substance of the question. Stack traces are useless: a failure shows operator frames, not the call path that produced the request, so "where did this come from" becomes guesswork without extra tooling. Debuggers do not step through an operator chain the way they step through a method. ThreadLocal breaks, so MDC logging, security context and tracing need explicit propagation through the reactive Context — and every library you use must cooperate. One blocking call poisons everything: a JDBC call on an event-loop thread stalls every request that thread multiplexes, and it fails under load rather than in testing. And the whole team must learn it, because a single imperative-minded change can undo the model.

Backpressure is the one thing reactive genuinely offers that Loom does not, and it is worth defining precisely: the subscriber signals how much it can accept with request(n), so demand flows upstream and a slow consumer causes the producer to slow down rather than an unbounded buffer to grow. With virtual threads you get flow control implicitly — a blocked thread stops pulling — but only within a request; across a streaming pipeline you must build bounded queues yourself.

So when is reactive still justified? Streaming with genuine backpressure requirements — server-sent events, long-lived subscriptions, high fan-out WebSocket delivery, pipelines where a fast producer must be throttled by a slow consumer. Also when you are already in a reactive ecosystem where mixing models would be worse.

For ordinary request/response services, virtual threads win: comparable throughput, readable code, working tooling, and no team-wide learning curve. Saying that plainly is the correct Software Engineer answer.

Java
// virtual threads: ordinary blocking code, real stack traces, working debugger
try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    exec.submit(() -> {
        var user  = userClient.fetch(id);      // blocks -> unmounts the carrier
        var prefs = prefsClient.fetch(id);
        return new Profile(user, prefs);
    });
}
// concurrency is now unbounded -> add the limit the pool used to provide
Semaphore db = new Semaphore(50);

// reactive: explicit demand signalling - the one thing Loom does not give you
flux.limitRate(100)                          // request(n) flows upstream
    .onBackpressureBuffer(1000, dropped -> metrics.dropped());
Follow-ups they will ask

Does Loom give you backpressure?

Implicitly and locally: a blocked thread stops consuming, so pressure propagates one hop. It does not give you explicit demand signalling across a multi-stage pipeline — for that you still need bounded queues or a reactive stream.

What is the single most common reactive production failure?

A blocking call on an event-loop thread — JDBC, a synchronous client, or a library that blocks internally. Throughput collapses under load in a way that looks like a capacity problem. BlockHound in tests is the defence.

What would you tell a team starting a new service today?

Virtual threads with ordinary blocking code, plus explicit semaphores to bound downstream concurrency. Choose reactive only for streaming or genuine backpressure needs, and choose it as a team, because it is a whole-codebase commitment.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The defining constraint is determinism, not throughput — and leading with that is what separates a real answer here. Two participants sending orders must produce exactly one outcome, reproducible on replay, because the exchange must be able to prove after the fact why a trade happened.

So the matching core is single-threaded per instrument. That sounds like a limitation and is actually the design: one thread processing a sequenced input stream gives you a total order with no locks, no race conditions, and perfect replayability. Scale by sharding across instruments — each symbol gets its own matching thread — not by parallelising within one book. This is the LMAX Disruptor architecture, and a single thread comfortably handles millions of orders per second because it never touches a lock and stays entirely in L1/L2 cache.

The order book is two sides, bids descending and asks ascending. Each side is a collection of price levels, and each price level holds a FIFO queue of orders. That structure directly encodes price-time priority: better price wins, and at the same price the earlier order wins. Use an array or a sorted structure indexed by price ticks rather than a general tree — prices are dense and bounded, so an array of levels gives O(1) access to the best bid and offer, which is the operation you perform constantly.

Matching is then simple: an incoming buy at or above the best ask consumes resting orders from that level in FIFO order, moving to the next level when exhausted, until filled or the price limit is reached; any remainder rests in the book.

Durability without sacrificing latency: journal the sequenced input to disk before processing, not the output. Because matching is deterministic, replaying the input reconstructs the exact book state — so recovery is replay from the last snapshot, and you never need to persist the book itself on the hot path.

Market data fan-out is a separate path: the matcher publishes events to a ring buffer that downstream consumers read independently, so a slow market-data subscriber can never back-pressure the matching engine. That separation is essential — the matcher must never wait on anything.

Order book
bids: price levels DESC   asks: price levels ASC
  each level -> FIFO queue of resting orders     <- price-time priority

single thread per instrument:
  sequencer -> journal input to disk -> match -> emit events -> ring buffer
                                                                  |
                                        market data / risk / persistence consumers

deterministic => replay the journal reconstructs the exact book
scale => shard by instrument, never parallelise one book
the matcher never blocks on a consumer
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is a single thread faster than a concurrent implementation here?

No lock acquisition, no cache-line contention, no memory barriers, and the entire working set stays in cache. A lock-free concurrent book would spend more time coordinating than matching — and would lose determinism, which is non-negotiable.

How do you recover after a crash?

Load the most recent book snapshot, then replay journaled input from that sequence number. Determinism guarantees you arrive at exactly the state you had, which is why the input rather than the output is what you persist.

What happens if a market-data consumer is slow?

Nothing to the matcher — it publishes into a ring buffer and moves on. The slow consumer falls behind and either catches up or is disconnected. Coupling the matcher to consumer speed would be the fatal design error.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Give a framework and then apply it, because frontend system design rounds reward structure over trivia.

1. Requirements and scope (5 min). Who uses it, on what devices and connections, what is the scale, what must work offline, what are the accessibility and internationalization requirements. For a photo feed: infinite scroll, images dominate the payload, mobile-first on variable networks.

2. API contract and data model. Design the response shape before any component. Cursor-based pagination (offset breaks as new posts arrive), and the crucial decision — the feed returns image URLs at multiple sizes plus dimensions, so the client can pick a rendition and reserve space. Getting the API right removes half the client complexity.

3. Component architecture and rendering strategy. Which parts are server-rendered for LCP, which are client. For a feed: SSR or streaming the first screen, client-render the rest.

4. State and caching. Server state in a query cache keyed by the feed query, client state minimal, scroll position and loaded pages preserved for back-navigation — which is the single most-complained-about behaviour in feeds.

5. Performance budget. Virtualize the list, lazy-load images below the fold with loading="lazy" but never the LCP image, use srcset for responsive renditions, and always set width and height so there is no layout shift. State targets: LCP under 2.5 s and INP under 200 ms at p75 on a mid-range Android.

6. Accessibility. Alt text as a product requirement, keyboard-reachable actions, a real "load more" fallback for the observer, live-region announcements for new content.

7. Error, empty and offline states per region, with retry.

8. Observability. Field web-vitals, error tracking, and a bundle budget in CI.

The two things that most often decide the round: designing the API first and quantifying the performance target rather than saying "make it fast".

Photo feed
API (cursor, not offset - the feed grows while you scroll)
  GET /feed?cursor=...&limit=20
  { items:[{ id, author, caption,
             image:{ w, h, srcset:[{url,w:400},{url,w:800},{url,w:1600}] } }],
    nextCursor }

render:  SSR/stream the first screen (LCP) -> client for the rest
list:    virtualized; images lazy below the fold, NEVER the LCP image
layout:  w/h from the API -> reserve space -> CLS ~ 0
state:   query cache keyed by feed query; restore pages + scroll on back
budget:  LCP < 2.5s, INP < 200ms at p75 on a mid-range Android
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the most common mistake in a frontend design round?

Jumping straight to components. Requirements and the API contract determine most of the client design — candidates who start with the data shape sound like they have built one, and those who start with a component tree usually have not.

Why does the API return image dimensions?

So the client can reserve exact space before the image loads, which eliminates layout shift. It is a one-field change on the server that removes an entire class of client-side workaround.

How do you decide what to server-render?

Whatever contributes to LCP and SEO. For a feed, the first screen; for a dashboard behind a login, often nothing. Server rendering the whole infinite list would be slow and pointless.

To add a value across a range many times, record only the change at each end. One prefix-sum pass at the end materialises the result.

CostO(1) per update, O(n) to finaliseReach for itMany range updates followed by one read — flight bookings, car pooling, interval counting.
def range_updates(n, updates):        # updates = [(l, r, val), ...]
    diff = [0]*(n + 1)
    for l, r, val in updates:
        diff[l]     += val            # start adding here
        diff[r + 1] -= val            # stop adding after r
    out, run = [], 0
    for i in range(n):
        run += diff[i]; out.append(run)
    return out

# 1000 range updates on a 1e5 array: O(1) each instead of O(n) each.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A Spliterator is the stream framework's source abstraction, and it does two jobs: traverse (tryAdvance, forEachRemaining) and split (trySplit). The split is what makes parallelism possible, and its quality is what determines whether a parallel stream is fast or pointless.

How work is divided: the framework calls trySplit recursively, building a tree of tasks that Fork/Join then distributes. A good spliterator splits in half, cheaply, and evenly. An ArrayList or array does this perfectly — halve the index range, O(1), balanced. A LinkedList must walk to find the midpoint; Files.lines and iterator-backed sources cannot split meaningfully at all and return null, so the framework falls back to a conservative batching strategy that is usually slower than sequential.

Characteristics let the pipeline optimize: SIZED and SUBSIZED mean the framework knows exact sizes and can pre-allocate and balance splits; ORDERED forces encounter-order preservation, which makes parallel distinct and limit far more expensive; DISTINCT lets distinct() become a no-op; IMMUTABLE and NONNULL remove defensive work. Declaring unordered() when you genuinely do not need order is a real and easy win.

Custom collectors connect to the same story through the combiner. A collector's five parts are supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher and characteristics — and the combiner is only ever called in a parallel stream. That is the trap: a wrong combiner passes every sequential test and silently corrupts results the day someone adds .parallel(). If you cannot write a correct one, say the collector is sequential-only rather than leaving a landmine.

The practical guidance: before writing either, check whether an existing collector composition covers it — groupingBy with a downstream, teeing, reducing handle most cases. And before reaching for parallel(), check that the source splits well and that N is large enough for the split-and-merge overhead to be repaid. Most parallel streams in production code are slower than the sequential version.

Java
Spliterator<String> sp = list.spliterator();
sp.estimateSize();
sp.hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.SIZED | Spliterator.SUBSIZED);
Spliterator<String> half = sp.trySplit();     // null if it cannot split

// custom collector - the combiner is called ONLY in parallel
Collector<Order, StringJoiner, String> ids = Collector.of(
    () -> new StringJoiner(", ", "[", "]"),   // supplier
    (j, o) -> j.add(o.id()),                   // accumulator
    StringJoiner::merge,                       // combiner  <- untested sequentially
    StringJoiner::toString);                   // finisher

// unordered() unlocks much cheaper parallel distinct/limit
stream.unordered().distinct();
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does an iterator-backed stream parallelize badly?

Because spliteratorUnknownSize has no SIZED characteristic and cannot split by index, so the framework batches conservatively and cannot balance the work. You pay the coordination cost without getting even distribution.

How do you test a combiner?

Run the collector on a parallel stream over an input large enough to actually split, and assert the result equals the sequential one. Property-based testing over random inputs is even better, since combiner bugs often only appear at particular split boundaries.

When would you write a Spliterator by hand?

Only when exposing a custom data structure as a stream and you want genuine parallel support. Otherwise wrap an Iterator with Spliterators.spliteratorUnknownSize and accept sequential execution.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Lead with the tension the question is built around: sharding requires independence, and a ledger requires a global invariant. Everything must balance to zero, but you cannot afford a global transaction at 50k writes/sec.

Resolve it by choosing a shard key that keeps most transactions single-shard. Shard by account id: a single account's entries live together, so per-account reads, balance computation and per-account transactions are local. Most activity in a real ledger — deposits, fees, interest, a customer's own history — is single-account and therefore single-shard.

Cross-shard transfers are the residual problem, and the answer is an explicit pending state rather than a distributed transaction. Debit shard A in a local transaction, writing the entry as pending; publish an event; credit shard B in its own local transaction; then mark the transfer complete. Every step is idempotent and keyed by transfer id, and a reconciler sweeps transfers stuck in pending. Two-phase commit would hold locks across the network at 50k/sec and is not viable — say that explicitly.

The critical honesty: during the pending window the money is genuinely in neither place, so the intermediate state must be modelled in the domain, not hidden. Reporting, balance display and reconciliation all have to understand "in flight". Pretending the transfer is atomic is what produces the bugs.

Balances at this write rate cannot be a running total or a full scan. Keep a per-account snapshot — balance as of a sequence number — updated periodically, and compute current balance as snapshot plus the entries after it. Snapshots are derived and rebuildable, which preserves the property that the entries are the only source of truth.

Ordering and idempotency: a monotonic per-account sequence number gives a total order within the account (which is the only ordering that matters), and every write carries an idempotency key with a unique constraint — because at 50k writes/sec, retries are constant.

Auditability: entries are append-only with no UPDATE or DELETE grant; corrections are reversing entries. Partition by time so old partitions tier to cold storage. And run a continuous invariant check: the sum of all entries across all shards must be zero — if it is not, you want to know within minutes.

Sharding a ledger
shard key = account_id      -> a single account's entries stay together
                               per-account txns, balances, history are LOCAL

cross-shard transfer (no 2PC):
  shard A: BEGIN debit(from, amt, status=PENDING, transfer_id) COMMIT
  event -> shard B: BEGIN credit(to, amt, transfer_id) COMMIT   (idempotent)
  mark complete; reconciler sweeps stuck PENDING
  -> the PENDING state is modelled in the domain, not hidden

balance = snapshot(as_of_seq) + SUM(entries WHERE seq > as_of_seq)
invariant: SUM(all entries, all shards) == 0   -> checked continuously
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not two-phase commit for cross-shard transfers?

It holds locks across a network round trip and blocks indefinitely if the coordinator fails. At 50k writes/sec that is both a throughput ceiling and an availability risk. A saga with an explicit pending state degrades gracefully instead.

How do you keep both sides of a transfer on one shard?

Route on a transfer group id rather than the account where possible, or co-locate accounts that transact frequently (a customer and their linked accounts). It does not eliminate cross-shard transfers but it substantially reduces them.

What does the continuous invariant check actually catch?

Bugs in transfer logic, partially-applied cross-shard transfers, and data corruption. It is cheap relative to its value — an unbalanced ledger discovered by an auditor months later is vastly more expensive than one caught the same day.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The first and most important decision: never store the document as an HTML string. Store a structured node tree — blocks containing inline content with marks — as ProseMirror and Slate do. HTML as the model means every operation is string surgery, the valid states are undefined, and you inherit every browser's contentEditable quirks as your data model.

With a structured model, operations are well defined: insert text at a position, toggle a mark over a range, split or merge a block, wrap in a list. Each has a computable inverse, which is what makes undo, collaboration and validation possible at all. A schema defines which nodes may contain which — so a heading cannot end up inside a list item unless you allow it — and invalid documents are rejected rather than rendered.

Selection is a first-class part of the model, expressed in document coordinates rather than DOM ranges. Every operation maps the selection through the change, so the caret ends up where the user expects after an edit, an undo, or a remote collaborator's change.

Undo/redo is a stack of invertible operations with coalescing — merge consecutive same-type contiguous edits within a short window, and break the group on a pause, a caret move, or a different operation type. Store the selection with each entry so undo restores the caret, not just the text.

Plugins are how this stays maintainable: a plugin contributes schema nodes and marks, key bindings, input rules (typing ## becomes a heading), decorations for visual overlays such as spellcheck or collaborator cursors, and commands. Core stays small; everything product-specific is a plugin.

Paste sanitization is a security requirement, not a formatting nicety. Pasted HTML from Word or a website carries scripts, event handlers, external styles and enormous nested markup. Run it through a parser that maps into your schema — anything not expressible in the schema is dropped — which is stronger than sanitizing HTML, because the schema is an allowlist by construction. Offer plain-text paste on Ctrl+Shift+V, and normalize pasted content rather than trusting it.

And the honest closing: contentEditable is a minefield — IME composition for CJK input, browser-specific behaviours, and Android soft keyboards that lie about what they are doing. Use ProseMirror or Lexical rather than building on raw contentEditable.

Model
// structured document, never an HTML string
{ type: 'doc', content: [
  { type: 'paragraph', content: [
    { type: 'text', text: 'Hello ', marks: [] },
    { type: 'text', text: 'world', marks: [{ type: 'bold' }] },
  ]},
]}

// operations are invertible and map the selection through the change
{ type: 'addMark', from: 6, to: 11, mark: 'bold' }   // inverse: removeMark

// paste: parse INTO the schema (allowlist by construction), do not sanitize HTML
const slice = DOMParser.fromSchema(schema).parseSlice(pastedDom);
// anything not expressible in the schema is simply dropped
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is schema-based paste parsing safer than HTML sanitization?

Because the schema is an allowlist: only node and mark types you defined can exist in the document, so a script tag or an onclick attribute has nowhere to go. Sanitization is a blocklist and must anticipate every vector.

What makes contentEditable so difficult?

IME composition (a CJK user's in-progress characters must not be treated as committed input), inconsistent behaviour across browsers for the same key, Android soft keyboards that batch and reorder events, and the browser mutating the DOM behind your back. Libraries exist because these take years to get right.

How does the structured model help with collaboration later?

Operations are exactly what OT transforms or a CRDT merges. Storing snapshots or HTML strings gives you nothing to merge — so the model choice made on day one determines whether real-time collaboration is feasible at all.

A compact array supporting prefix sums with point updates, both in log time. Fifteen lines — make it your default over a segment tree.

CostO(log n) update and query, O(n) spaceReach for itRunning counts with updates, counting inversions, and 'how many so far are less than x'.
class BIT:
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n; self.t = [0]*(n+1)
    def add(self, i, v):              # 1-indexed
        while i <= self.n:
            self.t[i] += v
            i += i & -i               # move to the next responsible node
    def sum(self, i):                 # prefix sum of 1..i
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += self.t[i]
            i -= i & -i
        return s
    def range(self, l, r): return self.sum(r) - self.sum(l - 1)

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

All three are probabilistic structures: they trade exactness for sublinear memory, and each answers a different question.

Bloom filter — set membership. A bit array plus k hash functions; adding sets k bits, querying checks them. If any bit is zero the element is definitely absent; if all are set it is probably present. So it has false positives but never false negatives, which is exactly what makes it useful as a cheap pre-check. Size it from expected n and target false-positive rate — roughly 10 bits per element gives 1%. You cannot delete (a counting Bloom filter can, at 4x the space).

Where I would use one in a Java service: in front of an expensive lookup to avoid the call entirely — checking a cache or database for a key that probably does not exist (cache penetration defence); LSM-tree SSTable probing, which is how Cassandra and RocksDB avoid reading files that cannot contain a key; and deduplication pre-checks, where a positive sends you to the authoritative store and a negative is instantly conclusive.

HyperLogLog — cardinality. Counts distinct elements in fixed memory (~12 KB for billions of items, ~2% error) by observing the maximum run of leading zeros in hashed values across buckets. Use it for unique visitors, distinct IPs, distinct keys — anywhere you need "how many different" and a couple of percent error is fine. Crucially, HLLs are mergeable, so per-shard counters combine into a global one without re-scanning.

Count-Min Sketch — frequency. A 2-D array of counters with several hash functions; increment all rows, and query by taking the minimum, which bounds overestimation. It overestimates but never underestimates. Use it for heavy hitters — finding the hot keys saturating a cache shard, top talkers by IP, per-key rate limiting at volumes where exact counters do not fit.

The framing to close on: each accepts a specific, bounded error in exchange for constant memory — Bloom false-positive-only, HLL a small percentage, CMS overestimate-only. Choosing one means the error direction is acceptable for your use, which is the question to ask before reaching for any of them.

Java
// Guava BloomFilter - 1% FPR, ~10 bits per element
BloomFilter<String> seen = BloomFilter.create(
        Funnels.stringFunnel(UTF_8), 10_000_000, 0.01);
seen.put(id);
if (!seen.mightContain(id)) return null;   // definitely absent - skip the DB entirely
// might contain -> do the real lookup (false positives are just a wasted check)

// Redis: HLL for cardinality, mergeable across shards
PFADD visitors:2026-08-29 user123
PFCOUNT visitors:2026-08-29            // ~2% error, ~12KB regardless of volume
PFMERGE visitors:week visitors:day1 visitors:day2

// CMS: overestimates, never underestimates -> safe for heavy-hitter detection
Follow-ups they will ask

Why can a Bloom filter never have false negatives?

Because adding an element only ever sets bits, and bits are never cleared. If any of an element's k bits is zero, it was definitively never added. That one-sided error is what makes it safe as a skip-the-lookup guard.

What happens if you undersize a Bloom filter?

The false-positive rate climbs as the bit array saturates, until nearly everything reports 'might contain' and the filter stops saving you anything. Size from the expected element count, and monitor the actual fill ratio.

Why does Count-Min Sketch take the minimum across rows?

Because collisions only ever add to a counter, so every row's value is an overestimate. The smallest is the tightest bound — which is why the error is one-sided and you can safely use it to find heavy hitters without false alarms in the other direction.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The central question is the one in the prompt, so answer it directly: a timeout is not a failure — it is an unknown outcome. The request may have been received, processed and charged, with only the response lost. Treating a timeout as a failure and retrying naively double-charges the customer; treating it as a failure and giving up loses the payment. Everything else in this design follows from that.

Idempotency keys are the mechanism. Generate a key per logical payment attempt — not per HTTP request — and send the same key on every retry. Every serious provider (Stripe, Adyen) supports this and will return the original response rather than charging again. Store the key with your local record before calling out, so a retry after a crash reuses it.

A local state machine tracks the truth: initiated → pending → succeeded | failed | unknown. On a timeout you move to unknown, never to failed. From unknown you resolve by polling the provider's status endpoint by idempotency key or reference with backoff — that is the fallback that makes timeouts recoverable.

Webhooks plus polling, not webhooks alone. Webhooks are lost, delayed, delivered out of order, and delivered more than once. So: verify the signature, dedupe on the provider's event id, tolerate out-of-order arrival (a succeeded after a pending is normal; ignore a pending arriving after succeeded), and run a reconciliation sweep for anything still unresolved after an SLA window.

Retries: only for network errors, timeouts and 5xx, with exponential backoff and jitter and a small attempt cap. Never retry a 4xx — a declined card or invalid request will decline identically forever, and retrying it looks like an attack.

Daily reconciliation is the safety net and the part people omit: fetch the provider's settlement file and diff it against your ledger, producing three buckets — matched, in our ledger but not theirs (we think we charged and they did not), and in theirs but not ours (they charged and we lost the record, the dangerous one). Both mismatch buckets go to an exceptions queue for human resolution. Without reconciliation you have no way to detect the money you have silently lost or double-taken.

Timeout handling
charge(order):
  key = idempotency_key(order.id, attempt_group)   # SAME key across retries
  persist(state=INITIATED, key)
  try:      resp = provider.charge(key, amount)
  except Timeout:
            persist(state=UNKNOWN)      # NOT failed
            schedule poll(key, backoff) # resolve by asking the provider

webhook: verify signature -> dedupe on event_id -> tolerate out-of-order
polling: fallback for lost webhooks + sweep of stale UNKNOWN/PENDING

daily reconciliation vs the settlement file:
  matched | ours-not-theirs | theirs-not-ours  -> exceptions queue -> human
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the correct idempotency key scope?

One logical payment attempt, generated before the first call and reused across every retry of that attempt. If the customer deliberately retries after a genuine decline, that is a new attempt with a new key — otherwise you would return the old declined response forever.

Why never retry a 4xx?

Because it is deterministic: an invalid card or malformed request fails identically every time. Retrying wastes capacity, can trigger the provider's fraud controls, and delays telling the customer something they need to act on.

Which reconciliation bucket is most dangerous?

Charges in their records but not in yours — you have taken the customer's money without a corresponding ledger entry, so nothing in your system will ever fulfil the order or refund it. It must be surfaced and resolved by a human, not auto-corrected.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Model every state explicitly, because the classic bug is treating buffering as paused. The states are idle, loading, ready, playing, buffering, paused, seeking, ended, error — and buffering is playing but starved, so the UI must keep the pause button showing pause, keep the timeline live, and overlay a spinner. Collapsing it into paused makes the player appear to have stopped when it is actually working, and users press play, which makes it worse.

Adaptive quality is mostly the streaming library's job (hls.js or dash.js) — it measures throughput and buffer level and switches rendition at segment boundaries. Your responsibility is the UI: expose Auto plus manual levels, show the level actually in use rather than the one requested, and persist a manual choice for the session. Never silently override a manual selection.

Buffering feedback should distinguish initial load from a mid-playback stall, and show buffered ranges on the timeline so the user can see how much runway they have. A spinner with no context is the least informative thing you can display.

Keyboard shortcuts are expected and cheap: Space/K play-pause, arrows seek five seconds and adjust volume, J/L for ten seconds, M mute, F fullscreen, number keys jump to percentage points. Scope them to the player container so they do not hijack typing elsewhere on the page, and make every one reachable through a visible control too.

Captions are an accessibility requirement, not a feature: WebVTT tracks with a real toggle, and — often forgotten — user control over size, colour and background, because default captions are unreadable over bright content. Also provide a transcript where possible; it serves search, skimming and users who cannot use audio.

Resumable playback: persist position debounced (every few seconds and on pause, seek and visibilitychange), keyed by user and asset, and resume with an explicit "Resume from 12:34 / Start over" choice rather than silently jumping — silently resuming is disorienting when the user wanted to rewatch.

One more the interviewer usually waits for: autoplay policy. Browsers block autoplay with sound, so an autoplay attempt returns a rejected promise. Catch it and either start muted with a visible unmute affordance or show a play button — never assume playback started.

JSX
// buffering is PLAYING-but-starved, not paused
type State = 'idle'|'loading'|'ready'|'playing'|'buffering'|'paused'|'seeking'|'ended'|'error';
const isPlaying = state === 'playing' || state === 'buffering';   // control shows Pause

// autoplay is blocked by policy - handle the rejection
try { await video.play(); }
catch { video.muted = true; await video.play(); setShowUnmute(true); }

// resume position: debounced, and offer a choice rather than jumping silently
const save = useDebouncedCallback(() => store(assetId, video.currentTime), 3000);
['pause','seeked','timeupdate'].forEach(e => video.addEventListener(e, save));
document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => save.flush());

// buffered ranges on the timeline - show the user their runway
for (let i = 0; i < video.buffered.length; i++)
  ranges.push([video.buffered.start(i), video.buffered.end(i)]);
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is treating buffering as paused so bad?

Because the controls flip to a play button while the player is actively trying to continue. The user presses play, which does nothing or restarts a request, and the experience reads as broken when the player is simply waiting for data.

How should manual quality selection interact with adaptive switching?

A manual choice pins the level and disables adaptation until the user returns to Auto. Silently overriding their selection when bandwidth changes is the behaviour people complain about most in video players.

What does autoplay policy require of your UI?

That you never assume playback started. play() returns a promise that can reject; the standard fallback is to start muted with a prominent unmute control, because muted autoplay is generally permitted.

A binary tree over array ranges. More code than a Fenwick tree, but it handles any associative operation — min, max, gcd — not just sums.

CostO(log n) query and update, O(n) spaceReach for itRange min/max/sum with point updates. Reach for it only when a Fenwick tree cannot express your operation.
class SegTree:
    def __init__(self, a):
        self.n = len(a)
        self.t = [0]*(2*self.n)
        self.t[self.n:] = a
        for i in range(self.n - 1, 0, -1):
            self.t[i] = min(self.t[2*i], self.t[2*i+1])
    def update(self, i, v):
        i += self.n; self.t[i] = v
        while i > 1:
            i //= 2; self.t[i] = min(self.t[2*i], self.t[2*i+1])
    def query(self, l, r):            # [l, r)
        res = float('inf')
        l += self.n; r += self.n
        while l < r:
            if l & 1: res = min(res, self.t[l]); l += 1
            if r & 1: r -= 1; res = min(res, self.t[r])
            l //= 2; r //= 2
        return res

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Give the rule for each type, then apply it — the mapping is the answer.

Instant is a point on the global timeline, in UTC, with no zone. LocalDateTime is a wall-clock reading with no zone at all — it is not an instant and cannot be converted to one without supplying a zone. ZonedDateTime is a local time plus a zone id, so it applies that zone's DST rules. OffsetDateTime is local time plus a fixed offset, with no DST rules attached.

A DB timestamp → Instant, stored as UTC (timestamptz in Postgres). Something happened at a moment; the moment is the fact, and the display zone is a presentation concern.

A user-facing meeting time → ZonedDateTime, storing the local time and the zone id — not an offset, and not an Instant. This is the one people get wrong. If you store the instant, a government changing DST rules moves the meeting: a 9 a.m. standup becomes 8 a.m. The business intent is "9 a.m. in Asia/Kolkata", so store that and resolve to an instant at display time.

A birthday → LocalDate. It has no time and no zone; someone born on 14 March was born on 14 March everywhere. Storing it as an instant means it renders as the 13th for some users.

An event log → Instant, always UTC, always machine time.

On money: never double — use BigDecimal or integer minor units. With BigDecimal, three rules: never the double constructor (new BigDecimal(0.1) captures the already-wrong binary value — use the String form or valueOf); always specify scale and RoundingMode on divide, or a non-terminating result throws; and compare with compareTo, not equals, because equals also compares scale so 2.0 does not equal 2.00.

One more worth volunteering: SimpleDateFormat is mutable and not thread-safe — a static instance shared across threads produces corrupted output under load. DateTimeFormatter is immutable and safe.

Java
Instant now = Instant.now();                       // DB timestamp, event log: UTC
LocalDate dob = LocalDate.of(1998, 3, 14);        // birthday: no time, no zone

// meeting: store LOCAL TIME + ZONE ID, not an instant, not an offset
ZonedDateTime meeting = ZonedDateTime.of(
        LocalDateTime.of(2026, 3, 14, 9, 0), ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata"));
// survives a DST rule change; "+05:30" would freeze a decision that may become wrong

new BigDecimal(0.1);          // 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827...
new BigDecimal("0.1");        // exactly 0.1
total.divide(new BigDecimal(3), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);   // scale + mode required
new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00"));      // false - scale differs
new BigDecimal("2.0").compareTo(new BigDecimal("2.00"));   // 0 - equal in value
Follow-ups they will ask

Why store the zone id rather than the offset for future events?

Offsets change with DST and with legislation — countries have abolished or shifted DST with a few months' notice. A zone id survives a rule change and resolves to the correct offset at display time; a stored offset freezes a decision that can become wrong.

How do you split 100.00 three ways without losing a paisa?

Round each share down, then distribute the remainder one minor unit at a time. Rounding each share independently and summing produces 99.99 or 100.01, which reconciliation will catch and an auditor will ask about.

Which RoundingMode for money?

HALF_UP or HALF_EVEN — banker's rounding reduces cumulative bias across many operations, which is why financial standards often mandate it. The important thing is that it is a stated business decision rather than a library default.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The naive design fails on the poll query, so lead with that. A single jobs table polled with WHERE run_at <= now() across millions of rows means every worker repeatedly scans a growing index, and contention rises as workers multiply.

Time bucketing fixes it: partition jobs by their due minute — a table partition or a Redis sorted set per minute, keyed jobs:2026-08-29T14:03. A worker only ever reads the buckets that are due, so the query is bounded regardless of how many jobs exist in total. Far-future jobs sit in buckets nobody touches until their minute arrives.

Claiming with leases is how you get at-least-once without duplicate execution in the normal case: a worker atomically claims a job with an owner and an expiry (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in Postgres, or an atomic move in Redis), executes, then deletes it. If the worker crashes, the lease expires and another worker picks it up. SKIP LOCKED is the key detail — workers step over each other's claims instead of blocking.

At-least-once means duplicates are guaranteed, so handlers must be idempotent. A worker that is merely slow — a long GC pause — can have its lease expire while it is still running, so two executions genuinely overlap. State that plainly: leases bound the damage, they do not prevent it. Long jobs should heartbeat to extend their lease.

Second-level accuracy comes from polling the current bucket at a sub-second interval with a small look-ahead, plus enough workers that the claim step is not the bottleneck. Accuracy is a scheduling floor, not a guarantee — say what you can promise: fired within a second of the due time under normal load.

Clock skew and DST are the hazards. Bucket on UTC epoch time, never local time, or a DST transition either skips an hour of jobs or fires them twice. Keep workers NTP-synced, and be aware that a worker whose clock is ahead will claim jobs early.

Finally, scheduling is not execution: the scheduler should enqueue onto a work queue rather than run the job itself, so a slow handler cannot delay the firing of everything behind it.

Bucketed scheduler
# bucket by due minute -> the poll query is bounded regardless of total job count
ZADD jobs:2026-08-29T14:03  <due_epoch_ms>  <job_id>

# claim with a lease; workers step over each other rather than blocking
UPDATE jobs SET owner = :w, lease_until = now() + interval '60s'
 WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM jobs
               WHERE bucket = :b AND run_at <= now() AND owner IS NULL
               ORDER BY run_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING *;

# crash -> lease expires -> redelivered   => handlers MUST be idempotent
# long job -> heartbeat to extend the lease
# bucket on UTC epoch, never local time (DST would skip or double-fire an hour)
Follow-ups they will ask

Why SKIP LOCKED rather than a plain FOR UPDATE?

Without it, workers queue behind each other on the same rows and throughput collapses to serial. SKIP LOCKED lets each worker claim a disjoint set immediately, which is what makes a database-backed queue scale across many workers.

Can you guarantee exactly-once firing?

No. A lease can expire while a worker is still alive but paused, so two executions can overlap. At-least-once plus an idempotent handler is the achievable guarantee — anyone claiming exactly-once here is describing the happy path only.

How do you handle a job scheduled a year out?

It sits in its far-future bucket, untouched. That is the advantage of bucketing over a single sorted structure — the scheduler's working set is the next few minutes, not the entire backlog.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Use the Intl APIs and never hand-roll. Intl.NumberFormat, Intl.DateTimeFormat, Intl.RelativeTimeFormat, Intl.PluralRules and Intl.ListFormat are built in, locale-aware, and correct for cases you will not think of.

Pluralization is not count === 1 ? 'item' : 'items'. English has two plural forms; Arabic has six, Polish has four with rules based on the last two digits, and Japanese has one. Hard-coding the English branch produces text that is simply wrong in most languages. Use ICU MessageFormat, where the translator controls the categories.

Never concatenate translated fragments. t('you have') + count + t('messages') breaks because word order differs between languages — the verb may go last, the number may be positioned differently. Pass the whole sentence as one message with placeholders, so the translator can reorder freely.

RTL is a layout problem, not a text problem. Set dir="rtl" and use CSS logical properties — margin-inline-start, padding-inline-end, inset-inline-start, text-align: start — instead of left/right. Then the entire layout mirrors automatically. Icons that imply direction (a back arrow, a progress chevron) must flip; icons that do not (a play button, a logo) must not, so that is a per-icon decision rather than a blanket transform.

Dates and timezones: keep the instant in state (an ISO string or epoch) and format only at render, in the user's chosen zone. The single most common bug is trusting Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone — the browser's zone — for business logic. A user travelling sees different data; a user with a misconfigured machine sees wrong data. Let the user set a preferred zone, store it server-side, and use the browser zone only as an initial default.

What breaks when you get this wrong: text that reads as broken grammar in half your markets, layouts with buttons in the wrong corner and text clipped, dates off by one day near midnight, and — the expensive one — a report that shows different totals depending on where the viewer is sitting.

JSX
// whole sentence with placeholders - the translator controls order and plurals
t('inbox.unread', { count })
// en: "{count, plural, one {# unread message} other {# unread messages}}"
// pl: four categories; ar: six - the message file decides, not your code

// format at render, in the USER'S zone (not the browser's)
new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, {
  dateStyle: 'medium', timeStyle: 'short', timeZone: user.timeZone,
}).format(new Date(instant));

/* RTL: logical properties mirror the whole layout automatically */
.card { margin-inline-start: 16px; padding-inline-end: 8px; text-align: start; }
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is trusting the browser timezone a bug?

Because it reports where the device currently is, not where the user's data belongs. A user in a different city, or with a wrong system clock, sees shifted dates — and for anything financial or scheduled, that is a correctness issue, not a display preference.

What does ICU MessageFormat give you over a template string?

Locale-correct plural categories, gender selection, and nested formatting, all controlled from the message file. The translator can restructure the sentence entirely without a code change, which is exactly what other languages require.

What is the most common RTL mistake?

Mirroring everything with a blanket CSS transform, which flips logos, photos and non-directional icons. Mirroring is per-element intent: use logical properties for layout and flip only the icons that genuinely encode direction.

Range updates on a segment tree without touching every leaf: store the pending change at a node and push it down only when needed.

CostO(log n) for range update and range queryReach for itAdd a value to a whole range, or assign a range, while still answering range queries. The step up from a plain segment tree.
# Store a pending delta per node; apply it before reading children.
def push(node, l, r):
    if lazy[node]:
        tree[node] += lazy[node] * (r - l + 1)
        if l != r:                       # not a leaf: defer to children
            lazy[2*node]   += lazy[node]
            lazy[2*node+1] += lazy[node]
        lazy[node] = 0

def update(node, l, r, ql, qr, val):
    push(node, l, r)
    if qr < l or r < ql: return          # no overlap
    if ql <= l and r <= qr:              # total overlap - stop here
        lazy[node] += val; push(node, l, r); return
    m = (l + r) // 2
    update(2*node, l, m, ql, qr, val)
    update(2*node+1, m+1, r, ql, qr, val)
    tree[node] = tree[2*node] + tree[2*node+1]

Prefer static factories with names over overloaded constructors. Make the common case one line and the complex case possible.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design for the fact that you cannot take anything back. Every public element is a promise, so the guiding rule is: make the surface as small as possible, make the common case one line, and make the complex case possible.

Nulls. Never return null for a collection — return an empty one, which composes correctly with loops and streams and costs nothing (List.of() is a shared instance). Use Optional as a return type where absence is meaningful, never as a field or parameter. Validate parameters at the boundary with Objects.requireNonNull so the failure points at the caller rather than surfacing three frames deeper. Document nullability explicitly — annotations or javadoc — because the type system does not.

Overloading versus named factories. Prefer static factories with meaningful names over constructors or overloads that differ only in parameter type: Money.ofMinor(1250, INR) versus new Money(1250, INR). Names document intent, can return cached or subtype instances, and avoid ambiguity. Overloads that differ only in long versus Long, or in the order of two same-typed parameters, are a trap for callers.

Builders when there are many optional parameters — beyond about four, telescoping constructors become unreadable and error-prone. Validate in build() so an invalid object cannot exist.

Defaults should be the safe, conservative choice, because most callers never change them. A default timeout of "infinite" is a production incident waiting to happen.

What counts as a breaking change in Java — and this list is longer than people expect: removing or renaming anything public; adding an abstract method to an interface (use default instead); changing a return type; widening a thrown checked exception; reordering enum constants that are persisted by ordinal; changing a method from static to instance or vice versa; and — subtly — adding an overload can break source compatibility by creating ambiguity at existing call sites. Also, tightening a parameter type or loosening a return type breaks callers even when it looks like a safe narrowing.

Version with semver, deprecate with @Deprecated(since=, forRemoval=) plus a migration note, and give consumers a real window.

Java
public final class Money {
    public static Money ofMinor(long minor, Currency c) { ... }   // named factory
    public static Money zero(Currency c) { ... }

    public Money plus(Money other) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(other, "other");    // fail at the boundary
        requireSameCurrency(other);
        return new Money(minor + other.minor, currency);   // immutable, fluent
    }
    public List<Tag> tags() { return List.copyOf(tags); }   // never null, never mutable
}

// non-breaking interface evolution
interface Validator {
    List<String> errors(Object v);
    default boolean isValid(Object v) { return errors(v).isEmpty(); }  // added later
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why can adding an overload break source compatibility?

Because an existing call site that previously resolved unambiguously may now match two candidates equally well, producing a compile error for consumers when they upgrade — even though nothing they wrote changed.

How do you evolve an interface without breaking implementors?

Add the method as default with a sensible implementation. If it genuinely cannot have one, you need a new interface or a major version — which is why the initial interface design deserves care.

What is the cost of a bad public API?

You keep it forever. Every consumer depends on it, so fixing it means a major version and a migration for everyone. That asymmetry is why the smallest possible public surface is always the right default.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Estimate first, because the numbers drive the storage design. Ten thousand hosts each emitting a thousand series at ten-second resolution is 1M data points per second — roughly 86 billion points a day. At a naive 16 bytes per point that is 1.4 TB/day, which is why specialised time-series compression exists rather than a general database.

Ingestion is a write-optimized path: agents push or are scraped, points land in a buffer (Kafka or an in-memory WAL), and the writer appends to per-series blocks. Writes are append-only and time-ordered, which is the property everything else exploits.

Storage uses the Gorilla techniques, and naming them is the depth signal: delta-of-delta encoding for timestamps (regular intervals compress to a couple of bits each) and XOR encoding for values (consecutive floats usually differ in few bits). Together they get typical series down to ~1.4 bytes per point — a 10x reduction that turns 1.4 TB/day into something affordable. Data is organised into immutable time-bucketed blocks, so expiry is dropping a block rather than deleting rows.

Rollups make dashboard queries fast: precompute downsampled series (1m, 5m, 1h) as data ages, and route a query to the coarsest resolution that satisfies the requested time range. Nobody renders 86,000 raw points into 800 pixels — so a query for the last 30 days reads hourly rollups, not raw data. Retention is tiered: raw for days, 5-minute for weeks, hourly for a year.

Query path: an inverted index from label pairs to series ids selects the matching series, then the engine reads the relevant blocks. That index is what makes {service="api", status="500"} fast.

Cardinality is the failure mode and the thing to volunteer. Every unique label combination is a separate series with its own index entry and memory footprint. Putting a user id, request id, or raw URL in a label multiplies series into the millions and takes the ingestion tier down — this is the single most common way monitoring systems die, and it is usually caused by one team's well-meaning deploy. Defend with per-tenant series limits, label-value allowlists, and alerting on series creation rate rather than only on total count. High-cardinality detail belongs in traces and logs, which are built for it.

Storage
1M points/s -> buffer (WAL/Kafka) -> per-series append-only blocks

compression (Gorilla):
  timestamps: delta-of-delta   (regular intervals -> a few bits each)
  values:     XOR with previous (consecutive floats differ in few bits)
  ~16 bytes/point -> ~1.4 bytes/point

rollups: raw (7d) -> 5m (30d) -> 1h (1y);  query routes to the coarsest that fits
index:   label pairs -> series ids (inverted index)
expiry:  drop a time block, never DELETE rows

CARDINALITY = series count. user_id/request_id/raw URL in a label -> outage.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is high cardinality so much worse for metrics than for logs?

Because each series is a persistent object with an index entry, in-memory head block and retention — the cost is ongoing and proportional to the number of distinct combinations. A log line is written once and read rarely, so unbounded values cost storage, not a live index.

How do you catch a cardinality explosion before it takes the system down?

Alert on the rate of new series creation per tenant, not just the total. An explosion is a step change on deploy, so a rate alarm fires within minutes while a total-count alarm fires after the damage.

Why not store metrics in Postgres?

The write rate and the compression. A relational row per data point is orders of magnitude more expensive in storage and index maintenance, and it cannot exploit the time-ordering and value-similarity that make time-series compression possible.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Three constraints define this SDK, and stating them up front frames every decision: it must never break the host application, it must not measurably slow the page, and it must not lose events on navigation.

Batching: queue events in memory and flush on whichever comes first — a size threshold (say 20 events), a time threshold (5–10 seconds), or a page-lifecycle event. One request carrying twenty events beats twenty requests carrying one, both for the network and for your ingestion tier.

Delivery on unload is the hard part. beforeunload is unreliable on mobile, where the browser frequently kills or backgrounds a page without firing it, and it cannot await an async request. The correct approach is to flush on visibilitychange when the document becomes hidden — which fires reliably on tab switch, app backgrounding and navigation — using navigator.sendBeacon or fetch with keepalive: true. Both survive the page going away, which a normal fetch does not. Note sendBeacon's ~64 KB payload limit, so cap the batch size accordingly.

Sampling must be at the session level, not the event level. Sampling 10% of individual events destroys funnels — you see a checkout completion whose preceding page view was dropped, and every conversion rate is wrong. Decide once per session (hash the session id against the rate) and then send all or none of that session's events. Always keep 100% of errors and conversions regardless of the sample rate.

Bundle footprint: the SDK must be a few kilobytes. That means no dependencies, no polyfills for browsers you do not support, feature detection rather than a UA parser, and lazy-loading anything optional (session replay, heatmaps) rather than shipping it to every page.

Never throw into the host application. Wrap every public entry point in try/catch, fail silently, and degrade to a no-op if the endpoint is unreachable. An analytics library that breaks checkout is infinitely worse than one that loses data. Also queue to localStorage for offline resilience, with a cap so a long offline session cannot fill storage.

And use an idempotency key per event so retries after a failed flush do not double-count.

JS
// flush on hidden - reliable on mobile, unlike beforeunload
document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === 'hidden') flush();
});

function flush() {
  if (!queue.length) return;
  const body = JSON.stringify({ events: queue.splice(0, 50) });
  // sendBeacon survives page teardown; ~64KB limit
  if (!navigator.sendBeacon(ENDPOINT, body)) {
    fetch(ENDPOINT, { method: 'POST', body, keepalive: true }).catch(() => {});
  }
}

// SESSION-level sampling - event-level sampling destroys funnels
const sampled = hash(sessionId) % 100 < SAMPLE_RATE;
function track(e) {
  try { if (sampled || e.critical) { queue.push(e); maybeFlush(); } }
  catch { /* never throw into the host app */ }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is beforeunload the wrong hook?

Mobile browsers often terminate or background a page without firing it, and it cannot wait for an async request. visibilitychange to hidden fires in all those cases and is the pattern the platform now recommends.

Why does event-level sampling break funnels?

Because a funnel needs the whole session's sequence. Dropping 90% of individual events leaves you with conversions whose preceding steps are missing, so every step-to-step rate is computed from inconsistent denominators.

How do you avoid double-counting on retry?

Give each event a client-generated id and dedupe server-side. A flush that times out may well have been received, so retrying without an id inflates every metric — the same reasoning as an idempotency key on a payment.

Design VII - calendars & intervals
  • My Calendar IMedium
  • My Calendar IIMedium
  • My Calendar IIIHard

A double-ended queue kept in sorted order, so the window's maximum is always at the front. Each element enters and leaves once.

CostO(n) total — beats the heap's O(n log n)Reach for itSliding window maximum or minimum, and any 'best value in the last k' query.
from collections import deque
def sliding_max(a, k):
    dq, out = deque(), []             # dq holds INDICES, values decreasing
    for i, v in enumerate(a):
        while dq and a[dq[-1]] <= v: dq.pop()      # v dominates them
        dq.append(i)
        if dq[0] <= i - k: dq.popleft()            # front fell out of window
        if i >= k - 1: out.append(a[dq[0]])
    return out

Code review round: given a snippet with a non-thread-safe SimpleDateFormat field, a @Transactional self-invocation, a leaked ExecutorService, and an N+1 - find every bug and propose fixes.

Noisy neighbor: per-tenant rate limits and query cost budgets, separate pools for large tenants. Every query must be tenant-scoped by construction, not by convention.
