Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Narrate a code review in severity order — correctness, then concurrency, then performance, then style — and ask about context before rewriting. Interviewers score prioritisation and communication as much as detection.

1. Non-thread-safe SimpleDateFormat as a shared field (concurrency, high). It holds mutable parsing state, so two threads formatting concurrently interleave and produce corrupted dates or a NumberFormatException — and it only appears under load, which is why it survives testing. Fix: replace with DateTimeFormatter, which is immutable and thread-safe. If it must stay, a ThreadLocal works but then needs remove() in a pooled thread.

2. @Transactional self-invocation (correctness, high). A call to this.method() bypasses the AOP proxy entirely, so the annotation does nothing — silently. The work runs without a transaction, so a partial failure leaves inconsistent state with no rollback and no error. Fix: move the method to another bean, or restructure so the transaction boundary is at the external entry point. Same failure applies to private and final methods.

3. Leaked ExecutorService (resource, high). An executor created per request or per call and never shut down leaks its threads permanently — each reserving around a megabyte of stack — until you hit OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread. Fix: a single shared, bounded, named pool as a managed bean with a lifecycle, or a try-with-resources executor on modern JDKs.

4. N+1 query (performance, medium-high). One query for parents plus one per parent for a lazy association — 200 rows becomes 201 round trips. Passes tests with ten rows, dies in production. Fix per query with JOIN FETCH, an @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection — not by switching the mapping to EAGER, which is a global change for a local problem.

The framing that scores well: lead with the two that cause incorrect data (the transaction and the date formatter), because they corrupt state rather than merely being slow, and note that the N+1 is the one most likely to be found by monitoring rather than by a user. Then ask what load this runs under, since that determines the urgency of the executor leak.

Java
class ReportService {
    // 1. mutable, not thread-safe, shared -> corrupted output under load
    private static final SimpleDateFormat FMT = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd");
    private static final DateTimeFormatter FIXED = DateTimeFormatter.ISO_DATE;  // fix

    @Transactional
    public void process(List<Long> ids) {
        // 3. new pool per call, never shut down -> thread leak
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);   // fix: shared bean

        for (Long id : ids) {
            Order o = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
            o.getLines().size();          // 4. N+1 -> use JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph
            audit(o);                     // 2. self-invocation: @Transactional IGNORED
        }
    }
    @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void audit(Order o) { }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Which do you raise first and why?

The @Transactional self-invocation and the date formatter — both silently produce wrong data. The thread leak and the N+1 degrade the system but do not corrupt it, so they are urgent rather than critical.

How would you catch these before review?

Static analysis catches shared SimpleDateFormat and unclosed executors; a datasource-proxy asserting query counts in tests catches N+1; the self-invocation trap needs either an integration test asserting rollback, or a team convention that transaction boundaries live at the service entry point only.

What question would you ask the author?

What load this runs under, and whether audit is intended to survive a rollback of the main transaction. The second determines whether the fix is REQUIRES_NEW in a separate bean or an after-commit event.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The three isolation models, with their real trade: Silo — a separate database (often separate infrastructure) per tenant. Strongest isolation, easiest compliance story, per-tenant backup and restore, no noisy-neighbour risk — and operationally expensive: migrations across a thousand databases, poor resource utilisation, slow onboarding. Pool — all tenants share tables with a tenant_id column. Cheapest and most efficient, trivial onboarding, one migration — and one query missing a tenant filter is a cross-tenant data leak. Bridge — a schema per tenant in a shared database. A middle ground: better isolation than pool, cheaper than silo, but schema count becomes a migration problem in the thousands.

Most platforms run a hybrid, and saying so is the mature answer: pool for the long tail of small tenants, silo for large or regulated customers who pay for it. Design the data-access layer so a tenant can be migrated between models without application changes.

Tenant scoping must be structural, not by convention. "Remember to add WHERE tenant_id = ?" fails eventually — one forgotten filter in one query is a breach. Enforce it with Postgres row-level security plus a session variable set from the authenticated context, or a repository layer that physically cannot issue an unscoped query. The tenant id should come from the verified token, never from a request parameter a client can change.

Noisy neighbours need limits at several layers: per-tenant rate limits at the gateway; per-tenant concurrency caps (a semaphore or a separate connection-pool partition) so one tenant cannot exhaust the pool; query cost budgets with statement timeouts; and separate worker queues or pools for large tenants — the bulkhead pattern applied to customers. Without these, one tenant running a report degrades everyone.

Operationally, track per-tenant usage and cost so you know who is expensive, and make it possible to move a tenant to dedicated infrastructure without a rewrite. Also plan for per-tenant restore: in a pool model, restoring one tenant's data after they delete something is genuinely hard, and customers will ask.

Enforcement
-- structural, not by convention: RLS makes an unscoped query impossible
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);

-- set from the VERIFIED token per request/connection, never from a parameter
SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = '...';

noisy neighbour:
  gateway   per-tenant rate limit
  service   per-tenant concurrency cap (semaphore / pool partition)
  database  statement_timeout + per-tenant query budget
  workers   separate queues for large tenants (bulkhead)
Follow-ups they will ask

Where must the tenant id come from?

The verified authentication token, resolved server-side. Taking it from a header, path or body lets a client set it — which is the most direct possible cross-tenant data access, and it has shipped in real products.

How do you migrate a tenant from pool to silo?

Dual-write to both, backfill their historical rows, verify counts and checksums, cut reads over behind a flag, then stop writing to the pool and delete their rows. The same expand-contract discipline as any migration — which is why the data layer must not hardcode the model.

What is hardest about the pool model operationally?

Per-tenant restore and per-tenant deletion. Restoring one tenant to a point in time from a shared table means extracting and replaying their rows, and a contractual deletion request means proving their data is gone from backups too.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Build on CSS custom properties, and make the tokens semantic rather than literal. A token named --color-grey-200 tells you nothing about where to use it and breaks in dark mode; --surface, --surface-raised, --text-primary, --border-subtle describe role, so a theme can redefine them freely and every component follows automatically.

Two layers of tokens is the structure that scales: a primitive palette (--blue-500) that never changes per theme, and a semantic layer (--accent: var(--blue-500)) that each theme remaps. Components reference only the semantic layer. That is what lets a per-tenant brand override change the palette without touching a single component.

Three theme states, not two. A user can choose light, choose dark, or leave it on system — and the third is the default. So define the complete light palette on bare :root, redefine the tokens inside @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) guarded against an explicit light choice, and redefine them again under an explicit [data-theme="dark"] attribute so the toggle wins in both directions. A theme defined only inside a media query silently fails for users who have explicitly chosen.

Per-tenant brands layer on top: serve the tenant's semantic overrides as a small block of custom properties scoped to :root or a wrapper, injected server-side or fetched before first paint. Because only the semantic layer changes, no component code is brand-aware.

Avoiding the flash of wrong theme is the crux of the question. The stored preference lives in localStorage, which JavaScript can only read after the document starts parsing — so if you apply the theme in React, the browser has already painted the default and the user sees a white flash before dark mode appears. The fix is a tiny blocking inline script in <head>, before any stylesheet, that reads the preference and sets data-theme on the root element. It must be inline and synchronous; a deferred or bundled script is too late.

With SSR there is an additional constraint: the server does not know the user's preference, so render with the attribute absent (system default) and let the inline script stamp it — trying to guess produces a hydration mismatch.

CSS + HTML
/* primitives never change; semantics are what themes remap */
:root { --blue-500:#3B5B92; --accent: var(--blue-500);
        --surface:#FCFCFA; --text-primary:#191D19; }

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:not([data-theme="light"]) {      /* explicit light must still win */
    --surface:#1C1F1A; --text-primary:#E9EBE3;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --surface:#1C1F1A; --text-primary:#E9EBE3; }

<!-- BLOCKING inline script in <head>, before any stylesheet: no flash -->
<script>
  try { var t = localStorage.getItem('theme');
        if (t) document.documentElement.dataset.theme = t; } catch (e) {}
</script>
Follow-ups they will ask

Why must the script be inline and blocking?

Because it has to run before the first paint. A deferred or bundled script runs after the browser has already painted the default theme, so the user sees the wrong colours for a frame or two — which is exactly the flash you are trying to prevent.

How do you avoid a hydration mismatch with SSR?

Render the server HTML with no theme attribute, so both server and client start from the system default, and let the inline script stamp the attribute before React hydrates. Guessing the theme server-side produces markup the client disagrees with.

Why semantic tokens rather than a palette?

Because a component referencing --grey-200 is wrong in dark mode and wrong for a tenant whose brand is not grey. --surface expresses intent, so every theme and brand can satisfy it without the component knowing anything.

Design VIII - leaderboards
  • Design a LeaderboardMedium
  • Design File SystemMedium
  • All O`one Data StructureHard

Precompute, for each prefix, the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. On a mismatch, jump there instead of restarting.

CostO(n + m) time, O(m) spaceReach for itSubstring search without hashing, period detection, and 'shortest palindrome' style problems.
def build_lps(p):
    lps, k = [0]*len(p), 0
    for i in range(1, len(p)):
        while k and p[i] != p[k]: k = lps[k-1]
        if p[i] == p[k]: k += 1
        lps[i] = k
    return lps

def kmp(text, p):
    lps, k, hits = build_lps(p), 0, []
    for i, ch in enumerate(text):
        while k and ch != p[k]: k = lps[k-1]
        if ch == p[k]: k += 1
        if k == len(p): hits.append(i - k + 1); k = lps[k-1]
    return hits
680/4

StudySystem Design Primer →

StudyARIA Authoring Practices Guide — patterns →
Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Treat this as a rehearsal with a scoring rubric, not as another practice problem — the point is the process, which is what actually gets assessed.

The time-box. Minutes 0–5: clarify. Restate the problem in your own words, ask about input size, ranges, duplicates, empty input, and what to optimise for. Minutes 5–10: state a brute force with its complexity, out loud, before optimising — this proves you understand the problem and gives you a fallback. Minutes 10–15: derive the optimal approach and state its complexity before writing code. Minutes 15–35: write it. Minutes 35–45: test by hand on a small case and an edge case, then discuss follow-ups.

Narrate continuously. Silence for more than about twenty seconds is the single most common way strong candidates fail — the interviewer cannot score reasoning they cannot hear. When you are stuck, say what you are considering and why you rejected it; that is still signal. Saying "let me think for thirty seconds" and then thinking is fine; going quiet for three minutes is not.

Write compiling code. Real method signatures, real types, no pseudocode drifting into hand-waving. Handle nulls and empty input explicitly rather than saying "I'd validate this". If you use a helper, either write it or state precisely what it does.

Test by hand — walk one small input through your code line by line, out loud. Most bugs surface here, and finding your own bug scores far better than the interviewer finding it.

Score yourself on five axes afterwards: clarifying questions asked; brute force stated before optimising; complexity stated correctly and unprompted; edge cases enumerated before coding; and whether you tested by hand. Those five, not whether you got the optimal solution — a working suboptimal solution with excellent communication frequently beats a silent optimal one.

Record it. Watch it back at 1.5x and note every silence over twenty seconds and every moment you jumped to code before stating an approach. That is the feedback loop that actually improves the round.

Rubric
0-5    clarify: input size, ranges, duplicates, empty, what to optimise for
5-10   brute force OUT LOUD + its complexity        <- your fallback
10-15  optimal approach + complexity BEFORE coding
15-35  compiling code, real signatures, edge cases handled
35-45  hand-trace a small input, then follow-ups

score yourself:
  [ ] asked clarifying questions
  [ ] stated brute force first
  [ ] stated complexity unprompted
  [ ] enumerated edge cases BEFORE coding
  [ ] tested by hand and found your own bugs
  [ ] never silent for >20s
Follow-ups they will ask

What if you cannot find the optimal solution?

Ship the brute force, state its complexity, and say specifically what you would improve and why you think it is possible. A working solution plus a clear articulation of the gap beats an unfinished optimal attempt in most rubrics.

How do you handle a hint from the interviewer?

Take it, say what it unlocked, and integrate it visibly. Hints are expected and are not automatically a mark against you — ignoring one, or pretending you had already thought of it, is.

What is the most common self-inflicted failure?

Coding immediately. It skips the clarification and approach steps the interviewer is scoring, and it usually means solving a subtly different problem than the one asked.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Run the time-box strictly, because the most common failure in this round is spending twenty-five minutes on requirements and never reaching a design — or the reverse, drawing boxes at minute two.

0–5 requirements. Functional: what must it do, for whom. Non-functional: scale, latency target, consistency needs, availability target. Write them down where the interviewer can see them and explicitly scope out what you will not cover. Ask the read:write ratio — it drives most later decisions.

5–10 estimates. DAU, requests per user, QPS, peak multiplier, storage per record, retention. Round aggressively to one significant figure; you are deciding "one box or a hundred", and that survives a 2x error. State your assumptions rather than hiding them.

10–20 high level. Draw the boxes and the data flow: clients, load balancer, services, stores, queues, caches. Keep it coarse — this is the map, not the destination. Then say out loud which component you consider most interesting and ask the interviewer where they want to go deep. That question is itself scored, and it stops you deep-diving into the part they do not care about.

20–40 deep dive. One or two components, properly: the data model with actual fields, the partition key and why, the index, the API contract, the failure behaviour. This is where the round is won — vague breadth loses to concrete depth.

40–45 tradeoffs and risks. Close by naming your top three risks and what you would build first. That is the single highest-leverage ninety seconds available, because it demonstrates engineering judgement rather than recall.

The failure mode to watch for in yourself: jumping to boxes-and-arrows before pinning requirements, and never quantifying anything. Watch the recording and check two things — did you drive the conversation or wait to be prompted, and did any number appear on the board? If the interviewer had to ask "how much data is that?", you left points behind.

Time-box
0-5    requirements  functional + non-functional; scope OUT loudly; read:write ratio
5-10   estimates     DAU -> QPS -> peak -> storage -> bandwidth (1 sig fig)
10-20  high level    boxes + data flow; then ASK where to go deep
20-40  deep dive     data model, partition key, indexes, API, failure behaviour
40-45  tradeoffs     top 3 risks + what you would build first

self-check on the recording:
  did I drive, or wait to be prompted?
  did any NUMBER reach the board?
  did I name risks unprompted?
Follow-ups they will ask

What if you do not know a technology the prompt implies?

Say so, and reason from first principles about what it must do. "I have not used Cassandra in production, but I need a store with multi-region writes and known access patterns, so I would evaluate it against these criteria" scores far better than inventing details.

How much detail is too much in the high-level phase?

If you are naming table columns before minute twenty, you are too deep too early. Keep it to components and data flow, then let the interviewer steer the deep dive — they usually have a specific area they want to probe.

What separates a hire from a strong-hire in this round?

Quantification and risk-naming. Most candidates can draw a reasonable architecture; far fewer size it with numbers and volunteer what they are most worried about and what they would validate first.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Frontend rounds are usually deliberately vague — "build a search interface", "build a comment thread" — because the scoring is about how you handle ambiguity and what you remember to include, not whether you can write JSX.

Confirm scope first (3–5 min). Ask what data comes from where, how much of it, what interactions matter, and whether design is provided. Then say explicitly what you will build in the time and what you will describe rather than implement. Interviewers respect scoping; silently attempting everything and finishing nothing is the failure.

Sketch the API and the state before any markup. What does the endpoint return, what shape does the component hold, what is derived versus stored. Most implementation problems in this round are actually state-shape problems, and a minute of design here saves ten of refactoring.

Build the happy path first and get something rendering early — a working narrow thing beats a half-finished broad thing, and it gives the interviewer something concrete to react to.

Then add the states that are actually scored: loading, error, and empty. These are the most commonly skipped and the cheapest to include. An interface that renders nothing on failure is indistinguishable from one that found no results, and pointing that out yourself is a strong signal.

Then accessibility: semantic elements, labels, keyboard operation, focus management. Mentioning it and doing the cheap parts — a real <button>, a label, an aria-live for async updates — puts you ahead of most candidates.

Then performance, if the data volume warrants it: debounce, cancellation, memoization, virtualization. Say which apply and why rather than adding them reflexively.

Close by saying what you would do with more time — tests, edge cases, the design polish you skipped, the API changes you would request. That converts an unfinished implementation into demonstrated judgement, and it is the difference between "ran out of time" and "scoped deliberately".

Order
1. scope        ask; state what you WILL and WILL NOT build in the time
2. API + state  response shape, component state, derived vs stored
3. happy path   get something rendering early
4. states       loading / error / empty          <- most often skipped, cheapest points
5. a11y         semantic elements, labels, keyboard, focus, aria-live
6. perf         debounce, cancel, memo, virtualize - only if warranted, and say why
7. close        "with more time: tests, X, Y"    <- judgement, not an excuse
Follow-ups they will ask

What if the prompt is too vague to start?

That is the test. Make an explicit assumption, say it out loud, and build against it — "I will assume the API returns twenty results per page and I will design for that" is exactly the behaviour being assessed.

Should you write tests in a 45-minute round?

Usually not, unless asked — but say what you would test and why. Naming the two or three behaviours worth covering demonstrates the same judgement in a fraction of the time.

What is the highest-value thing most candidates omit?

The error state, and cancellation on a search input. Both take a couple of minutes and both are things a real reviewer would flag in a pull request, so including them reads as production experience.

MOCK - 45 min, design round
  • Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)Medium
  • LFU CacheHard

Design-heavy coding round. Sketch the data structures and their invariants before writing a single method.

Treat a string as a number in some base. Sliding the window updates the hash in O(1), so substring comparison becomes a number comparison.

CostO(n + m) average, O(1) per substring compareReach for itSubstring search, finding duplicate substrings, and comparing many substrings quickly. Often replaces heavier suffix structures.
def rabin_karp(text, pat, base=256, mod=10**9+7):
    n, m = len(text), len(pat)
    if m > n: return []
    high = pow(base, m-1, mod)
    ph = th = 0
    for i in range(m):
        ph = (ph*base + ord(pat[i]))  % mod
        th = (th*base + ord(text[i])) % mod
    hits = []
    for i in range(n - m + 1):
        if ph == th and text[i:i+m] == pat: hits.append(i)   # verify!
        if i < n - m:
            th = ((th - ord(text[i])*high) * base + ord(text[i+m])) % mod
    return hits

# Always verify on a hash match, or use two moduli - collisions happen.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Clarify before designing — that is scored in an LLD round. Ask: is it a single lot or multiple, are spots typed (motorcycle, car, EV, accessible), is pricing hourly or slabbed, is entry ticket-based or plate-recognition, and do we need to find a specific car later. Then state your assumptions out loud.

The core model. ParkingLot holds Floors, each holding ParkingSpots. A Vehicle has a type. A Ticket links vehicle, spot, entry time, and later exit time and fee. Keep Spot dumb — it knows its type and occupancy, nothing about pricing or allocation.

The two things being assessed are extensibility points, so make them explicit rather than hard-coding: allocation and pricing are both Strategy interfaces. SpotAllocationStrategy decides which free spot to give a vehicle (nearest to entrance, lowest floor first, EV-preferring); PricingStrategy computes the fee (flat hourly, slabbed, weekend rates, free first 15 minutes). Adding an EV-charging spot type or a new pricing rule must not touch existing classes — that is the test the interviewer will apply at minute 40.

Spot typing is an enum plus a compatibility rule (a car may take a large spot if no compact is free), which belongs in the allocation strategy rather than scattered in conditionals.

Concurrency is the correctness question even though it sounds like a modelling exercise: two vehicles must never be assigned the same spot. Do not iterate a list and set a boolean — that is a check-then-act race. Either hold a lock around allocate-and-mark, or keep free spots per type in a ConcurrentLinkedQueue and poll(), which is atomic by construction and scales better. Say which and why.

Interfaces to expose: Ticket park(Vehicle) and Receipt unpark(Ticket) — small surface, everything else internal. And mention what you would add for a real system: persistence, an availability display per floor, and reservations, which change allocation from "any free spot" to "any free unreserved spot".

Java
enum SpotType { MOTORCYCLE, COMPACT, LARGE, EV, ACCESSIBLE }

interface SpotAllocationStrategy { Optional<Spot> allocate(Floor[] floors, Vehicle v); }
interface PricingStrategy       { Money price(Ticket t, Instant exit); }

class ParkingLot {
    private final Map<SpotType, Queue<Spot>> free = new EnumMap<>(SpotType.class);
    private final SpotAllocationStrategy allocation;
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;

    Ticket park(Vehicle v) {
        Spot s = free.get(compatible(v)).poll();      // atomic claim - no race
        if (s == null) throw new LotFullException(v.type());
        return new Ticket(v, s, Instant.now());
    }
    Receipt unpark(Ticket t) {
        Money fee = pricing.price(t, Instant.now());
        free.get(t.spot().type()).offer(t.spot());     // return to the pool
        return new Receipt(t, fee);
    }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

How does your design handle adding EV charging spots?

A new enum constant, a compatibility rule in the allocation strategy, and optionally a pricing strategy that adds a charging fee. No existing class changes — which is the Open/Closed test the interviewer is applying.

Why a queue rather than scanning a list for a free spot?

poll() is atomic, so two threads cannot claim the same spot; scanning and then setting a flag is check-then-act and races. It is also O(1) rather than O(n).

What changes for multiple lots or reservations?

Allocation moves behind a service that can consult reservations, and spot state gains a RESERVED status. The strategy interface absorbs it — which is the point of having made allocation pluggable.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Distinguish this from a scheduler immediately: a scheduler answers "run this at time T"; a job queue answers "one of N workers should do this, exactly once if possible, as soon as capacity allows". The core mechanic here is competing consumers with visibility timeouts.

Visibility timeout is the central idea. A worker receives a message rather than deleting it — the message becomes invisible to other consumers for a configured window. The worker processes, then explicitly deletes it. If the worker crashes, the timeout expires, the message becomes visible again, and another worker picks it up. That is how at-least-once delivery is achieved without a distributed transaction.

The consequence to state plainly: a worker that is merely slow — a long GC pause, a stalled downstream — can have its visibility timeout expire while it is still working, so the job runs twice concurrently. Visibility timeouts bound the damage; they do not prevent duplication. Therefore handlers must be idempotent, and long-running jobs should extend their own visibility (a heartbeat) rather than relying on a generous initial timeout.

Priority is best implemented as separate queues per priority with weighted polling, not as an in-queue sort. Sorting inside a queue destroys the O(1) head operation and creates contention; separate queues let you also scale their consumers independently. Guard against starvation by always polling the low-priority queue at some minimum rate.

Dead-lettering: track a receive count on each message and move it to a DLQ after N deliveries, preserving the last error and the full history. Classify first — a deserialization or validation failure should go straight to the DLQ, since retrying is pure waste. And a DLQ nobody monitors is just delayed data loss: alert on depth and have a documented, idempotent replay path.

Fairness deserves a mention: one tenant enqueuing a million jobs must not starve everyone else. Either shard queues per tenant or apply a per-tenant in-flight cap during dispatch.

Semantics
receive(queue, visibility=60s):
  message becomes INVISIBLE to other consumers for 60s
  worker processes -> delete(receipt)        # explicit ack
  crash / timeout  -> becomes visible again  # at-least-once => idempotent handler

long job: heartbeat -> extendVisibility(receipt, +60s)

priority: separate queues + weighted polling (never sort inside a queue)
          always poll low-priority at a minimum rate -> no starvation

dlq: receive_count > N -> DLQ with last error + history
     permanent failures (deserialize/validate) -> DLQ immediately, no retries
     alert on DLQ depth; replay must be idempotent
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you choose the visibility timeout?

Longer than the p99 processing time, plus margin — too short and healthy jobs get duplicated, too long and a crashed worker's job sits idle. Better still, set it modestly and heartbeat, so the timeout tracks actual progress.

Queue or log for this workload?

Queue. You need per-message acknowledgement, per-message retry with visibility timeouts, and priority. A log like Kafka replays by offset, which makes "retry just this one message later" awkward — that is why Kafka deployments add retry topics.

How do you stop one tenant starving the others?

Per-tenant queues with weighted dispatch, or a per-tenant in-flight cap enforced at dispatch time. Without it, a bulk import from one customer becomes an outage for everyone else.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Four requirements drive the design: it must open instantly from anywhere, search must feel immediate over hundreds of commands, it must be fully keyboard-operable, and it must be accessible to screen readers. Say those, then build to them.

Opening: a global Cmd/Ctrl+K listener registered once at the app root, with preventDefault so the browser's own shortcut does not fire. Store focus before opening and restore it on close — a command palette that dumps focus to document.body strands keyboard users.

Fuzzy search over a few hundred commands is fast enough to run synchronously on every keystroke, so no debounce is needed and the UI feels instant. Score matches (prefix match beats substring, consecutive characters beat scattered ones, and weight by recency and frequency of use) and sort. Above a few thousand items, move matching into a worker or precompute an index — but say that the common case does not need it.

Grouping and recents: group results by category with non-focusable headings, and show recent commands when the input is empty — that turns the palette from a search tool into a genuinely faster path than the menu, which is the actual product goal. Persist recents in localStorage.

Accessibility is the combobox pattern, and it is what most implementations get wrong. The input carries role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-controls, and crucially aria-activedescendant pointing at the highlighted option's id — so DOM focus stays in the input while the screen reader announces the highlighted item. Moving real focus into the list would break typing entirely. The list is role="listbox" with role="option" children and aria-selected; group headings must not be options. Add an aria-live region announcing the result count.

Keyboard: arrows move the highlight (clamped or wrapping — pick one and be consistent), Enter executes, Escape closes and restores focus, and the highlighted row must be scrolled into view programmatically. Virtualize the list only if the command count justifies it.

Executing a command should close the palette first, then run the action, so a command that opens a dialog does not fight the palette for focus.

JSX
// global open, once at the root
useEffect(() => {
  const onKey = e => {
    if ((e.metaKey || e.ctrlKey) && e.key === 'k') { e.preventDefault(); open(); }
  };
  document.addEventListener('keydown', onKey);
  return () => document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey);
}, []);

// focus STAYS in the input; the screen reader follows activedescendant
<input role="combobox" aria-expanded={true}
       aria-controls="cmdk-list"
       aria-activedescendant={active >= 0 ? `cmdk-opt-${active}` : undefined}
       value={q} onChange={e => setQ(e.target.value)} onKeyDown={onKey} />

<ul id="cmdk-list" role="listbox">
  {results.map((r, i) =>
    <li id={`cmdk-opt-${i}`} role="option" aria-selected={i === active}>{r.label}</li>)}
</ul>
<div aria-live="polite" className="sr-only">{results.length} commands</div>
Follow-ups they will ask

Why aria-activedescendant instead of moving focus?

Because the user must keep typing while arrowing through results. Moving DOM focus into the list would take focus off the input and stop keystrokes reaching it — activedescendant lets assistive technology announce the highlighted option without relocating focus.

Do you need to debounce the search?

Not for a few hundred local commands — synchronous filtering is sub-millisecond and debouncing would make it feel laggier. Debounce only when matching hits the network or the dataset is large enough to be measurable.

What makes a palette actually faster than the menu?

Recents and frequency weighting. Without them users must type the full command name every time, which is often slower than clicking. The ranking is the product, not the search box.

Concurrency I (Java-specific)
  • Print in OrderEasy
  • Print FooBar AlternatelyMedium
  • Design Bounded Blocking QueueMedium

Expand around every centre — there are 2n-1 of them, counting the gaps between characters for even-length palindromes.

CostO(n²) time, O(1) spaceReach for itLongest palindromic substring, counting palindromic substrings. Short, and fast enough almost always.
def longest_palindrome(s):
    best = ''
    def expand(l, r):
        while l >= 0 and r < len(s) and s[l] == s[r]: l -= 1; r += 1
        return s[l+1:r]
    for i in range(len(s)):
        best = max(best, expand(i, i), expand(i, i+1), key=len)
        #                     ^ odd length   ^ even length
    return best

# Longest palindromic SUBSEQUENCE is different: it is LCS(s, reversed(s)).

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Clarify first: how many floors and cars, is there an express car serving only high floors, are there separate up/down hall buttons, and what should happen at idle — park at the lobby, or stay put. Then state assumptions.

Model. An ElevatorCar has a current floor, a direction (UP, DOWN, IDLE), a door state, and two sets of pending stops — one for each direction. A Request is either a hall call (floor + desired direction) or a car call (a passenger pressing a floor inside). A Dispatcher assigns hall calls to cars; each car independently decides its next stop.

State machine per car is the right structure: IDLE → MOVING_UP / MOVING_DOWN → DOORS_OPENING → DOORS_OPEN → DOORS_CLOSING → …. Modelling it explicitly matters because the illegal states are the bugs — moving with doors open, or accepting a direction change mid-travel. Transitions are guarded, and the door states are not optional detail; door timing is most of the real behaviour.

The scheduling policy must be pluggable — that is the extensibility point the interviewer will probe. Make DispatchStrategy an interface: nearest car is the naive one, but the standard is LOOK/SCAN — a car continues in its current direction serving all stops that way, then reverses. That is why a real elevator passes your floor going up when you pressed down: your call is queued for the downward sweep. Being able to explain that is a strong signal, because it shows you understand the domain rather than just the classes.

Dispatch cost function: prefer a car already moving toward the caller in the same direction, then an idle car, then anything else — weighted by distance and current load. Keep it in the strategy so a building can swap in a different policy.

Concurrency: button presses arrive from many threads. Each car owns its stop sets behind its own lock (or a single-threaded event loop per car, which is cleaner and deterministic), and the dispatcher is the only component that assigns hall calls — so there is exactly one writer per decision.

Testing is the follow-up they usually ask: inject a simulated clock so a full journey runs in microseconds, and assert invariants — never moves with doors open, every accepted request is eventually served, no car reverses with stops remaining ahead.

Java
enum Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE }
enum DoorState { OPEN, OPENING, CLOSED, CLOSING }

interface DispatchStrategy { ElevatorCar select(List<ElevatorCar> cars, HallCall c); }

class ElevatorCar {
    private int floor; private Direction dir = IDLE; private DoorState doors = CLOSED;
    private final NavigableSet<Integer> up   = new TreeSet<>();          // ascending
    private final NavigableSet<Integer> down = new TreeSet<>(reverseOrder());

    // LOOK: keep going in `dir`, serving stops that way; reverse only when empty
    Optional<Integer> nextStop() {
        if (dir == UP)   return Optional.ofNullable(up.ceiling(floor))
                                 .or(() -> Optional.ofNullable(down.first()));
        if (dir == DOWN) return Optional.ofNullable(down.floor(floor))
                                 .or(() -> Optional.ofNullable(up.first()));
        return Optional.ofNullable(up.ceiling(floor));
    }
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is nearest-car dispatch a poor policy?

It ignores direction and load. A car one floor away travelling the opposite way must finish its sweep first, so it arrives later than a car three floors away already heading toward you. Cost must include direction agreement and existing stops, not just distance.

How do you test this without waiting in real time?

Inject a clock abstraction and drive it in a test. A full multi-floor journey then runs in microseconds, and you can assert invariants and exact stop sequences deterministically — which is impossible with wall-clock sleeps.

What are the safety invariants worth asserting?

Never move while the doors are not CLOSED; never reverse direction while stops remain ahead in the current direction; every accepted request is eventually served (no starvation). Those three catch most real bugs.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The requirement that shapes everything: flag evaluation must never be a network call. A flag is checked dozens of times per request, so a remote lookup would add latency and — worse — make your service depend on the flag service's availability. So the design is: evaluate locally, distribute the ruleset.

Architecture: an SDK in each service holds the full ruleset in memory and evaluates flags synchronously. The ruleset is pushed via a streaming connection (SSE or WebSocket) with polling as a fallback, so changes propagate in seconds. On startup the SDK fetches a snapshot; if the control plane is unreachable it uses a bundled default file, so a flag service outage degrades to "last known good" rather than an outage.

Deterministic bucketing is the subtle correctness requirement. A user must get the same variant on every evaluation, in every service, without any shared state — so bucket by hash(flagKey + userId) % 10000 compared against the rollout percentage. Including the flag key in the hash matters: without it, the same users land in the first bucket for every flag, so the same unlucky cohort receives every experiment. And because it is deterministic, the frontend and backend independently compute the same answer, which is what stops a user seeing a UI for a feature the API refuses to serve.

Targeting rules are an ordered list evaluated top-down: explicit user or account overrides first, then attribute rules (plan, region, beta opt-in), then the percentage rollout, then the default. First match wins, which makes behaviour predictable and debuggable.

Kill switches must propagate faster than normal changes and be dead simple — a boolean with no targeting, evaluated first. In an incident nobody wants to reason about rule precedence.

The operational discipline to volunteer: flags are tech debt with a half-life. Every flag needs an owner and an expiry date, and stale flags should be reported automatically — because N flags means 2^N code paths, and past a few dozen nobody can reason about the combinations. Also emit evaluation telemetry so you know which flags are actually being read and can safely delete the ones that are not.

Evaluation
// local, in-process, no network call per check
bucket = hash(flagKey + ":" + userId) % 10000     // flagKey in the hash is essential

rules (ordered, first match wins):
  1. explicit overrides   userId in [...]            -> variant
  2. attribute rules      plan == "enterprise"       -> variant
  3. percentage rollout   bucket < rollout * 100     -> variant
  4. default

distribution: snapshot on boot -> streaming updates (SSE) -> polling fallback
              control plane down -> last known good / bundled defaults

kill switch: plain boolean, evaluated first, propagates in seconds
hygiene:     every flag has an owner + expiry; report stale flags automatically
Follow-ups they will ask

Why include the flag key in the bucketing hash?

Otherwise every flag buckets users identically, so the same 5% of users are in the first bucket for every rollout. They receive every experiment simultaneously, which corrupts your results and gives one cohort a permanently unrepresentative experience.

What happens when the flag service is unreachable?

The SDK serves its last known ruleset, or bundled defaults on a cold start. A flag system must never be able to take down the services that depend on it — that is the difference between a control plane and a dependency.

How do you keep flags from accumulating?

Owner and expiry on every flag, automated reporting of flags past expiry or with no recent evaluations, and treating removal as part of the feature's definition of done. Otherwise you accumulate hundreds and the combinatorial state space becomes untestable.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The core is a registry plus a resolver. A schema describes fields; a widget registry maps each field type to a component; a renderer walks the schema and renders the matching widget. That indirection is what makes the builder extensible — a new field type is a registry entry, not a change to the renderer.

Derive validation from the same schema the backend uses (JSON Schema or Zod), so client and server rules cannot drift. That is the main argument for schema-driven forms in the first place: one definition, two enforcers.

Conditional fields are the hard part, and the interesting question is what happens to hidden values. When a field is hidden by a condition, do you clear it or preserve it? Both are defensible and the answer must be deliberate: clear if the value would be meaningless or misleading when submitted (a spouse's name after changing marital status), preserve if the user may toggle back and would be annoyed to retype. Whichever you pick, hidden fields must be excluded from validation, or the form blocks submission on an error the user cannot see or fix — which is the classic bug.

Nested sections and arrays need path-based field names (addresses.1.postcode) so state, validation errors and registration all address the same node. Array items need stable ids for React keys — never the index, or removing an item strands the wrong row's state.

Performance: as the schema grows, a single form-level state object re-renders every field on every keystroke. Use a subscription-based form library (react-hook-form) so each field subscribes only to its own value and error, and only components watching a condition's source field re-render when it changes. Memoize the compiled schema and the resolved widget map so they are not rebuilt per render.

Accessibility must come from the renderer, not from each widget author: every field gets a label associated by id, errors are linked with aria-describedby and aria-invalid, and on submit focus moves to the first invalid field with a summary in a live region. Building it centrally is the main reason to have a form builder at all.

JSX
const widgets = { text: TextField, select: SelectField, date: DateField };

function Field({ node, path }) {
  const Widget = widgets[node.type] ?? Unsupported;
  const visible = useWatchCondition(node.visibleWhen);   // re-renders only on its source
  if (!visible) return null;
  return <Widget name={path} label={node.label} {...node.props} />;
}

// hidden fields must not block submission
const schema = z.object({...}).superRefine((v, ctx) => {
  for (const f of hiddenFields(v)) ctx.path !== f;      // skip validation for hidden
});

// arrays: stable ids, never the index
{fields.map((field, i) =>
  <Section key={field.id} path={`addresses.${i}`} node={node.items} />)}
Follow-ups they will ask

Clear or preserve a hidden field's value?

Deliberate either way. Clear when the value becomes semantically wrong for the new branch and would be submitted incorrectly; preserve when the user may toggle back. The non-negotiable part is excluding hidden fields from validation.

How do you keep client and server validation in sync?

Define the schema once and share it — a Zod schema imported by both, or JSON Schema compiled on each side. Duplicated rules always drift, and the drift shows up as a form that submits successfully and then fails server-side.

What limits a schema-driven form?

Anything genuinely bespoke — a complex custom interaction, an unusual layout, cross-field UI that is not a simple show/hide. Provide an escape hatch that renders a custom component for a named field rather than contorting the schema to express it.

Concurrency II (Java-specific)
  • Fizz Buzz MultithreadedMedium
  • Building H2OMedium
  • The Dining PhilosophersMedium

To fit the most non-overlapping intervals, always take the one that finishes earliest. Sorting by end time is the algorithm.

CostO(n log n) time, dominated by the sortReach for itMaximum meetings in one room, minimum arrows to burst balloons, non-overlapping intervals to remove.
def max_meetings(iv):
    iv.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])          # by END time - this is the insight
    count, last_end = 0, float('-inf')
    for s, e in iv:
        if s >= last_end:
            count += 1; last_end = e
    return count

# Sorting by START or by DURATION both give wrong answers. The exchange
# argument: finishing earliest leaves the most room for everything after.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Say the headline immediately: this whole interview is the double-booking race. The modelling is straightforward; the scoring is whether you put the concurrency control in the right place.

Model: Movie, Screen, Show (movie + screen + start time), Seat (screen + row/number + type), ShowSeat (show + seat + status), Hold, Booking, Payment. The key modelling decision is ShowSeat as its own entity — seat availability is per show, not per seat, and conflating them is a common mistake.

Seat lifecycle: AVAILABLE → HELD (with expiry) → BOOKED, with HELD reverting to AVAILABLE on expiry or cancellation. Selecting seats creates a hold with a short TTL (5–10 minutes) so the user has time to pay without seats being locked indefinitely.

The concurrency control must be explicit and it must be in the database. Two acceptable answers: a conditional update that claims the seats atomically (UPDATE … SET status='HELD' WHERE show_seat_id IN (…) AND status='AVAILABLE', then check the affected-row count equals the number requested and roll back if not); or SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the seat rows inside the transaction, in a deterministic order (by seat id) to avoid deadlock between two users selecting overlapping seats in different orders. That ordering detail is worth stating.

What is not acceptable: reading availability into the application, checking, and then writing. And an application-level or Redis lock is not sufficient on its own for correctness — a GC pause past the lock TTL means two holders. The database constraint is the invariant.

Confirmation: a unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) for active bookings makes overselling structurally impossible, independent of any application logic.

Payment timeout is the case to raise unprompted: the hold can expire while payment is in flight. Either extend the hold for the payment window, or accept it and refund automatically — but never charge for a seat you cannot deliver. Reconcile payment state against booking state rather than assuming. And expire holds both with a sweeper and lazily on read, so a dead sweeper cannot lock inventory permanently.

Java / SQL
-- atomic claim: affects N rows or none. No read-then-write anywhere.
UPDATE show_seats
   SET status='HELD', held_by=:user, held_until=now() + interval '8 minutes'
 WHERE show_id=:show AND seat_id IN (:seats)
   AND (status='AVAILABLE' OR (status='HELD' AND held_until < now()));
-- rowsAffected != seats.size()  ->  ROLLBACK, tell the user which seats went

-- the invariant lives in the DB, not in application logic
ALTER TABLE bookings ADD CONSTRAINT one_active_booking_per_seat
  UNIQUE (show_id, seat_id) WHERE status = 'CONFIRMED';

-- if using SELECT FOR UPDATE instead: lock rows in seat_id ORDER to avoid deadlock
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is a Redis lock not enough here?

Because a process pause longer than the lock TTL means another client legitimately acquires it while the first still believes it holds it. For money and inventory the invariant must be enforced by the database constraint, with the lock as an optimisation at most.

What happens if the hold expires during payment?

Decide in advance: extend the hold for the payment window (preferred), or refund automatically with a clear message. The unacceptable outcome is charging a customer for a seat someone else now holds, so the payment must be reconciled against booking state.

How do you handle group bookings of adjacent seats?

Allocate the whole group in one atomic update — all seats or none — and expose an allocator that finds contiguous runs. Partial success is worse than failure here, because a group split across the cinema is not what was asked for.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Separate the three concerns, because they have different accuracy requirements — that separation is the answer. Enforcement (is this request allowed) must be fast and can be approximate. Metering (how much was used) must be complete. Billing (what do we charge) must be exact and reconcilable.

Enforcement lives at the gateway: a counter in Redis checked per request, updated atomically with a Lua script, with a local in-process cache to avoid a network hop on every call. Being slightly permissive at the boundary is acceptable — over-counting a few requests during a race matters far less than adding latency to every request.

Metering must be at-least-once and deduplicated. Emit a usage event per billable operation to Kafka with a unique request id. Because delivery is at-least-once and money depends on the count, dedupe by request id before aggregating — otherwise a redelivery inflates a customer's bill, which is the failure that generates support tickets and refunds.

Aggregation is two-tier, mirroring the click-aggregation pattern: a streaming job maintains near-real-time counters for dashboards and quota display, while a batch job over the retained raw events produces the authoritative figure for invoicing. Billing cannot use the streaming number because windows close on watermarks and late events may be excluded. Reconcile the two daily and alert on divergence.

Quotas versus overage is a product decision the design must support: hard cap (reject at the limit), soft cap (allow and charge overage), or throttle (degrade rather than reject). Expose remaining quota in response headers so customers can self-manage, and notify at 80% rather than only at 100%.

Invoices must reconcile exactly, which means retaining the raw events, not just the aggregates. When a customer disputes a bill you must be able to show them the underlying requests. Store raw usage for at least the dispute window, make the aggregation deterministic and re-runnable, and version the pricing rules so an invoice can be recomputed exactly as it was originally calculated — a price change must never retroactively alter last month's bill.

Three tiers
ENFORCE (fast, approximate)
  gateway -> Redis counter (Lua, atomic) + local cache; 429 + X-RateLimit-Remaining

METER (complete, deduplicated)
  per billable op -> Kafka event { request_id, tenant, op, ts }
  dedupe on request_id  <- at-least-once delivery would otherwise inflate bills

BILL (exact, reconcilable)
  streaming aggregate -> dashboards / quota display   (approximate)
  batch over RAW retained events -> invoice           (source of truth)
  reconcile daily; retain raw events for the dispute window
  version pricing rules -> re-running an old invoice reproduces it exactly
Follow-ups they will ask

Why can the enforcement counter not be the billing number?

Because it is optimised for speed: approximate under races, held in a volatile store, and reset on window boundaries. Billing needs completeness and an audit trail, which means durable raw events and a deterministic aggregation.

What happens if a usage event is lost?

You under-bill, which is commercially bad but not a customer-facing failure. That asymmetry is why the pipeline is tuned for at-least-once with dedupe rather than at-most-once — duplicates are correctable, losses are not detectable.

Why version the pricing rules?

So an invoice can be recomputed exactly as issued. If a price change silently applies to historical aggregation, re-running last month's invoice produces a different number than the one the customer paid — which is an audit failure.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The critical point first: an SVG of paths is invisible to assistive technology. A screen reader encounters a decorative graphic and announces nothing useful, so a chart with no alternative is simply unavailable to those users. Solving that is the requirement, not an enhancement.

What a screen reader gets: the chart container is role="img" with an aria-label summarising what it shows and the headline finding — "Revenue by month, 2026. Rising from 1.2M in January to 3.4M in August." A summary sentence is worth more than any amount of markup, because it delivers the insight rather than the data. Then provide the underlying data as a real table, either visually toggleable or visually hidden — that is the most reliable alternative, since tables are a well-supported navigation structure. Mark decorative parts (gridlines, axes) aria-hidden.

Keyboard navigation: make the chart a single tab stop, then arrow keys move between data points within a series and up/down switch series. Each move updates a aria-live="polite" region announcing the value — "March, 1.9 million, up 12% on February". Announcing the delta as well as the value is what makes it genuinely usable rather than technically compliant. Home and End jump to first and last; Escape exits the chart.

Do not rely on colour alone to distinguish series: add shape markers, direct labels, or pattern fills, and check contrast for both themes. Roughly 8% of men have some colour vision deficiency, so a red/green comparison chart fails for a meaningful share of users.

50,000 points is a rendering problem with two answers. First, downsample for display — a 800-pixel-wide chart cannot show 50,000 points, so use LTTB (largest-triangle-three-buckets), which preserves visual peaks and troughs far better than naive sampling and typically reduces to a few thousand points with no perceptible difference. Second, render to canvas rather than DOM: 50,000 SVG elements is tens of megabytes of DOM and will freeze the browser, whereas canvas draws in one pass. Keep interaction working by hit-testing against the underlying data with a spatial index rather than relying on DOM events.

With canvas you lose the DOM-based accessibility entirely — which is precisely why the table alternative and the live region are mandatory rather than optional.

JSX
<figure role="img"
        aria-label="Revenue by month 2026. Rises from 1.2M in January to 3.4M in August.">
  <canvas ref={ref} aria-hidden="true" />        {/* 50k points: canvas, not SVG */}
</figure>

{/* the reliable alternative: real data, real table semantics */}
<table className="sr-only">
  <caption>Revenue by month, 2026</caption>
  <tbody>{data.map(d => <tr key={d.month}><th scope="row">{d.month}</th>
                            <td>{format(d.value)}</td></tr>)}</tbody>
</table>

{/* keyboard: one tab stop, arrows move, live region announces value AND delta */}
<div tabIndex={0} onKeyDown={onKey} aria-describedby="chart-live" />
<div id="chart-live" aria-live="polite" className="sr-only">{announcement}</div>

// downsample for display: LTTB preserves peaks; naive sampling loses them
Follow-ups they will ask

Why LTTB rather than taking every Nth point?

Naive sampling can miss a spike entirely, which changes what the chart says. LTTB selects the point in each bucket that maximises the triangle area with its neighbours, so visual extremes survive — the shape stays honest at a fraction of the points.

Canvas or SVG?

SVG below a few thousand points, because you get DOM accessibility and easy hit-testing for free. Canvas above that, because SVG element count becomes the bottleneck — and then you must supply the accessibility layer explicitly.

What should the live region announce?

The value and its context — the label, the number, and the change from the previous point. Announcing only the raw value forces the user to hold the whole series in memory to interpret it.

The proof technique that makes a greedy trustworthy: show that swapping any pair towards your chosen order never makes the result worse.

CostUsually O(n log n) — the sort is the algorithmReach for itAny greedy you are about to submit. Two minutes trying to break it saves a wrong answer.
# Task scheduling to minimise total waiting time: shortest job first.
# Exchange argument: if a longer job runs before a shorter one, swapping
# them reduces total waiting. So no optimal order has that inversion.

tasks.sort(key=lambda t: t.duration)

# Fractional knapsack: sort by value/weight ratio.
items.sort(key=lambda i: i.value / i.weight, reverse=True)

# GREEDY FAILS on 0/1 knapsack - you cannot take a fraction, so the
# exchange argument breaks. That is exactly why 0/1 needs DP.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Two problems, and they test different things — say that and split your time.

Chess: the point is avoiding a giant switch on piece type. Model Piece as an abstract type with List<Move> candidateMoves(Board, Position) implemented per piece, so adding a variant piece means adding a class. Board is an 8×8 array of optional pieces plus game state that is easy to forget: castling rights, en passant target, halfmove clock, side to move. Move is a value object (from, to, promotion, flags).

Validation layers cleanly: a piece generates pseudo-legal moves from its movement rules; the board filters those that leave your own king in check. That separation is the key insight — piece classes stay simple because they do not know about check. isInCheck(colour) asks whether any enemy pseudo-legal move attacks the king's square; checkmate is "in check and no legal move exists", stalemate is "not in check and no legal move exists". Generate-and-filter is the clean implementation and is fast enough for an interview.

The in-memory database is a different exercise: data structure choice per query type. A HashMap primary index by id for equality lookups; a TreeMap-based secondary index per indexed column for range queries; and — the detail that matters — because a secondary key is not unique, each index entry maps to a set of row ids, and every write must update every index atomically with the row.

Transactions: the same stack-of-overlays approach as a transactional key-value store — begin pushes an overlay, get walks the stack top-down, rollback pops, commit merges down one level. Deletions need a tombstone or a delete inside a transaction silently falls through to the committed value. Say explicitly what isolation you have implemented: read-your-own-writes within a transaction, and nothing between concurrent transactions unless you add locking or MVCC.

The connecting theme to state: both are about choosing the structure that makes the required operation cheap, and keeping the varying part (piece rules, index type) behind an interface so the core does not grow a conditional per case.

Java
// chess: rules per piece, check handled once on the board
abstract class Piece {
    abstract List<Move> pseudoLegal(Board b, Position from);   // no check awareness
}
List<Move> legalMoves(Colour side) {
    return pseudoLegalFor(side).stream()
            .filter(m -> !leavesKingInCheck(m, side))          // filtered centrally
            .toList();
}
boolean isCheckmate(Colour s) { return isInCheck(s) && legalMoves(s).isEmpty(); }
boolean isStalemate(Colour s) { return !isInCheck(s) && legalMoves(s).isEmpty(); }

// in-memory DB: index per access pattern, non-unique -> set of ids
Map<Long, Row> primary = new HashMap<>();                       // equality
NavigableMap<Comparable<?>, Set<Long>> byAge = new TreeMap<>();  // range queries
// every write updates row + ALL indexes in one unit
Follow-ups they will ask

What game state do people forget in chess?

Castling rights, the en passant target square, the halfmove clock for the fifty-move rule, and position repetition for threefold draw. Modelling only the piece placement means several legal moves and draw conditions are unrepresentable.

Why a set of ids in the secondary index?

Because secondary keys are not unique — many rows share an age. Mapping to a single id silently loses rows, and it is the first bug an interviewer will probe with a duplicate value.

What isolation does your transaction implementation actually provide?

Read-your-own-writes within a transaction, and no isolation between concurrent transactions. Real isolation needs locking or MVCC with per-transaction snapshots — being precise about that is better than implying you built a database.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design it as a tiered funnel, because the cost per item varies by three orders of magnitude and you cannot run the expensive check on everything.

Tier 1 — cheap deterministic filters on ingestion: hash matching against known-bad content (PhotoDNA-style perceptual hashes for images), URL and domain blocklists, and simple pattern rules. Milliseconds, near-zero cost, catches known material outright. Tier 2 — classifiers: ML models scoring for each policy category, producing a confidence. Tier 3 — human review for the uncertain band, which is expensive and slow and therefore the resource the whole design exists to conserve.

Latency requirements differ per content type, and that is the key design decision. High-risk categories — child safety, terrorism — are pre-publish blocking: the content does not go live until it clears, and a few seconds of delay is an acceptable cost. Everything else is post-publish asynchronous: publish immediately for a good user experience, scan within seconds, and take down if it fails. Live video is a third case, sampled frame-wise in near-real time. Blocking everything would make the product unusable; blocking nothing is negligent — so the policy tier drives the path.

Reviewer queues need prioritisation by predicted severity and reach (something already going viral outranks an unseen post), assignment with a lease so two reviewers do not duplicate work, and sampling for quality control — a percentage of decisions re-reviewed blind to measure reviewer accuracy and calibrate the model's thresholds. Reviewer throughput is the binding constraint, so the tiers above exist to keep this queue small.

Appeals are a first-class flow, not an afterthought: every enforcement action records the policy, the evidence and the decision path, so an appeal can be reviewed by a different reviewer with full context. Regulatory regimes increasingly require this, and it is also your feedback signal for model error.

The measurement framing to close on: false positives and false negatives have asymmetric costs that differ per category, so you tune thresholds per policy rather than globally — and you must track both, because a system optimised only against false negatives quietly removes large amounts of legitimate content.

Tiers
ingest
  T1 hash match / blocklist        ~1ms, ~free   -> known-bad: block outright
  T2 classifiers (per policy)      ~50ms         -> score + confidence
       high confidence bad  -> auto-action
       high confidence ok   -> publish
       uncertain band       -> T3
  T3 human review queue             minutes-hours -> the scarce resource

path by policy tier:
  child safety / terrorism -> PRE-publish blocking (delay is acceptable)
  everything else          -> POST-publish async (publish now, scan, take down)
  live video               -> sampled frames, near real time

queue: prioritise by severity x reach; lease per reviewer; sample for QC
appeals: full decision record -> different reviewer -> feeds model error analysis
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not review everything pre-publish?

Latency and cost. Blocking every post behind a classifier plus a possible human review makes the product feel broken, and the reviewer capacity does not exist. The tiering exists so that only genuinely high-risk categories pay the blocking cost.

How do you set the uncertainty band?

From the cost asymmetry per policy. Where a false negative is catastrophic, widen the band so more goes to humans; where false positives are the bigger harm, narrow it. Measure both rates continuously — a threshold set once will drift as content changes.

What is the feedback loop?

Reviewer decisions become labels, appeals surface false positives, and QC sampling measures reviewer accuracy. All three feed retraining — and appeals are the most valuable because they identify errors the system was confident about.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The design principle is local-first: the client writes to local storage and treats the server as a replica, not the other way round. That inverts the usual model and is what makes the app fully usable offline rather than degraded.

Storage: notes in IndexedDB (asynchronous, structured, gigabytes — never localStorage, which is synchronous and blocks the main thread), plus a service worker caching the app shell so it loads with no network at all. Reads render from IndexedDB immediately; a background fetch refreshes and the UI updates when it lands.

Writes go to an outbox. Every mutation is applied locally and appended to a queue in IndexedDB with a client-generated id, a base version, and an idempotency key. On reconnect (or via Background Sync) the outbox replays in order. Because every operation carries an idempotency key, replaying something the server already applied is harmless — which is what makes an interrupted sync safe to retry.

Conflict resolution is the hard part and needs an explicit decision. Each note carries a version; a push including the base version gets a 409 if the server has moved on. Then: last-writer-wins silently destroys someone's work and should be rejected for a notes app; automatic merge is only sound for structured operations; so the honest answer for text is keep both versions — save the remote as the note and the local as "Conflicted copy (this device)", exactly as Dropbox does. Users forgive an extra file; they do not forgive lost writing.

Be honest in the UI about sync state. Show per-note status — saved locally, syncing, synced, conflict — because a user who believes their work is safe when it is not is the worst failure this app can have. Never present stale data as authoritative without indicating when it last synced.

The constraint to acknowledge: browser storage is evictable. Safari expires it aggressively and any browser may clear it under pressure. Request persistent storage where available, but design for the cache being empty on any load — so unsynced work should be surfaced and pushed as soon as possible rather than accumulating for days.

JSX
// write: local first, then queue for sync
async function saveNote(note) {
  await db.put('notes', { ...note, dirty: true, updatedAt: Date.now() });
  await db.add('outbox', {
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),            // idempotency key - replay is safe
    op: 'upsert', noteId: note.id, baseVersion: note.version, body: note.body,
  });
  scheduleSync();
}

// sync: replay in order, stop on conflict rather than plowing through
for (const op of await db.getAll('outbox')) {
  const res = await api.push(op);
  if (res.status === 409) {
    await db.put('notes', res.serverNote);                 // remote wins the id
    await db.add('notes', { ...local, id: newId(),
                            title: local.title + ' (conflicted copy)' });  // keep BOTH
  }
  await db.delete('outbox', op.id);
}
Follow-ups they will ask

Why keep both versions rather than merging?

Because merging free-form text without user intent produces a document neither person wrote. A conflicted copy is visibly imperfect but loses nothing — and the user can reconcile it with full context, which no algorithm has.

When would a CRDT be the right answer here?

If the product required simultaneous editing of the same note by multiple people with live cursors. For single-user multi-device with occasional conflicts, version checks plus conflicted copies are simpler, correct, and easier to reason about.

Can you rely on IndexedDB persisting?

No — it is evictable under storage pressure and Safari expires it after a period of inactivity. Request persistent storage, but treat local data as a cache that may be empty on any load, and push unsynced work promptly rather than letting it accumulate.

Keep a max-heap of the smaller half and a min-heap of the larger half, balanced in size. The median sits at one or both tops.

CostO(log n) insert, O(1) medianReach for itMedian from a data stream, sliding window median, and 'balance two sides' problems.
import heapq
class MedianFinder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lo = []    # max-heap (negated) - smaller half
        self.hi = []    # min-heap            - larger half
    def add(self, v):
        heapq.heappush(self.lo, -v)
        heapq.heappush(self.hi, -heapq.heappop(self.lo))   # pass the largest up
        if len(self.hi) > len(self.lo):                    # rebalance
            heapq.heappush(self.lo, -heapq.heappop(self.hi))
    def median(self):
        if len(self.lo) > len(self.hi): return -self.lo[0]
        return (-self.lo[0] + self.hi[0]) / 2
730/4
