Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The purpose of a rapid-fire round is calibration, not learning. Sixty seconds each, out loud, no notes. Anything you hesitate on goes on tomorrow's list — that is the entire mechanism.

Language and object model: the string pool and why == deceives on literals; the Integer cache range (−128..127) and why equals is the only safe comparison; pass-by-value and why swap is impossible; final versus effectively final and why lambdas require it; static versus instance initialization order and why calling an overridable method from a constructor sees nulls; finally versus finalize; interface private and static methods; var's limitations; why array covariance throws at runtime while generics do not compile.

Collections: the hashCode contract and the exact HashMap failure when you break it; treeify at 8, untreeify at 6, capacity ≥ 64, and why the hysteresis; load factor 0.75; why capacity is a power of two; fail-fast modCount and why it is best-effort only; Arrays.asList fixed-size versus List.of null-rejecting; why LinkedList loses to ArrayList despite the Big-O; when CopyOnWriteArrayList is right.

Concurrency: what volatile guarantees and what it does not; why i++ is still a race; happens-before edges you can name; the ThreadPoolExecutor submission order and the unbounded-queue trap; CPU-bound versus IO-bound sizing; ConcurrentHashMap's Java 8 mechanism and why size() is an estimate; the four deadlock conditions and how to break each; why ThreadLocal leaks in a pool; what unmounts a virtual thread and what pins it.

JVM: heap versus Metaspace versus native and why -Xmx = container limit gets you OOMKilled; the OOM message variants and what each means; retained size versus shallow size; what escape analysis enables; why a cold JVM is slower.

Scoring: a confident, correct answer in under sixty seconds is a pass. A correct answer that took ninety is a partial. Anything you had to reason your way to from first principles is a fail for this exercise — under interview pressure that hesitation reads as uncertainty even when the answer is right.

Drill
25 questions, 60s each, OUT LOUD, no notes, recorded.

score each:  PASS (confident, <60s) | PARTIAL (correct, slow) | FAIL (had to derive)

any PARTIAL or FAIL -> tomorrow's list -> re-drill until PASS

the four that appear in nearly every Java Software Engineer loop - be perfect on these:
  1. hashCode contract + the exact HashMap failure
  2. volatile vs atomic, and happens-before
  3. thread pool sizing + the unbounded queue trap
  4. @Transactional proxying + self-invocation
Follow-ups they will ask

What if you go blank on one?

Say the shape of the answer rather than freezing — "it relates to visibility rather than atomicity, let me be precise". A structured partial answer scores; silence does not. Then log it and drill it.

How many passes does this take?

Three, spaced a few days apart. The list shrinks each time, and by the third pass what remains should fit on a physical card you can review before the interview.

Should you memorise numbers like 0.75 and 8?

Yes for these specific ones, because they come up and knowing them signals you have read the source rather than a summary. But always pair the number with the reason — 0.75 balances space against collision probability.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Prepare this as a story with numbers, because the interviewer will drill until they find the edge of your involvement. The claim invites five specific questions, and vagueness on any of them is worse than a smaller claim.

How many partitions, and why that number? Partitions cap your consumer parallelism and cannot be reduced. Know the count, and know that you chose it with headroom — a few times current need — because increasing it later changes key-to-partition mapping and breaks ordering for in-flight keys.

What was the partition key? This is the most revealing question, because it shows whether you understood that ordering is per-partition only. If you keyed by account or entity id, say so and say what that bought: a single entity's events processed in order, different entities in parallel. If the key was null, say that and say you accepted no ordering guarantee.

What was consumer lag, and what was the alert threshold? Lag is the key SLI. Have the normal value, the alert threshold, and — importantly — what you did when it grew: scaled consumers up to the partition count, and what you would have done next once at that ceiling.

What happened on a poison message? The expected answer is bounded retries with backoff, then a DLQ, committing the offset so the partition advances. If you did not have a DLQ, say so and say what happened instead — a blocked partition is a real and common answer.

What was the throughput ceiling? Thousands per minute is roughly tens per second, which is modest — so be honest about that rather than implying you operated at scale you did not. The stronger answer is: "the volume was moderate; what was interesting was the ordering and idempotency requirements" — then talk about the part that was genuinely hard.

If you do not know a number, say what you would measure and why. That is an acceptable answer. Inventing one is not, because the follow-up will expose it. And spend an hour before week 11 pulling the real figures from dashboards, runbooks and old tickets — this is the single highest-return preparation available to you.

Numbers to recover
[ ] topics, and partitions per topic          (+ why that count)
[ ] partition KEY and what ordering it bought
[ ] consumer instances; concurrency per instance
[ ] avg and p99 processing time per message
[ ] normal lag; alert threshold; what you did when it grew
[ ] DLQ volume; what a poison message did
[ ] acks / min.insync.replicas / auto-commit setting
[ ] what broke first at peak, and what you would do at 100x

"thousands per minute" ~ tens per second. Be honest about the scale, and
pivot to what was genuinely hard: ordering, idempotency, failure handling.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if the real numbers are unimpressive?

Say them plainly and move to the interesting part. An honest modest number with a sophisticated discussion of ordering and idempotency beats an inflated number that collapses under one follow-up — and interviewers are specifically listening for inflation.

What if you inherited the system and did not choose the partition key?

Say that, then say what you would have chosen and why. Explaining a design decision you did not make, correctly, still demonstrates the understanding being tested — pretending you made it does not survive the next question.

How deep will they actually go?

Typically three levels: what did you build, how did it work, what happened when it failed. The third is where prepared candidates separate — most can answer the first two.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Prepare the self-critique, because that is the actual test. An interviewer asking about a personal project is assessing whether you can evaluate your own work critically — a candidate who says "it works well" learns nothing new; a candidate who names their design's weaknesses sounds like a Senior Engineer.

OAuth2 flow. Be precise: authorization code with PKCE, where the code exchange happens (server-side, so the client secret never reaches the browser), where the tokens live, and how you handle refresh. Then the critique: if you stored the token in localStorage, say so and say the tradeoff — XSS-readable, and the alternative is an httpOnly cookie which reintroduces CSRF. Owning that tradeoff explicitly is stronger than claiming you got it perfect.

The edit-approval workflow's concurrency is where they will push. The question to have an answer for: what happens if two people request edits to the same page simultaneously? If the second proposal was written against a version the first has since changed, applying it silently produces a page nobody wrote. The correct design is optimistic concurrency — each proposal carries a base version and the server returns a conflict if the page has moved, requiring a rebase or rejection. If you did not implement that, say so and describe it as the fix, which is a better answer than pretending it was handled.

AI generation: what is your timeout, what happens when the provider is slow or down, is the call on the request path or queued, do you cap cost per user, and do you handle the case where generation returns something inappropriate. Unbounded latency on a third-party call inside a request handler is the most common weakness in AI-integrated side projects.

What you would redesign — have two or three ready and be specific: the concurrency control on approvals, moving AI generation off the request path to a queue with a status poll, and adding an idempotency key to the proposal endpoint so a double-submitted approval cannot apply twice.

The framing that lands: "here is what I built, here is the constraint I was designing under, here are the two things I would change and why". Confidence plus specific self-criticism reads as judgement; either alone does not.

Prepared critique
be ready to say, unprompted:

1. concurrency on approvals
   two proposals against the same base version -> silent overwrite
   fix: base_version on the proposal, 409 on conflict, rebase or reject

2. AI generation on the request path
   third-party latency is unbounded -> your endpoint inherits it
   fix: queue + status poll, hard timeout, per-user cost cap, fallback copy

3. token storage
   localStorage: XSS-readable | httpOnly cookie: needs CSRF protection
   say which you chose and WHY - there is no free option

4. idempotency on approve/reject - a double submit must not apply twice
Follow-ups they will ask

How much detail should the walkthrough have?

Four minutes: the problem, the constraint you designed under, one hard tradeoff, and the outcome. Then stop and let them choose where to go deep — a ten-minute monologue loses the room and wastes the questions you wanted.

Is it bad that it is a side project rather than production?

No, provided you are clear about the scale and constraints. Side projects are excellent interview material precisely because you made every decision — so you can answer any "why" question, which is often not true of work systems.

What if they find a flaw you had not considered?

Say so, think about it out loud, and propose a fix. That is a good outcome — the round is testing how you reason about a problem you have not pre-rehearsed, and a genuine real-time answer scores better than a polished one.

A hash map for O(1) lookup plus a doubly linked list for O(1) reordering. Every access moves the node to the front; eviction takes the tail.

CostO(1) get and putReach for itCache design questions, and the classic 'combine two data structures' interview problem.
from collections import OrderedDict
class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        self.cap = cap; self.d = OrderedDict()
    def get(self, k):
        if k not in self.d: return -1
        self.d.move_to_end(k)                   # mark as recently used
        return self.d[k]
    def put(self, k, v):
        if k in self.d: self.d.move_to_end(k)
        self.d[k] = v
        if len(self.d) > self.cap:
            self.d.popitem(last=False)          # evict least recent

# In an interview, implement the doubly linked list by hand - that is
# what is actually being tested.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Second rapid-fire pass, framework-focused. Same rules: sixty seconds, out loud, no notes, score each as pass, partial or fail.

Spring core: bean scopes and what breaks when a prototype is injected into a singleton; the bean lifecycle and where proxies are created; @Configuration CGLIB proxying and what proxyBeanMethods=false changes; why constructor injection is the default and why field injection hurts testability; how a circular dependency is resolved for setter injection and why constructor injection cannot be; how auto-configuration decides (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean) and how to see the report.

@Transactional — expect at least two of these: proxy mechanics and self-invocation; that checked exceptions commit by default; REQUIRED versus REQUIRES_NEW and the second-connection deadlock risk; what readOnly actually does; why you must never make a remote call inside a transaction; how to write something that survives a rollback.

JPA: the persistence context as first-level cache; dirty checking and why you do not call save(); flush versus commit; N+1 and the three correct fixes (and why EAGER is not one); LazyInitializationException and why OSIV is a bad fix; optimistic versus pessimistic locking and when each; cascade types and orphanRemoval; why Page costs an extra COUNT query and when to use Slice.

Testing: @Mock versus @MockBean and why the latter slows the suite (context cache misses); test slices versus full @SpringBootTest; why you should not mock what you do not own; why Awaitility rather than Thread.sleep; what Testcontainers buys over H2.

Build: Maven nearest-wins versus Gradle highest-wins; what NoSuchMethodError tells you; what a BOM is for.

The four to be perfect on, because they appear in nearly every Spring interview: @Transactional self-invocation, N+1 diagnosis and fix, bean scopes and the singleton trap, and constructor injection's advantages.

Drill
25 questions, 60s each, out loud, scored.

perfect on these four - they appear in nearly every Spring loop:
  1. @Transactional: proxy, self-invocation, checked exceptions commit
  2. N+1: how you DIAGNOSE it (count queries) and the 3 correct fixes
  3. bean scopes: prototype injected into singleton -> one instance forever
  4. constructor injection: final fields, fail-fast, testable without Spring

trap answers to avoid:
  "EAGER fixes N+1"          -> no, it makes it global
  "OSIV fixes lazy loading"  -> no, it holds a connection for the whole request
  "@Transactional rolls back on any exception" -> only unchecked, by default
Follow-ups they will ask

Which single Spring question is asked most often?

@Transactional self-invocation. It is the perfect interview question because it has one root cause — the proxy — that explains several unrelated-looking symptoms, so it separates people who understand the mechanism from people who have memorised the annotation.

How do you answer a question about a Spring feature you have not used?

Reason from the mechanism you do know. Most Spring behaviour follows from proxies, the bean lifecycle, and conditional configuration — deriving the answer out loud from those is a better signal than a memorised fact.

What should be on the physical card you carry?

Whatever is still a partial after three passes. For most people that is the propagation table, the exact N+1 fixes, and the OOM message variants — things that are pure recall rather than reasoning.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Structure the answer as an incident narrative, not a result: symptom → measurement → hypothesis → change → verification → guardrail. That shape is what an interviewer is listening for, because it demonstrates method rather than luck.

Symptom. What did someone actually notice — a slow endpoint, a timeout, an alert, a customer complaint? Name the endpoint and the p99 before. "Queries were slow" is not a symptom; "the transaction history endpoint's p99 was 1.4 s against a 300 ms SLO" is.

Measurement. This is the part that separates a real story. Name the tool: pg_stat_statements to find the offending statement by total time (not just mean — a fast query run a million times can dominate), then EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on it. Say what you saw: a sequential scan on a large table, or estimated rows wildly diverging from actual (stale statistics), or a sort spilling to disk, or a nested loop over far more rows than expected.

Hypothesis and change. State what you believed and what you changed — a composite index in the right column order for the predicate and sort, a projection so you stopped selecting columns you never rendered, keyset pagination replacing a deep offset, or an ANALYZE because the planner was working from stale statistics. Crucially, say what you considered and rejected: that shows judgement rather than pattern-matching.

Verification. How did you know it worked in production, not just locally? Re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, compare p99 in the APM over a comparable traffic window, and confirm on the endpoint's dashboard rather than a synthetic test. Also confirm you did not make something else worse — an index costs write throughput.

Guardrail. What stops it regressing? A query-count assertion in tests, a slow-query alert, a dashboard someone actually looks at.

On the percentage itself: 30–40% is a range, so be ready for "which query, and what were the actual numbers?" Have one concrete before-and-after. If you cannot recover the figures, say exactly what you would measure — that is acceptable; a vague gesture at "we optimised the queries" is not.

Narrative
symptom      "/transactions p99 was 1.4s against a 300ms SLO"
measurement  pg_stat_statements (by TOTAL time) -> EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
             saw: seq scan on 12M rows | est 40 rows vs actual 48,000 (stale stats)
hypothesis   missing composite index matching the predicate + sort order
change       CREATE INDEX (account_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (amount)
             rejected: caching (data changes per request), denormalising (premature)
verification EXPLAIN after -> index scan; APM p99 1.4s -> 0.9s over a comparable window
             checked write throughput did not regress
guardrail    slow-query alert + a query-count assertion in the integration test
Follow-ups they will ask

What if you cannot find the original numbers?

Say what you would measure and how you would verify — that is an acceptable answer. What fails is a percentage with no method behind it, because the follow-up question exposes it immediately.

Why sort pg_stat_statements by total time rather than mean?

Because a 5 ms query executed a million times consumes more database capacity than a 2 s query run twice. Optimising by mean sends you to the dramatic outlier while the actual load stays untouched.

What would you say if the fix was simply adding an index?

Say it plainly — most query optimisation is. The interesting part is how you found which index, why that column order, and how you confirmed it helped without hurting writes. The mechanism is the answer, not the exotic-ness of the fix.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

This claim invites a correctness question, not a performance one — and answering the performance part only is how candidates lose the round. 1s → 40ms is a large number; the interviewer's real question is what did you trade for it?

What was cached. Be specific: which endpoint, which data, and why it was cacheable. The strongest version names the property that made it safe — the data was read-heavy and changed rarely, or it was derived and reconstructible. "We added Redis" is not an answer; "we cached the reference-data lookup that every request performed and that changed at most daily" is.

Where the cache sat. In-process (fast, per-node, independently stale) or shared Redis (consistent across nodes, one network hop)? Both are defensible; the choice tells the interviewer whether you thought about multi-instance staleness.

The TTL, and why that value. A number with a reason — "five minutes, because the upstream data changed at most hourly and five minutes of staleness was invisible to the workflow". A TTL chosen arbitrarily is the tell that the caching was not reasoned about.

Invalidation. TTL only, or explicit eviction on write? If TTL only, say so — that is a legitimate choice and far more honest than claiming an invalidation scheme you did not build. If explicit, mention the race: a concurrent read can repopulate the old value just after the delete.

The worst-case staleness outcome — this is the question that actually scores. Name the concretely wrong thing a user could see and for how long. "For up to five minutes a user could see a rate that had just changed; the workflow tolerated that because the value was advisory and confirmed downstream." A Software Engineer answer names the risk it accepted. A mid-level answer only names the speedup.

Then volunteer what you did not handle: cache stampede on expiry (did you have single-flight?), what happens when Redis is down (does the cache outage become a database outage?), and TTL jitter so entries populated together do not expire together.

Prepared answer
what   the <X> lookup on /<endpoint> - read-heavy, changed at most <daily>
where  <in-process Caffeine | shared Redis>  (say why: staleness vs a network hop)
TTL    <N> minutes, because upstream changed at most <hourly>
invalidation  <TTL only | explicit evict on write>  - be honest which

WORST CASE (the question that scores):
  "a user could see a value up to <TTL> old. That was acceptable because
   <the value was advisory / confirmed downstream / non-financial>."

volunteer what you did NOT handle:
  stampede on expiry (single-flight?)  |  Redis down -> DB overload?
  TTL jitter so entries do not expire together
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is naming the accepted risk so important?

Because caching is a correctness trade, not a free optimisation. An engineer who reports only the speedup has not thought about what the cache can be wrong about — and that is precisely what a Software Engineer is expected to reason about.

What if the honest answer is that you did not consider staleness at the time?

Say that, then say what you know now — what the worst case actually was and what you would add. Demonstrating growth on a real decision is a strong answer; claiming foresight you did not have collapses under one follow-up.

What is the follow-up you should expect?

"What happens when the cache goes down?" The good answer names load shedding, a circuit breaker, or a small local cache absorbing the first seconds — because a cache outage becoming a database outage is the classic failure this question probes.

Dynamic programming where the state lives on tree nodes and is combined from children during a DFS. Usually dp[node][state].

CostO(n · states) timeReach for itHouse robber on a tree, maximum independent set, tree colouring, and subtree aggregate problems.
def rob_tree(root):
    def dfs(node):
        if not node: return (0, 0)          # (rob this, skip this)
        L = dfs(node.left)
        R = dfs(node.right)
        rob  = node.val + L[1] + R[1]       # take it -> children must skip
        skip = max(L) + max(R)              # skip it -> children free
        return (rob, skip)
    return max(dfs(root))

# The pattern: return a TUPLE of states per node, combine at the parent.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

This question is not about the mistake — it is about whether you can evaluate your own work and extract a transferable principle. Prepare one story properly rather than three vaguely.

Choose well. It must be a decision you genuinely owned, technical enough to go three levels deep, and consequential enough to matter — but not so catastrophic that the story becomes about damage. Good candidates: a data-model choice that made a later feature painful; caching without an invalidation plan; an abstraction introduced before the second use case existed, which then fitted neither; choosing a technology for a scale that never arrived; skipping a test seam that made later changes risky.

Structure: the context and constraint you were under → the decision and why it was reasonable at the time → what it cost, concretely → how you found out → what you did about it → the general principle.

The middle part matters most. Explain why it was a defensible decision given what you knew, because "I did something obviously stupid" is not a useful story — it suggests poor judgement rather than learning. The interesting version is a reasonable decision that turned out wrong for a reason you can now articulate.

Be concrete about the cost. Not "it caused problems" but "every new report needed a join across three tables that should have been one, and it added about a day to each of the next four features". Specificity is what makes it credible.

Then the principle, stated generally — for example: introduce an abstraction at the second use case, not the first, because a single case does not tell you which axis will vary. That generalisation is what the interviewer is actually listening for.

Tone: own it without self-flagellation. "I made this call, here is what it cost, here is what I do differently now" — no blaming a deadline, a manager or a predecessor, and no excessive apology. Confidence plus specific self-criticism reads as senior; either alone does not.

Rehearse for depth. They will ask "what would you do instead?" and then "what would that have cost?" — have both answers, because every alternative has a tradeoff too.

Structure
context     the constraint you were under, what you knew at the time
decision    what you chose - and why it was REASONABLE then
cost        concrete: "+1 day on each of the next 4 features", not "it caused issues"
discovery   how you found out - a bug, a slow feature, a review
response    what you actually did about it (or why you deliberately left it)
principle   the transferable rule  <- what the interviewer is listening for

tone: own it, no blame, no over-apology
prepare the two follow-ups:  "what instead?"  and  "what would THAT have cost?"
Follow-ups they will ask

What if your biggest mistake was on a team decision, not yours alone?

Take the part you owned — the recommendation you made, the objection you did not raise. Sharing credit for a decision is fine; the story fails only if you cannot identify your own contribution to it.

Should the story have a happy ending?

Not necessarily. "We decided the cost of fixing it exceeded the cost of living with it, and here is how we contained it" is a mature answer. Pretending every mistake was fully remediated is less believable than an honest tradeoff.

How long should this take to tell?

Two to three minutes, then stop. The value is in the follow-up questions, and a five-minute monologue uses up the time in which you would have demonstrated depth.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The point of this exercise is that Software Engineer hiring tests whether you identify problems, not only whether you solve assigned ones. Prepare one genuine proposal from your own experience, with a cost/benefit argument — that is what distinguishes a Senior Engineer from a productive one.

Start from a real pain point, not from an interesting technology. Good sources: something that repeatedly wakes people up; a manual process someone does weekly; a class of bug that keeps recurring; a deploy step everyone fears; a piece of data nobody can answer questions about. If you cannot name who is currently in pain, the proposal is a solution looking for a problem.

Quantify the cost of the status quo — this is the part that turns an opinion into a proposal. Hours per week spent, incidents per quarter, mean time to recovery, engineer-days lost to a recurring bug class, revenue at risk. Even rough numbers with stated assumptions are dramatically more persuasive than "this is painful".

Then the design, briefly — requirements, the shape of the solution, and what you would deliberately not build in v1. Scoping down is itself a signal; a proposal that requires six months before anything ships will not be approved.

Rollout plan: how you land it incrementally so value arrives early and risk stays bounded. Shadow mode, one team first, a feature flag, an incremental migration. "We rewrite it and switch over" is the answer that gets rejected.

Success metrics defined up front, with the honesty to say what would make you abandon it. "If incident count has not dropped by half after a quarter, this was the wrong bet" is a much stronger position than open-ended optimism.

And the cost side: engineer-weeks, ongoing operational burden, what you are not doing instead. A proposal that ignores opportunity cost reads as naive. The strongest closing is a comparison: this costs roughly N weeks and saves roughly M hours per month, so it pays back in a quarter.

Proposal
problem     who is in pain, and how often
cost today  hours/week | incidents/quarter | MTTR | engineer-days lost
            (rough numbers with stated assumptions beat adjectives)
proposal    requirements -> design -> what is deliberately OUT of v1
rollout     shadow mode -> one team -> flag -> incremental migration
metrics     what improves, measured how, by when
kill criteria  "if X has not moved by Y, this was the wrong bet"
cost        engineer-weeks + ongoing ops + what we are NOT doing instead
payback     N weeks of work, M hours/month saved -> pays back in a quarter
Follow-ups they will ask

What if your proposal was rejected in real life?

That is a fine story, and often a better one. Explain the counter-argument, whether it was right, and what you learned about how decisions get made. Being able to articulate why you lost the argument fairly is a strong signal.

How technical should the proposal be?

Technical enough to be credible, business-framed enough to be approvable. Lead with the cost of the status quo and the payback; keep the architecture to the level of detail a staff engineer would need to sanity-check it.

What makes a proposal get rejected?

No quantified problem, no incremental path, and no acknowledgement of opportunity cost. Any one of those is usually enough — the third most often, because every proposal competes with the roadmap.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The skill being drilled is narrating while coding, which is genuinely hard and which most candidates lose points on — they go quiet the moment they start typing, and the interviewer stops being able to score anything.

Set it up like the real thing: a vague one-line prompt, thirty minutes on a clock, recorded, and a rule that you must speak continuously. Pick something small enough to finish: a search box with results, a multi-select filter, a comment box with optimistic posting, a toast system.

What to narrate, in order. The scope decision — "in thirty minutes I will build the happy path plus loading and error states, and describe the accessibility work". The state shape before markup — "I will model this as a discriminated union so loading-with-an-error cannot be represented". Each tradeoff as you hit it — "I am debouncing the request rather than the input so typing stays instant", "I am using an AbortController rather than an ignore flag because this fires on every keystroke and I want to cancel the network work too".

The habit to build is saying the alternative you rejected. "I could keep this in a parent and pass it down, but that re-renders every row, so I will colocate it" is worth far more than silently making the right choice — the interviewer cannot score a decision they did not hear you make.

When you get stuck, narrate the stuckness. "I am trying to remember the exact IntersectionObserver signature — the idea is to observe a sentinel and load when it intersects, let me write the shape and fix the details." That keeps the signal flowing and is far better than a ninety-second silence, which reads as being lost.

Record and watch it back specifically for silence. Mark every gap over twenty seconds and note what you were doing — typically it is typing a block of JSX or debugging. Those are precisely the moments to describe what you are writing. On the second and third repetitions of this drill, the silences should shrink measurably; that trend is the metric, not whether the component was good.

Thirty minutes is deliberately short so you practise finishing something small rather than starting something large. Scoping down under time pressure is itself the skill.

Drill
30 min | vague one-line prompt | recorded | speak continuously

narrate in this order:
  scope      "I'll build X + loading/error; I'll describe the a11y work"
  state      "discriminated union so illegal states can't be represented"
  tradeoffs  "debouncing the request, not the input, so typing stays instant"
  rejected   "could lift this, but it re-renders every row - colocating instead"
  stuck      "trying to recall the exact signature; the idea is X - shape first"

watch back: mark EVERY silence > 20s and what you were doing
metric: silence count should drop across repetitions - not component quality
Follow-ups they will ask

Is it distracting to talk while coding?

At first, yes — which is why it is a drill. It becomes automatic after a handful of reps, and it is the single highest-return habit for interview performance because everything else you do is only scored if it is audible.

What if narrating slows you down and you do not finish?

Finish less, deliberately. A well-narrated two-thirds of a component beats a silent complete one in nearly every rubric — and scoping to what you can finish while talking is exactly the calibration this drill builds.

What should you narrate when the code is routine?

Say why it is routine — "this is just mapping over the results, nothing interesting here" — and move faster. Signalling which parts are boilerplate and which are decisions helps the interviewer follow where the thinking is.

TEMPLATES - write from memory, no IDE

Write the code template for all 20 patterns from memory on paper: sliding window, two pointers, binary search on answer, monotonic stack, fast/slow pointers, BFS, DFS, topological sort, union-find, Dijkstra, trie, backtracking, 1-D DP, 2-D DP, heap top-K, merge intervals, prefix sum, bit tricks, matrix traversal, and cyclic sort.

Precompute each node's 2^k-th ancestor. Any jump up the tree then decomposes into powers of two, so LCA takes log time.

CostO(n log n) preprocess, O(log n) per queryReach for itMany LCA queries, k-th ancestor, and distance between nodes in a tree.
LOG = 20
up = [[-1]*n for _ in range(LOG)]      # up[k][v] = 2^k-th ancestor of v
# up[0] = direct parent, filled by a DFS
for k in range(1, LOG):
    for v in range(n):
        if up[k-1][v] != -1:
            up[k][v] = up[k-1][up[k-1][v]]     # 2^k = 2^(k-1) twice

def lca(u, v):
    if depth[u] < depth[v]: u, v = v, u
    d = depth[u] - depth[v]
    for k in range(LOG):                       # lift u to v's depth
        if d >> k & 1: u = up[k][u]
    if u == v: return u
    for k in reversed(range(LOG)):             # lift both as high as safe
        if up[k][u] != up[k][v]: u, v = up[k][u], up[k][v]
    return up[0][u]

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

This is mock loop 1 — treat it as the real thing. No notes, no pausing, no restarting when it goes badly. The whole value is in reproducing the pressure, because that is the variable you are trying to control.

Set it up properly: a peer or an AI interviewer, camera on, screen shared, forty-five minutes on a clock, and a problem you have not seen. Practising on a problem you know tests recall, not performance.

Record it. This is non-negotiable and it is where nearly all the value is — you cannot observe your own silences, filler words or moments of visible panic while you are inside them. Watch it back at 1.5x the same day.

Ask for written feedback on four axes, and ask for it in writing rather than a verbal "that was good": communication (was the reasoning audible and followable), structure (clarify → brute force → optimal → code → test), correctness (did it work, were edge cases handled), and speed (working solution with time left for follow-ups). A generic "you did fine" is useless — push for the axis where you were weakest.

What to watch for in the recording: every silence over twenty seconds; whether you stated a brute force before optimising; whether complexity came out unprompted; whether you tested by hand or waited to be asked; and whether you drove the conversation or waited for prompts.

Then the part that makes mocks compound: log every gap in one place. A single running weak-spots list — topic, what went wrong, and whether it was knowledge or performance. That distinction matters: a knowledge gap is fixed by studying, a performance gap by more reps. Day 78 exists to clear this list, so the log is the deliverable, not the mock itself.

Expect the first one to go badly. That is the point — you are failing cheaply now so you do not fail expensively later. A mock that goes well teaches you nothing.

Protocol
setup     peer or AI interviewer | camera on | 45 min on a clock | UNSEEN problem
record    always. watch it back same day at 1.5x.

feedback (in writing, on four axes):
  communication  was the reasoning audible and followable?
  structure      clarify -> brute force -> optimal -> code -> test
  correctness    worked? edge cases? found your own bugs?
  speed          working solution with time left for follow-ups?

watch the recording for:
  [ ] silences > 20s          [ ] brute force stated first?
  [ ] complexity unprompted?  [ ] tested by hand, or waited to be asked?

LOG EVERY GAP -> one list -> tag each: KNOWLEDGE or PERFORMANCE
Follow-ups they will ask

Why distinguish knowledge gaps from performance gaps?

Because they need different fixes. Not knowing how ConcurrentHashMap works is solved by an hour of study; going silent under pressure is solved only by more mock reps. Treating the second as a study problem is why people plateau.

How many mocks are enough?

Six or more before the real loop, spread across problem types and interviewers. The plan schedules them on days 76, 77, 79, 80, 81, 83 and 86 — the spacing matters as much as the count, because you need time to repair between them.

What if you cannot find a mock partner?

An AI interviewer is a reasonable substitute for structure and problem delivery, and recording yourself still catches the communication issues. But get at least one or two rounds with a real Senior Engineer before the loop — a human asks the unscripted follow-up that a script will not.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Run the full forty-five minutes on an unseen prompt with the time-box enforced, because the most common failure in this round is not lack of knowledge — it is spending twenty-five minutes on requirements and never reaching a design, or drawing boxes at minute two.

The time-box: 5 minutes requirements, 5 estimates, 10 high level, 20 deep dive, 5 tradeoffs and risks. Put a visible timer where you can see it. If you are still gathering requirements at minute eight, move on with a stated assumption.

Record it, and watch it back for two specific things. First: did you drive, or did the interviewer drive? Count how many times they had to prompt you with "what about…" — every one of those is a point you left on the table, because the round is testing whether you can lead a design discussion. Second: did any number reach the board? If they had to ask "how much data is that?", you skipped the estimation step that justifies every subsequent decision.

Two more things to check in the recording: whether you asked where they wanted to go deep before diving (which stops you spending twenty minutes on the component they do not care about), and whether you volunteered risks and tradeoffs at the end or ran out of time first.

Ask for feedback on depth versus breadth specifically. The characteristic mid-level failure is naming many components without going deep on any — a tour of the architecture rather than an engineering discussion. Ask your partner directly: did I go deep enough anywhere to demonstrate real understanding?

Choose the prompt to be genuinely unseen and outside your comfort zone. Designing a payments system when you work in payments tests recall; designing a video pipeline or a search system tests whether you can reason from principles, which is what the round actually measures.

Log the gaps into the same weak-spots list, tagged as knowledge or performance, and — specifically for design — note any diagram you could not draw from memory. Day 78 rebuilds those on a blank page.

Protocol
45 min, UNSEEN prompt, visible timer, recorded.

 0-5   requirements  functional + non-functional; scope OUT loudly; read:write
 5-10  estimates     DAU -> QPS -> peak -> storage (1 sig fig, assumptions stated)
10-20  high level    components + data flow; then ASK where to go deep
20-40  deep dive     data model, partition key, indexes, API, failure behaviour
40-45  tradeoffs     top 3 risks + what you would build first

watch the recording for:
  [ ] how many times did they prompt me?   (each one = a point lost)
  [ ] did any NUMBER reach the board?
  [ ] did I ask where to go deep?
  [ ] did I volunteer risks, or run out of time?

log: any diagram you could not draw from memory -> day 78
Follow-ups they will ask

What if you have never worked on anything like the prompt?

Say so and reason from first principles — requirements, estimates, and the building blocks you do know. Interviewers routinely give prompts outside a candidate's domain precisely to see that reasoning, and admitting unfamiliarity while still driving is a strong answer.

How deep is deep enough?

Concrete enough to be wrong. Actual field names, an actual partition key with a justification, an actual index, an actual failure behaviour. If everything you said would be true of any system, you have not gone deep.

What is the single highest-leverage ninety seconds?

The closing risks. Almost no candidate volunteers "here are the three things I am most worried about and what I would validate first" — and it is the clearest available demonstration of engineering judgement.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Run a full forty-five-minute frontend round on an unseen, deliberately vague prompt — "build a search interface", "build a comment thread", "build a file uploader". The vagueness is the test.

Follow the order and check afterwards whether you did: scope and confirm what you will build → sketch the API and state shape → build the happy path → add loading, error and empty states → accessibility → performance if warranted → close with what you would do with more time.

The two axes to ask your partner about specifically are the two most commonly missed, and asking about them by name gets you better feedback than "how did I do": did I handle the error and empty states, and did I address accessibility unprompted. Both take a couple of minutes to include and both read as production experience, so omitting them is a disproportionate loss.

In the recording, check whether you scoped or just started typing. The failure pattern is attempting everything the prompt might mean and finishing none of it. Saying "in forty-five minutes I will build X and Y properly and describe Z" at minute three is what separates a controlled round from a scramble.

Also check whether you designed the state before writing markup. Most implementation trouble in this round is actually state-shape trouble — a discriminated union for loading/error/success takes thirty seconds to declare and removes an entire class of impossible-state bugs you would otherwise debug live.

Watch for silent typing. Frontend rounds tempt candidates into heads-down coding because there is visible output. The interviewer still needs to hear the reasoning — narrate the tradeoffs as you make them.

Log the gaps into the same weak-spots list. For React specifically, note anything you had to look up: hook signatures, ARIA attributes, the exact AbortController pattern. Those are pure recall and are worth putting on a card.

Protocol
45 min, UNSEEN vague prompt, recorded.

order (check afterwards whether you followed it):
  1. scope       "I'll build X and Y properly, and describe Z"   <- by minute 3
  2. API + state response shape, then the state SHAPE (discriminated union)
  3. happy path  get something rendering early
  4. states      loading / error / empty        <- most commonly missed
  5. a11y        semantics, labels, keyboard, focus, aria-live  <- 2nd most missed
  6. perf        debounce / cancel / memo / virtualize - only if warranted
  7. close       "with more time: tests, X, Y"

ask your partner specifically:
  did I handle error + empty states?
  did I address accessibility WITHOUT being prompted?
Follow-ups they will ask

Why are error and empty states weighted so heavily?

Because they are the cheapest possible signal of production experience. Anyone can render a happy path; someone who has shipped software knows a failed request must look different from zero results, and reviewers notice their absence immediately.

Should you use a component library in a mock?

Ask. If allowed, use it and spend the time on behaviour and states; if not, hand-roll the minimum. Either way, say what you are doing and why — the decision itself is part of the assessment.

What if you finish early?

You will not, but if you do: add tests, add keyboard support, or handle a harder case out loud. Sitting silently having finished is a wasted five minutes in which you could still be demonstrating depth.

  • Number of IslandsMedium
  • Longest Increasing SubsequenceMedium

Get written feedback on communication, structure, correctness, and speed. Log every gap.

Split the input in half, enumerate each half separately, then combine. Turns 2ⁿ into two lots of 2^(n/2) plus a join.

CostO(2^(n/2) · n) time and spaceReach for itThe constraint n ≤ 40 is effectively a label for this — too big for 2ⁿ, too small for polynomial.
from bisect import bisect_right
def count_subsets_at_most(a, target):
    m = len(a) // 2
    def sums(part):
        out = [0]
        for v in part:
            out += [s + v for s in out]
        return out
    A, B = sums(a[:m]), sorted(sums(a[m:]))
    total = 0
    for s in A:
        if s <= target:
            total += bisect_right(B, target - s)   # join with binary search
    return total

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The rule for mock 2 is deliberate discomfort: pick a different problem class from mock 1. If mock 1 was arrays and hashing, do graphs or dynamic programming. Repeating a class you are comfortable with feels productive and teaches nothing — the purpose of a mock is to fail cheaply, and you cannot fail cheaply on material you already know.

Why problem class matters more than difficulty. Most candidates have an uneven distribution: strong on arrays and strings, weak on graphs or DP, and they practise what feels good. A real loop draws randomly, so your expected performance is closer to your weakest class than your average. Two hours on your weakest class moves the expected outcome more than ten hours on your strongest.

Keep the process identical — clarify, brute force with complexity, optimal with complexity, code, hand-test — because the process is what you are making automatic. Changing the problem class while holding the process constant is what isolates the variable you are training.

For DP specifically, watch for the failure that shows up under pressure: jumping to a table without stating the recurrence. Say the recurrence and the base case out loud, then the memoized version, then bottom-up, then space optimisation if there is time. Candidates who go straight to a two-dimensional array usually get an index wrong and cannot debug it because they never wrote down what the cell means.

For graphs, the failure is choosing the traversal before understanding the problem — BFS versus DFS versus topological sort versus union-find each answer a different question. State which and why before writing.

Expect this one to go worse than mock 1, because you deliberately chose harder ground. That is the correct outcome, and reacting to it by retreating to comfortable problems is the trap. Log the gaps, tag them knowledge or performance, and note specifically whether the difficulty was recognising the pattern or executing it — those need different remedies.

Selection
mock 1 was arrays/hashing  ->  mock 2 is graphs or DP

why: a real loop draws randomly, so your expected score tracks your WEAKEST
     class, not your average. Practise the weak one.

DP under pressure - state these OUT LOUD before any code:
  1. what does dp[i] MEAN (one sentence)
  2. the recurrence
  3. the base case
  4. iteration order
  then: memoized -> bottom-up -> space-optimised

graphs - state WHICH traversal and why before writing:
  BFS (shortest unweighted) | DFS (reachability/cycles) |
  topo sort (dependencies)  | union-find (connectivity)  | Dijkstra (weighted)

log each gap: RECOGNITION (didn't see the pattern) or EXECUTION (saw it, botched it)
Follow-ups they will ask

Why separate recognition failures from execution failures?

Different fixes. Recognition is fixed by seeing more problems in that class until the trigger phrases become obvious; execution is fixed by writing the template from memory until it is muscle memory. Treating one as the other wastes weeks.

What if you cannot solve it at all?

Get the brute force down, state the complexity, and articulate specifically what you cannot see. Then afterwards study that one problem properly rather than moving on — an unsolved problem you fully understand afterwards is worth more than three you skimmed.

Should mock 2 be harder than mock 1?

Different, not necessarily harder. Difficulty within a class you know is less informative than moderate difficulty in a class you avoid.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Deliberately pick a design in your weakest area — the whole point of a mock is to fail cheaply, and a comfortable prompt gives you a pleasant hour and no information.

How to identify the weakest area honestly: go back through weeks 4 to 10 and find the designs you skimmed, the ones where you read the answer rather than attempting it, and any diagram you could not draw from memory. That last test is the sharpest — recognition feels like knowledge and is not.

Common weak spots for a backend engineer with your background: anything media or streaming (video pipelines, transcoding), search and ranking, geospatial matching, real-time collaboration, and machine-learning serving paths. Those feel foreign because they are outside the fintech and Kafka world you work in — which is exactly why an interviewer might pick one, and exactly why reasoning from first principles matters more than domain recall.

The technique when the domain is unfamiliar: fall back on the building blocks, which do not change. Requirements and estimates work identically. Then ask what is being stored, what is being queried, what the read:write ratio is, what must be consistent, and what can be eventual. Almost every unfamiliar system decomposes into ingestion, storage, indexing, a serving path and a background pipeline — say that out loud and the design assembles itself.

Say when you are outside your experience, then keep driving. "I have not built a transcoding pipeline, so I will reason from the constraints: the work is CPU-heavy and embarrassingly parallel, the output is immutable and segment-based, so I want a queue, a worker fleet and object storage." That is a strong answer. Silently pretending familiarity and getting a detail wrong is a weak one.

Afterwards, note whether the difficulty was the domain or the method. If your framework held and you simply lacked domain facts, you are in good shape — facts are cheap to acquire. If the framework fell apart under unfamiliarity, that is the thing to drill, and day 78 is for exactly that.

Choosing the prompt
pick from weeks 4-10 where you:
  - read the answer instead of attempting it
  - could not draw the diagram from memory
  - felt relieved when you moved on

likely weak areas given your background:
  video/transcoding | search + ranking | geospatial | realtime collab | ML serving

unfamiliar domain -> fall back on the invariant method:
  requirements -> estimates -> what is stored / queried / read:write
  -> ingestion | storage | indexing | serving path | background pipeline

say "I have not built one of these" then KEEP DRIVING from constraints

afterwards: was the gap DOMAIN (cheap to fix) or METHOD (drill it on day 78)?
Follow-ups they will ask

Is it acceptable to admit you have never built something?

Yes, and it is expected — nobody has built everything. What is assessed is whether you can reason from constraints to a defensible design anyway. Feigning familiarity fails at the first specific follow-up.

How do you prepare for a domain you have never worked in?

Learn the two or three domain-specific facts that unlock it — for video, that output is segmented and adaptive bitrate is client-driven; for search, the inverted index. Those facts plus your existing framework covers most of what a round requires.

What is the sign your framework is solid?

That an unfamiliar prompt slows you down but does not stop you. If you can still produce requirements, estimates and a sensible decomposition in a domain you have never touched, the method is working.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A component design plus API design prompt is a different round from "build this" — it is closer to a system design interview than a coding one, and preparing for it as coding is why people underperform.

Typical prompts: design the API for a Table, a Select, a DatePicker, a Modal, or a Form library. Sometimes framed as "forty teams will use this — design it." Almost no code is required; what is assessed is API judgement.

The structure to follow. First, who uses it and for what — a component for one product is a different design from one for forty teams. Second, the props versus composition split: which things are configuration (behaviour flags, data) and which are markup (rendering variations). Anything that exists to customise rendering should be composition, not a render* prop, or you end up with forty props. Third, controlled and uncontrolled duality per feature, so simple cases need no state and complex cases stay possible. Fourth, accessibility built into the core, because it is the main argument for a shared component at all. Fifth, versioning and deprecation, since you cannot coordinate forty teams.

The single strongest move is to refuse the god component. When the prompt implies twenty features, say explicitly: "a flat prop API does not scale past about ten props, so I would build a headless core hook plus composable subcomponents" — and then name the cost honestly, which is that the API becomes implicit and needs much better documentation and examples.

Be concrete about naming and defaults, because that is where API judgement actually shows. Defaults should be the safe, common case. Names should describe intent rather than implementation (appearance rather than variant2). Booleans should be positive (disabled, not notEnabled).

Close with the migration story: semver, deprecation warnings in development, codemods for mechanical changes, and adoption tracking before removal. That closing is what turns a component design into a platform answer.

Afterwards, ask your partner one specific question: would you be able to build an unusual variant with this API without asking me for a new prop? If the answer is no, the design failed.

Structure
1. audience     one product, or 40 teams? (changes everything)
2. props vs composition
     configuration/behaviour -> props    (multiple, disabled, sortable)
     rendering variation     -> composition (Table.Cell, Select.Option)
     rule: if it exists to customise MARKUP, it is composition
3. controlled/uncontrolled duality per feature (value + onChange optional)
4. accessibility in the CORE (roving tabindex, aria-sort, focus) - the main reason
                                                                  to share at all
5. versioning: semver + dev deprecation warnings + codemods + adoption tracking

the strong move: refuse the god component, propose headless core + composition,
                 and NAME the cost (implicit API, needs real docs)

ask afterwards: "could you build an odd variant without asking me for a new prop?"
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you decide between a prop and composition?

Ask whether it configures behaviour or customises markup. sortable is behaviour and belongs as a prop; a custom cell with a badge in it is markup and belongs as composition. A renderCell prop is composition wearing a prop's clothes.

What is the most common API design mistake?

Adding a prop for every request. Each one is individually reasonable and the tenth makes the component unusable. The moment you are adding a render* prop, the answer was composition.

Should you write code in this round?

A little — the API surface as a usage example is worth more than an implementation. Show how a consumer would call it for the simple case and for a hard case; that demonstrates the design better than the internals would.

Merge sort that counts, during the merge, how many left-side elements are greater than each right-side one.

CostO(n log n) time, O(n) spaceReach for itCounting inversions, 'reverse pairs', and any 'count pairs across a split' problem. The template for the whole tag.
def count_inversions(a):
    def sort_count(a):
        if len(a) <= 1: return a, 0
        m = len(a)//2
        L, x = sort_count(a[:m])
        R, y = sort_count(a[m:])
        merged, inv, i, j = [], x + y, 0, 0
        while i < len(L) and j < len(R):
            if L[i] <= R[j]: merged.append(L[i]); i += 1
            else:
                merged.append(R[j]); j += 1
                inv += len(L) - i        # ALL remaining L are > R[j]
        return merged + L[i:] + R[j:], inv
    return sort_count(a)[1]

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

No new material today. The rule is rebuild, not re-read — because recognition feels like knowledge and is not. If you read your notes on the Java Memory Model and nod, you have learned nothing; if you explain it out loud to an empty room and stumble, you have found the gap.

Pick exactly three topics from your weak-spots list — the ones tagged knowledge rather than performance. Three is the limit; attempting eight means eight shallow passes and no consolidation.

The method for each, in order. First, explain it out loud from memory as if teaching a Junior Engineer, without notes, and record it. Teaching is the highest-fidelity test available because it exposes the joins in your understanding — the places where you know two facts but not how they connect. Second, write working code demonstrating it: a deadlock and its three fixes, a stale-closure bug and its repair, a self-invocation that silently skips the transaction. Code you wrote today beats notes you read today. Third, only then open the reference and note precisely what you got wrong or vague.

Then go one level deeper than the answer requires. If the topic is volatile, do not stop at "visibility not atomicity" — be able to say which happens-before edge it creates and why double-checked locking needs it. Interviewers probe until they find your limit, so the goal is to move the limit rather than to have a good first answer.

Write a one-paragraph summary from memory afterwards, in your own words, and keep it. That paragraph becomes your week-13 revision material, and the act of compressing it is itself consolidation.

How to know you are done with a topic: you can explain it out loud in under two minutes, write the demonstrating code without reference, and answer two follow-up questions. Anything short of that is not finished, and it should stay on the list rather than being ticked optimistically — ticking what you skimmed corrupts the only signal you have.

Method
pick THREE knowledge-tagged gaps. Not eight.

for each:
  1. teach it OUT LOUD from memory, recorded, as if to a junior
       -> the stumbles ARE the gaps
  2. write working code that demonstrates it
       deadlock + 3 fixes | stale closure + fix | self-invocation skipping the txn
  3. THEN open the reference; note exactly what was wrong or vague
  4. go one level deeper than the answer needs
  5. write a one-paragraph summary from memory  -> week 13 revision material

done when:
  [ ] explained out loud in <2 min, no notes
  [ ] wrote the code with no reference
  [ ] answered two follow-ups
otherwise it stays on the list
Follow-ups they will ask

Why teaching out loud rather than writing notes?

Writing lets you pause and reorder; speaking does not. The places you stall, backtrack or say "sort of" are precisely the joins in your understanding, and they are invisible when you write.

What if all three topics are still shaky at the end of the day?

That is useful information — it means the estimate was wrong, not that you failed. Carry them to day 84 and reduce the count. Three genuinely closed topics beats eight partially touched.

Should you do this for performance gaps too?

No — performance gaps (silence under pressure, poor time management) are fixed by mock reps, not study. That is why the list is tagged; today is only for the knowledge column.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The test for system design is drawing from memory on a blank page. If you cannot produce the diagram without prompts, you cannot produce it on a whiteboard with an interviewer watching — and recognition of a diagram you have read is not the same capability at all.

Pick three designs you fumbled or skipped. For each: blank page, no notes, draw the full architecture, then annotate it with the data flow, the storage choices, the partition key, and the failure behaviour of each component. Time yourself — ten minutes per design, which is roughly the high-level phase of a real round.

Then compare against your original notes and mark what you missed. The misses cluster predictably, and knowing your own pattern is worth as much as the individual fix. The usual ones are: no numbers at all; the queue or cache drawn but never explained; no partition or shard key; and no failure story — what happens when this component is unavailable.

Redraw immediately after comparing, from memory again. The second pass is where it consolidates; stopping after the comparison leaves you having read the answer rather than produced it.

Then do the harder version: say it out loud while drawing, as if to an interviewer. Design rounds are performed, not written — you have to draw and narrate simultaneously, and doing both at once is measurably harder than either alone. Record it and check whether the narration went silent while you were drawing boxes.

For each design, be able to state three things unprompted: the partition or shard key and why, the consistency requirement per operation, and the top three risks. Those three cover most of what separates a strong design round from an adequate one, and they are recall-able if you drill them.

Keep the drawings. Five or six hand-drawn architectures you produced from memory are far better week-13 revision material than any document you read, because re-drawing them is a two-minute test rather than a twenty-minute read.

Method
three designs you fumbled. Blank page. No notes. 10 minutes each.

draw + annotate:
  components and data flow
  storage choice per component (and WHY)
  partition / shard key
  what happens when each component is unavailable

then compare -> mark the misses. The usual pattern:
  [ ] no numbers anywhere
  [ ] cache/queue drawn but never justified
  [ ] no partition key
  [ ] no failure story

redraw from memory again (this is where it sticks)
then: draw AND narrate simultaneously, recorded  <- the actual round is performed

for each, unprompted: partition key + why | consistency per operation | top 3 risks
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is drawing from memory the right test?

Because that is the actual task. A design round is produced live on a whiteboard while talking — so practising by reading is training a different skill and gives false confidence.

What if you can draw it but cannot justify the choices?

That is the more common failure and the more important one. Interviewers rarely challenge the shape of a diagram; they challenge "why that database" and "what is your partition key". Annotating with reasons is the part to drill.

How many designs should you have drawable from memory before the loop?

Six to eight covering distinct shapes — a read-heavy cached service, a write-heavy pipeline, a fan-out feed, a transactional ledger, a search system, and a real-time system. Most prompts are variations on those.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Same rule as the other tracks: rebuild rather than re-read — but for React the rebuild is a small working example, because React knowledge that is not in your fingers evaporates under interview pressure.

Pick three topics from the weak-spots list and, for each, write a minimal working demonstration from scratch in a scratch file or a sandbox. Not a copied snippet — typed from memory, run, and observed. The observation matters: seeing the stale closure actually produce the wrong number is what makes it stick in a way reading about it never does.

The examples worth building if they are on your list: a stale-closure bug in an interval and its three fixes; a React.memo that is silently defeated by an inline object prop, then fixed; a context whose value identity changes every render and the memoized version; a debounced search with AbortController handling out-of-order responses; a focus trap with restore-on-close; a virtualized list with the windowing maths written by hand.

For each, then break it deliberately and observe the failure. Remove the cleanup and watch two subscriptions accumulate. Swap useLayoutEffect for useEffect and watch the tooltip flicker into place. That deliberate-breakage step converts "I know the rule" into "I have seen what it prevents", which is what lets you answer the follow-up.

Say it out loud while building, since the frontend round is narrated too, and check the recording for silence during typing.

Keep the examples in one scratch project. By week 13 you have a small file of runnable demonstrations that is far better revision material than notes — re-reading a snippet you wrote and ran recalls the whole reasoning in seconds.

Done when you can rebuild the example without reference, explain what it demonstrates in under a minute, and answer why the naive version is wrong. Anything less stays on the list.

Method
three topics -> one minimal WORKING example each, typed from memory, run

high-value examples if they are on your list:
  stale closure in setInterval + the 3 fixes
  React.memo defeated by an inline object prop, then fixed
  context value identity changing every render, then memoized
  debounced search + AbortController + out-of-order responses
  focus trap + restore focus on close
  virtualized list - windowing maths written by hand

then BREAK each one deliberately and watch it fail:
  remove the cleanup      -> two subscriptions accumulate
  useEffect not useLayout -> visible flicker on reposition

keep them all in one scratch project -> week 13 revision in seconds
Follow-ups they will ask

Why deliberately break the working example?

Because knowing the rule and having seen the failure are different depths. The follow-up question is always "what goes wrong if you do not?" — and having watched it go wrong makes that answer specific rather than theoretical.

Is a sandbox enough, or should it be a real project?

A sandbox is fine and faster. The value is in typing it from memory and observing the behaviour, not in the build tooling.

What if a topic is conceptual rather than code-shaped?

Find the code-shaped consequence. Hydration mismatch is conceptual until you render Date.now() on the server and watch React discard the markup. Almost every React concept has an observable consequence you can produce in ten lines.

REPAIR - re-solve failures from scratch

Re-solve every problem you failed or needed a hint on, from a blank file, with no reference. If you cannot, that pattern is not learned - go back to its template.

Turn intervals into start and end events, sort them by position, and sweep left to right maintaining a running count.

CostO(n log n) time, dominated by the sortReach for itMaximum overlapping intervals, meeting rooms II, skyline, and 'how many active at once' problems.
def min_rooms(intervals):
    events = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        events.append((s, 1))      # a meeting starts
        events.append((e, -1))     # a meeting ends
    events.sort()                  # ends sort before starts at equal times,
                                   # because -1 < 1. That is intentional.
    cur = best = 0
    for _, delta in events:
        cur += delta
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

This is the calibration mock — the one where you find out whether the preparation worked. Full interview intensity, unseen problem, no notes, recorded, and a partner who will push.

The bar to measure against: you should now consistently land a working, optimal or near-optimal solution with continuous narration, inside forty-five minutes, with time left for follow-ups. Not occasionally — consistently. One good round after three poor ones is variance, not readiness.

The specific checklist: clarifying questions asked unprompted; brute force stated with complexity before optimising; optimal approach and complexity stated before writing code; edge cases enumerated before coding rather than discovered during; compiling code with real signatures; hand-tested on a small input, finding your own bugs; and no silence over twenty seconds anywhere.

If you are hitting all of that, you are ready on this axis and should shift remaining effort to system design and behavioural, which have longer tails.

If you are not, the diagnosis matters more than another rep. Sort the failure into one of three: pattern recognition (you did not see what kind of problem it was) — fix by working through more problems in that class specifically; execution (you saw it and botched the implementation) — fix by writing the pattern templates from memory until they are automatic, which is what days 75 and 85 are for; or performance (you knew it and froze) — fix only with more mock reps, because it is a pressure problem rather than a knowledge one.

Do not respond to a bad round by studying more theory. That is the common and comfortable mistake — at this stage the gap is almost always execution or performance, and both are fixed by repetition under pressure rather than reading.

Log the result honestly. With eleven days left, an accurate assessment is worth more than an encouraging one: it determines whether the remaining time goes to more mocks, targeted repair, or — if the picture is genuinely poor — whether to move the interview timeline.

The bar
consistently, not occasionally:
  working optimal solution | narrated throughout | <45 min | time for follow-ups

checklist:
  [ ] clarifying questions, unprompted
  [ ] brute force + complexity BEFORE optimising
  [ ] optimal approach + complexity BEFORE coding
  [ ] edge cases enumerated before coding, not discovered during
  [ ] compiling code, real signatures
  [ ] hand-tested; found your own bugs
  [ ] no silence > 20s

if failing, diagnose - do NOT just study more theory:
  RECOGNITION -> more problems in that class
  EXECUTION   -> write pattern templates from memory (days 75, 85)
  PERFORMANCE -> more mock reps. It is pressure, not knowledge.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if this round goes badly with eleven days left?

Diagnose which of the three failure types it was, then spend the remaining time on that specifically. Eleven days is enough to fix execution or performance; it is not enough to learn a whole problem class from scratch, so scope accordingly.

How do you tell execution failure from performance failure?

Ask yourself whether you could solve the same problem calmly on your own in twenty minutes afterwards. If yes, it was pressure; if no, it was execution. Do that check the same day, while the round is fresh.

Is one good round enough evidence?

No. You want two consecutive rounds meeting the bar on unseen problems from different classes. A single good round is as likely to be an easy draw as genuine readiness.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Do this one with a real Senior Engineer if you possibly can — someone who has interviewed candidates. An AI or a peer can deliver the prompt; only an experienced interviewer produces the unscripted follow-up that finds the edge of your understanding, which is what the round actually is.

Full forty-five minutes, unseen prompt, time-boxed, recorded. By now the framework should be automatic: requirements, estimates, high level, deep dive, tradeoffs and risks — with numbers on the board and you driving throughout.

Then ask the question directly: "Based on that round, would you hire me at Software Engineer? Where would you have hesitated?" Ask it plainly and let the silence sit. People soften feedback unless you make it explicit that you want the real answer, and a vague "that was solid" is worth nothing eleven days out.

Push for specificity on three axes if they do not volunteer it: did I go deep enough anywhere to demonstrate real understanding, or was it a tour? Did I quantify, or did you have to ask? Did I drive, or did you? Those three separate a hire from a no-hire far more often than knowledge gaps do.

What a strong-hire round looks like, so you can compare: requirements pinned and scoped in five minutes; numbers on the board by minute ten; a deep dive concrete enough to be wrong — actual fields, an actual partition key with a justification, an actual failure behaviour; tradeoffs volunteered rather than extracted; and top risks named unprompted at the end.

Take the answer at face value rather than arguing with it. If they hesitate, the hesitation is the signal — ask what would have removed it. Defending the round you just did is the least useful possible response and it costs you the honest version of everything they say next.

Then act on it with the time remaining. If the gap is depth, pick two designs and go three levels deeper on each. If it is quantification, drill estimation until numbers are reflexive. If it is drive, that is a performance fix — more rounds, and consciously narrating your next step before taking it.

Follow-ups they will ask

What if they say they would not hire you?

That is the most valuable eleven-days-out information available, and far better than finding out in the real loop. Ask exactly what was missing, and decide whether it is fixable in the time — if not, moving the interview is a legitimate and often correct choice.

Where do you find a Senior Engineer to do this?

A senior colleague not on your team, a former manager, someone from your network, or a paid mock platform. It is worth paying for one or two rounds with a real interviewer at this stage — it is the highest-information hour available.

What if the feedback contradicts an earlier mock?

Weight the more experienced interviewer, and look for what both agree on. Contradictions usually mean the round was near a boundary — which itself tells you that consistency, not capability, is the remaining problem.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Final frontend calibration: an unseen, deliberately vague prompt at full intensity. The single thing to verify is that you handle ambiguity by asking rather than assuming — that is what the vagueness is testing, and it is the most common reason candidates drift into building the wrong thing.

The check: in the first three minutes, did you ask what data comes from where, what scale, which interactions matter, and whether design is provided — and then state explicitly what you would build in the time and what you would only describe? If you started typing before that, the round is already compromised regardless of the code quality.

The bar to measure against: a working happy path, plus loading, error and empty states, plus at least the cheap accessibility work (semantic elements, labels, keyboard operation, a live region for async updates), narrated throughout, finished with a clear statement of what you would do with more time.

The two things to confirm you did unprompted, because they are the most-skipped and highest-signal: the error and empty states, and accessibility. Both cost a couple of minutes; both read immediately as production experience. If your partner had to ask about either, that is the fix for the remaining days.

Also verify the state shape came before the markup. Under time pressure the temptation is to start rendering and add state ad hoc, which is where impossible states and mid-round refactors come from. Thirty seconds declaring a discriminated union prevents both.

Ask your partner one specific question: did anything I built look like it came from someone who has shipped this to real users? Error handling, cancellation, focus management and empty states are the tells — and they are what separates a candidate who has built UIs from one who has completed exercises.

After this round, stop adding React material. Week 13 is consolidation only: your cheat sheet, your scratch project of worked examples, and rest.
