Follow-ups they will ask

What if the prompt is so vague you cannot start?

State an assumption out loud and build against it. "I will assume a REST endpoint returning twenty results per page" is exactly the behaviour being assessed — the round is testing decision-making under ambiguity, not clairvoyance.

Is it worth learning a new library before the loop?

No. Eleven days out, depth on what you already know beats breadth. A confident answer using plain React plus one familiar library is far stronger than a shaky one name-dropping something you read about last week.

What is the highest-value thing to fix if this round is weak?

Whichever of error states or accessibility you skipped. Both are checklist items rather than skills — you can close that gap in a single practice round, which makes them the cheapest available points.

MOCK 3 - final calibration
  • Top K Frequent ElementsMedium
  • Serialize and Deserialize Binary TreeHard

You should now consistently land a working optimal solution with narration. If not, that is the priority for the last two weeks.

Once a DAG is topologically sorted, DP over it in that order — every dependency is already computed when you reach a node.

CostO(V + E) timeReach for itLongest path in a DAG, course scheduling with weights, and 'longest increasing path in a matrix'.
from functools import cache
def longest_increasing_path(mat):
    R, C = len(mat), len(mat[0])
    @cache
    def dfs(r, c):
        best = 1
        for dr, dc in ((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)):
            nr, nc = r+dr, c+dc
            if 0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C and mat[nr][nc] > mat[r][c]:
                best = max(best, 1 + dfs(nr, nc))
        return best
    return max(dfs(r, c) for r in range(R) for c in range(C))

# The 'increasing' rule makes it acyclic, so memoisation is safe.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Today is design-round intensive, so keep Java deliberately light — fifteen minutes of rapid-fire recall, no new material. The purpose is to arrive at the design rounds warm rather than depleted, and managing your own energy across a long day is itself part of interview preparation.

Cover only your three weakest levels from the earlier rapid-fire passes, using the physical card you built on days 73 and 74. If the card is empty because everything passed, spend the fifteen minutes on the four that appear in nearly every Java loop — the hashCode contract and its HashMap failure, volatile versus atomic and happens-before, thread pool sizing and the unbounded queue trap, and @Transactional proxying with self-invocation.

Out loud, sixty seconds each, standing up. Standing sounds trivial and is not — it changes your voice and energy, and it is closer to whiteboard conditions than sitting hunched at a desk.

Then stop. The discipline of stopping is the actual lesson here. The instinct on a heavy day is to cram more, and it reliably makes the important rounds worse — you arrive at the second design round with nothing left, which is precisely the round where candidates fade.

If anything is still shaky after fifteen minutes, note it and move on. It goes on the day-84 repair list, not into today. One shaky Java topic will not decide your loop; a poor second design round might.

A useful frame for the rest of the plan: from here to day 90 the marginal value of new knowledge is close to zero, and the marginal value of consistency, stamina and rest is high. Days like this one, where the instruction is to do less, are as deliberate as the days that demand more.

Follow-ups they will ask

Why does energy management matter this much?

Because a real onsite is four to five hours and the last round often decides ties. Candidates who prepare only for individual rounds fade in the second half — which is exactly what today's back-to-back design rounds are training against.

Should you skip the warm-up entirely?

No — a short recall drill primes you and settles nerves. It is the difference between a warm-up and a workout: fifteen minutes helps, ninety minutes costs you the rounds that matter.

What if the Java card still has ten items on it?

Then the earlier passes were too generous or the list was never pruned. Take the three highest-frequency items today and schedule the rest for day 84 — spreading fifteen minutes across ten topics achieves nothing.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Two full forty-five-minute design rounds on unseen prompts, ten-minute break between, both recorded. This is a stamina drill as much as a skill drill, and it exists because that is the shape of a real onsite.

The specific thing being tested is the second round. Candidates rehearse individual rounds and then fade in the second half of the day — attention drops, the framework gets skipped, numbers stop appearing, and they stop driving. Simulating it is the only way to find out whether that happens to you and by how much.

Choose two structurally different prompts so the second is not a variation on the first: one storage- or consistency-heavy (a ledger, a booking system), one throughput- or streaming-heavy (a feed, a pipeline, a real-time system). Different shapes force the framework to do the work rather than recall.

Enforce the time-box in both — 5 requirements, 5 estimates, 10 high level, 20 deep dive, 5 risks — with a visible timer. Fatigue shows first as the time-box collapsing.

Then compare the two recordings directly, which is the whole point. Was there a number on the board by minute ten in both? Did you ask where to go deep in both? Did you volunteer risks at the end of the second, or run out of time? How many times did the interviewer have to prompt you in round one versus round two? That delta is your fatigue curve, and it is measurable.

If round two is materially worse, the fix is not more knowledge — it is more back-to-back reps, plus practical things that sound minor and are not: eat before the loop, keep water to hand, take the full break, and have a written framework you can glance at to restart the structure when your attention drops.

Note also which round you preferred. If you are consistently stronger on the storage-shaped prompt, that is useful — you can steer an ambiguous prompt slightly toward the ground you know, which is a legitimate skill.

Follow-ups they will ask

Why do candidates fade in the second round?

Attention and working memory, not knowledge. The framework is the first thing to go — people stop time-boxing, skip estimation, and start responding to prompts instead of driving. A written framework you can glance at restores the structure quickly.

Is a ten-minute break enough?

It mirrors a real onsite, so yes for the purposes of the drill. Use it properly — stand up, drink water, do not review notes. Reviewing between rounds feels productive and costs you the recovery.

What if both rounds are equally strong?

Excellent, and worth knowing. Then stamina is not your constraint and the remaining time should go to depth or to whichever track your day-79 feedback flagged.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Review only today — fifteen minutes, no building. Redraw your frontend system design framework from memory on a blank page, then apply it to one prompt in fifteen minutes rather than the usual forty-five.

The framework, from memory: requirements and scope → API contract and data model → component architecture and rendering strategy → state and caching → performance budget → accessibility → error, empty and offline states → observability. If you cannot produce all eight without prompting, that is today's finding and the list goes on your card.

Then the compression drill: apply it to a prompt in fifteen minutes instead of forty-five. One minute on requirements, two on the API, three on architecture, three on state, two on performance, two on accessibility and states, two on close. You will not go deep anywhere — that is deliberate. Compression forces you to identify what actually matters in each phase, because you cannot afford to say anything that is not load-bearing.

What the drill reveals is which phases you pad. Most people discover they spend disproportionate time on component architecture, which is the least differentiating part, and skip the API contract, which is the most. Fixing that ratio is worth more than any additional React knowledge at this stage.

Say it out loud and time each phase. Write the actual seconds spent next to each one and compare against the plan — the gap between intended and actual allocation is the finding.

Then stop. Today is design-round intensive; the React track is deliberately light so you arrive at the second system design round with something left. Adding a build exercise here would cost you the round that matters.

Keep the framework page. A single hand-drawn sheet with the eight phases and the two or three things that matter in each is exactly the right week-13 revision artefact — glanceable in thirty seconds before a round.

Follow-ups they will ask

Why compress rather than practise the full round?

Because compression forces prioritisation. In fifteen minutes you can only say what is load-bearing, which exposes what you have been padding — and that insight transfers directly to the full-length round.

What if you cannot recall all eight phases?

Write down the ones you have, then check. The missing ones are almost always accessibility and observability, which is exactly why they get skipped under pressure — put them on the card.

Should the framework be memorised verbatim?

The phases yes, the contents no. You want the structure automatic so your attention goes to the actual problem, not to remembering what comes next.

Warm-up pair - keep it light
  • Kth Largest Element in an ArrayMedium
  • Merge IntervalsMedium

Today is design-round intensive. Keep the coding light so you arrive fresh.

Count numbers with a property up to N by building them digit by digit, tracking whether you are still hugging N's prefix.

CostO(digits · states · 10) timeReach for itCount numbers with no repeated digits, with a digit sum, or without a forbidden digit, up to a huge bound.
from functools import cache
def count_up_to(N):
    s = str(N)
    @cache
    def go(i, tight, started, state):
        if i == len(s): return 1 if started else 0
        limit = int(s[i]) if tight else 9
        total = 0
        for d in range(0, limit + 1):
            total += go(i + 1,
                        tight and d == limit,      # still hugging the bound?
                        started or d > 0,          # past the leading zeros?
                        new_state(state, d))
        return total
    return go(0, True, False, 0)

# 'tight' is the whole technique: once you go below N's digit, the rest
# is unconstrained.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

LLD rounds are increasingly common at Software Engineer and candidates prepare for them least, which makes this an unusually high-return hour. Sixty minutes, unseen prompt, produce a class design and working core code.

Structure the hour deliberately. 0–10: clarify requirements and state assumptions out loud. 10–20: identify entities and draw the class relationships. 20–45: write the core classes and the main flow — real compiling code, not boxes. 45–55: the extension question they will ask. 55–60: what you would add for production.

The clarifying phase is scored and is usually rushed. For a vending machine: does it give change, what denominations, is inventory per slot, can a purchase fail mid-way, is it single-user. For an ATM: card and PIN or just account, what happens on insufficient funds, is there a daily limit, does it dispense specific notes. For Splitwise: equal or arbitrary splits, multi-currency, do we simplify debts across a group. Each of those changes the design materially.

The two things being assessed are the same in every LLD prompt. First, where did you put the variation? Anything likely to change should sit behind an interface — pricing, payment method, split strategy, note-dispensing algorithm. The interviewer will ask at minute 45 "how would you add X", and a design where X requires editing existing classes has failed the test. Second, where is the state machine? Most LLD prompts contain one — a vending machine's idle/selecting/paying/dispensing, an ATM's session — and modelling it explicitly rather than with a pile of booleans is the difference between a clean design and a tangle.

Write real code for the core flow, not for everything. One complete path — insert money, select item, dispense, return change — with real types and real validation beats twelve half-written classes.

Volunteer the concurrency question even if the prompt is single-threaded, because it is the standard follow-up: what happens when two threads buy the last item. The answer is an atomic claim, not a check-then-act.

Score yourself on: requirements clarified, patterns named as you used them, extension question answered without editing existing classes, and code that would compile.

Hour plan
 0-10  clarify + state assumptions out loud   <- usually rushed, always scored
10-20  entities + relationships (draw it)
20-45  core classes + ONE complete flow in real compiling code
45-55  "how would you add X?"  <- the extension test
55-60  production concerns: persistence, concurrency, observability

the two things always assessed:
  1. where did you put the VARIATION?   (Strategy behind an interface)
     - adding X must not edit existing classes
  2. where is the STATE MACHINE?        (explicit states, not booleans)

volunteer: "two threads buy the last item" -> atomic claim, not check-then-act
Follow-ups they will ask

What if you cannot finish the code?

Finish one complete flow rather than sketching all of them. A working purchase path with real types demonstrates more than twelve stubbed classes, and you can describe the rest.

Which patterns should you name explicitly?

Strategy for pluggable policy, State for the lifecycle, Factory for creation by type, Observer for notifications. Naming them as you use them — "this is Strategy so a new pricing rule is a new class" — is what signals deliberate design rather than accident.

How is an LLD round different from a coding round?

A coding round tests algorithmic problem solving; an LLD round tests modelling, extensibility and API design. Optimal complexity is irrelevant here — whether adding a feature requires touching existing classes is everything.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

This is the standard LLD follow-up and it catches people, because every single-process assumption you made silently becomes a distributed problem. Go through your design and name each one.

In-memory state becomes shared state. A HashMap of inventory, a set of held items, a counter — each was correct in one JVM and is now wrong across fifty. Either move it to the database, or move it to Redis and accept the consistency implications. The question to ask per piece of state: does correctness depend on it, or is it a cache?

synchronized becomes a distributed coordination problem. A lock that protected "two threads must not buy the last item" protects nothing across fifty servers. The correct answer is almost always to push the invariant into the database — a conditional update whose affected-row count you check, or a unique constraint — rather than reaching for a distributed lock. Say why: a distributed lock can be lost to a GC pause past its TTL, so it cannot be the thing guaranteeing correctness.

Singletons and in-process schedulers multiply by fifty. A background job that expired holds now runs fifty times concurrently. Fix with leader election, or a lease claimed atomically, or by making the job idempotent and letting duplicates be harmless — the last is usually simplest.

Generated ids collide. An in-process counter is fine in one JVM; across fifty you need a database sequence, UUIDv7, or a Snowflake-style generator.

Local caches diverge. Each server has its own copy with independent staleness, so either accept a short TTL or add invalidation — and note that pub/sub invalidation is fire-and-forget, so a TTL is still needed as a backstop.

The framing that scores: the shared database is now the coordination point and the bottleneck, so the design question becomes which invariants must be enforced there (correctness) and which state can live elsewhere (performance). And with fifty servers sharing one database, connection pool sizing becomes the real constraint — fifty servers times twenty connections is a thousand, far more than a Postgres primary wants.

What breaks
single process              ->  50 servers + shared DB

in-memory map of inventory  ->  DB rows; correctness invariant lives in the DB
synchronized block          ->  conditional UPDATE (check rowsAffected) or
                                UNIQUE constraint. NOT a distributed lock -
                                a GC pause past the TTL breaks it.
in-process scheduler        ->  runs 50x. Leader election, lease, or make it idempotent
local counter for ids       ->  DB sequence / UUIDv7 / Snowflake
local cache                 ->  50 divergent copies -> short TTL (+ optional pub/sub)

NEW bottleneck: 50 servers x 20 connections = 1000 -> use a pooler (PgBouncer)

ask per piece of state: does CORRECTNESS depend on it, or is it a cache?
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not just use a distributed lock everywhere?

Because it is not a correctness mechanism — a process pause longer than the lock TTL means two holders. Locks are a performance optimisation to reduce contention; the invariant must be enforced by a database constraint or a conditional update.

What is the new bottleneck once the app tier scales out?

The database, and specifically its connection limit. Fifty servers each holding a pool exhausts a Postgres primary quickly, so you need a connection pooler in front and much smaller per-server pools than intuition suggests.

How do you decide what moves to Redis versus the database?

Correctness-critical invariants go to the database. High-churn, low-value, recomputable state — sessions, locations, rate-limit counters — goes to Redis. If losing it silently would be a bug rather than an inconvenience, it belongs in the database.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Designing the UI for the system you just modelled is the most underrated exercise in this plan, because it forces the three vocabularies — frontend, backend, and design — to describe one system. Interviewers at Software Engineer increasingly ask a candidate to reason across that boundary.

Start from the state machine you already wrote. The domain states map almost directly to UI states: a vending machine's idle → selecting → awaiting payment → dispensing → returning change is exactly what the screen must represent. Reusing the same state names on both sides is a real practice benefit — it makes conversations between frontend and backend unambiguous.

Then the question that matters: what state lives where? The rule is that the server owns anything that is a fact about the world; the client owns anything that is a fact about this user's current interaction. Inventory counts, prices, whether a purchase succeeded — server. Which item is highlighted, whether the confirmation dialog is open, the partially-entered amount — client. Duplicating a server fact into client state is how the two drift.

Design the API contract explicitly, because that is where the two designs meet. For each action: what does the client send, what does the server return, and what does the client do on failure. Two specifics worth naming: the mutation should carry an idempotency key so a double-tap cannot buy twice, and the response should return the new authoritative state rather than just success, so the client does not have to guess or re-fetch.

Optimistic updates need a judgement call here — and the answer is usually no for anything involving money or scarce inventory. Showing a purchase as complete before the server confirms is not a UX improvement, it is a lie you may have to retract. Show a pending state instead.

Then the states that are always underspecified: what does the UI show when inventory is exhausted mid-selection, when the payment times out (unknown, not failed), when the network drops between submit and response. Those three are exactly the cases the backend design already had to handle, which is why doing both halves together surfaces them.

Mapping
reuse the domain state machine as the UI state machine:
  idle -> selecting -> awaiting_payment -> dispensing -> complete | failed

state ownership:
  SERVER  facts about the world: inventory, price, purchase outcome
  CLIENT  facts about this interaction: highlighted item, open dialog, draft input
  never duplicate a server fact into client state -> they drift

API contract:
  POST /purchases  { itemId, Idempotency-Key }   <- double-tap cannot buy twice
  -> returns the NEW AUTHORITATIVE STATE, not just 200

no optimistic update for money or scarce inventory -> show pending

the three always-underspecified states:
  inventory exhausted mid-selection | payment TIMEOUT (unknown, not failed) | network drop
Follow-ups they will ask

Why should the mutation response return the new state?

So the client never has to guess what happened or issue a follow-up read. It also removes a whole class of race where the client's optimistic guess differs from what the server actually computed.

When is an optimistic update appropriate?

When the operation almost always succeeds, is cheap to reverse, and being briefly wrong is harmless — a like, a reorder, a draft save. Never for money, scarce inventory, or irreversible actions.

What is the value of designing both halves?

It surfaces the gaps that only appear at the boundary — timeouts that are neither success nor failure, idempotency, and who owns which piece of state. Those are exactly the questions a system design round probes, so practising them together is efficient.

LLD CODING - build it, do not solve it

From a blank file in 60 minutes: an LRU cache with per-entry TTL, thread-safe, with a pluggable eviction policy and unit tests. This is what an LLD round actually feels like.

A position loses if every move leads to a winning position, and wins if any move leads to a losing one. Compute the first few by hand and look for a pattern.

CostO(states · moves) timeReach for itNim-style games, stone games, 'can the first player force a win'. The pattern is usually periodic.
def can_win(n, moves):
    win = [False] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        # winning if ANY move leaves the opponent in a losing position
        win[i] = any(i >= m and not win[i - m] for m in moves)
    return win[n]

# Nim: a position is LOSING exactly when the XOR of all pile sizes is 0.
# Sprague-Grundy: independent games XOR their Grundy numbers together;
#   grundy(pos) = mex({grundy(next) for each move})

Third and final rapid-fire pass on Spring, JPA and testing. Same protocol: twenty-five questions, sixty seconds each, out loud, standing, scored pass/partial/fail.

By the third pass the list should be short. If it is not — if you are still failing a third of the questions — that is important information eight days out: it means the earlier passes were scored generously, and the remaining time should go to those specific topics rather than to more mocks.

The rule for anything still failing after three passes: it goes on a physical card you carry to the interview. Not a document, not an app — an index card you can read in the five minutes before a round. The act of deciding what earns a place on one small card is itself the final compression, and the constraint is what makes it useful.

What typically survives to the card is pure recall rather than reasoning: the propagation table for @Transactional, the exact set of N+1 fixes, the OOM message variants and what each means, the treeify/untreeify thresholds, the Maven-versus-Gradle resolution rule. Things you cannot derive under pressure and simply have to know.

What should not be on the card is anything you can reason to from a mechanism you understand. If you know @Transactional is a proxy, you can derive self-invocation, private methods, and final classes from that one fact — so the card carries the mechanism, not the three symptoms.

Then stop drilling Java. From here to day 90 the marginal value of another Spring fact is near zero compared with rest and consistency. The card exists so you can stop carrying the material in working memory, which is the actual benefit.

Why a physical card rather than notes on a phone?

Because the constraint of one small card forces genuine prioritisation, and because you can glance at it between rounds without opening a device. The selection process is most of the value.

What if nothing is failing by pass three?

Then Java recall is not your constraint and the remaining days belong to system design, behavioural preparation, and rest. Continuing to drill what you already know is the most comfortable way to waste the last week.

Should you drill on the day of the interview?

A five-minute glance at the card, nothing more. Cramming on the day raises anxiety and displaces the calm you need for the rounds that actually decide the outcome.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Thirty system design questions at sixty seconds each — definitions, tradeoffs, and crucially "when would you not do this", which is the part that separates recall from judgement.

The set to cover: CAP and why PACELC is the more useful framing; the consistency models and the symptom of each violation; how you choose a shard key and what breaks after sharding; the cache patterns and what each fails at; queue versus log and the three delivery semantics; why exactly-once delivery is impossible and what is achievable instead; the circuit breaker states and what trips one; the isolation levels and the anomaly each prevents; write skew and why snapshot isolation does not prevent it; consistent hashing and what it does not solve; saga versus 2PC; idempotency keys and the outbox pattern; CDC; SLO and error-budget arithmetic; the latency ladder; keyset versus offset pagination; B-tree versus LSM; and load shedding versus rate limiting.

For every one, force the third question: when would you not do this? That is the discriminator. "Use a cache" is a first-year answer; "cache when reads dominate and staleness is tolerable, and do not when the data changes as often as it is read or when you cannot invalidate reliably" is a Software Engineer answer. Anyone can name a pattern; naming its cost is what demonstrates you have paid it.

Answer out loud in the shape you would use in a round: one sentence defining it, one naming the tradeoff, one giving a concrete case. Sixty seconds is enough for exactly that, which is why the format is useful — it rehearses the compression a real answer needs.

Anything still slow goes on the same physical card — realistically the latency ladder, the isolation-level table, and the availability arithmetic, since those are pure recall.

Then stop. Eight days out, the value is in consistency and rest, not in one more pattern.

  2. the tradeoff      (what it costs)
  3. when NOT to do it <- the discriminator

Why is "when would you not do this" the key question?

Because every pattern has a cost, and recognising the cost is what distinguishes someone who has operated systems from someone who has read about them. It is also the follow-up interviewers use to test depth.

How do you answer a design question in sixty seconds?

Definition, tradeoff, concrete case. That structure fits and it is the same shape you want inside a full design round — so the drill rehearses the compression, not just the recall.

What if you disagree with a common answer?

Say so with reasoning. "Most people reach for a distributed lock here; I would put the invariant in the database instead, because a lock cannot survive a GC pause past its TTL" is a strong answer, provided you can defend it.

Because React's APIs exist to prevent specific bugs, and naming the bug demonstrates you have hit it. "Keys let React match children across renders" is textbook; "without stable keys, deleting a row leaves the typed text on the wrong row" is experience.

Say so and explain what problem it solves and what it costs. Honest conceptual understanding is fine; claiming production experience you do not have collapses at the first specific follow-up.

None beyond the cheat sheet. It is your third track and the marginal return is lowest — protect the time for system design consolidation and rest.

Pick k items uniformly from a stream of unknown length, in one pass, using O(k) memory.

CostO(n) time, O(k) spaceReach for itRandom sample from a stream, random node from a linked list, and any 'pick uniformly without knowing n' problem.
import random
def reservoir(stream, k):
    res = []
    for i, item in enumerate(stream):
        if i < k:
            res.append(item)
        else:
            j = random.randint(0, i)     # keep with probability k/(i+1)
            if j < k: res[j] = item
    return res

# Proof sketch: by induction, after seeing i items every one of them is
# in the reservoir with probability exactly k/i.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Two forty-five-minute coding rounds at hard difficulty, back to back, different problem classes. This is deliberate fatigue training, and the second round is the one being measured.

Why hard, and why two. By now you should be reliable on mediums; the failure mode left is what happens when the problem is genuinely difficult and you are already tired. A real onsite may put the hardest technical round third or fourth, so practising a single fresh round overstates your readiness.

Keep the process identical under difficulty — that is the actual test. Under pressure the discipline is the first thing to go: people skip the brute force, skip stating complexity, and start coding a half-formed idea. Clarify, brute force with complexity, optimal with complexity, then code. If the optimal approach does not come, implement the brute force and say what you would improve — a working suboptimal solution with clear articulation of the gap is a pass in most rubrics; an unfinished optimal attempt is not.

The specific hard-problem trap is spending twenty minutes silently searching for the elegant solution. Give yourself a rule: if you have not found the optimal approach within ten minutes, start on the brute force out loud while continuing to think. You then always have something working, and interviewers frequently give a hint once they see you are moving.

Compare the two recordings for the fatigue signature: did you still clarify in round two, or dive in? Did complexity still come out unprompted? Did you still hand-test, or run out of time? How much silence in round two versus round one? That delta is what you are training against, and it is measurable.

The practical fixes if round two is materially worse are unglamorous and real: eat beforehand, water to hand, take the full break away from the screen, and have a written checklist you glance at to restart the process when your attention drops.

Then stop coding for the day. A third round would produce noise, not signal.

Protocol
round 1  45 min, HARD, class A (say DP)
  break  10 min - away from the screen
round 2  45 min, HARD, class B (say graphs)
then a 45-min design round with NO break   <- the real fatigue test

  while still thinking. Always have something working.

              round 1   round 2
  clarified?              __        __
  complexity unprompted?  __        __
  hand-tested?            __        __
  silence > 20s (count)   __        __

that delta is the thing you are training. Then STOP for the day.
Follow-ups they will ask

Is a working brute force really a pass?

Frequently, yes — with clearly stated complexity and a specific articulation of how you would improve it. Interviewers score problem-solving process and communication heavily, and a candidate who is honest about the gap reads better than one who stalls silently chasing optimal.

What if you cannot even get the brute force?

Then narrate the sub-problem you can solve and build outward. Producing a partial solution with clear reasoning still generates signal; going quiet produces none, which is the only guaranteed failure.

Why not three or four rounds?

Diminishing returns and distorted data. Two plus a design round already exceeds most onsite densities, and beyond that you are measuring exhaustion rather than interview performance.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A forty-five-minute design round immediately after two hard coding rounds, with no break. This is the hardest thing in the schedule and it is deliberately placed here.

Why no break: in a real onsite the design round often lands after two technical rounds, and it is the one where fatigue costs the most — because it demands sustained structure and continuous driving rather than solving one well-defined problem. Candidates who have only practised fresh discover this on the day.

What fatigue does to a design round, specifically. The time-box collapses first — you drift in requirements or dive into a component too early. Then quantification disappears, because estimation takes deliberate effort. Then you stop driving and start answering, waiting for the interviewer to prompt the next area. Then risks and tradeoffs never get said because you run out of time. Knowing that sequence lets you catch yourself in it.

The countermeasure is a written framework you glance at. Have the five phases and their minute markers on a card in front of you. When attention drops, the structure carries you rather than your memory — that is precisely what the card is for, and using it is not cheating, it is what a whiteboard's structure does in a real room.

Deliberately front-load the numbers. Since estimation is the first casualty of tiredness, do it early and write it where the interviewer can see it, so even if you fade later the quantification is already on the board.

Check the recording for one thing above all: how many times did they prompt you? Compare against your day-76 round. A rising prompt count under fatigue is the clearest measurable signal, and it tells you whether your framework is genuinely internalised or only holds when you are fresh.

If this round falls apart, the fix is stamina reps and logistics — not more system design study. Eat before the loop, keep water to hand, and if the real schedule allows, ask for a short break before the design round. That request is normal and interviewers accommodate it.

  3. you stop driving            (answering prompts instead of leading)
  4. risks/tradeoffs never said  (ran out of time)

  FRONT-LOAD the numbers: get them on the board by minute 10 while fresh

fix is stamina + logistics, NOT more study.
Follow-ups they will ask

Is it acceptable to ask for a break in a real onsite?

Yes, and it is normal. A two-minute break between rounds to stand up and drink water is routinely accommodated and materially improves the round that follows. Not asking is the mistake.

What if fatigue is clearly the problem seven days out?

That is fixable, unlike a knowledge gap. Schedule two more back-to-back sequences before the loop, and fix the logistics — sleep, food, hydration, and asking for breaks. Stamina responds quickly to targeted practice.

Should you use notes in a real design round?

A blank page for drawing, yes. A framework card is usually fine to have in a remote interview and unnecessary in person, because the whiteboard itself gives you the structure. Practise with it so you do not need it.

For a function that rises then falls with a single peak, repeatedly discard a third of the range to find the extremum.

CostO(log n) iterationsReach for itOptimising a unimodal function — minimum of a convex cost, best position on a line. Prove unimodality first or the answer is confidently wrong.
def ternary_search(f, lo, hi, iters=200):
    for _ in range(iters):               # fixed count beats an epsilon test
        m1 = lo + (hi - lo) / 3
        m2 = hi - (hi - lo) / 3
        if f(m1) < f(m2): lo = m1        # for a MAXIMUM
        else:             hi = m2
    return (lo + hi) / 2

# Integer version: shrink until hi - lo <= 2, then check each by hand.
# Binary search finds a THRESHOLD; ternary search finds a PEAK.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Second repair day, and the list should now be short and specific. Take every Java gap logged during mocks 4 and 5 (days 80 and 83) and rebuild those topics from first principles, out loud, with working code.

The method is the same as day 78 and it works because it is uncomfortable: teach it out loud from memory first, write the demonstrating code second, open the reference third. Reversing that order — reading then nodding — produces recognition, which feels like learning and is not.

The diagnostic that matters today: if the list is still broad, that is a signal about the timeline rather than about today. With six days left, a short specific list is repairable; a list of eight or ten distinct topics is not. In that case the honest options are to narrow ruthlessly to the three highest-frequency items and accept the rest, or to move the interview. Both are legitimate; pretending a broad list will close in six days is not.

Prioritise by interview frequency, not by discomfort. The instinct is to fix whatever felt worst; the better rule is to fix whatever is most likely to be asked. For Java that ordering is roughly: the hashCode contract and HashMap internals, the memory model and volatile versus atomic, thread pool sizing and the unbounded queue trap, @Transactional proxying, and N+1 diagnosis. An exotic topic you fumbled matters far less than a common one you are merely adequate on.

Separate knowledge gaps from performance gaps once more. Only the knowledge column belongs today. If a mock failure was actually freezing under pressure, no amount of study fixes it — that is day 86's dress rehearsal.

Finish by writing the one-paragraph summary from memory for each repaired topic and adding it to your week-13 material. Then update the physical card: anything that survived two repair days is pure recall and belongs on it.

How do you decide whether to move the interview?

If the mock feedback on day 79 was a clear no-hire and the gaps are knowledge-shaped and numerous, moving it is usually correct — a failed loop often carries a six-to-twelve-month cooldown, which is far more expensive than a delay.

What if the same topic keeps reappearing on the list?

Then the repair method is not working for it — usually because you keep reading rather than producing. Force the code: write it from a blank file, break it deliberately, and explain it to someone. If it survives that, it is genuinely learned.

Should you add new topics you discover you do not know?

No. Six days out, close the known gaps and stop expanding scope. Discovering an unknown is normal and does not mean you are unprepared — no candidate knows everything, and interviewers expect "I have not worked with that" as an answer.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Redraw from memory every design you fumbled in mocks 4 and 5. Blank page, no notes, ten minutes each, then compare against your originals — the same method as day 78 because it is the only test that distinguishes recognition from production.

By this point you should have a stable set of six to eight architectures you can draw cold, covering the distinct shapes rather than specific products: a read-heavy cached service, a write-heavy streaming pipeline, a fan-out feed, a transactional ledger, a search system, a real-time system, and a job scheduler. Most prompts are variations, so the shapes are what transfer.

Check the same four failure patterns in what you produce: no numbers anywhere; a cache or queue drawn but never justified; no partition or shard key; and no failure story per component. Those four account for most of the gap between an adequate and a strong design round, and they are all recall-able once you know they are your pattern.

Then the harder version: draw and narrate simultaneously, recorded. Design rounds are performed — you must draw and talk at once, and doing both is measurably harder than either alone. Check the recording for narration going silent while you draw, which is the specific failure this drill catches.

Prioritise by likelihood again. If your target companies are fintech, spend the time on the ledger, payments, reconciliation and fraud shapes rather than on video transcoding. Being outstanding on the designs adjacent to their product is worth more than being adequate on everything.

Finish by making the framework card, if you have not already: five phases, minute markers, and the three things to say at the close — top risks, what you would build first, and what you would validate. That card is what carries you through a tired round on day 86 and in the real loop.

Keep the drawings. Six hand-drawn architectures you produced from memory are the best possible week-13 revision material, because re-drawing one is a two-minute test rather than a twenty-minute read.

How many designs should be drawable cold?

Six to eight distinct shapes. Beyond that you are memorising products rather than internalising building blocks, and an unseen prompt will still be unseen — the shapes are what generalise.

What if a design still will not stick?

Draw it three times across three days rather than three times today. Spaced repetition works and massed repetition does not, and with six days left you still have room for two or three spacings.

Should you prepare designs specific to your target companies?

Yes — two per company, adjacent to their actual product. It signals genuine interest and it gives you home-field advantage if the prompt lands anywhere near their domain.

Topological sort with a twist: use a heap instead of a queue for the lexicographically smallest order, or track levels for parallel scheduling.

CostO(V log V + E) with a heapReach for itCourse schedule II, alien dictionary, minimum time to finish all tasks with unlimited workers.
import heapq
def lexicographically_smallest_topo(n, edges):
    g = [[] for _ in range(n)]; indeg = [0]*n
    for u, v in edges: g[u].append(v); indeg[v] += 1
    h = [i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0]
    heapq.heapify(h)                     # heap instead of deque
    out = []
    while h:
        u = heapq.heappop(h); out.append(u)
        for v in g[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0: heapq.heappush(h, v)
    return out if len(out) == n else []

# Level-by-level instead gives the minimum time with unlimited parallelism.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Behavioural rounds at Software Engineer probe until they find the limit of your actual involvement, so prepare each story to survive three levels of "and then what happened". A story that is compelling at level one and vague at level three reads as someone else's work — which is the specific thing the interviewer is checking for.

Level one is the story itself in STAR form: the situation, your task, the actions you took, and the result with a number. Two minutes maximum. Level two is the technical detail: what exactly did you change, which files, what was the design, what did you measure. Level three is the counterfactual: what would you do differently, what did you consider and reject, what would have happened if you had not done it, what broke afterwards.

Prepare eight stories covering the standard territory: conflict with a colleague, a failure you owned, taking ownership beyond your remit, working through ambiguity, influencing without authority, disagreeing with someone senior, a tight deadline and what you cut, and mentoring or helping someone. One story can serve two prompts, but do not stretch one across four.

The technical depth is the part to actually rehearse, because that is where Software Engineer candidates separate. For each story, be able to name the code, the numbers and the alternatives — "we reduced the release cycle by 35%" needs "by parallelising the integration test stage and moving the smoke tests behind a flag; the pipeline went from 42 to 27 minutes; I rejected caching the build because the flakiness was in the tests, not the compile".

Use "I" rather than "we" for your own actions, while crediting the team for outcomes. Interviewers are assessing your contribution specifically, and a story told entirely in "we" is impossible to score.

Rehearse out loud and time it. Most people's stories run four minutes when two is right, and the excess is context nobody needed. Cut to the situation in two sentences, then spend the time on your actions and the result.

Have one genuine failure story where the outcome was bad and you learned something specific. A candidate with no failures either has not taken responsibility or is not being honest, and both read poorly.

Follow-ups they will ask

What if a story's number is unimpressive?

Use it honestly and spend the time on the reasoning. A modest, well-understood result beats an impressive one you cannot explain — and interviewers are specifically listening for inflation, so an honest small number builds credibility for everything else you say.

How do you handle a question you have no story for?

Say so and offer the nearest thing: "I have not led a team through that, but here is a smaller version I handled." Inventing a story is worse, because level-three questions will expose it and the round becomes about your honesty rather than your work.

Why is the failure story so important?

Because it tests self-assessment, which is the trait that determines whether someone grows at the next level. A candidate who cannot name a real failure either has not owned anything significant or is not being candid — neither is a hire signal.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Two things to prepare today, and both are about signalling seniority rather than knowledge.

First, your own proposal. Software Engineer hiring tests whether you identify problems, not only whether you solve assigned ones — so have one genuine proposal from your work at FIS, framed as: who is in pain and how often, what the status quo costs in hours or incidents, what you would build, what you would deliberately leave out of v1, how you would roll it out incrementally, what success looks like, and what it costs in engineer-weeks. The quantified cost of the status quo is what turns an opinion into a proposal.

Second, your questions for the interviewer — and these are scored, which most candidates do not realise. Weak questions ask what is publicly knowable ("what stack do you use?"). Strong questions ask how decisions get made, because that is what you actually need to know and it demonstrates you think like someone who will be making them.

The ones worth asking: How does a technical decision get made here — who decides to adopt a new datastore, and what does that process look like? What does on-call actually look like — how many pages a week, and who fixes what they find? How much of the last quarter went to tech debt versus features, and who decides that split? What is the deploy cadence, and how long from merge to production? How is the step from Software Engineer to Senior Engineer evaluated here — what does someone need to demonstrate?

That last one is disproportionately valuable. It signals you are thinking about growth rather than just the offer, it gets you a concrete answer about what the company rewards, and the quality of the answer tells you a great deal — a team with a vague answer usually has vague progression.

Ask one or two per round, not a list, and vary them by interviewer: on-call and deploy cadence for an engineer, tech debt split and progression for a manager. And listen to the answers — a question you asked but did not react to reads as rehearsed.

Prepare a follow-up for each, because the interesting part is usually the second question: "you mentioned two pages a week — what were the last two about?"

strong: "how do technical decisions get made here?"

Follow-ups they will ask

Why does the progression question work so well?

It shows you are evaluating the role rather than just wanting it, and the answer is genuinely useful to you. A team that can describe exactly what Senior Engineer requires has thought about growth; one that cannot usually promotes by tenure.

What if you have no questions left because earlier interviewers answered them?

Say that — "the earlier rounds covered on-call and deploy cadence; what I would still like to understand is X." It shows you were listening across the loop, which reads better than repeating a question.

Should you ask about salary or level in these rounds?

No — that belongs with the recruiter, not the technical interviewers. Asking here shifts the conversation away from the assessment and is usually mildly negative.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Record two things today and cut both by 20%: your ninety-second introduction and your four-minute project walkthrough. These are the most-used and least-rehearsed artefacts in the whole loop — you will deliver the introduction four or five times in one day.

The introduction sets the interviewer's prior for the entire round, and almost everyone's is too long and too chronological. The failure pattern is starting at university and walking forward through every role. Nobody asked for a timeline.

The structure that works is: what you do now and what you own, one concrete thing you built with a number, and one sentence on why you are in this conversation. Ninety seconds. "I'm a backend engineer at FIS working on payment processing — Java, Spring Boot and Kafka. Most of my work is on the event pipeline that processes our transaction flow; the piece I'm most pleased with is cutting an endpoint's latency from a second to forty milliseconds by caching a reference-data lookup. I'm looking for a role with more ownership of system design, which is why this one interested me."

Lead with what you own, not when you joined. Recency and ownership are what the interviewer is calibrating; the chronology is on the CV in front of them.

The four-minute walkthrough needs a diagram you can draw live, because "let me draw this" is far more engaging than describing it. Structure: the problem and its constraint, your design, one hard tradeoff, the outcome with a number, and what you would change now. That tradeoff is the part that makes it a senior story rather than a feature description.

Watch both recordings and cut a fifth. The cuts are always the same: context nobody needed, hedging ("I sort of, kind of, helped with"), and detail that belongs in the answer to a follow-up rather than in the opening. Leave room for questions — the walkthrough should invite them, not pre-empt them.

Rehearse until it is effortless rather than memorised. A recited introduction sounds recited; the goal is knowing the three beats so well that the words vary each time.

Follow-ups they will ask

Why cut 20% specifically?

Because almost every first recording is that much too long, and the excess is context the interviewer did not need. Forcing a fixed cut makes you choose what is load-bearing rather than trimming evenly.

Should the introduction change per company?

The last sentence should — why this role. The first two beats stay constant, which is what makes it deliverable without thinking after a long day.

What if the interviewer interrupts the walkthrough?

Excellent — that is the goal. The walkthrough exists to provoke questions, so stop and follow them. Insisting on finishing your prepared version wastes the part of the conversation that actually generates signal.

Express a linear recurrence as a matrix, then binary-exponentiate it to jump billions of steps in log time.

CostO(k³ log n) for a k-term recurrenceReach for it'n up to 1e18' with a linear recurrence — that constraint is effectively a label for this technique.
MOD = 10**9 + 7
def mat_mul(A, B):
    n = len(A)
    return [[sum(A[i][k]*B[k][j] for k in range(n)) % MOD
             for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]

def mat_pow(M, e):
    n = len(M)
    R = [[int(i == j) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]   # identity
    while e:
        if e & 1: R = mat_mul(R, M)
        M = mat_mul(M, M); e >>= 1
    return R

# Fibonacci: [[1,1],[1,0]]^n gives F(n) in the corner. n = 1e18 is fine.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The full loop in one day, in order, with no notes: forty-five minutes coding, forty-five LLD, forty-five system design, forty-five frontend, forty-five behavioural. Four to five hours with short breaks, exactly as an onsite is scheduled.

The point is stamina and consistency, not any individual round. You have already tested each round type in isolation; what you have not tested is whether round four is as good as round one. That variance is what decides real loops, because a strong first round and a weak fourth averages to a no-hire.

Run it properly: same day, same order, real timers, someone else delivering the prompts, all recorded. Take the breaks you would get — five to ten minutes — and use them as you would on the day: stand up, water, no reviewing notes. Reviewing between rounds feels productive and costs you the recovery.

For the coding round specifically, keep the process identical to when you were fresh: clarify, brute force with complexity, optimal with complexity, code, hand-test. The discipline is the first casualty of fatigue, so this round is measuring whether the process is genuinely automatic or only holds when rested.

Afterwards, compare rounds one and four on the same axes: did you clarify, did complexity come out unprompted, did you hand-test, how much silence. Write the numbers down — a fatigue curve you can see is actionable in a way a vague sense of tiredness is not.

Then ask for a hire/no-hire call on the loop as a whole, not per round, because that is how the real decision is made. Ask specifically: which round would have sunk this, and what would have changed it.

And after today, stop adding material. Days 87 to 90 are consolidation and rest. Whatever is not known now will not be learned in four days, and arriving rested is worth more than any remaining topic — this is the last day of the schedule that demands anything from you.

Follow-ups they will ask

Is a full simulation really necessary?

It is the only way to find out how you perform in hours three and four, which is where most loops are decided. Every round you have practised was a fresh round; the real one will not be.

What if you cannot get someone to run five rounds?

Split it across two consecutive days, or use an AI interviewer for the middle rounds and a person for the first and last. Preserve the ordering and the lack of breaks between — that is the variable being tested.

What if the dress rehearsal goes badly?

Diagnose whether it was fatigue or knowledge. Fatigue is fixable with logistics and rest in the remaining days; a knowledge gap this late is not, and the honest response is to narrow scope or consider moving the interview.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The design round of the dress rehearsal, on a prompt you have never seen, in hour three of the day. That placement is deliberate — it is where the design round usually falls in a real onsite and where the framework is most likely to collapse.

Run the time-box with a visible timer and front-load the numbers, because estimation is the first casualty of fatigue. Get a QPS figure and a storage figure on the board by minute ten while you still have the attention to compute them.

Use the framework card. You built it on day 84 precisely for this — when attention drops, the structure should come from the card rather than from working memory. That is not a crutch; it is what the whiteboard's own structure does in a real room.

Then ask the question that matters and let the silence sit: "Would you hire me at Software Engineer based on that round?" Ask it plainly. People soften feedback unless you make it explicit that you want the real answer, and four days out an encouraging non-answer is worth nothing.

Push for the specific version if they hedge: which part would have caused a debrief objection, and what single change would have removed it. "Solid" is not actionable; "you never named a partition key, so I could not tell whether you had thought about the data layer" is.

Take the answer at face value and do not defend the round. Arguing costs you the honest version of everything they say afterwards, and the hesitation itself is the signal regardless of whether you think it was fair.

That answer is the input to your final week. If it is a clear yes, days 87 to 90 are consolidation and rest as planned. If it is a hesitant yes, spend day 87 on whatever caused the hesitation and then consolidate. If it is a no and the gaps are knowledge-shaped and numerous, moving the interview is a legitimate and often correct decision — a failed loop typically carries a six-to-twelve-month cooldown, which is far more expensive than a delay of a few weeks.

Whatever the answer, this is the last assessment. From tomorrow the work is compression and rest.

Follow-ups they will ask

Is moving the interview really a reasonable option?

Yes, and it is under-used. Most companies have a cooldown of six to twelve months after a failed loop, so a four-week delay to close real gaps is cheap by comparison. The instinct to push ahead because the date is booked costs people a year.

What if different mock interviewers disagree?

Weight the most experienced one, and look for what they agree on. Disagreement usually means you are near the boundary — which tells you consistency rather than capability is the remaining problem, and that is fixed by reps.

What if the feedback is a clear yes?

Believe it, stop assessing, and switch entirely to consolidation and rest. Continuing to seek reassurance through more mocks in the final days costs energy and changes nothing.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The frontend round of the dress rehearsal, in hour four. This is the round most likely to be affected by fatigue, because it demands sustained narration while typing — two things that both degrade when you are tired.

The specific check today: did you still scope in the first three minutes, or did you start typing? Under fatigue the temptation is to skip straight to code because it feels like progress. Compare against your day-79 round — if you scoped then and did not now, that is your fatigue signature, and it is fixable with logistics rather than study.

Verify the two highest-value habits held: the loading, error and empty states, and the cheap accessibility work. These are checklist items, so they are exactly what a tired candidate drops — and dropping them is a disproportionate loss because they are the clearest signal of production experience in the whole round.

Check the recording for silence while typing. Frontend rounds tempt you into heads-down coding because there is visible output on the screen, and in hour four that temptation is much stronger. The interviewer still needs to hear the reasoning; visible code is not a substitute for audible thinking.

Close the round the way you would on the day: "with more time I would add X and Y". That closing converts an unfinished implementation into demonstrated judgement, and it takes twenty seconds.

Then ask your partner one question: across the whole day, which round was weakest and why. Not per-round feedback — you have had plenty of that — but the comparison, because a real debrief compares rounds and a single weak round can sink an otherwise strong loop.

And then stop. This is the last assessment in the plan. From tomorrow the work is compression onto three pages and rest — nothing you learn in the remaining four days will change the outcome, and arriving rested will.

Follow-ups they will ask

Why is the frontend round most affected by fatigue?

Because it requires narrating and typing simultaneously for forty-five minutes. Both degrade with tiredness, and the visible output on screen makes it feel like you are still performing when the audible signal has stopped.

What if you drop the states and accessibility under fatigue?

That is a logistics fix, not a study fix — eat, hydrate, take the breaks, and keep a four-item checklist visible. Those items are recall under pressure, and a written prompt restores them instantly.

What should you do with the whole-day feedback?

Use it to decide where the last consolidation day goes. If one round was clearly weakest and the gap is small, day 87 addresses it; if the gap is large, that is information about the timeline rather than about tomorrow.

DRESS REHEARSAL - unseen pair

One medium and one hard you have never attempted - pick blind from the NeetCode 150. Full interview conditions: no notes, narrate throughout, 45 minutes.

Insert numbers into a binary trie of their bits. To maximise XOR with a query, greedily walk toward the opposite bit at every level.

CostO(n · 32) timeReach for itMaximum XOR of two numbers, maximum XOR subarray, and XOR queries with constraints.
class BitTrie:
    def __init__(self): self.root = {}
    def insert(self, x):
        node = self.root
        for b in range(31, -1, -1):
            bit = x >> b & 1
            node = node.setdefault(bit, {})
    def max_xor(self, x):
        node, res = self.root, 0
        for b in range(31, -1, -1):
            bit = x >> b & 1
            want = 1 - bit                # opposite bit maximises XOR
            if want in node: res |= 1 << b; node = node[want]
            else:            node = node[bit]
        return res

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

One page, written from memory, no notes open. That constraint is the entire exercise — what you cannot recall today is what you must review tomorrow, and copying from your notes tells you nothing.

What earns a place on the page. Collections complexity: the operations for ArrayList, LinkedList, ArrayDeque, HashMap, TreeMap, PriorityQueue, and why LinkedList loses to ArrayList despite the Big-O. HashMap internals: load factor 0.75, treeify at 8, untreeify at 6, capacity ≥ 64, and why capacity is a power of two. Concurrency primitives: what volatile guarantees and what it does not, the happens-before edges, CAS and the ABA problem, LongAdder versus AtomicLong, the ThreadPoolExecutor submission order and the unbounded-queue trap, CPU versus IO pool sizing. JVM: the memory areas, why -Xmx = container limit gets you OOMKilled, the OOM message variants, retained versus shallow size, the diagnostic sequence for high CPU. The five contracts: equals, hashCode, compareTo, clone, toString. Spring: the proxy mechanism and the three symptoms it explains, propagation, the N+1 fixes.

What does not earn a place is anything derivable from a mechanism you hold. If "it is a proxy" is on the page, self-invocation, private methods and final classes do not need to be — write the mechanism, not its consequences. That compression is what makes the page useful rather than a second set of notes.

If it does not fit on one page, you have not compressed enough. The constraint forces you to distinguish what you must recall from what you can derive, and that distinction is exactly what you need under interview pressure.

Write it by hand if you can. Handwriting is slower, which forces selection, and the physical page is glanceable between rounds in a way a document is not.

Then note the gaps. Anything you reached for and could not produce goes on tomorrow's short review list — that list, not the page, is the real output of today.

Follow-ups they will ask

Why from memory rather than curated from notes?

Because the page is not the deliverable — the retrieval attempt is. A beautifully organised page copied from notes tells you nothing about what you actually hold, which is the only thing that matters in four days.

What if the page is mostly blank?

Then you have found a genuine problem while there is still time to act, which is better than finding it in the loop. Fill the blanks from your notes, mark them, and re-attempt the page tomorrow from memory.

Should you keep adding to it over the remaining days?

Only by removing. Each day, cross off anything that has become automatic. A shrinking page is evidence of consolidation; a growing one means you are still learning, which is the wrong activity now.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

One page, from memory. System design has the most material and compresses the best, because most of it derives from a small number of numbers and a fixed framework.

The latency ladder — L1 ~1ns, RAM ~100ns, SSD random read ~100µs, same-datacentre round trip ~0.5ms, cross-continent ~150ms. These anchor every estimate and every caching argument you will make, so they must be reflexive rather than recalled.

Capacity estimation formulas: DAU × requests per user ÷ 86,400 for average QPS, times two or three for peak; records per day × size × retention × replication × index overhead for storage; and the reminder to always ask the read:write ratio first, because it drives the storage decision more than any other input.

The building blocks, as a checklist you can run down in a round: load balancer, CDN, API gateway, cache, queue or log, database with replication and sharding, object storage, search index, and a background pipeline. Having them as a list means you never stare at a blank board.

The decision rules that come up most: the consistency models with the symptom of each violation; the cache patterns and what each fails at; queue versus log and the three delivery semantics; why exactly-once delivery is impossible; the isolation levels and their anomalies; keyset versus offset pagination; saga versus 2PC; and availability arithmetic — serial multiplies, 99.9% is 43 minutes a month.

Your framework with minute markers — 5 requirements, 5 estimates, 10 high level, 20 deep dive, 5 risks — plus the three things to say at the close: top risks, what you would build first, what you would validate.

The page should be mostly numbers and lists, not prose, because that is what you cannot derive under pressure. Everything conceptual you can reason to; the latency ladder and the availability arithmetic you cannot.

One page
LATENCY LADDER  L1 ~1ns | RAM ~100ns | SSD ~100us | same-DC ~0.5ms | cross-cont ~150ms

ESTIMATION  QPS = DAU x req/user / 86,400;  peak = 2-3x
            storage = rows/day x size x retention x replication(3) x index(1.3)
            ALWAYS ask read:write ratio first

AVAILABILITY  serial multiplies (0.999^3 = 99.7%)
              99.9% = 43 min/month | 99.99% = 4.3 min

BUILDING BLOCKS  LB | CDN | gateway | cache | queue/log | DB (replica, shard)
                 object store | search index | background pipeline

DECISIONS  consistency models + the SYMPTOM of each violation
           cache patterns + what each fails at | queue vs log | delivery semantics
           isolation levels + anomalies | keyset vs offset | saga vs 2PC

FRAMEWORK  5 req | 5 est | 10 high level | 20 deep dive | 5 risks
           close with: top 3 risks | build first | what to validate
Follow-ups they will ask

Why prioritise numbers over concepts on this page?

Because concepts are derivable under pressure and numbers are not. You can reason your way to why a cache helps; you cannot reason your way to the fact that a cross-continent round trip is 150ms, and that number is what makes your argument concrete.

Should the framework be on the page if you have it on a card?

Yes — the card is for glancing at during a round, the page is for revision. Writing it again from memory is another retrieval rep, which is the point of the exercise.

What if you cannot recall the latency numbers?

Then they are the highest-priority item for the remaining days, because every estimate and every caching justification depends on them. They are pure memorisation and take fifteen minutes to fix.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

One page, from memory, same rule. React compresses well because almost everything derives from the render model — so the page should hold the mechanism plus the small set of facts you cannot derive.

The render model first, because it is the root: setState enqueues and schedules; the render phase is pure and interruptible and produces a new element tree; the commit phase applies mutations synchronously, then layout effects, then paint, then passive effects. Reconciliation matches children by position unless a key overrides it. Automatic batching covers promises and timeouts since React 18.

Hook rules and why: hooks are stored in a linked list on the fiber and resolved by call order, so a conditional call misaligns every subsequent hook. That one mechanism explains the whole rule set — write the mechanism, not the four rules.

The performance levers in the order you would apply them: identify whether the problem is render count, render duration, or a blocked main thread; then memo and selectors for count, virtualization and memoized derivations for duration, and workers or transitions for blocking. Note that memo is defeated by inline objects, JSX children, and context.

The facts you cannot derive and therefore must write down: the ARIA combobox and dialog attribute sets, the AbortController pattern, the windowing maths (start = floor(scrollTop / rowHeight), visible = ceil(viewportHeight / rowHeight), plus overscan), the three XSS vectors in React, and when CSRF applies.

Your frontend design framework — requirements, API contract, component architecture, state and caching, performance budget, accessibility, error and empty states, observability — with the reminder that the API contract is the differentiating phase and component architecture is the one people over-spend on.

Keep it to one page, and remember this is your third track: if the Java or system design page is weak, spend the remaining time there instead. Knowing where not to spend the last days is its own judgement.

One page
RENDER MODEL  setState enqueues -> render phase (pure, interruptible)
              -> commit (sync DOM) -> layout effects -> PAINT -> passive effects
              reconciliation matches by position unless a key overrides
              batching covers promises + timers (React 18)

HOOKS  stored in a linked list on the fiber, resolved BY CALL ORDER
       -> that one fact explains every rule. Write the mechanism, not the rules.

PERF   diagnose first: render COUNT | render DURATION | blocked main thread
       count    -> memo, selectors, state placement, split context
       duration -> virtualize, memoize derivations
       blocked  -> worker, transitions
       memo is defeated by: inline objects | JSX children | context

NOT DERIVABLE (write these down):
  ARIA combobox + dialog attributes | AbortController pattern
  windowing: start = floor(scrollTop/rowH), visible = ceil(viewportH/rowH) + overscan
  XSS vectors: dangerouslySetInnerHTML | javascript: URLs | spread onto DOM
  CSRF applies only with COOKIE auth

FRAMEWORK  requirements | API contract | architecture | state | perf | a11y |
           error+empty | observability      (API contract is the differentiator)
Follow-ups they will ask

Why write the mechanism rather than the rules?

Because one mechanism generates many rules, and under pressure you can regenerate them. Memorising four hook rules is four things to forget; knowing they are a positional linked list is one thing that produces all four.

How much time should React get in the final days?

Least of the three, unless the day-86 feedback said otherwise. It is your third track and the Software Engineer bar is decided primarily on backend and design — deliberately under-investing here is the right call.

What if the page ends up mostly the not-derivable list?

That is a good sign — it means the conceptual material is genuinely internalised and only the arbitrary facts remain. Those are exactly what a glanceable page is for.

Light - stay warm
  • Valid PalindromeEasy
  • Maximum Depth of Binary TreeEasy

For each bar, find how far it extends left and right before hitting something shorter. One monotonic stack pass gives both.

CostO(n) time, O(n) spaceReach for itLargest rectangle in a histogram, maximal rectangle in a binary matrix, trapping rain water.
def largest_rectangle(h):
    st, best = [], 0                      # st holds indices, heights increasing
    for i, x in enumerate(h + [0]):       # sentinel 0 flushes the stack
        while st and h[st[-1]] >= x:
            height = h[st.pop()]
            left = st[-1] + 1 if st else 0
            best = max(best, height * (i - left))
        st.append(i)
    return best

# Maximal rectangle in a 0/1 matrix: run this on each row's running
# column heights. That is the whole reduction.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Interview formats vary more than people expect, and preparing for the wrong one is a self-inflicted wound. Two days out, an hour of research changes what you rehearse.

The three broad styles. Algorithm-heavy — product companies and most FAANG-style loops: LeetCode-shaped problems, optimal complexity expected, one or two rounds. LLD-heavy — increasingly common at Indian product companies and at many fintechs: a sixty-minute class-design round on a vending machine, parking lot, Splitwise or an ATM, where extensibility and pattern use matter far more than complexity. Core-Java-heavy — common at services companies and some enterprise teams: rapid-fire questions on collections internals, concurrency, JVM and Spring, with less coding.

How to find out, in rough order of reliability: ask the recruiter directly — they will usually tell you the round structure and often the format, and asking signals preparation rather than weakness; check Glassdoor and LeetCode discuss for recent reports on that specific company and role; ask anyone in your network who has interviewed there; and read the job description for tells — "low-level design" or "object-oriented design" in the requirements is a strong signal.

Then rehearse accordingly. If it is LLD-heavy, spend today on one more LLD prompt with the extension question, since that round rewards a different skill from algorithms and you have only practised it twice. If it is core-Java-heavy, run the rapid-fire cards again. If it is algorithm-heavy, do one timed medium and stop.

Also confirm the practical shape: how many rounds, how long, on what platform, whether you can use an IDE or must write in a shared editor without autocomplete, and whether there is a take-home. Writing Java without autocomplete is a genuinely different experience — if that is the format, practise once in a plain editor today rather than discovering it live.

Do not learn new material today. The purpose is to point the rehearsal you have already done at the right target, not to expand scope two days out.

Research

  algorithm-heavy  LeetCode-shaped, optimal expected      -> 1 timed medium, stop
  LLD-heavy        60-min class design + extension test   -> 1 more LLD prompt
  core-Java-heavy  collections/concurrency/JVM rapid fire -> re-run the cards
