  ask the recruiter - they will usually tell you, and asking signals preparation
  Glassdoor / LeetCode discuss, filtered to recent + this role
  anyone in your network who has interviewed there
  the JD itself - "low-level design" / "OOD" in the requirements is a tell

confirm the practical shape:
  rounds, duration, platform, IDE or plain shared editor, take-home?
  no autocomplete? -> practise once in a plain editor TODAY
Follow-ups they will ask

Is it acceptable to ask the recruiter about the format?

Yes, and it is expected — recruiters want you to do well because their metrics depend on it. Ask what the rounds are, how long, and what each focuses on. Candidates who ask are usually better prepared, and recruiters know that.

What if you cannot determine the format?

Prepare for algorithm-heavy as the default, since it is the most common, but spend thirty minutes reviewing your LLD structure so a design round does not catch you cold. The two require different openings but share the clarify-first discipline.

Should you learn a new topic if the research reveals a gap?

No. Two days out, point your existing preparation at the right target and accept the gap. Learning something new now is shallow and displaces rest, which costs more than the gap does.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Prepare two design prompts per target company, drawn from their actual product domain. This is one of the highest-return hours available this late, for three reasons.

It gives you home-field advantage. Interviewers frequently pick prompts adjacent to what they build, because that is what they can evaluate deeply. If you interview at a payments company and have already worked through a payment gateway integration and a ledger design, there is a real chance the prompt lands on ground you have covered.

It signals genuine interest. Being able to say "I imagine the interesting problem for you is idempotency across retries when the provider times out" reads completely differently from a generic answer. It shows you thought about their business rather than just their job posting.

And it surfaces good questions for the end of the round, which is separately scored.

How to choose the two: pick their core product flow and their hardest-looking scaling problem. For a payments company: an idempotent charge API with reconciliation, and a double-entry ledger at scale. For a lending or banking product: a KYC workflow and a risk-scoring pipeline. For a trading platform: an order matching engine and market-data fan-out. For a general SaaS: multi-tenancy isolation and a metering and billing pipeline.

Work each one to the level of your framework, not exhaustively: requirements, rough numbers, the components, the one interesting deep dive, and the top three risks. Thirty minutes each is enough — the goal is familiarity with the shape, not a memorised answer, because a memorised answer sounds memorised and collapses at the first variation.

Given your background, the fintech shapes are where you are strongest, so lean into that: ledgers, payment retries and reconciliation, idempotency, and fraud pipelines. That is your differentiator — most candidates cannot design a ledger, and you have spent a week on it.

Two per company
pick: (1) their core product flow  (2) their hardest scaling problem

payments   -> idempotent charge API + reconciliation | double-entry ledger at scale
banking    -> KYC workflow | risk scoring pipeline
trading    -> order matching engine | market data fan-out
SaaS       -> multi-tenancy isolation | metering + billing
marketplace-> search + ranking | matching / dispatch

30 min each, to framework depth only:
  requirements | rough numbers | components | ONE deep dive | top 3 risks

not a memorised answer - that sounds memorised and breaks on any variation.
familiarity with the SHAPE is the goal.

your edge: ledgers, payment retries, reconciliation, idempotency. Lean into it.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if the prompt is nothing like what you prepared?

You lose nothing — the framework is the same and the preparation was thirty minutes. The asymmetry is favourable: small cost, occasionally a large payoff, and it improves your questions either way.

Is it obvious if you have pre-prepared a design?

Only if you recite it. Work the framework live as you would with any prompt; the preparation shows up as fluency with the domain vocabulary and better instincts about what matters, not as a rehearsed script.

How does this help with the questions you ask?

It gives you specific ones. "How do you handle the timeout-but-charged case with your provider?" demonstrates far more than any generic question about culture or stack, and it usually starts a genuine engineering conversation.

Today's version is the tailored walkthrough with a live diagram, which is different from the general one you recorded on day 85. Same four minutes, but pointed at each specific company.

The diagram is the point. Saying "let me draw this" and producing a clean architecture in ninety seconds changes the register of the conversation — it becomes a discussion between engineers rather than a recitation. Practise drawing it until it is fluid: the same boxes, the same order, every time. On a whiteboard or a shared canvas, hesitancy while drawing is very visible.

Keep the structure — problem and constraint, design, one hard tradeoff, outcome with a number, what you would change — but tailor which tradeoff you lead with to the company. Interviewing at a payments company: lead with the idempotency and concurrency question on the approval workflow. At a product company that cares about frontend: lead with the state and rendering decisions. At an infrastructure-leaning team: lead with the deployment and CI pipeline. Same project, different emphasis.

Prepare the honest weakness for each version, because the follow-up is always "what would you change?" For Unsent that is the concurrency control on approvals, the AI generation sitting on the request path with unbounded third-party latency, and the absence of an idempotency key on the approval endpoint. Volunteering those reads as judgement; being shown them reads as inexperience.

Rehearse the drawing separately from the talking, then together. Doing both at once is measurably harder, which is why the day-78 drill applies here too — record it and check the narration does not go silent while your hand is moving.

Time it at four minutes and stop there. The walkthrough exists to provoke questions, not to pre-empt them; if you are still talking at seven minutes you have used up the part of the conversation where you would have demonstrated depth.

Then stop preparing React. Days 89 and 90 are review and rest only.

Why does drawing matter so much?

It converts a monologue into a shared artefact you can both point at, and it demonstrates you can communicate architecture visually — which is most of what a design discussion is. It also slows you down usefully.

What if you are asked to walk through a work project instead?

Have that version ready too — the FIS Kafka pipeline, same structure. Some interviewers prefer production work because the constraints are real; have both and let them choose.

Should you volunteer the weaknesses unprompted?

Yes, one of them, at the end: "the thing I'd change is X". It pre-empts the question, demonstrates self-assessment, and steers the follow-up onto ground you have thought about.

Trading a guaranteed answer for a much simpler or faster one that is correct with overwhelming probability. Randomisation also defends against adversarial inputs.

CostVaries — usually O(n) expectedReach for itRandomised quicksort pivots, reservoir sampling, randomised hashing bases, and shuffling.
import random

# Fisher-Yates shuffle - the only correct in-place shuffle
def shuffle(a):
    for i in range(len(a) - 1, 0, -1):
        j = random.randint(0, i)          # 0..i INCLUSIVE. Getting this
        a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]           # range wrong biases the result.
    return a

# Randomise to defend against worst cases:
#   quicksort pivot        -> avoids the O(n^2) adversarial input
#   hash base chosen at runtime -> defeats anti-hash tests
#   randomised treap       -> balanced without rotation bookkeeping

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Review your cheat sheet only. No new topics — none. This is the instruction and it is the hardest one in the plan to follow, because anxiety the day before an interview manifests as an urge to study.

Why cramming now actively hurts. New material twenty-four hours out is shallow, so it does not become recallable under pressure — but it does consume working memory and sleep, both of which the loop measures directly. The trade is unambiguous: you swap a small chance of being asked the new thing for a large certain cost to everything else.

What to actually do: read your one page from day 87, out loud, once. Note anything that feels shaky and give it fifteen minutes maximum. Then close it. Twenty to thirty minutes of review is enough; two hours is counterproductive.

Specifically confirm the four that appear in nearly every Java Software Engineer loop — the hashCode contract and the exact HashMap failure, the memory model with volatile versus atomic, thread pool sizing with the unbounded-queue trap, and @Transactional proxying with self-invocation. If you can explain each in under two minutes without notes, the Java track is done.

Then handle logistics, which is the genuinely productive use of today: confirm the time and time zone, test the platform and your camera, microphone and internet, have water and paper and a pen to hand, book a quiet room, charge everything, and check nothing is scheduled immediately before or after. Removing avoidable stress from tomorrow is worth more than any revision.

And sleep. Sleep affects recall speed and working memory more than anything else you could do today. A well-rested candidate who knows 85% of the material outperforms an exhausted one who knows 95%, because the loop tests retrieval under pressure rather than storage.

The discipline of stopping is the same one you will need between rounds tomorrow. Practise it today.

Follow-ups they will ask

What if you realise you do not know something important?

Accept it. Nobody knows everything, and "I have not worked with that" is a perfectly acceptable interview answer. Trying to learn it tonight produces a shallow answer that collapses at the follow-up and costs you sleep.

Is any review counterproductive?

Reviewing your own summary is calming and useful. Opening new material, watching tutorials, or attempting fresh problems is not — those raise anxiety by revealing gaps you cannot close in time.

How much sleep actually matters?

A great deal. Retrieval speed, working memory and emotional regulation under pressure all degrade measurably with a short night, and all three are exactly what the loop measures. Treat sleep as part of the preparation, not as what is left over.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Two things today, both about the conversation rather than the technical content.

First, finalise your questions. Have four or five ready, varied by interviewer, and remember these are scored — a candidate with sharp questions reads as someone evaluating the role rather than hoping for it. The strong ones ask how decisions get made: how a technical decision is made and who decides to adopt a new datastore; what on-call actually looks like in pages per week and who fixes what they find; how much of the last quarter went to tech debt versus features and who decides that split; the deploy cadence from merge to production; and how the step from Software Engineer to Senior Engineer is evaluated. Prepare a follow-up for each, because the second question is where the honest answer is — "two pages a week, what were the last two about?"

Second, prepare for the compensation conversation, because it usually starts before you are ready. The rules are simple and worth rehearsing out loud once. Do not name a number first — when asked your expectation, deflect once: "I'd rather understand the role and level first; what's the band for this position?" Most recruiters will share it. If pressed, give a researched range rather than a point, anchored on market data for the level and city, not on your current salary. Never disclose your current compensation — it anchors the offer to your past rather than the role's value, and in many places you are not obliged to.

Evaluate the whole package, not just base: base, bonus, equity and its vesting schedule, and — for a Software Engineer role — the level, which matters more than a few percent of salary because it determines your next three years of scope and progression.

When an offer arrives, always ask for time — a few days is completely standard — and never accept on the call, however enthusiastic you feel. And if you negotiate, do it once, politely, with a specific number and a reason.

Then stop. No system design study today. Read your one page once and close it.

     follow-up: "what were the last two about?"
  tech debt vs features last quarter - who decides the split?
  deploy cadence: merge to production, how long?
  how is Software Engineer -> Senior Engineer evaluated? what must someone demonstrate?

COMPENSATION
  do NOT name a number first -> "what's the band for this position?"
  if pressed: a researched RANGE for the level + city, not your current salary
  never disclose current compensation - it anchors the offer to your past
  evaluate: base + bonus + equity (and vesting) + LEVEL   <- level matters most
  always ask for a few days. Never accept on the call.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if they insist on a number before proceeding?

Give a researched range with a stated basis: "based on market data for Software Engineer in this city, I'd expect X to Y, and I'm flexible depending on the overall package." A range with a reason is defensible; a number without one becomes the ceiling.

Why does level matter more than salary?

Because level determines scope, the problems you are trusted with, and your trajectory for the next few years — and salary follows level. Accepting a lower level for slightly more money is the most common expensive mistake candidates make.

Is negotiating risky?

Very rarely. Offers are almost never withdrawn for a polite, single, specific counter with a reason. The far more common outcome is a modest improvement and no downside.

Do a full dry run of your introduction and resume walkthrough today, timed — the introduction at ninety seconds, the walkthrough at four minutes. These are the two things you will deliver most often tomorrow, and they are the two people rehearse least.

The introduction sets the interviewer's prior for the entire round. You will give it four or five times, to people who have skimmed your CV in the ninety seconds before the call. Whatever you lead with is what they will believe you are — so lead with what you own now, not with when you graduated.

Time it honestly and cut to fit. If it runs past ninety seconds, the excess is almost always chronology or context nobody needed. Three beats only: what you do now and what you own, one concrete thing you built with a number, one sentence on why this conversation.

The goal is effortless, not memorised. Rehearse until you know the three beats so well that the words vary each time — a recited introduction is audibly recited and it makes everything after it sound rehearsed too. If you find yourself reciting, do it three more times deliberately changing the wording.

Then the walkthrough with the diagram, four minutes, drawn live. Check that the narration does not go silent while you draw, because that is the specific failure and it is very visible on a shared screen.

Record both once more and watch them at normal speed. Look for hedging — "I sort of helped with", "we kind of built" — which undercuts everything it touches. Say "I built", "I designed", "I chose", and credit the team for outcomes rather than for your own actions.

Then stop. No React study today. Read your one page from day 87 once, close it, and spend the remaining time on logistics and rest. Tomorrow is skim and go.

Follow-ups they will ask

Why does the introduction matter so much?

Because it is delivered four or five times to people forming a first impression in the first ninety seconds, and impressions formed early colour how ambiguous answers later in the round are interpreted. It is the highest-leverage ninety seconds you control completely.

How do you stop it sounding rehearsed?

Rehearse the beats rather than the sentences, and deliberately vary the wording each time you practise. Memorising a script produces a delivery that is audibly a script, which undercuts the content.

What if you are nervous and it comes out badly?

Note it, take a breath, and carry on — interviewers discount early nerves far more than candidates expect. What they do not discount is a candidate who never settles, which is precisely what rehearsing this to the point of effortlessness prevents.

Java · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Skim your one page. Confirm four things. Then stop.

The four that appear in nearly every Java Software Engineer loop, each explainable in under two minutes without notes: the hashCode contract and the exact HashMap failure when you break it — the entry sits in an unreachable bucket, so get returns null and it can never be removed; the Java Memory Model — happens-before, what volatile guarantees (visibility and ordering) and what it does not (atomicity of compound actions), and why i++ is still a race; thread pool sizing — cores for CPU-bound, cores × (1 + wait/service) for IO-bound, and the unbounded-queue trap where maximumPoolSize is never reached; and @Transactional proxying — it is an AOP proxy, so a self-call bypasses it entirely, private and final methods do nothing, and checked exceptions commit by default.

If you can explain all four cleanly, the Java track is ready. That is the whole check — do not extend it into a general review, because a broad skim today finds gaps you cannot close and costs you calm you cannot replace.

Then genuinely stop. No new problems, no new topics, no tutorials. The instinct on the morning of an interview is to fill the time with study, and it reliably makes the rounds worse — you arrive with a full working memory and a raised heart rate, which are the two worst conditions for retrieval under pressure.

What actually helps in the last hours: eat properly, be somewhere quiet ten minutes early, have water and paper to hand, and give yourself a few minutes of nothing before the first round rather than cramming up to the moment it starts.

And between rounds tomorrow, do not review. Stand up, drink water, reset. The temptation to look something up after a round that felt shaky is strong and it costs you the next one — which, in a debrief, is weighted just as heavily.

You have done ninety days of this. The preparation is done; today is only about arriving able to use it.

Final check
explain each in under 2 minutes, no notes:

  1. hashCode contract  -> equal objects must have equal hashCodes
     break it: entry lands in bucket A, lookup computes bucket B
     -> get() returns null, entry is unreachable and unremovable

  2. JMM  -> happens-before; volatile = visibility + ordering, NOT atomicity
     i++ is read-modify-write, so still a race

  3. pool sizing -> CPU: cores | IO: cores x (1 + wait/service)
     unbounded queue -> maximumPoolSize never reached -> OOM instead of reject

  4. @Transactional -> AOP proxy. Self-call bypasses it. Private/final: nothing.
     Checked exceptions COMMIT by default.

all four clean? -> done. Close the page.
no new problems. No new topics. Between rounds: stand up, water, do NOT review.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if one of the four is shaky this morning?

Give it ten minutes with your own summary, then stop regardless. Ten minutes on a known topic is repair; an hour is anxiety, and it displaces the composure that matters more than the topic does.

Should you do a warm-up problem before the first round?

One easy problem you have solved before, purely to get into the rhythm — not a new one. A failed warm-up half an hour before a loop is the worst possible start.

What do you do if a round goes badly?

Let it go completely and reset before the next. Debriefs weigh the whole loop, and candidates recover from one weak round constantly. Carrying it forward is what turns one weak round into three.

System Design · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Skim your one page. Confirm you can drive the framework end to end without prompting. Then stop.

The framework, said out loud once: five minutes requirements — functional, non-functional, and what you are explicitly scoping out; five minutes estimates — DAU to QPS to peak to storage, at one significant figure, with assumptions stated; ten minutes high level — components and data flow, then ask where they want to go deep; twenty minutes deep dive — a data model with real fields, a partition key with a justification, indexes, the API contract, and failure behaviour; five minutes tradeoffs — and close with your top three risks and what you would build first.

Confirm the numbers are reflexive, because they are the only part you cannot derive: the latency ladder (L1 ~1ns, RAM ~100ns, SSD ~100µs, same-datacentre ~0.5ms, cross-continent ~150ms), the QPS formula, the peak multiplier of two to three, and the availability arithmetic — serial dependencies multiply, and 99.9% is 43 minutes a month.

The two behaviours that decide this round, and they are worth saying to yourself once this morning: get a number on the board by minute ten, and drive rather than wait to be prompted. Almost every piece of feedback on design rounds reduces to one of those two.

Then stop. Do not review designs, do not read another architecture, do not open your notes between rounds. If a design round tomorrow lands on something unfamiliar, the framework is what carries you — and the framework is the thing you have rehearsed most.

One last reframe worth holding: a design round is a conversation between two engineers about a problem, not an examination. Ask questions, state assumptions, say when you do not know something and reason from constraints anyway. Candidates who treat it as a discussion perform better than candidates who treat it as a test, and that is as much a decision as a skill.

You are prepared. Go and have the conversation.

Final check

  10  high level    components + data flow, then ASK where to go deep
  20  deep dive     real fields | partition key + WHY | indexes | API | failure behaviour
   5  tradeoffs     top 3 risks + what you would build first

numbers must be reflexive (the only part you cannot derive):
  L1 ~1ns | RAM ~100ns | SSD ~100us | same-DC ~0.5ms | cross-continent ~150ms
  serial availability multiplies | 99.9% = 43 min/month

the two behaviours that decide the round:
  1. a number on the board by minute 10
  2. DRIVE - do not wait to be prompted

then stop. It is a conversation between engineers, not an examination.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if the prompt is a domain you have never touched?

Say so and reason from constraints — requirements, estimates, and the building blocks, which do not change. Interviewers give unfamiliar prompts deliberately to see exactly that, and driving through unfamiliarity is a stronger signal than recalling a familiar design.

What if you freeze at the start?

Start with requirements out loud, because it is the one phase that needs no knowledge — just questions. Asking three clarifying questions gets you talking and buys you the minute you need to settle.

Is it acceptable to say you do not know something?

Yes, and it is expected. "I have not used that; here is how I would evaluate it against these criteria" is a strong answer. Inventing detail is the failure, because the next question always finds it.

React · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Skim your one page. Confirm two things. Then you are done.

The render model, explainable cleanly: setState enqueues an update and schedules work — it does not change anything immediately, which is why state is a snapshot of the current render. The render phase is pure and interruptible and produces a new element tree, which React diffs against the previous one, matching children by position unless a key overrides it. The commit phase applies mutations synchronously, then runs layout effects, then the browser paints, then passive effects run. That single sequence explains keys, effect timing, the useLayoutEffect flicker, and why render must be pure.

Your performance toolkit, in the order you apply it: diagnose first — is it render count, render duration, or a blocked main thread? Then render count is fixed with memoization, selector granularity, state placement and splitting context; render duration with virtualization and memoized derivations; and a blocked main thread with a worker or a transition. And remember memo is defeated by inline objects, JSX children, and context.

If both are clean, the React track is ready. It is your third track and it does not need to be your strongest — be confident about the render model and the common failure modes, and honest that your depth is on the backend. A clear self-assessment reads far better than uniform shallow claims.

Then stop. No new material, no tutorials, nothing between rounds.

Ninety days is a long programme and you have worked through it. The material is in place; today is only about arriving able to use it. Eat properly, be early, keep water to hand, and give yourself a few quiet minutes before the first round rather than filling them with revision.

Good luck.

Final check
1. THE RENDER MODEL, cleanly:
     setState enqueues + schedules (state is a snapshot of THIS render)
     render phase  - pure, interruptible, diffs; children matched by position
                     unless a key overrides
     commit phase  - sync DOM mutations -> layout effects -> PAINT -> passive effects
   that one sequence explains keys, effect timing, the useLayoutEffect flicker,
   and why render must be pure.

2. PERF TOOLKIT - diagnose before fixing:
     render COUNT    -> memo, selectors, state placement, split context
     render DURATION -> virtualize, memoize derivations
     BLOCKED thread  -> worker, transitions
     memo is defeated by: inline objects | JSX children | context

both clean -> done. Close the page.
Eat. Be early. Water. A few quiet minutes before round one.

Good luck.
Follow-ups they will ask

Is it a problem that React is your weakest track?

No, for a backend-focused Software Engineer role — it is expected. Be strong on the render model and the common failure modes, and say plainly that your depth is on the backend. Interviewers respect an accurate self-assessment far more than an inflated one.

What if a React round goes deeper than you expect?

Reason from the render model, which generates most React answers, and say when you are outside your experience. "I have not used that in production, but based on how reconciliation works I would expect…" is a legitimate and often correct answer.

What is the last thing to remember?

That every round is a conversation. Ask questions, think out loud, and say when you do not know something. Candidates who engage rather than perform do better — and after ninety days, you have the material to engage with.

Rest completely

No problems. Skim your cheat sheets once, review your stories, sleep eight hours.

Not a new algorithm — the map connecting all 89. Recognising which family a problem belongs to is what the last three months were for.

Cost—Reach for itBefore every practice session, and in the first two minutes of any interview problem.
ARRAYS      two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, Kadane,
            binary search on answer, cyclic sort, Dutch flag
STACK       monotonic stack, histogram, next greater, parentheses
HEAP        top-K, two heaps, merge k sorted, Dijkstra, Prim

TREES       DFS orders, BFS levels, return-a-value recursion,
            BST validation, LCA, trie, tree DP, binary lifting
GRAPHS      DFS components, BFS shortest, topo sort, cycle detection,
            union-find, MST, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, 0-1 BFS, bipartite
DP          1-D, knapsack 0/1 and unbounded, LCS, edit distance,
            LIS n log n, bitmask, digit, tree, DAG
BACKTRACK   subsets, permutations, combinations, N-Queens, grid search
BITS        basics, XOR tricks, bitmask enumeration, bit trie
MATH        gcd, sieve, modular power, nCr, matrix exponentiation
STRINGS     frequency, KMP, rolling hash, palindrome expansion
ADVANCED    Fenwick, segment tree, lazy propagation, line sweep,
            meet in the middle, reservoir sampling

If you can name the family in 60 seconds, the rest is implementation.

Resume defence

Every number on your resume is an invitation. Week 11 attacks each one — but find the real figures before you get there. If a figure is unrecoverable, prepare what you would measure. That is an acceptable answer; vagueness is not.

  • 1,000s+ events/minute via KafkaPartition count and key, consumer instances, p99 processing time, lag alert threshold, DLQ volume.
  • 30–40% query latency reductionBaseline, the tool you measured with, the actual change made, how you verified it in production.
  • 96% API latency reduction (1s → 40ms)What was cached, the TTL, the invalidation strategy, and the worst-case staleness you accepted.
  • 80%+ code coverageWhat kinds of tests, and what coverage does not tell you about correctness.
  • 35% release-cycle reductionWhat specifically changed in the pipeline, and what the bottleneck had been.
  • Zero P1 defectsWhat your review, testing, and rollout process actually was.
